Hi Alicia,
I spoke with Jerry Barsz at Adheris (copied here) about potential pharmacy programs that we could execute to get the
word out about the Voltaren Gel and Opana formulary win. We can schedule a call to discuss further, but here are his
initial thoughts:
Opana ER: Normally for managed care wins we would have some solid options. However in the case of
OPANA ER we are not going to have much to offer due to the nature of the product. Our retailers won't accept
much messaging for the products in this category. Any messaging around managed care, targeting other
meds, has an extremely high likelihood of rejection.
VGel: Unfortunately, one of your competitors in this space has the inventory locked up and we don't have any
messaging options. There are potentially other targets, but moving away from the topicals probably gets you
into a less desirable space. The only other option is if you have market research or existing data on where
VGel patients come from. Maybe this data would help us determine other suitable targets?

> Hi Demir,
> Yes, after much conversation and review, this is what we suggest.

> We recommend that we focus solely on the business rationale (e.g., "streamlining" and
"prioritization of production") to announce the removal of the 7.5 mg and 15 mg doses of
extended release oxymorphone instead of including "crush resistance" or "patient safety"

> If we tried to communicate to key audiences that "Endo is removing two doses of its extended
release oxymorphone franchise because we want to blunt generic competition that won't have

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL

EPI000623381

 crush-resistance properties" (or something similar), we anticipate the FDA may misinterpret
this message as misleading or even off-label promotion. With the hypersensitivity of the FDA
and its increased scrutiny on marketing messages, it seems to be better to err on the side of
caution.

> Even if we adjusted the message to suggest that "Endo is pursuing a crush-resistant
formulation of its extended release oxymorphone product, and wants to remove two doses facing
generic competition to help ensure future patient safety by granting access to only crushresistant tablets," we run the risk of positioning Endo as a pharma company that is trying to
"spin" its desire for more dollars.

> As such, below are the recommended messages (Please note that these are NOT FINAL, but we
feel they are close if you agree with this approach).

> • Endo is committed to meeting the medical needs of patients requiring continuous, aroundthe-clock opioid treatment for an extended period of time. In doing so, we continually
evaluate our product lines to ensure we meet client demands and maximize efficiencies.
> • Endo is prioritizing production of the dosages of extended release oxymorphone that are
most utilized for patients in need of a long-acting opioid.
> • On February 15, 2011, Endo will stop shipping 7.5 mg and 15 mg dosages, but will continue
to supply a wide range of dose strengths including 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg, and 40 mg tablet
strengths for oral administration
> • Focusing on the most commonly prescribed dosages enables Endo to streamline our
manufacturing and distribution operations to better serve the needs of our customers, while
continuing to supply a wide range of dose strengths.

Institutional Sales Contracting Info

Clark,
As a new member of the Institutional Pilot Team, I wanted to get your thoughts and input on some
feedback we received from a local speaker in Southern CA after a recent Opana ER Dinner program.

We spoke to Dr. Scott martin post the speaker program, and he shared his perception of OER
and discussed some strategies on how to improve our current market share.
The most important strategy discussed was getting OER onformulary at Mission Hospital. In
fact, Dr. Martin attributes Nucynta ER's recent success in our territory to its availability on
Mission'sformulary. He argued that oncology patients needpain medications that do not
interact with CYP450 system since many of them are on antidepressants. The only LAO that
fulfills this need and that is available on Mission'sformula!), is Nucynta ER, which he believes
would not compete too well with OER if our product was on formulary at the hospital. The
reason he stated is that Nucynta ER's SNRIproperties can cause unwanted side effects (for
example, serotonin syndrome) for cancer patients who are already on many medications that
cause much discomfortfor them. Best of all, he said that he would have no issues championing
OER and getting us a meeting with headpharmacist.
We'd like to take advantage of the insights provided by this doctor and utilize his support as a
champion. We think that with Dr. Martin championing Opana ER, we may be able to gain some
headway with the Pharmacy Dept. My question is...what could we offer this hospital with regard to
contracting as it is not a pilot hospital. Also, as I was not privy to the early information shared for
the pilot...could you forward me the contracting information for the pilot?
Please let me know your thoughts,

;NE ARE

twers

— A premier team
offering valued solutions to our partners through
expertise and a tenacious desire for success.

Congratulations on your performance with Opana ER and the strong week
you had with Fortesta Gel!!

From: Davison, Christopher
Sent: Thursday, September 13, 2012 8:43 AM
To: Wilfert, Kenneth; Bullard, Lori; Castro, Esther; Johnson, Steven; Lee, Robin; Nakabayashi, Jane; Peyton, Barrett;
Sanderson, Scott; Slater, Gregory; Smith, Lisa; Spear, David
Cc: Bonk, Tom; Keane, Ellen
Subject: Conference Call Recap
Team,
I would like to thank everyone for participating on our district conference call yesterday. Over the last 4 weeks
everyone has shown a high degree of professionalism and positivity as we work through adversity, I am very proud of
the effort. During our call we talked about finishing the month strong by ensuring that we increase our effort on call
plan doctors. I would like to highlight Barry, Robin, Lori, and Steve who are all above 8 calls per day on targets (Scott
Sanderson is above 8 on total calls). By increasing our calls on targets deciled 5-10 we will be able to drive growth.
We have been doing a very nice job in completing our Spendtrax forms and ensuring they are scanned into the system
in addition to being entered into the online tool. As we move forward we are going to make sure the dates are a
complete match in Interplex vs. the Spendtrax as sometimes data entry errors can occur that make it more difficult to
match up activity. You guys also agreed to make me aware when something is a double expense in Interplex but only
captured one time (total spend) in Spendtrax so that I can reconcile and get expenses reimbursed quicker.
During the call we were able to review the new ECR form (Barry Peyton has already used on a field ride). These
changes will help us to create stronger feedback and ultimately drive growth over the remainder of this year. As always
the goal remains to get the feedback into your hands within 48 hours so that we can continue to work towards moving
all products above 100% to goal.
Performance
Currently at the district level we are 100.5% to goal with Opana ER which is outstanding as we have a 48.5% weighting
with this product. Our second best product is Lidoderm at 98.1%, this would be a great product to put incremental
PDEs because we have a real opportunity to hit 100% with this brand which is a positive step forward in portfolio
selling. Voltaren Gel is sitting at 88.4% to goal which is right around where we started the quarter, If we are going to
keep pace with the quota, which accelerates at a strong rate in the month of September we are going to have to have
a better success creating business with some of those doctors who have held out prescribing due to lack of samples.
With Fortesta Gel we are 90.6% to quota which represents the best job we have done to date. In fact we had 48
prescriptions last week which was an all-time high coming out of the Northwest and also 1 prescription over quota for
the week. It looks like we are starting to have some breakthroughs that could really have us ending the quarter strong.
As we close out the week let's make sure we put some focus on the following items.
-Make sure you understand your customer's needs, this way we can ensure that our solution (products) are positioned
in a way that provides a valid solution.

CONFIDENTIAL

ENDO-OR-CID-01317053

 -Make sure you are not just selling to the old customer but to the new. I have worked with Barry this week who has had
great success with Fortesta Gel over the course of the entire year and he has been able to do this by bringing on new
prescribers every month (while maintaining the old), this strategy has worked better than bringing on 4-5 people who
drive all his growth as that strategy would leave him more vulnerable to vacations, relocation or a doctors losing
confidence.
-We need to understand every aspects of our doctors business. One good way to do that is to engage the Medical
Assistants in a higher level of conversation during our wait time.
-Stay positive. People tend to feed off positive energy and in many cases the doctor is buying into you just as much
as our solutions.
-Let's end this month with a sense of urgency as all our products are currently ranked right there with the nation, we
really have an opportunity to move up the ladder with a strong end to the month.

Thanks,

Christopher Davison

CONFIDENTIAL

ENDO-OR-CID-01317054

Mark,
I agree with all of the great comments by the team. Here is some additional points that I hope do not duplicate
previous responses.
Belbuca
What's working well
• Consistently asking effective questions to uncover each individual HCP's needs, key priorities and preferences
in treating chronic pain in each office. In Addition gain a complete understanding of their business model and the
type of practice they are running. This has opened up great dialogue and allowed us to be more targeted in our
approach.
We have been taking a step back and ensuring that we understand all of our current writers individual
protocols for titration and when they bring the patient back in after initiating therapy. We need to ensure
effective follow up resulting in patients achieving their optimal dose.
• Patient profiles have been great as it has allowed us to humanize the appropriate patient type we are looking
for. We spent way too much time early on talking about SAO to LAO. Our customers are relating much better to
"Susan and Roberto" type of discussions.
Challenges
There is a Buprenorphine knowledge and experience gap both with our reps and HCP's. We have worked
hard with increasing our HCP knowledge and comfort level with Buprenorphine by continuing to differentiate
Belbuca from Suboxone and others as well as dealing with the misconceptions (weaker, partial agonist) by
those that have not used Buprenorphine in the past.
Managed care! Some physicians are taking the easy way out with the patients that are on 3-4 SAO. They
say It's easier to add another generic SAO pill vs. switching to a branded LAO and having to the prior
authorization.
Opana ER
What's' Working
Simply giving more time to Opana ER and ensuring that we are having a clinical discussion vs. a reminder
call.
DMVA efficacy page and our core messaging is still our bread and butter (i.e. True 12 hours dosing, durable
efficacy, limited utilization of rescue medication)
United health care formulary leave behind. Powerful example of our good coverage for Opana ER as well
as help reinforce our messaging about non AB rated oxymorphone which is in a triple step edit along with other
branded products.
Challenges
Manage care misconceptions exist and has been a challenge . It's critical that we consistently educate our
customers on the actual coverage for Opana ER to dispel misconceptions of Opana ER access due to lack of share of
voice for Opana ER that we have had over the past two years.
Pharmacist causing issues with non AB rated oxymorphone due to their desire to generate switches due to their
creating misconceptions to our customers.
Constant changing market conditions and external pressures on our customer with the long acting opioid
class. We must understand what happening in our local market and states with regards to guidelines. So we

Northeast Leadership Team,
In preparation from my presentation next week with Rajiv I am asking for your assistance. Can you please provide me

challenge extends to the providers and payers.

Hi y'all —
Sunday was the first day of the UCD-SF Pain Conf and we're off to a good start.
There were about 140 pre-registered attendees and more people doing same-day registration at the desk. The
anticipated total is 200 attendees.
First day, we are the only pharmaceutical company displaying, so we had steady traffic by the table. The physicians,
nurses, physical therapists, and psychologists who came our display either asked really good questions about our
products, seemed genuinely interested in learning more about the medications, or provided good feedback on the
efficacy of our medications as they use them with their patients. (It's always nice to get good feedback about our
medicines and the benefits they bring patients.)
Highlights:
Bobbie-Sue Brown is participating in the conference as attendee...and getting to know some key participants...like....
Jeffrey Reinking, MD (Yippee!) and his associates Robert Kelly Otani, MD and Linda Glazier, NP.
Had time with Drs Scott Fishman and Gagan Mahajan from UCDavis Dept Anesthesia & Pain Medicine. Discussed Dr
Charles Argoff coming out here Oct 1 and they are looking forward to seeing him.
Munish Lal, MD from Chico Pain Clinic is an attendee, spent time speaking with us at the booth extolling Lidoderm's
benefits and is signed up for the breakout session taught by Daniel Rockers, PhD on use of hypnosis in the management
of chronic pain.
Physicians from Kaiser (Oakland & Vallejo) stopped by the table to ask questions about Opana-ER. They told us that
Kaiser pharmacy has done an excellent job of instructing Kaiser physicians about how to dose, convert, and titrate
Opana-ER because the physicians have been instructed to convert OxyContin patients to Opana-ER. Opana-ER is on
Kaiser formulary and is in preferred position ahead of OxyContin. (Yeah!) Their questions revolved about understanding
the food effect, for the most part. Also of interest, the Kaiser doctors said they saw great benefit for their patients from
Lidoderm and were willing to do the necessary paperwork to get Lidoderm for them as Lidoderm is a non-formulary
medication.

clinic in the very rural area around Minden, NV.

RESTRICTED DATA:
New data restrictions were implemented with the data reports for week ending August 11. There are two
different restrictions affecting the pharmaceutical industry: one in New Hampshire, and the other nationwide based
upon an AMA Opt-Out (PDRP) program.
In New Hampshire, we cannot show Rxs for any physician who prescribes in that state. We also cannot show
any Rxs that are filled in NH but are written by prescribers in other states. We WILL have this data at the zip code level
for IC purposes.
In the rest of the country, we cannot show Rx data for any physician who has asked the AMA to restrict the use
of their information. These prescribers will be listed at the bottom of the report. We WILL have this information for use
in calculating IC, but will not be able to share it with anyone in the field.
We will continue to show the historical data for prescribers in both categories.
A FEW KEY POINTS:
There are 4 tabs per file: Lidoderm report, Frova report, Opana report and a tab with three line graphs.
Each report contains TRxs for your call plan doctors individually and a last line for all other profiled prescribers in
your territory combined.
Manager reports contain summarized data for each of their territories or districts.
The arrow indicates whether the Lidoderm or Frova TRxs are up or down for the most recent 4 weeks compared
to the previous 4 weeks.
This information should be close to, but not the same as, your monthly IC TRxs. Weekly TRxs are provided to
help you monitor your prescribers, but IC is based on final monthly data.
Weekly data is naturally more volatile than monthly data. Please do not overreact to week-to-week changes.
When opening your report in Excel, click the "Enable Macros" button. This is necessary to turn on some of the
features of the report.
TO SORT THE REPORTS:
Above the Endo logo, there will be a toolbar with 4 pull-down lists and three buttons.
The lists work in pairs to allow you to sort by one or two fields.
The buttons will apply or remove the sort you choose.
You can sort by Prescriber Name, Prescriber ID, Specialty, Zip Code, Current Week TRx, Current Four Week or
Prior 13 week total TRx in either Ascending or Descending order. The default order is Ascending.
In the first drop-down list on the left, select the primary sort field.
In the second drop-down list, select the order for the primary sort field.
(Optional) In the third drop-down list, select the secondary sort field.
(Optional) In the fourth drop-down list, select the order for the secondary sort field.
When you have specified your sort options, click the "Sort" button to apply the sort.
If you want to return to the original sort order, click the "Reset" button.
The "Exit" button will close the report.
TO PRINT:
The report and graph tabs are already formatted for reporting.
To print any tab, click the "File" menu and choose "Print...".

From: Oehler, Sesilie

Subject: Need BL and Brand Team Approval- CIGNA and HealthSpring Part D 2015 RFP Response- Due 12/16/2013
Importance: High
NEED Brand Team and Brian Lortie's Approval
Mary Jo,
We have just received the CIGNA and HealthSpring (combined) 2015-2016 Part D RFP, representing —1M Part D
lives, with a due date of December 16th. In 2012, CIGNA acquired the HealthSpring Part D business, and beginning
with the 2014 Part D Bid cycle, CIGNA and HealthSpring became a combined solicitation; although they were still
separate entities under CMS, and maintained separate manufacturer Agreements and Formularies. Per the customer,
for 2015, CIGNA/HealthSpring will be considered a single Part D plan under CMS and 2015 formularies will be
combined for the first time. As such, they are mandating that the offering be the same for both CIGNA and
HealthSpring, whereas, previous bids allowed for some differentiation.
We have had individual Part D Agreements in place with CIGNA and with HealthSpring since January 2008. Currently
including Lidoderm, Opana ER, and Voltaren Gel, the Agreements are due to expire on 12/31/2015, and 12/31/2014
respectively. Recently, CIGNA and HealthSpring announced a new arrangement with Catamaran PBM of Illinois,
under which Catamaran will take over the contracting and rebate invoicing to manufacturers for CIGNA and
HealthSpring utilization effective 1/1/2014. As a result, they have requested that all manufacturers Assign the existing
Commercial and Part D Agreements to Catamaran, and have also asked that all 2015 bids be provided directly to
Catamaran, who will be managing the overall bid process.
Given that Catamaran is a client of Express Scripts (ESI) until 12/31/2015, and ESI does not allow manufacturers to
contract directly with their clients, we are in discussions with ESI and Catamaran regarding this conflict. ESI has
indicated that they will absorb CIGNA & HealthSpring as downstream plans of their client Catamaran, and will bill all
related utilization under the terms of the ESI Agreements. Conversely, Catamaran has indicated that, they will bill the
utilization under the terms of the CIGNA/HealthSpring Agreements, at minimum, where such terms are more favorable

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-01891418

 than ESI's.
Since we do not want to risk duplicative eligibility under two separate agreements, we are hoping to receive a final
decision from ESI/Catamaran on the billing method that will be used, prior to any assignment of existing Agreements
to Catamaran for 2014; however, since we do not want to risk being excluded from formulary consideration for 2015,
we must proceed with our bid submission to Catamaran by the December 16th due date, while concurrently pursuing
resolution of the issues noted above.
Enhanced (fixed pricing) terms for Lidoderm (LOE) were implemented with CIGNA effective 9/15/2013. HealthSpring
was not willing to consider LOE terms during our discussions with them earlier this year, and is not expected to
participate going forward, though this offering will be available to them through this combined bid process. There is
some concern about Catamaran being made aware of the availability of 'fixed pricing' opportunities through Endo,
since, as they become a more significant player in the PBM space, they may push for this option during future product
negotiations; however, if we do not maintain this LOE offering, we will likely put at risk CIGNA's continued brand over
generic coverage, if applicable for 2015.
In response to this 2015 RFP, Carle Randesi and Tim VanDeVelde have proposed that we renew the current terms for
Lidoderm (LOE), maintain Voltaren Gel terms as currently contracted (HealthSpring rates), and revise the Opana ER
terms with additional options to block or disadvantage Oxycontin and generic oxymorphone ER, as shown below.
Price protection will continue as currently contracted.
Financial analysis was prepared for the above offerings during the 2014 bid cycle (as attached). No current analysis
has been performed.

Demir,
I wanted to share another MC Opportunity success story out of the Detroit, MI territory of Amy Goble and Mark Radwan.
Starting in May, I have been serving as a mentor with Amy and Mark to identify 5 physicians to hyper target for a 10 week
contest. They would compare their 5 targets vs. the rest of their district headed by Bijal. They had 2 goals: one was 10-15%
growth from their targets, the other was to beat their district.
I am attaching the excel file used to track progress as well as a power point file to summarize our findings similar to what we
reviewed with Pittsburgh.
As with previous MC Opportunity contests in Pittsburgh and St. Louis this goal of 10-15% growth was lofty yet attainable. I sent
out weekly trackers to keep them updated on their progress in addition to check-ins along the way after speaker programs, etc

As you will see with the attached documents, with each of them being in the offices 1x/wk, utilizing all available resources, and
emphasizing a message of Opana ER for the elderly patient and pulling through Medicare Part D plans they finished stronger
than we had even hoped!

Amy and Mark grew their 5 physician hyper targets a whopping 45%! This was triple what their
1st
goal was and they also beat their district handily as well which grew 7.1%.
In addition, their average baseline among these 5 was 10.2 prescriptions. The week of 7/23 they finished with 38! Their
territory market share at baseline was 6%, it is now 11.4%. Their territory has grown 41% over the last 4 weeks and 16% over
the last 16 weeks.
I thought you would be excited to hear this success story out of Detroit and Amy and Mark did a great job of devising a plan
together and executing! I thought these results were worthy of your attention.

- The Opana IR data will not be incorporated in Strong Opioid market sales or market share calculations
- As with all other products, the Opana IR data will be normalized TRxs (not divided by 4, as used for IC calculations)
DO NOT reply to this email or call WK. If you have any questions about this report, please contact your manager.
RESTRICTED DATA:
- Due to the AMA Opt-Out program (PDRP), we cannot show Rx data for any physician who has asked the AMA to restrict the
use of their information.
- The call plan prescribers who have elected to have their data masked will be displayed at the bottom of the report. Their
historical data will be displayed up to the point they requested opt-out.
- AMA opt-out prescriber level TRxs' are masked, but are included in territory totals.
KEY POINTS:
- Weekly data is more volatile than monthly data.
- IC calculations are based on monthly WK data which can be found in the Prescriber Sales report.
USING THE REPORT:
- When opening your report in Excel, if prompted, click the "Enable Macros" button. This is necessary to turn on some of the
features of the report
- Use the sorting toolbar above the Endo logo to sort on various fields (Ascending or Descending)
- When you have specified your sort options, click the "Sort" button to apply the sort.
- If you want to return to the original sort order, click the "Reset" button.
- The "Exit" button will close the report.
- The report and graph tabs are already formatted for reporting.

BUSINESS <http://online.wsj.com/public/search?article-doctype=°/07BBusiness°/07D&HEADER TEXT=Business> : The Wall Street Journal
Generic OxyContin Pains the FDA
Patent Expiration Brings Debate Over Abuse Deterrents
By TIMOTHY W. MARTIN
<http://online.wsj.com/search/term.html?KEYWORDS=TIMOTHY+W.+MARTIN&bylinesearch=true>
The first patent on OxyContin expires Tuesday, a milestone in the history of one of the most powerful and
abused painkillers on the market.
But it could be quite some time before generic versions of the drug are available.
Generic-drug makers have lined up to make their own versions of the medication, which has become
synonymous with painkiller abuse. But first, they must wait for the Food and Drug Administration to
decide whether they may produce the original version of OxyContin—the one losing patent protection—or
whether they may make only newer versions designed to impede abuse, which won't come off patent for
several more years.

The agency's decision is likely to have significant implications for the fight against prescription-drug
abuse. Overdoses from painkillers caused more deaths in 2010 than heroin and cocaine combined,
according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Yet the agency must weigh that problem
against legitimate demand from patients for effective, inexpensive, generic painkillers. OxyContin is
prescribed for a broad range of ailments, from chronic back pain to cancer.
The FDA's ruling also will dictate whether profits in the $9.4 billion annual painkiller industry are shuffled
and could influence proposed federal legislation to require that most prescription painkillers be made with
so-called abuse-deterrent formulations. OxyContin, with $2.8 billion in annual sales, represented about
30% of the market for painkillers last year, according to research firm IMS Health Inc.
The original version of OxyContin helped spawn addiction because the pill was easy to heat or crush,
breaking its extended-release function. Users then could inject, snort or smoke the contents for a heroin
like high.
But OxyContin maker Purdue Pharma LP in 2010 infused the blockbuster drug with a polymer that made
the pill more difficult to crush, an innovation that the company spent about $100 million to develop. The
patent on that formulation, the only one Purdue now sells, doesn't expire until 2025.
The FDA for years has been reviewing whether generic OxyContin should be required to have such an
abuse deterrent and, if so, what kind.
2

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_OPIOID_OHAG-00050510

 The FDA has several options, and there is no assurance it will rule by Tuesday. The agency could allow
generic drugs to be sold using the original formulation, that would make inexpensive versions available
almost as soon as the FDA ruled. It could also allow only versions using Purdue's abuse deterrent. And the
agency could permit generic-drug makers to market versions with their own abuse deterrents. That would
make it possible for lower-priced OxyContin to hit the market before Purdue's abuse-deterrent version
loses patent protection in 2025, though probably not until late next year.
Douglas D. Throckmorton, a deputy director in the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research,
declined to say when a decision would be made. "We are working to take action, as soon as the science
and law allow us to do so," he said.
The agency is under pressure from lawmakers who believe that delays are contributing to painkiller abuse.
"If the FDA doesn't act this time, there will be consequences," said Rep. Hal Rogers (R., Ky.), co-chairman
of the Congressional Prescription Drug Abuse Caucus, referring to his previous efforts to get the FDA to
take action.
Israel-based Teva Pharmaceutical Industries
<http://online.wsj.com/public/quotes/main.html?type=djn&symbol=TEVA> TEVA -1.20%
<http://online.wsj.com/public/quotes/main.html?type=djn&symbol=TEVA?mod=inlineTicker> Ltd.; Impax
Laboratories <http://online.wsj.com/public/quotes/main.html?type=djn&symbol=IPXL> Inc., IPXL 1.58% <http://online.wsj.com/public/quotes/main.html?type=djn&symbol=IPXL?mod=inlineTicker> of
Hayward, Calif.; and Covidien
<http://online.wsj.com/public/quotes/main.html?type=djn&symbol=COV> COV +0.46%
<http://online.wsj.com/public/quotes/main.html?type=djn&symbol=COV?mod=inlineTicker> PLC's
Mallinckrodt unit, which is based in St. Louis, are awaiting FDA approval to make generic versions of the
original OxyContin. Purdue, meanwhile, is in court trying to fend off old and new generic versions of
OxyContin.
The average retail price for all strengths of the drug, is $7.50 a pill, or $450 a prescription, according to
Purdue. The generic versions would be 30% to 40% less expensive, said Shibani Malhotra, a
pharmaceutical analyst for RBC Capital Markets.
The ultimate question: Is the newer form of OxyContin, which is further from patent expiration, safer than
the original?
Purdue says, yes.
OxyContin's sales have declined more than 10% since the Stamford, Conn., company introduced the
abuse-deterrent version in 2010, according to IMS.
"Purdue does not think that the public safety will be served by an influx of opioids from multiple sources
that do not employ abuse-deterrent technology," said Purdue spokesman James Heins.
The answer won't be so simple for the FDA. Much of the research on the effectiveness of abuse-deterrent
formulations was funded and conducted by Purdue and Endo Pharmaceuticals
<http://online.wsj.com/public/quotes/main.html?type=djn&symbol=ENDP> Inc., ENDP -0.13%
<http://online.wsj.com/public/quotes/main.html?type=djn&symbol=ENDP?mod=inlineTicker> which
makes another powerful painkiller, Opana.
Public-health and addiction experts have said that allowing a generic form of OxyContin with no
safeguards would be like throwing gasoline on a fire.
"It's going to mean more dead kids," said Jeffrey Reynolds, executive director of the Long Island Council
on Alcoholism and Drug Dependence. He said there was a shift to a version of Opana without safeguards
after OxyContin was reformulated in 2010.
OxyContin's sales fell 7% the first year it was reformulated, according to IMS Health, while Opana's
3

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_OPIOID_OHAG-00050511

 revenue rose 72%, to $640 million. Opana's sales dropped 25% to $479.5 million last year, after it was
reformulated with an abuse deterrent.
The FDA has signaled preliminary support for safety features. In January it issued draft guidance on how
companies could demonstrate that their painkillers have abuse deterrents. But the guidance stopped short
of requiring safeguards. The FDA is seeking input ahead of a public meeting scheduled for the fall.
Blocking generic drugs could mean "leaving behind the millions of patients who stand to benefit from
access to lower-cost versions" of OxyContin, said David Gaugh, a senior vice president at the Generic
Pharmaceuticals Association, an industry group.
Endo's Opana ER is an early example of the situation. That extended-release drug was reformulated last
year so that the pill's contents turned into a jellylike goop when heated, meaning it couldn't easily be
injected to produce a high. A generic version of higher-dosage forms—without abuse-deterrent features—
was introduced in early January. The total number of prescriptions written for branded Opana ER has
remained steady, yet the market share for the new generic version is growing.
"Branded Opana is not being substituted out; the generic market-share growth means it's being abused,"
said Corey Davis, a specialty-pharmaceuticals analyst with Jefferies & Co.
Endo's initial analysis of substance-abuse and poison-control centers showed that versions of Opana
without abuse-deterrent features were abused about 80% more often than the version with the
safeguards, said Blaine Davis, a senior vice president for the Malvern, Penn., company.
Meanwhile, makers of generic drugs are debating whether they should find ways to incorporate abusedeterrent formulations proactively, rather than wait for the FDA to provide definitive guidance, according
to a drug-company executive.
Political pressure is mounting for the FDA to take action. The National Association of Attorneys General
last month sent the agency a letter signed by 48 members, urging the FDA to require abuse-deterrent
features on generic drugs.
"We want to see, as these drugs are coming off patent, that the same rules apply across the board," said
Alabama Attorney General Luther Strange, who signed the letter.

Dear Pain Solutions Sales Team,
The Opana® ER Brand Team is looking forward to a great 2013 and we looking forward to sharing the 2013 strategies and
resources for POA I with you on the January 7 Pain Solutions Kickoff WebEx.
In follow-up to Larry's voicemail this morning and our competitive readiness for a generic oxymorphone HCI extendedrelease from Impax Labs, please review the following information and the attached memo:
At this time, our competitive intelligence indicates that the Impax product is not yet commercially available. However, we
have confirmed that product has been manufactured at all dosage strengths. Product can be commercially launched any day
now. We will keep you updated, but in the meantime we need to be prepared. As we have discussed, Impax's generic
oxymorphone HCI extended-release tablets are not considered therapeutically equivalent to Endo's Opana ER with INTAC,
which is designed to be crush-resistant. Therefore, the generic non-crush-resistant form of Opana ER should not be
considered as therapeutically substitutable for a prescription written for Opana ER.
During the January 7 WebEx, you will be fully trained on additional core selling messages highlighting the difference between
Opana ER with INTAC and generic oxymorphone ER, as well as trained on new promotional resources. The following new
resources will ship to you for arrival on January 7 in response to this new market dynamic. Although you will be trained on the
new messages and resources on January 7, we will not utilize these resources in with customers until we know Impax has
launched. We will let you know when the resources are approved for use with customers. In the meantime, please review
the attached memo which will provide you with the current, approved response to customer questions at this time.

Dear RDs,

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_SF-00290501

 The OPANA Marketing Team is excited to expand the 2006 OPANA Speakers Bureau Initiative with the launch of field-driven
dinner programs. The objective of this initiative is to drive your OPANA ER and OPANA business in markets of highest
potential by providing customers with programs to learn more about the benefits of OPANA ER and OPANA in small
educational settings with their peers. The key programs in 2006 for this initiative are the teleconference series (beginning
October 17) and field-driven dinner programs. Additional programs will be included in 2007 such as web casts, 1:1 thought
leader briefings, and meet-the-expert sessions.

In order to launch the field-driven dinner programs, please review the following important information with your DM teams.

The allocation of programs for 2006 is as follows:
- Specialty Division: 70 programs (35 programs per division)
- Pharma Division: 37 programs (1 program per DM)
- Hospital Division: 12 programs (1 program per DM and 5 programs for key accounts per RD direction)

RD and DMs will determine the most appropriate placement of these programs. Programs should be placed in markets of
greatest business potential with targeted attendees from Deciles 10-6 of the call plan. In order to maximize the success of
these programs, we would like the different sales teams to partner together on programs, where appropriate. For example, for
the Pharma programs, the DM/Rep should reach out to specialty counterpart who have higher decile healthcare professionals
(HCPs), rather than inviting lower decile HCPs from the Pharm call plan. The same will be important for the Specialty DM/Rep
to reach out to their Pharma counterpart to include high decile Primary Care HCPs in the area where their dinner meeting will
be held.

The following key documents explain the dinner programs in great detail and provide DM/Reps tools for planning and
executing these programs:
* Program Description: provides a comprehensive overview of the program
* Checklist: key document to assist in planning and understanding responsibilities
* FAQ Document
* Program Request Form: rep will complete to initiate a program
* Dinner Meeting Invitation: rep will customize both pages of the invitation, print, and distribute to customers in deciles 10-6
on the call plan
* Invitee Tracking Form
* Onsite Checklist
* Program Evaluation Form
* Onsite Sign in Sheet
* OPANA Promotional Speaker List: list of trained speakers (those expected to attend the Chicago speaker training meeting
or participated in the 10/5 telecon); only trained speakers will be permitted as faculty. When recommending faculty, local
faculty should be given priority.
It is critical that all of these documents are reviewed by the DM and Reps in order to facilitate successful implementation of the
program. All of the documents can be found at the following link: http://endonet/sites/commbiz/sales/opana/default.aspx

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_SF-00290502

 You must be logged into your Endo account on the Endo network to access these intranet files.
A few important notes regarding the field-driven dinner programs:
* EHC Communications is the medical communications agency who will support the reps in the planning and execution of the
programs
* Program Approval Flow: 1.) Rep will complete Program Request Form and forward to DM for review/approval; 2.) DM will
forward approved Program Request Form to EHC (per the request form); 3.) EHC will confirm receipt of the Program Request
Form via email to sales rep no later than 2 days of DM message receipt and will scheduled the planning conference call with
the Rep
* Program Timing: We understand that some sales representatives may have already begun planning certain logistical
aspects of their dinner program (le, securing a venue or speaker). It will be critical that the rep provides EHC an update on
these arrangements during their first planning conference call (which will be held after receipt of the Program Request Form)
* Program Invitations: The invitation is 2 pages. Each page needs to be customized by the sales representative (Page 1:
Program Date, Program Location, Address, City, State, Zip, Program Time, Speaker, Sales Rep Name, and Sales Rep
Phone Number and Page 2: Program Date, Program City, and Sales Rep Name). The reps will then print the invitation and
distribute to customers in Deciles 10-6 on the call plan. As with all promotional materials, invitations must be distributed with a
copy of the OPANA ER and OPANA prescribing information.
* Program Metrics: We will be looking at a number of key metrics to measure the impact and success of these programs,
including prescribing data, number of program attendees, sale force evaluations, attendee and faculty evaluations, etc.
* All other important program information is included in the documents found on the link above
Please share this information with your DM teams in order to begin planning programs. DMs can then forward this message to
Reps in the markets where the programs will be targeted.
Thank you for your help in launching these programs. If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me.

Cc: Davison, Christopher; Keane, Ellen; Kamins, Lori
Subject: ACTION: MCPTR Sorts to Hyperfocus on Key Targets
Importance: High

RAPTORS and Northern COMETS!
Thank you all for spending some time this morning re-thinking our approach to using the Fortesta Gel
instant savings cards in light of what Joe Marino learned about ISC denials for patients with commercial
coverage from plans that do not presently pay for Fortesta Gel.

ISC denials for patients with commercial coverage:
We agreed on the need to:
Confirm with the new Formulary Compass report which plans in your state offer T2-T3 access to
Fortesta Gel.
Sort the MCPTR to confirm which high potential providers have disproportionate numbers of
patients in these plans and hyper-focus on these offices.
Set appropriate expectations for how the ISCs will work: "Dr., when submitted to the pharmacy
with a prescription, these cards have the potential to afford patients a free one month trial
and subsequent monthly discounts on their co-pays depending on their health plan." In an
office where there are one or more pre-eminent plans paying for FG you can mention these plans
with the assurance of the benefits that these cards convey. But the key is spending your selling
time where most of the covered patients are!
Set appropriate expectations around the challenge providers will face — step therapy, PAs, etc. —
for patients in other plans. (If someone is really sold, they'll do whatever it takes.)

LOA and PHN markets: Increasing Opana ER and Lidoderm
Plans

arket Share in Key

You'll recall we also discussed the utility of the Access and Share report to help you quickly assess the
potential upside for pull-through on Opana ER and on Lidoderm in plans with T2-T3 coverage. Using this
report you can see which plans offer T2-T3 coverage for these products and which of these T2-T3 plans
offer the greatest potential for you to increase your market share. (Please see below the "keys" to the
tabs in this report.) Once you've identified those plans, run MCPTR sorts for the LOA and PHN markets,
CONFIDENTIAL

ENDO-OR-CID-01295042

 respectively; then drill down in the MCPTR on those plans you identified from the Access and Share
report as offering you the best opportunity to increase share. (You do this by clicking on the plan name.)
What you will see then is the list of providers who have patients covered by the plan you clicked on. Then
you can drill down on these providers — again, by clicking on them — and you'll see what % of their
patients are participants in that high-potential plan. The ideal candidates for hyperfocus to increase
pull-through are already using your product, but have potential to use more in one or more of these
high-potential plans. While some providers have great awareness of plans, again the key benefit to
targeting these customers is that you'll be fishing where the fish are! Effective clinical selling of
our products in offices with disproportionate numbers of patients with good access to them gets
more Rxs filled! However, don't neglect the total office call. Talk to the staff handling the administration
of the Rxs and confirm that these high-potential plans are plans they are familiar with. Assure them of the
excellent access their patients have to our products in these plans. They may be influential in the
prescribing decision.

CTIO By Tuesday have someone from every territory get back to me with the
names of 5 customers / product you've uncovered in your Fortesta Gel, Lidoderm,
and Opana ER MCPTR sorts that you will be concentrating on for pull-through
between now and June 30th. Keep it simple: list the provider names under each
product and mention the plans that represent opportunity in those offices. THEN GO
GET `EMU!
The key to the first tab "Access & Share" report:
A — Product Market
B — Region Number (should match the MCPTR) P60000 is Ellen
C — Region of the country
D — Footprint number is the district number (P6 is Ellen, 03 is the district, AO is the footprint)
E — Footprint City/State
F — State
G — Monthly average of scripts for the 3 month (Dec 2010 — Feb 2011) roll-up total
H - % of T2 and T3 access with LAO or PHN
I — Endo's share for plans with T2 and T3 access
— Expected Share — where we should be at with the T2 and T3 access
K — Potential upside of the number of scripts we'd have with expected share
Here's the "key" second tab:
Green means Endo share for that product (column O) in that plan (column ]) is greater than the total footprint
share for that product. Pink is the opposite. The TRx's have been normalized, and LTC and Medicaid scripts
have been removed.
Column Explanations:
A — Market (currently we just have LAO & PHN)
F — Footprint ID Territory
G — Footprint City/State
H — State
I — Plan rank by number of scripts
— Plan Name
K — Plan Entity (Commercial or Medicare Part D)
L — Formulary Coverage
M — This is total market basket TRX with a monthly average of the 3 month roll-up total, consistent with how
the MCPTR is set up.
N — Percent the plan has in that footprint
O — Endo's product market share for that plan in that footprint
P — Percent of Endo product market share in that fooprint vs. Endo product market share performance in the
entire footprint (all plans). Compares how our product performs at that plan in that footprint vs how our
CONFIDENTIAL

ENDO-OR-CID-01295043

 product performs in that footprint in total.
Q — Share growth —vs- prior year
R — Share growth —vs- prior quarter

Attachments: END01_112948_210308_20060908.xls
RESTRICTED DATA:
- New data restrictions were implemented with the data reports for week ending August 11. There are two different
restrictions affecting the pharmaceutical industry: one in New Hampshire, and the other nationwide based upon an AMA OptOut (PDRP) program.
- In New Hampshire, we cannot show Rxs for any physician who prescribes in that state. We also cannot show any Rxs that
are filled in NH but are written by prescribers in other states. We WILL have this data at the zip code level for IC purposes.
- In the rest of the country, we cannot show Rx data for any physician who has asked the AMA to restrict the use of their
information. These prescribers will be listed at the bottom of the report. We WILL have this information for use in calculating
IC, but will not be able to share it with anyone in the field.
- We will continue to show the historical data for prescribers in both categories.
A FEW KEY POINTS:
- There are 4 tabs per file: Lidoderm report, Frova report, Opana report and a tab with three line graphs.
- Each report contains TRxs for your call plan doctors individually and a last line for all other profiled prescribers in your
territory combined.
- Manager reports contain summarized data for each of their territories or districts.
- The arrow indicates whether the Lidoderm or Frova TRxs are up or down for the most recent 4 weeks compared to the
previous 4 weeks.
- This information should be close to, but not the same as, your monthly IC TRxs. Weekly TRxs are provided to help you
monitor your prescribers, but IC is based on final monthly data.
- Weekly data is naturally more volatile than monthly data. Please do not overreact to week-to-week changes.
- When opening your report in Excel, click the "Enable Macros" button. This is necessary to turn on some of the features of
the report.
TO SORT THE REPORTS:
- Above the Endo logo, there will be a toolbar with 4 pull-down lists and three buttons.
- The lists work in pairs to allow you to sort by one or two fields.
- The buttons will apply or remove the sort you choose.
- You can sort by Prescriber Name, Prescriber ID, Specialty, Zip Code, Current Week TRx, Current Four Week or Prior 13
week total TRx in either Ascending or Descending order. The default order is Ascending.
- In the first drop-down list on the left, select the primary sort field.
- In the second drop-down list, select the order for the primary sort field.
- (Optional) In the third drop-down list, select the secondary sort field.
- (Optional) In the fourth drop-down list, select the order for the secondary sort field.
- When you have specified your sort options, click the "Sort" button to apply the sort.
- If you want to return to the original sort order, click the "Reset" button.
- The "Exit" button will close the report.
TO PRINT:
- The report and graph tabs are already formatted for reporting.
- To print any tab, click the "File" menu and choose "Print...".
- When the print window opens, select the options you want and click the "Print" button.
Please DO NOT reply to this email or call WK. If you have any questions about this file, please contact Chris Speaker by email
(speaker.chris@endo.com) or phone (x4052).

I had a chance to listen in on the three hour Opana ER Webcast tonight. Faculty included Dr. Joseph Pergolizzi and Dr.

speakers to conduct programs from one of the five Opana/Opana ER slide decks (hence the duration of the call):
As you know, the 5 NEW presentations your representatives will be able to request are as follows:
1. Core Slide Presentation — This is the current core module and is most appropriate for prescribers who have
had little or no exposure to OPANA and OPANA ER. Provides the primary studies and background information

1. Primary Care — This is the current core module (number "1" above) presented in a case study format that is
focused towards primary care prescribers. It is most appropriate for those who have had little or no experience
with OPANA and OPANA ER.
1. Conversion and Dosing — This module focuses on how to convert and dose OPANA ER using a case study
approach. It is most appropriate for prescribers who have had some experience, but have had difficulty dosing
patients and would like more information.

Aetna Opana ER 2011 Part D

I wanted to provide you an update on a situation/negotiation that has been occurring with
Aetna for their 2011 formulary on their Part D business for Opana ER.
In 2010, Opana ER. Kadian, and Oxycontin are all in a preferred position (Tier3 in a 5 tier
plan design, Tier 1 and 2 are generic tiers). Aetna was very concerned about the cost of
this category and originally informed us that they were going to remove all branded
products from their 2011 formulary. Our account executive, Ken Smith immediately started
discussing potential ways they could control utilization. At the request of Aetna, Ken
engaged Mark Rubino from the HOPE team to present some of our pharmacoeconomic
information that would address Aetna's specific questions.
As a result of this negotiation, Aetna has verbally accepted the following
1.
2.
3.
4.
5.

Opana ER will be listed as the only branded opioid on formulary. All other branded products will be
non-formulary
30% Flat Rebate (down from 40% in 2010)
Opana would be in a non-preferred position requiring a higher co-pay than this year but the only
product generally available
For the closed formulary (85% of current membership) there will be a single step through generics for
Opana ER. All other brands will require Medical Exception.
For the open formulary there will be a single step through generics for Opana ER. For all other brands
there will be a double step through generics.

Although they have verbally accepted, the process to official acceptance will still take some
time. They will now submit this through their internal committees and then to CMS and we
should know formally in late summer to early fall.
The key takeaway here is that we executed very well cross functionally with extremely tight
timelines. We may come away from this with an advantaged position at a lower rebate level
with an opportunity for increased gross and net sales!
Great job, Ken and Mark!

Subject: Re: Hello & TRF survey

We ask that you please take a few minutes to render your expert opinion on the subject of abuse resistant opioids, keeping in
mind that the information collected will be used in an aggregatefashion and will be kept confidential and not used for
sales/marketing purposes. Thank You.
Background on the issue: Extended-release formulations of prescription opioids are designed to release the active ingredient
slowly over a prolonged period. If the integrity of the delivery system is compromised prior to use, the entire contents could
become immediately available for ingestion, intranasal or injection use. The result would be opioid plasma concentrations
which may lead to overdose, respiratory depression, and death. As a result, abuse-resistant formulations have been
developed in an attempt to confer physical and/or physiochemical properties which may reduce the accidental misuse (i.e.,
breaking, chewing, and/or crushing for patient convenience) and deter certain methods of intended abuse (i.e., chewing or
crushing for snorting and/or injection).
1. When it comes to knowledge of the various abuse-resistant opioids available and/or in development, I am:
a. Very knowledgeable
b. Moderately knowledgeable
c.

Somewhat knowledgeable

d. Not very knowledgeable

2. My experience with abuse-resistant opioids to date has been (please indicate all answers that apply):

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_SF-00146023

 a.

I currently prescribe abuse-resistant opioids for my patients

b. I have used abuse-resistant opioids in clinical trials
c. I have read about/attended talks on subject
d. I have no experience with abuse-resistant opioids

3. How successful do you believe abuse-resistant formulations will be in preventing the misuse/abuse of prescription
opioid medications?
a. Highly effective
b. Moderately effective
c. Minimal to no effectiveness
4. I believe that prescribing abuse-resistant opioids for my patients will help mitigate my risk as a clinician.
a. True
b. False
5. When I think about using abuse-resistant opioids in my practice, I think:
a. I believe these should be the drugs of choice for all patients
b. I would consider using them for all patients
c.

I am somewhat reluctant to use them; would consider for select patients only

d. They do not fit into my practice; I won't use them

6. What would motivate you to switch patients to abuse-resistant formations from their current prescriptions?
(please indicate all answers that apply)
a. History of substance abuse
b. Abnormal urine drug test
c. Concern regarding family/caretaker access to the patient's medication
d. Pattern of aberrant behavior (requests for early refills, lost prescriptions, etc.)
e. Other (Please specify): price was equivalent to the same opioid that is currently on the market
7. What would be the primary reason you would not prescribe abuse-resistant formulations?
a. Price/Payer issues
b. Lack of guidelines/recommendations endorsing abuse resistant opioids
c. Patient perception (I must think they are an abuser if I prescribe abuse-resistant opioids)
d. No reason not to prescribe
e. Other (Please specify):
8. When it comes to recommendations advocating the use of abuse-resistant opioids, I would (please indicate all
answers that apply):
a. Want to be actively involved in developing guidelines, committee recommendations, etc.
b. Support guidelines developed by my peers and/or professional societies
c. Need to have more information and/or experience with abuse-resistant opioids before I could make
recommendations
d. Not advocate the use of abuse-resistant opioids

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_SF-00146024

 In the space below, please provide any final thoughts related to abuse resistant formulations that have not been addressed
in this survey, or clarification of opinions on any of the above questions.
Abuse resistant/deterrant formulations will have minimal et ctiveness if price is an issue
Abuse resistantideterrant formulations will have minimal effectiveness if you only apply it to the long-acting opioid and
avoid applying it to the short-acting version of the same opioid.
By prescribing abuse resistant/deterrent formulations to ail patients, it removes the issue of deciding who gets it and who
does not and eliminates the issue of stigma.
You need to clarify to prescribers that these new formulations will not prevent issues of patients
buying/stealing/borrowing other people's prescribed med for the purpose of using it in a non-tampered state.

Thank you for your participation.

Press Releases

Dec 11 2012
McConnell Engages FDA on Behalf of Kentucky Organizations Seeking Assistance to
stop "Crushable' Generic Pain Pills from Flooding Into the Commonwealth
WASHINGTON, DC U.S. Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell reached out to the Commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration
(FDA) today on behalf of Kentucky law enforcement and health care providers "expressing concern about generic versions of long-release opiates
coming to market without the tamper-resistant technology."
Brand name long-release opiates, such as Opana ER and Oxycontin, are particularly potent and were subject to rampant drug abuse prior to the
deployment of tamper-resistant technologies. These technologies prevent addicts from destroying the time release mechanism of the extended release
opiates, designed to treat severe pain, by crushing the pills in order for the user to achieve an immediate heroin-like high. However, generic versions
of the same drugs lacking the tamper-resistant formulations are expected to pour into the market in early 2013. Senator McConnell heard from some
of Kentucky's top law enforcement and health care providers about their concerns, including: the Kentucky Primary Care Association, Inc.,
Appalachian Regional Healthcare, Inc., Norton Healthcare, KentuckyOne Health, the Kentucky Narcotic Officers' Association (KNOA), and
Operation UNITE.
Senator McConnell contacted FDA Commissioner Margaret Hamburg on their behalf to relay their concerns on the issue. In a letter to
Commissioner Hamburg, Senator McConnell pressed the FDA to identify what authority the agency may have to act should they recognize this
legitimate public safety concern. He also questioned if there's precedent to remove a generic drug from the market that lacks a safety mechanism now
included as a part of the brand drug. Senator McConnell also asked Commissioner Hamburg what steps can be taken for FDA approval of the same
generic drugs to include the tamper-resistant formula.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07118495

 "In Kentucky, the pain pill epidemic has destroyed thousands of lives and ravaged communities," Senator McConnell said. "In my travels across the
Commonwealth, I'm often told heartbreaking stories about the individuals who needlessly lost loved ones to opiate drug overdose. The problem is so
acute that more Kentuckians die from drug overdose than from car accidents each year."
Senator McConnell's office has also worked closely with Congressman Hal Rogers on this effort. Senator McConnell added, "I appreciate the
leadership of my friend, Congressman Rogers, on this issue and I applaud his efforts to combat drug abuse in Kentucky. I look forward to our
continued partnership in this fight."
Jerry Haynes, President and CEO of ARH, wrote to McConnell about the issue recently. "Our service area of Eastern Kentucky has been plagued by
prescription drug abuse for many years. Painkiller addiction has destroyed the lives of numerous people and the potential release of these generics
threatens to escalate the problem."
Karen Kelly, President and CEO of Operation UNITE, wrote: "At a time when painkillers are responsible for more deaths than heroin and cocaine
combined, and illegal trafficking continues to confound aggressive law enforcement efforts, we do not need to expand the playing field by flooding
the market with more • and potentially just as deadly drugs under the guise that they are cheaper."
In addition to writing FDA Commissioner Hamburg, Senator McConnell also forwarded the letters he received from the Kentucky organizations to
the FDA and asked for a prompt review and response.

Sue,
The problem is multi-factorial but experts agree the following factors contribute:
Ease of access — keeping old medicines, unlocked medicine chest, etc. with no instruction of how to dispose
Oversupply - 30 tablets of Vicodin or oxycodone prescribed for 3rd molar extraction or a sprain in the ER
Poor patient selection— physicians prescribing inappropriately
Poor monitoring — not checking the prescription drug database before prescribing or dispensing ("doctor
shopping")
Tennessee governor Bill Haslam announced "Prescription for Success" in early June. A number of strategies have
been developed to meet the following seven goals of the "Prescription for Success" plan to fight this epidemic:
1.
2.
3.
4.
5.
6.
7

Decrease the number of Tennesseans that abuse controlled substances
Decrease the number of Tennesseans who overdose on controlled substances
Decrease the amount of controlled substances dispensed in Tennessee
Increase access to drug disposal outlets in Tennessee
Increase access and quality of early intervention, treatment and recovery services
Expand collaborations and coordination among state agencies
Expand collaboration and coordination with other states

There will be mandatory checking of prescription drug database, limits on daily opioid dose, training of physicians
including pain specialists, more places to dispose of old meds, and more treatment and intervention. All of which
should reduce ease of access and oversupply along with less patients getting these drugs.

respective customers. During the Opana ER supply disruption we kept the patient front and center as our
area of priority — that has not changed.

Please do not proactively discuss this article but in the event, a customer brings it up the best response is to
reinforce these key points:
•
•

Endo takes very seriously the problem of prescription drug abuse and is also strongly committed to
providing solutions to the medical needs of patients suffering with chronic pain.
Part of our corporate mission is a commitment to educating physicians and patients about the
appropriate and responsible use of pain management therapies.

•

REBOUND to pre-event levels
RECLAIM lost patients

Subject: Ad hoc: Opana Injectable - PCA and Epidural Administration MITA 105725
Hi Nancy and Oksana,
For the BRC request for a "formulary packet for Numorphone use for IV PCA and intrathecal," we performed a search of the
Opana Injection PI, SRLs, previous ad hocs, and Medline literature (attached). Please see our findings/proposed response
below.
IV-PCA
Provide OFF - PCA SRL, which summarizes literature reports of administration of oxymorphone via PCA (including IV-PCA).
Intrathecal
Provide response from previous ad hoc (attached and copied below). An updated Medline literature search (attached) did not
reveal any additional citations.
Provide information from the Opana Injection PI (under 'Description'):
Opana Injection is available in 1 mg/mL, 1 mL ampules of oxymorphone hydrochloride. In addition, each 1 mg/mL ampule
contains 8.0 mg/mL sodium chloride. pH is adjusted with hydrochloric acid.
Endo Pharmaceuticals has not conducted any studies on the intrathecal use of Opana and cannot make any
recommendations regarding such use. As a professional courtesy, a literature search was performed and identified a few
reports of intrathecal oxymorphone use [Note that this is not meant to be a comprehensive list. Provide citations below, along
with the descriptions if requested]:
1.) Aldrete JA, Couto da Silva JM. Leg edema from intrathecal opiate infusions. Eur J Pain. 2000;4:361-365.
• This was a report of the incidence of pedal/leg edema in 23 patients who received intrathecal opioids for chronic noncancer pain (patients had pseudoarthrosis/arachnoiditis) via permanently implanted pumps. Five out of the 23 patients
developed pedal/leg edema 6 months after treatment initiation; 3 of the patients were receiving oxymorphone (6-13
mg/day) and 2 were receiving morphine (12-16 mg/day). Pre-existing risk factors included leg edema and venous
insufficiency prior to receiving the intrathecal opioid therapy, which may have been exacerbated by dose-dependent
vasodilation associated with the opioid.
2.) Sousa H de, Klein E. Intrathecal and Epidural Oxymorphone. Anesthesiology. 1989;71(3A):A699
• This study noted that the lack of spinal neurotoxicity of intrathecal oxymorphone was confirmed in 8 sheep receiving 9
daily injections of 0.5 mg oxymorphone. The study also reported 20 patients undergoing major orthopedic or intra-

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07567480

 abdominal surgery who received added oxymorphone to their intrathecal or epidural anesthetic. In these patients,
analgesia with intrathecal oxymorphone lasted a mean of 16 hr, compared with a mean of 11.5 hr (range 6-16 hr) with
epidural oxymorphone. Of the 7 patients who received intrathecal oxymorphone, 2 had bradypnea and 2 had nausea
and vomiting.
Thank you!
Nora

Proprietary 1FDA delays plans to release draft guidance on tamper-resistant opioid formulations to 2013 - sources BioPharm
Insight The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has pushed back publication of its draft guidance on demonstrating tamperresistance (TR) qualities in opioids to at least January 2013, pain drug sources said.
The agency declined to comment.
This news reported in July 2012 that the draft guidance was expected by the end of 2012 but could be delayed due to the
presidential election in November. A pain drug consultant noted the delay could possibly be due to a lack of internal agency
expertise on understanding TR formulations and drug extraction studies.
The pain drug industry is eagerly awaiting FDA guidance on TR demonstration, in particular when it comes to whether generic
opioids makers should demonstrate TR as well. Generic filers to
Endo Health Solutions' (NASDAQ:ENDP) pain drug Opana Extended-Release (oxymorphone HCI) will likely have to demonstrate
that their products have comparable abuse-resistant mechanisms to Endo's product, this news service previously reported.
Endo announced 26 September it received Paragraph IV Certification Notices from

Subject: another BD lead
Linda,
On referral from Matt, I've been in conversation with Dr. Seabury Davies regarding a patented process for tagging a molecule
(such as Opana) with a stable, non radioactive isotope that can then be picked up in a urine sample to see if the appropriate
medication is in the urine vs. other compounds. This group has been before the FDA several times and the FDA was positive
about the process, but told them to come back with a product before they rule on it. Seems and aNDA would be the way to go.
The second and longer ppt is the one that addresses the FDA (basically the slides added on to the end). This physician is savvy
and truly engaging. I'd love to see him get before the right folks to present this. I had some questions for him regarding the
isotope and the FDA's seeming unwillingness to grant anything `abuse deterrent' status (I understand this is due to the fact that
the agency itself is unsure of what really constitutes a tleterrent'.) He had some good answers. I was thinking that because of
the chemistry involved, Sandeep would be the person to look at this, but I wanted to check with you first and see if you agreed
and/or wanted to walk this over as well. I know you are very busy and I don't consider you at my beck and call; I've just run
across some exciting stuff recently and want to do the best I can to see that it gets the attention it deserves. For all I know, we
could tag Opana with this isotope and then use the technology from Indevus to implant it...
Let me know how you want me to proceed,
Vicki
PS
I have copied a portion of a previous email below so that you get a flavor of Dr. Davies himself....
I trust you got attachments to the last email. I sent the presentation with the most slides that included a bit more of the
regulatory information about state prescription monitoring programs (PMP's).
Ultimately I feel this individual state model will give way to an integrated national then international registry for scheduled drug
administration. This registry will ultimately offer a good ROI in that it will enhance detection of diversion and illicit use early in the
life cycle of addictive behaviors, thus a far more cost effective approach. Not coincidentally it will identify providers that are lax.
However conscientious we may be about all those goals we must first make this a revenue generator for despite the events of
CONFIDENTIAL

EPI001038485

 the recent past with governmental purchase of equity in private enterprise we are CAPITALISTS. Thus if we are to make the
case that ENDO needs to pursue this there must be a tangible return from sales to both private and public enterprise.
Its easy to see where the government will like the applications of scheduled drug testing reliably in the military, TSA, intelligence
community etc. The quandary is how to get a private enterprise to jump through the hoops of actually creating a product with
isotopic labeling for the government will only bite after the product is available. Fortunately the timing here is pretty much perfect
inasmuch as the new administration will be eager to show its desire to innovate and improve health care.
Admittedly, the game plan as I see it consists of multiple steps and will frankly be pretty dynamic but is achievable. First things
first, we must convince the strategists at ENDO this is worth a whirl.
Evidence of a vast and enlarging marketplace as the indications for prescribing opioids for nonmalignant pain are expanding with
lots of champions in the medical community. This coupled with an emerging crisis in abuse despite the legitimacy of most users.
Thus advocates in the chronic pain community on both "ends of the needle" if you will. Demand established.
Supply is a function of the availability and cost of isotopic compounds used as building blocks in making the labeled drugs and the
ability to synthesize said compounds. While I am not an organic chemist my understanding is that this is not rocket science and
not prohibitively expensive. Supply not prohibitive and in fact perhaps attractive to the Mallinkrodts or Johnson Matheys to get
into a new line of manufacturing.
No one has a reliable means of following compliance now in prescribing scheduled drugs. The other paradigms (controlled
release, antagonist administration) are complementary not competitive to what we propose.
Thus we would be not only first in delivery but IP protected for ALL scheduled drugs elaborated in patent. Innovative, exclusive,
and adaptable.
Finally we seal the deal by letting the team know that despite the opportunity the cost is skinny relative to the potential. ENDO
gets the upside without the cumbersome baggage of buying this sort of thing from a big biotech concern because they are willing
to put sweat equity into developing this with DRPN. Lots of options.
That's the pitch.
There is a lot more detail that we can flesh out during brainstorming sessions.
All the best.

prescribing Opana ER brand, Mark Ritter confirmed that this is not a United Health requirement; in fact, in some of
United's plans, generic oxymorphone ER is subject to a triple step before being covered at all, and Opana ER is one
of the preferred agents that must be tried first.

specific to United patients, I can have Mark follow up again. If it's a step through immediate release, there shouldn't

just trying to ensure Abuse-Deterrent labeled formulations are available/covered. Since generic oxymorphone ER is

 From: Kan, Sarah

Subject: Take-aways/follow up from NASCSA Meeting

Hi Greg,

This week I attended the 28th Annual Education Forum of the National Association of State Controlled
Substance Authorities (NASCSA). Heather Thomson, Sr. HOPE Field Scientist was also in attendance and
served as one of the Parliamentarians for the meeting. I also had the good fortune to meet Kimberly Lee
who is responsible for DEA Compliance in Huntsville.

36 states were represented- mostly from Boards of Pharmacy, Departments of Health, and some Attorneys
General Offices- each representative has responsibility over their states Prescription Monitoring Program
(PMP). There were a number of industry representatives- Endo, Purdue, Mallinckrodt, Jansen, GW
Pharmaceuticals.

There were a number of presentations of note that may need further discussion/action:

1.
There was a presentation by Alan Santos, DEA Office of Diversion, with an update from the DEA. He
discussed trends in drug abuse and enforcement activities throughout the country. In particular, he
highlighted Florida, West Virginia, Ohio, New Mexico, New York, and Texas. Many of his statistics were at
least two years old and he had a slide with pictures of the old formulation of Opana ER with pictures of the
old pills and mentioned that there were a lot of concerns with field agents about Opana ER and the abuse
with addicts and dealers particularly interested in "stop signs." There was no discussion of the reformulation
or Endo's successful efforts to replace the old formulation with the new formulation that is designed to be
crush resistant. He also made a connection of abuse, misuse, and diversion when Oxycontin reformulated
and increased activities around Opana ER.

2.
Dr. Paul Coplan of Purdue Pharma made a presentation entitled "The Impact of Tamper Resistant
Formulations on Prescription Drug Abuse." He presented data from epidemiological studies he conducted
along with some universities using data from Poison Control, Mortality and Morbidity Data, Prescriber Data,
Adverse Event Data, etc. to determine if abuse of Oxycontin had changed one year following the
reformulation. This is similar information that is found in the Pain Med News article from August about their
posters during the American Pain Society meeting.
There is one item of significant note that was cited during the meeting. Dr. Coplan mentioned that while
Oxycontin abuse decreased 49% overall by all routes- oral, snorting, and injecting- Opana ER abuse
increased 196%. He did note that Opana ER has been reformulated as designed to be crush resistant this
year.

Dr. Jody Green of Denver Health Rocky Mountain Poison Control presented RADARS data and studied
Oxycontin and Exalgo in abuse reduction numbers with mention of Opana ER reformulation with no
conclusions or data.

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-02023509

 3.
There was significant discussion on clamping down on wholesalers by the DEA as well as by Bob
Twillman, American Academy of Pain Management. Mr. Twillman did cite significant concern that some of
these enforcement activities by the DEA are leading to shortages for legitimate pain patients and it was like
squeezing the balloon- not really leading to real solutions.

4.
Finally, there were no discussions about hydrocodone combination product rescheduling- either
consideration by the FDA or any states. New York was not in attendance and while hydrocodone abuse was
a significant discussion point in a number of presentations- state-by-state rescheduling was not
recommended.

I think there is significant opportunity for Endo in 2013 to provide additional information about the
reformulation of Opana ER, discussion of e-prescribing of controlled substances, as well as education on
REMS. While this was noted by Dr. Coplan and Dr. Green, as well as Bob Twillman, there were no
presentations on REMS.

Please let me know if you have any questions. I have an extra conference packet and will send it to Chadds
Ford. Some of the presentations are difficult to read, so if they are not available on the NASCA website, I
will ask Kathy Keough, the Executive Director, to share them electronically.
