Endo Pharmaceuticals Has Some Upside

Endo Pharmaceuticals Has Some Upside
by: MagicDiligence April 22, 2010 I about: ENDP / MRK / TEVA / WPI
Endo Pharmaceuticals (EN1DP) is a specialty drug company, with a focus on a few specific areas, namely pain
management, urology, and endocrinology. Pain management is the company's forte, led by Lidoderm, a
lidocaine medicated patch that is prescribed for a wide variety of pain-related problems. Lidoderm gained
traction after orally ingested pain killers such as Vioxx (MRK) faced well-publicized safety concerns in the
1

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-STAUBUS_LIT-00670529

 mid-2000's. Today, Lidoderm accounts for well over 50% of Endo's total sales, bringing in $763 million dollars
last year.
Another 16% of sales is generated by the Opana franchise. Opana is orally ingested and is used to treat severe
pain symptoms. It is used much like morphine. The third major drug marketed by Endo is Percocet, the wellknown painkiller for less severe pain indications. Percocet accounts for about 9% of Endo's total.
While far and away dominated by its pain franchises, the company in early 2009 purchased Indevus, which
specializes in urology (bladder and urinary tract) and endocrinology (endocrine system). Currently, the products
here account for a rather small portion of sales, about 4-5%.
Let's look at Endo through the filters of growth potential, competitive position, and financial strength. Growth
potential is a negative here. Endo faces a common problem in the branded drug industry - patent expiration and
the inevitable generic competition that follows. Both Lidoderm and Opana, collectively almost 70% of
revenues, have patent cliffs upcoming. Lidoderm has theoretical patent protection up until 2015, but already
faces a patent challenge from Watson Labs (WPI). Opana has seen similar challenges, and its patent protections
expire before 2013.
The most likely outcome of these challenges are settlements. For example, Endo recently settled generic
challenges to Opana from Teva (TEVA), which allow Endo to continue selling the drug until 2012, longer than
would have been possible had they lost the challenge, but also before the patents expire.
MagicDiligence expects similar settlements related to Lidoderm. It seems reasonable to assume that generic
versions of both Lidoderm patch and Opana will hit the market in the 2012-2013 time frame, meaning that Endo
will need to replace 60% or more of their sales in the next 3 years. That certainly does not bode well for longterm growth potential.
How Endo will replace those revenues is still in question. The Indevus purchase gives the company a wider
market to address, but those sales will have to ramp up fast. The pipeline has had recent problems. Aveed, a
long-acting testosterone injection, and Fortesta (testosterone gel), both acquired in 2009, received FDA inquiry
letters last December, which will at best postpone their approval. On the pain side, Endo continues to work its
strategy of buying the rights to late-stage drugs that improve on existing treatments. While this strategy usually
improves the likelihood of approval and limits R&D spending, it also limits the duration of patent protections.
All told, Endo will likely see solid growth into 2012, at which time generic competition could eat as much as
half of current revenues. This uncertainty will keep the valuation high on an earnings yield basis.
The other two factors, competitive position and financial health, are positives. Endo, like all branded
pharmaceuticals, enjoys strong regulatory barriers to entry through patent protection. This keeps competitors
out for a period of time and allows the firm to charge high prices for their drugs. Another competitive advantage
is Endo's large 800-person sales staff that focuses on the niche of pain management. This sales department is
considered one of the most productive in the industry, and should be an important factor in quickly growing
sales of acquired products.
Financial health is fine. The balance sheet has $734 million in cash vs. $322 million in long-term debt.
Operating margins are over 25% and stand to improve as Opana and, to a lesser extent, Lidoderm experience
volume gains. Free cash flow is outstanding, averaging almost 30% of sales over the past 5 years. This cash
flow will help the company acquire new compounds to plug their upcoming sales gaps.
Right now, Endo trades at a trailing, 1ViFI-adjusted earnings yield of 15%. Against expected 2010 results, that
figure is 16.2%. That looks too cheap for the profitability just mentioned. Going through a cash flow analysis, I
2

ENDO-STAUBUS_LIT-00670530

 come up with a fair value between $27-$32, depending on how long they can push back generic competition of
Lidoderm, and what kind of replacements they can find. So there appears to be upside from the current price
around $24... but not a tremendous amount. Therefore, while MagicDiligence has a positive rating, Endo doesn't
quite make Top Buy status. This doesn't assign any value to the potential of a bigger pharma player gobbling up
the company, either.

Rodney,
As always thank you for taking my call and calls these last few weeks.
I will try to cover two birds with one stone in this email.

I.

Stephenson Murder Case
follow upI tried to explain to the caller that there was often DNA analysis done for different
reasons; i.e. paternity, id etc. and that in my limited knowledge those test would take less time
and that the in depth analysis required for a murder investigation requires an extensive standard,
multiple profiles and methodical testing. . . because the evidence would be under great degrees of
scrutiny as it can provide the proof to arrest and prosecute. AND in a court case the evidence has
not only the power to identify but, convict a person/persons who if convicted may receive the
death penalty. ( hope that sounded correct)

As always, thank you for your help. As you understand and are more than aware, not having
answers is so difficult for the family.

H.

HB 377 Tamper Resistant or Abuse Resistant/Deterrent Opioids - My take on the proposed
bill, is another tool to combat prescription narcotic drug abuse that is taking a toll on Kentucky families. Ina nutshellwhen the physician feels it is in the best interest of the patient to write a prescription for the tamper resistant form of the
pain medication, pharmacists would be required to "fill as written" no substitution. The cost of tamper resistant is the

CONFIDENTIAL

EPI001073023

 same as the non tamper resistant form of the medication No one pharmaceutical company holds the patent, so generic
forms of the tamper resistant medications are also in the pipeline. Most importantly, this is about saving lives. Too many
lives lost, too maw futures destroyed and too many children suffer from the destructive effect on their young lives.
Family court judges report that 85% of their abuse, neglect and dependency cases are the result of substance abuse.

HB 377 is on the agenda for the House Health and Welfare Committee for next Thursday, Feb 23
and noon.
Testifying on the bill
•

A mother's story I have a mother who has lost two adult children to Opana over doses.
They began popping pills, the progressed to snorting and then IV.
(Some of the pharmacist say, " it doesn't stop abuse . because they can still take the pills
by mouth". My response is that as users progress and spiral in their addiction, the go for
a more intense high, that is why they crush pills etc.)

I do not call Tamper Resistant Opioids Formulations (TRF) the end all, but another tool in
the tool box to combat this scourge on Kentucky.

Michael Barnes, Interim Executive Director, Center for Lawful Access and Abuse
Deterrence (he will be here to testify and has sent a letter of support see a quote from
Michael below)

Judge Roberts, Cir. Court/ Eastern, KY. I have with spoken Judge Roberts and he feels
he can testify but is clearing it with AOC. Judge Roberts will speak on the extremely high
amount of cases related to narcotic abuse he sees in his court.

Comm. Rodney Brewer, KSP ( KSP knows better than any organization the toll the
substance abuse is taking. If you can just add your support and if standing with you we
could have some of the uniform Troopers in the room

Also, if you could provide me a brief statement of support etc for my fact sheet that would
be great. Please send by email and copy me and my assistant Allison.hartle@lrc.ky.gov. it
would be greatly appreciated.

CONFIDENTIAL

.

I have a call in to Tracey Corey, but she is out until next Wednesday morning. I may ask big John
with the coroners association to assist.

•

And I have myself and Dr. DeWeese or another physician.

EPI001073024

 FYI - Who is against the bill, pharmacist- they believe it would increase the cost to Medicaid patients, because
there is a limited number of brands TRF (5 currently approved and 12 in development) and generics TRF are still
forth coming. There is no difference in the cost of brand narcotic TRF or the same brand in the non TRF.

(my response, the physician prescribes TRF - tamper resistant formulas for opioids, i.e. OxyContin,
morphine, oxymorphone, at his/her discretion., not routinely for every patient. )
(there are no patent restrictions or ownership any company can obtain the patent to manufacture TRF.)
(personally, I am really not for cheap narcotics. . . . I really do not want a market flooded with $4 generic
OxyContin and Opana)
I want medication to be affordable but, the toll substance abuse is taking on this Commonwealth, we need
tools to assist in addressing the issue.

As always, thank you for your assistance with Thursday's testimony. I look forward to receiving your statement for
our fact sheet. Please see a few of the other quotes below.

Please do not hesitate to call me if you have any questions or concerns.

Warmest Regards,

Addia

P.S. CASA event last Friday- thank you and KSP for helping us. We are just going over the post conference surveys
and "Examining the Drug Problem in Kentucky" (KSP) has very high reviews and comments. Will forward once we
complete the process.

Quotes for fact sheet

Since 2009, CLAAD's National Prescription Drug Abuse Prevention Strategy has called for the adoption of
technologies to impede the intentional abuse of prescription medications.
The use of abuse-deterrent opioids is the new standard of care in pain treatment.
Abuse-deterrent medications are the new equivalent of child-proof medicine caps.

CONFIDENTIAL

EPI001073025

 Please heed the recommendations of the 30 organizations endorsing the National Prescription Drug Abuse
Prevention Strategy, and act in accordance with federal policy, by shepherding safe prescribing and dispensing
legislation through the Kentucky Legislature.
Michael C. Barnes
Interim Executive Director
Center for Lawful Access and Abuse Deterrence

Due to ongoing problems with drug diversion in the United States, NADDI is strong proponent of new tamper
resistant medicines that make it more difficult for an abuser and more helpful for law enforcement, yet still provide
quality relief to the patient. NADDI has a strong belief that the diversion of prescription medication, can many times
ultimately negatively affect legitimate patients, the vast majority of those who use controlled substances.
Charles F. Cichon
Executive Director
National Association of Drug Diversion Investigators, Inc. (NADDI)

The poll also showed more than 3 in 10 adults in Northern Kentucky and statewide reported that they have friends or
family members who have experienced problems as a result of misusing prescription pain relievers. — "The
Kentucky Health Poll"

Stephen J. Pasierb, President and CEO, The Partnership at Drugfree.org:
The Partnership at Drugfree.org believes that tamper resistant formulation can be one important piece of an overall
effort to deter the abuse of prescription medications.
While it is by no means a silver bullet, the prescribing and dispensing of tamper resistant formulations is an important
part of reducing the behavior of prescription drug abuse. That means that if more prescribers substitute TRF for
non-TRF opioid analgesics, it will be more difficult for drug seekers who steal pain medications from friends and
family to find drugs that they can easily crush and snort or inject.

Your thoughts?
Opana ER is formulated as a hard tablet to resist pulverization by using USP breaker force tester crushing forces in
excess of 800 Newtons. In standardized laboratory-based in-vitro manipulation studies, attempts to crush the tablet
with common methods including two metal spoons, a hammer, and a professional pill crusher resulted in a deformed,
flattened, and intact tablet. The pharmacokinetic profiles of an Opana ER tablet tampered with a professional pill
crusher and an intact Opana ER tablet are bioequivalent.

flattened tablet. Therefore, insufflation of the manipulated drug product would be extremely difficult. The product's
physicochemical barrier may result in meaningful reduced abuse by insufflation.

possible by the oral route or other manipulation methods.

product's actual abuse potential. Postmarketing studies of the actual abuse patterns associated with this product are

On May 5, 2016, at 9:36 PM, Clark, Paula <Clark.Paulara),endo.com wrote:
Hi all:
We are providing a summary of the Advisory Committee Meeting discussing 1) approval of Apadaz, and 2) addition
of abuse deterrence labeling for KemPharm's Apadaz, an IR formulation of hydrocodone/APAP. First section is
summary from briefing materials; second section provides high level summary of responses to questions to
committee and voting.
Please feel free to contact us with any questions you may have.
Thanks.
Meeting material: http://www.fda.ciov/AdvisoryCommittees/CommitteesMeetinciMaterials/Drucis
/AnestheticAndAnalgesicDrugProductsAdvisoryCommittee/ucm498783.htm
High level summary from the FDA briefing materials
Benzhydrocodone (KP201) is a prodrug for hydrocodone and is proposed to be available in a fixed dose
combination with acetaminophen. There are currently no approved immediate-release (IR) hydrocodone
formulations with abuse-deterrent properties on the market. FDA granted the product a priority review because
it's a novel ADF technology.
The primary development goal for APADAZ (proposed brand name) was to reduce the intranasal (IN) and
oral abuse potential of immediate-release (IR) hydrocodone/acetaminophen products. The product was
formulated with a benzyl group attached to the hydrocodone molecule by an ester bond, creating a
hydrocodone prodrug (benzhydrocodone, called KP201 during development), which is hydrolyzed to release
hydrocodone in the presence of esterases in the gastrointestinal system or blood.
10 clinical pharmacology studies were conducted — most were BE related. Essentially nothing of
significance in the BE studies - some minor deviations outside the 80-125% BE range, but nothing considered
by FDA to be clinically significant or meaningful under the various conditions (fasted, fed, etc).
Abuse Liability: Oral — no statistically significant separation between the active and comparator arms on
primary endpoint (drug liking)
Abuse Liability: Intranasal - no statistically significant separation between the active and comparator on
primary endpoint (drug liking)
A second intranasal liability study was also presented, but that one had major issues with the design — even
so FDA evaluated drug liking and found it showed no significant difference
In vitro studies were also done — Frank will have to look at that more closely, but it appears that there is
some concern over the ability of some solvents to allow separation of the API from the acetaminophen which
is not ideal
FDA is questioning whether intranasal abuse is important for this product, so that will be a big point of
discussion. Since the formulation also includes acetaminophen there is some question on whether this needs
to be done at all since FDA stated acetaminophen is already known to be a deterrent to nasal abuse.
Meeting Summary, Comments and Voting after Presentations:
HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-01109825

 Dr. Hertz Comments:
Products will remain abuseable — there is a formulation that makes it less amenable to abuse via methods or routes but Division does not expect abuse deterrence abuse proof
Expect incremental benefit to be an improvement; no absolute value for everything, incremental steps are acceptable
and apply to IR or ER.
Guidance of Industry - if abuse deterrent properties are expected to result in meaningful reduction can be included in
the labeling and use of relevant comparator per guidance is essential
Established through comparison to product that is relevant.
There were differences between FDA and Sponsor —interpretations is what are important and FDA looks at willingness
to take a drug again into account against all other parameters — cannot only rely on pk but also must have PD. FDA is
interested in products that subject find less desirable — willingness to take again provides context for Adverse Events
(i.e., irritating qualities could deter abuse).
Modern labeling is included in Guideline and — not just one victory — does not always support labeling inclusion per
guidance.
Difference in drugs already out there is important.
Questions for the Committee are
1.

Discussion: Please discuss whether the data presented for hydrocodone and APAP combination drug
products support that nasal route of abuse is relevant for KP201/APAP.
Most — route of nasal abuse is relevant for the product; but to be clear it is not the only route — and
need to look at different abuse patterns per region (urban versus rural). This product cannot stop
individuals for progressing to abuse (as in a comparable product) and people have options on how to
abuse — regarding likeability of one route
Intranasal is not always the preferred choice. But data collected was based on folks who take drugs
via intranasal route — the data did not show change in preference to nasal abuse
Committee Summary:
Nasal route is probably relevant even if there is only a small relevance — question whether or not nasal
route after oral route — appears that it may be relevant to adolescents who use nasal as abuse route.
Relevant for product — pathway implies that product in and of itself prevents progression and that is not
known.

2.

Discussion: Please discuss whether there is sufficient data to support a finding that KP201 has properties
that can be expected to deter abuse commenting on support for deterrent effects for each of the three possible
routes of abuse:
a.
b.
c.

Oral
Nasal
Intravenous — not relevant

Panel Comments:
Note data needs to be taken with a great deal of skepticism. Clear — A and C — no (with C no
relevance); little bit of data (pK/pD) — can't show any difference in liking or level of high; challenge that

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-01109826

 there was reliance on internet data. Also age — there is abuse in older generation above and beyond
data presented.
Chemistry is compelling — but no true data that it is hard to overcome. Far more broad ranging
aggressive ways to overcome abuse in other drugs than this one — this is a very small amount of data
and it could easily be overcome.
Nasal abuse was base case scenario — not compelling data that someone would not try to abuse
again.
Approvable drug and innovation in pro-drug is very "neat" and could be positive to what is currently
available. Nice option to have available whether abuse deterrent or not — similar to comparator and
how to label and promote is in question since abuse deterrent incremental benefit is small.
Only so much a user could snort for this product — may not be supportable. Comparing 2 products
on intranasal use could lead to assist for the on-line forum on how to abuse. It has some small
deterrence to abuse.
Drug liking data — measured at % hour so hard to assess. Challenge was it measured at right time
to have compelling data re intranasal data.
Hydrocodone scheduling meeting — discussion — APAP is an abuse deterrent over Zohydro that is
on the market (pure hydrocodone) so maybe this is where this product fits into the products available.
Human abuse potential studies - 2 failed to meet primary endpoints and 1 study had flaws - so
labeling could not support labeling for deterrent aspects of the product. Positive is that there is nothing
to be gained in mean plasma — nasal route vs. oral — so reduces importance of nasal route.
Nothing presented today make backward steps — but is a baby step forward in the opioid abuse
issue.
Challenges in analysis — what we expect in IR drugs this has missed the window (15-30 minutes) and
extrapolation of data for the abuse routes is lacking on extractable versus not extractable regarding
release data. Balance concerns against numbers of people in pain who need options - it is hard not to
say there is a tiny incremental benefit here that people will not abuse this product. But is it a big enough
increment forward to call it an abuse deterrent? This is a credibility issue for panel and not good for us
to state to "we can see what happens post-approval" so panel member is conflicted.
Size of incremental step if approving drug and providing labeling for abuse deterrence. The panel
warns FDA they have to think of impact of information in the package label for prescribers. This could
have prescribers feel it is "safer than" and then prescribe it more if we include in labeling with ADF
properties. The intended consequences of labeling inclusion has to be thoroughly considered.
Committee Summary: the panel is unconvinced of deterrent characteristics of snorting — no
compelling evidence. The deterrent can be overcome for this drug as FDA did describe.

3.

VOTE: Should KP201/APAP be approved for the proposed indication?
Indication: "moderate to severe acute pain" per Dr. Hertz
Yes - 16
No - 4
Abstain - 0
Yes o for the indication proposed and yes data and data bioequivalence was supportable

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-01109827

 No
o not supported by data; not safer and unintended uses weigh over indication support and
worried another opioid on market without robust abuse deterrence; drug liking was within 30
minutes; and product could be manipulated by simple solvents.

4.

VOTE: If approved should KP201/APAP be labeled as an abuse deterrent product?
Yes - 2
No - 18
Abstain — 0
Yes — incremental benefit; believe in "baby steps"
No:
o lack of evidence of clear distinction from other products; not sufficient data on deterrence;
o labeling concerns and crushing data not available; difficult to provide labeling that would be effective for
prescribers — could make labeling decisions by prescribers worse;
o could accelerate use of product; data not compelling — to small of an incremental change; issue with
marketing materials as well;
o need a very strong post market surveillance in order to support abuse deterrence.

5.

Discussion: If you think the product should be approved, discuss the route or routes of abuse for which
abuse-deterrent language should be included in the product label.
Yes — 2 persons — already stated.
Anything further that you wish to say on question 4:

No further comments of substance. One panel member did complement sponsor on presentation and this
should not be the
end for this technology in the future to be considered —
needs more information post
marketing for future and lead to labeling change.

Paula Clark
Senior Director, Regulatory Affairs Liaison

 Belbuca — Aspirational Positioning
Belbuca is an effective treatment for chronic pain that can lead to less opioid abuse and reduce opioid
addiction and death. It can also reduce corresponding costs associated with the opioid epidemic.
Belbuca is an effective pain medicine for many pain conditions, allowing for a segment of patients
that may need to progress to schedule II heavy hitter LAO's: Opana/Oxycontin.
Belbuca is hard to abuse.
o It is a buccal film that makes snorting and/or injecting very improbable.
o Because this film goes into the cheek, using more than two films at any one time makes
abuse of the product very improbable.
o The dose limit of 0.9 mg of buprenorphine makes abuse of Belbuca very improbable.
o The known slower development of tolerance associated with buprenorphine makes abuse of
Belbuca much less likely.
o The known psychological benefits of buprenorphine may be an advantage in deterring
patients from opioid abuse using Belbuca.
o Because Belbuca is not a pill, it cannot easily be put into the diversion market for illicit
purposes.
o Belbuca has no known street value.
o Belbuca is a schedule III drug. This means that the DEA and the FDA have determined that
Belbuca has less potential for abuse than schedule II drugs.
The opioid epidemic in the U.S. costs billions of dollars in productivity, medical costs, and
treatment. Belbuca reduces these costs by effectively treating chronic pain patients, while avoiding
the harmful effects of opioid abuse.
Belbuca is an effective treatment for chronic pain that can be used to replace schedule II narcotics.
Belbuca can be used in the first instance to avoid using SAO's which have become the face of the opioid
addiction and overdose crisis. It can also be used after a short course of SAO therapy when the
physician plans on transitioning the patient to chronic therapy----we believe that Belbuca can play a
transformational role in these patients and bend the curve on the opioid crisis. Lastly, Belbuca can be
used for chronic pain patients who might otherwise utilize very powerful LAO's such as Opana ER,
OxyContin, and/or fentanyl.
Belbuca offers physicians the opportunity to treat patients effectively while avoiding the negative impacts
associated with the U.S. opioid epidemic.

 Lifetree Clinical Research and Pain Clinic, Salt Lake City, Utah 84106, USA. lynnw@lifetreepain.com

Abstract
Two strategies should greatly improve pain management while minimizing opioid abuse. The first strategy involves the systematic
implementation in every clinical practice of "universal precautions," a set of procedures that help physicians implement opioid therapy in a safe
and controlled manner. These procedures include: 1) carefully assessing the patient's risk for opioid abuse; 2) selecting the most appropriate
opioid therapy; 3) regularly monitoring the patient to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of the treatment and to detect possible aberrant
behaviors; and 4) mapping out solutions if abuse and/or addiction is detected, or in case of treatment failure. The second strategy involves the
use of opioid formulations designed to deter or prevent product tampering and abuse. Results of clinical trials of new formulations of existing
opioids (including oxycodone, morphine, and hydromorphone) suggest the potential for reduced abuse liability and, if approved, will be
evaluated after launch for reduced real-world abuse. Integration of these formulations in clinical practices based on universal precautions
should help further minimize the risk of opioid abuse while fostering appropriate prescribing to patients with indications for opioid therapy.
PERSPECTIVE: Undertreated pain and prescription opioid abuse remain important public health problems. In the absence of strong empirical
evidence, common sense dictates that a universal-precautions approach-a systematic and easily adopted process that clinicians can quickly
put into practice-is advised to promote safe opioid prescribing. Abuse- and tamper-resistant opioid formulations are emerging tools that may
enhance safe opioid prescribing; further research and postmarketing analysis will clarify their utility and role in clinical practice.

Delaware Prescription Drug Abuse Summit Marks a Turning Point in National Epidemic, CLAAD Says.
NEWARK, Del., Nov. 16, 2012 /PRNewswire- USNewswire/ --Today, a not-for-profit organization presenting
at the Delaware Prescription Drug Abuse Summit appealed to the event's host, Attorney General Beau Biden,
for assistance in preventing medication overdoses. The Center for Lawful Access and Abuse Deterrence
(CLAAD) asked Biden to work closely with his father, Vice President Joe Biden, to ensure that federal
regulators properly implement Obama-Biden Administration drug policies.
During CLAAD's presentation at the summit, Director Michael Barnes warned that pain medications without
added safety features could flood back into communities in the coming weeks if the Food and Drug
Administration (FDA) fails to follow the Obama-Biden strategy.
In recent years, the makers of the opioid pain relievers OxyContin and Opana removed their traditional
products from the market in favor of new versions designed to impede certain forms of intentional abuse.
Preliminary, peer-reviewed evidence indicates that dealers and abusers have less interest in the new drugs with
abuse-deterrent features.[1] The new medications cost no more to consumers than their prior formulations.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_FLAG-01233718

 Several drug companies have asked the FDA for approval to bring the old, more readily abused formulations of
the drugs back to the market as early as January 2013.
"The Administration's prescription drug abuse prevention plan provides express support for abuse-deterrent
medications," Barnes said.
Earlier this month, CLAAD and nine other public health and safety organizations sent aletter to the FDA urging
it to implement Obama-Biden policy, foster the transition to abuse-deterrent medications, and prevent the
marketing of generic versions of the drugs that do not have similar safety features.
"At today's summit, I asked General Biden to work closely with his father to make certain that the FDA does
the right thing," Barnes said.
Vice President Biden is considered one of the most accomplished national leaders in drug policy, having served
as chairman of both the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee and Drug Caucus.
"I have confidence that the Bidens will ensure that the FDA supports the shift to abuse-deterrent medications,"
Barnes concluded. "We reached a turning point in our nation's prescription drug abuse epidemic at today's
summit."
[1] Cicero TJ, Ellis MS, Surratt HL. Effect of abuse-deterrent formulation of OxyContin. New England Journal

Subject: Paladin Requests

Hi Sue,
We have received requests from Paladin for information on 4 products that would be required to submit a
NDS for each. While we assess the information requested and how best to provide it, we wanted to
make you aware of some potential challenges for submitting a new NDS for each product. A summary for
each product is included below.
Best Regards,
Jeff
Opana IR Tablets

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-01285844

 Valeant filed the Opana IR NDS and subsequently withdrew the filing. At the time Health
Canada had outlined the below concerns (as summarized by Valeant):
Clinical Development
o The Cmax is 2x higher for IR compared with Opana ER - risk of overdose, prone to abuse.
o In acute post-operative pain the 20 mg ER lead to an unacceptable number of subjects
requiring naloxone therapy to treat an overdose. The risk with Opana IR might be higher.
o There was no evident benefit for IR 30 mg over the 20 mg dose and this dose was associated
with serious AEs particularly hypoxia
Opana ER Tablets (Abuse-deterrent formulation)
The original Opana ER formulation application was approved in 2012; however, only 4 dosage
strengths are approved 5, 10, 20, 40 mg. The other 3 dosage strengths were not approved as
Health Canada disagreed with the methodology we used in the US to support the approvals. No
other data was available therefore Valeant withdrew the additional dosage strengths (7.5, 15, 30).
Specifically Health Canada wanted an IVIVC and that is not available for Opana ER.
Currently Valeant still owns the original Opana ER dossier in Canada. It was never returned to
Endo.
Please note that Endo partners with Grlinenthal on the US NDA; it appears discussion with
GRT would be needed for any Canadian distribution (would need confirmed by legal)

Subject: Hospital Channel Strategy
Midwest Region Sales Team,
As we discussed on the region conference call today, given the regulatory complexities of the FDA decisions, we need to
reevaluate the long-term brand strategy and stop the promotion of Opana ER with INTAC into the hospital accounts. I
want to thank you for your efforts, I know a lot of hard work went into the training, credentialing, creating appointments
and establishing relationships with the 80 Hospital Accounts across the Midwest Region, you stepped up to the
challenge and did amazing job, thank you.
This is a difficult decision given the significant progress made thus far in 2013 including the 8 formulary wins including
wins at Cleveland Clinic, North Shore Health System, Port Huron and Holmes Regional Health System just to name a
few. However, with the potential for additional generic oxymorphone ER product launching into a setting we had to
make this tough business decision. With pricing having a significant impact on product decisions and the possibility of
additional generic oxymorphone ER products entering the market at further reduced pricing would likely have an
immediate impact on the ability of OPANA ER with INTAC to successfully compete and win in this setting.
Again, thank you for all that you have done with the hospital channel strategy, I appreciate everything you did to make it
successful. Please let me know if you have any questions.
Regards,
Kenny

Can we respond to these concerns?
Sent from my iPhone
Begin forwarded message:

From: "Greg Baran" <greg@michiganpharmacists.org >
Date: May 3, 2012 12:17:00 PM EDT
To: <moody.david@endo.com >
Cc: "Melissa Yutzey" <MYutzey@kelley-cawthorne.com>, <kjonas@michiganpharmacists.org >
Subject: Opioid Technology Legislation

David,

Based upon a review by our board, they have some created some very plausible scenarios that are everyday occurrences
and they have requested a response related to how the proposed legislation would impact day-to-day pharmacy practice.

1. A patient presents a prescription written for oxymorphone extended release 10mg, what would a pharmacist be required
to do prior to dispensing the prescription?

2. A prescription written for morphine 10mg/2m1 injectable is written for a patient in hospice, what would a pharmacist be
required to do prior to dispensing the prescription?

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07130194

 3. A medication order for morphine 10mg/2m1 injectable is written in a medical institution, what would a pharmacist be
required to do prior to dispensing the prescription?

4. A prescription, which is an authorization by a prescriber, is written for Vicodin© but the prescriber has not indicated
"DAW," what can the pharmacist dispense? Can they perform drug product selection?

5. Six months from now, a generic tamper resistant oxymorphone 10mg ER is available and the prescriber writes
generically and the pharmacists wishes to dispense Opana ER 10mg, what is the process that the pharmacist needs to
complete prior to dispensing?

We interpret the proposed legislation to require the pharmacist, prior to dispensing in any of the above scenarios as having
to check the Board's list and having to verify with the prescriber and document appropriately. If this is the case, this will create
additional steps for the pharmacist prior to dispensing any opioid medication, the pharmacist will be required to document
compliance which would create workflow and potential audit issues for pharmacist providers. Based upon this legislation, this
does not differentiate between outpatient, inpatient or medical institutional practice. Since schedule 2 prescriptions cannot be
taken verbally or via fax, this creates a potential access barrier for patients.

Hello Neil and Colleagues,
Jeff suggests that a general upward trend in the severity of patients could account for the differences in
patients seen at different times, without recourse to a theory of selective exit from NAVIPPRO. Under the
general time-trend hypothesis, it would be natural that sites that only participated in the pre-period would
have seen less severe patients than did those sites that only participated in the post-period, even if there were
no intrinsic differences between the sites coming in and going out. That there should be some secular effect
seems very plausible, I agree. You can't test whether this accounts for all of the evolution of the TN population
without knowing the full and pre- and post- data for all the sites, which you don't have.
Neil points out that in the pre-period, the sites that were destined to continue had patients who were more
severe than did the sites that were not destined to continue. This suggests a selective dropout of sites with
less severe patients. I notice that opposite is true in the post period. The new sites seem also to be better off
(less severe patients) than those who continued from earlier. My guess is that sites with severe patients have
better retention in NAVIPPRO than do those sites with less severe patients.
Useful time trend data might come from "same-store" comparisons. Among the continuing sites Opana
mentions go from 10% pre (origina) to 8% post (reformulated). Compared against all evaluations, injection
use goes from from 1.5% (15% of 10%) pre to 6% (76% of 8%) post. For Any Prescription Opioid the
corresponding numbers go from 13% (26% of 48%) pre to 19% (34% of 55%) post. In the analysis confined
to continuing sites in Tennesse, then, there is an upward secular trend in the prevalence of injection use
overall, as Jeff suggests. The prevalence of Opana injection use is rising faster than the prevalence of
injection use overall. We don't have the figures in the table, but it seems inevitable that non-injection use of
Opana must be dropping if overall use is dropping despite a rise in injection use.
All the prevalences are so high that Tennessee will dominate the national figures. My inclination would be to
stick with the point that Tennessee is different from the nation and that the high prevalence in Tennessee and
the dramatic over-representation of Tennessee in the NAVIPPRO data make it necessary to separate out that

Hi, Alec and Jeff,
We asked Inflexxion to do some additional analyses of the NAVIPPRO data in TN. You'll
remember that there were 26 sites participating during the pre-period, but 38 during the
post-period. We asked Inflexxion to do a more detailed look at those sites to see if a change
in the pattern in TN could be associated with a change in the sites. The analysis is
summarized on the attached spreadsheet.
Of the 26 sites that participated in the pre-period, 11 dropped and 15 continued into the
post-period. An additional 23 new sites in TN joined the NAVIPPRO system in the post-period,
providing the total of 38. What appears to be of interest is not so much the sites that joined,
but the sites that dropped. If my interpretation is correct, the 11 sites that dropped were
characterized as
Treating milder patients (lower ASI-MV score)
Using less residential treatment
Treating less patients with prescription opioid abuse
Treating less patients with injection abuse
Treating less patients who injected Opana ER
In other words, the centers that seemed to have treated less ill patients less prone to IV
abuse during the pre-period left the study, leaving behind centers that already were
pre-disposed to treat more severe patients and continued to do so in the post-period.
Thoughts?
Thanx, Neil

Washington Analysis: FDA Update
Ira S. Loss, 2i,5edacted - Privacyj
110Sswashingtonanalysis.corn

Despite an 18 to 8 vote from two advisory committees that the benefits of Endo International's Opana ER®
(oxymorphone hydrochloride) do not continue to outweigh the risks, we do not believe this will result in FDA
attempting to remove the product from the market, irrespective of immediate reports. At least half of the 18 negative
voters specifically urged that the product remain on the market, albeit with revised labeling that could include a Risk
Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) with Elements to Assure Safe Use (ETASU), but that nevertheless does
HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-02479783

 not imply market removal. There is a subset of patients who do not get pain relief from other opioids that need this
product, and we believe the FDA is ultimately like to heed that need, particularly as it falls under new leadership that
focuses on the needs of subcohort patients.
All that being said, a REMS with ETASU would be mandatory, and would limit the doctors that can prescribe the
drug, the pharmacies that sell the drug, and the patients who can receive the drug. It could also be expanded to
include all generic forms of long-acting oxymorphone hydrochloride marketed by Impax Laboratories (IPXL), Sun
Pharma (NSE:SUNPHARMA), Teva Pharmaceuticals' (TEVA) Actavis division, and Mallinckrodt (MNK). There
are indeed far reaching potential implications, but not the worst case scenario of market removal, in our opinon.
The issues of diversion and abuse of this product, which upon reformulation became easier to abuse through
intravenous means and harder to abuse through snorting, was the genesis of this meeting. The post-marketing data are
difficult to interpret due to numerous limitations.
However, from the FDA's perspective, we believe the post-marketing studies under discussion make it difficult to
determine if the increase in intravenous abuse rates are greater than they would have been without reformulation, as
increases had begun prior to the reformulation and rates were similarly high for generic oxymorphone ER during the
post-period among those being assessed for substance abuse treatment.
Beyond that, there was the chemical used to harden the surface of the tablet that was supposed to make it more
difficult to crush. It has been identified as a causal agent in reports of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)
in abusers who injected Opana ERt. TTP causes microscopic blood clots to form in small blood vessels. This
chemical was also tied to 59 cases of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) and 181 cases of HIV in one county in
Indiana where needle sharing was apparently commonplace.

King's Embeda Cleared as Abuse-Resistant Painkiller (Update2)
Share I Email I Print I A A A
By Catherine Larkin
Aug. 13 (Bloomberg) -- King Pharmaceuticals Inc., the drugmaker betting its future on safer painkillers, won U.S.
approval to sell the first pain pill that users may not easily manipulate to get high.
The Food and Drug Administration cleared the extended- release morphine product, Embeda, the agency said today in
an e- mail. Embeda contains a chemical designed to counteract the morphine if the capsule is crushed, chewed or
dissolved in alcohol to get the full dose at once. The company said, and the FDA agreed, the evidence wasn't
conclusive that the chemical truly interfered with the morphine high.
King moves in front of at least five companies that have been racing to develop new painkillers with chemical or
physical features to deter the most common methods of abuse. The approval also justifies the Bristol, Tennesseebased company's $1.3 billion December acquisition of Alpharma, which developed Embeda and submitted it to the
FDA on June 30, 2008, analysts said.
"We've been waiting for this approval for several months - - it's very exciting," said Gary Nachman, an analyst at
Leerink Swann & Co. in New York. "It is the key catalyst for King's stock that investors have been focused on. The FDA
's approval helps validate the whole abuse deterrent category, and King has other products in this area behind
Embeda that it's working on."
King gained 44 cents, or 4.3 percent, to $10.57 at 2:27 p.m. when New York Stock Exchange composite trading was
halted pending news about the company. King has fallen less than 1 percent so far this year, as investors wait for new
products to replace revenue lost when its former top-selling heart pill Altace went generic in late 2007.
Estimated $300 Million
Embeda sales may be $300 million in 2012, said Corey Davis, an analyst at Natixis Bleichroeder in New York, in a
June 24 note to clients. King still awaits an FDA decision on Remoxy, a tamper-resistant pill to compete with closely
held Purdue Pharma LP's OxyContin, and Acurox, a short-acting oxycodone pill that guards against overdose.
Doctors considered extended-release pain drugs such as OxyContin a major breakthrough when they were introduced
in the mid-1990s for cancer and chronic pain. Regulators then realized that teenagers and adults could manipulate the
drugs to get high and they have urged companies to develop tamper-resistant alternatives.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_MA_00075350

 Almost 5 percent of high school seniors say they have used OxyContin, according to the National Institute on Drug
Abuse's 2008 Monitoring the Future Survey. About 5.2 million Americans ages 12 and older misuse prescription
painkillers, according to the latest National Survey on Drug Use and Health.
Extra Ingredient
Embeda capsules contain pellets of long-acting morphine surrounding a sequestered core of naltrexone, an antagonist
used to help wean addicts off opioid painkillers. If taken as directed, the naltrexone passes through the system
without any effect. If the capsules are crushed or chewed, the naltrexone is released to counteract the sense of
euphoria from the morphine, according to the company.

FDA April 16, 2013 OxyContin Decision Media Wrap Up and Analysis

CC:
Sent:
Subject:

Team,
Below, please find a general wrap up and summary of media surrounding yesterday's FDA decision:
The overall tone of the articles addressed the reasons for ADF OxyContin, with concentration on the abuse of the
product, which lines up nicely with our Opana ER with INTAC story. Quotes in the stories were positively biased,
focusing on the decision as a favorable one for societal safety and concurring that FDA made the right decision.
Articles also pointed out the significance of the decision, calling it "a major policy move" and a "landmark decision".
Select Messages from Media Coverage:
...the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has determined that generic non-abuse-resistant
formulation of Purdue Pharma's drug OxyContin (oxycodone HCI) cannot be marketed, citing the drug's
original non-abuse-resistant formulation was withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness.
Specifically, FDA said: because it "poses an increased potential for certain types of abuse," and saying
"the benefits of original OxyContin no longer outweigh its risks"
The agency had concluded that it was enough to show that the new version of OxyContin was safer, in its
abuse resistance, than the original version.
o ....the product has physical and chemical properties that are expected to make abuse via injection
difficult and to reduce abuse via the intranasal route (snorting)." — Regulatory Focus
Select Opana ER or Endo References:
Fierce Pharma: "There is evidence that tamper-resistant versions can keep some addicts from using
them. Citing IMS Health stats, The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that when OxyContin was
reformulated, its sales dropped 7% in the first year while sales of an unreformulated painkiller from Endo
Pharmaceuticals ($ENDP) rose 72%. Then when Endo remade its Opana, the new drug's sales dropped
25%. The patent on Opana ER expired recently."
New York Times: "Along with Purdue Pharma, the manufacturer of another long-acting narcotic painkiller,
Endo Pharmaceuticals, has also petitioned the F.D.A. seeking a similar claim of abuse resistance for a
newer version of one of its drugs, Opana. If that claim proves successful, generic versions of the original
form of Opana would also be barred.
MedPage Today: An FDA spokesperson, however, did not comment on whether the agency would take
action against generic versions of original Opana (oxymorphone), which started shipping in January after
patents on original Opana expired. She said today's action specifically applies to OxyContin alone. Opana
drugmaker Endo Pharmaceuticals had sued the FDA to block generic versions of the drug, but the lawsuit
was dismissed...

We hope this wrap up provides some appreciation of the media's sentiment. Below is a list of links to full articles for
your reference. Please let the team know if you have any questions.
Regards,
Brian

Attached are my comments. A couple of overarching points:
The removal of "generic" from the entire document seems a bit confusing. If you are asking about
the entire oxymorphone ER HCL basket, that makes sense. When you are attempting to delineate
between Opana ER with INTAC and IMPAX or Activas the "generic" is meaningful in front of
oxymorphone ER HCL.
I did not comment on the managed care questions here, but they do seem pretty basic and ones
we should know the answers.
When planning out these research projects, it would be very helpful for me to see objectives and
key business questions we need to answer. That would frame the document as I read through. I
would also like to engage in pharmacy research earlier in the process to help guide the flow of the
dialogue and questions to increase the value to Endo.

My humble opinion: Overall. I am not sure this pharmacy research is necessary as we are continuing to
scrutinize our spend. The key questions around pharmacy behavior should either be captured in
previous waves of research or be institutional knowledge within Managed Markets (Payor and Trade).
Thanks for sharing with me. I am happy to elaborate on my thoughts.

RE: Data on Distribution of Opana ER Sales: Follow-Up from Teleconference to Discuss
TTP Cases with Opana ER

I think there may not be any difference. Certainly, our analysis so far doesn't find any significance difference. Also,
anecdotally, several of the cases with infection continued to have TTP-like illness after the infection resolved and/or UP
was the primary diagnosis and infection was a secondary diagnosis. However, we decided to make the distinction since
many clinicians would exclude the diagnosis of TTP for patients with sepsis or endocarditis. We would exclude patients
with malignancy or malignant HTN or pregnancy.

Best regards, Neil

analysis.
David

I have received information from our marketing analytics department regarding the state distribution of Opana ER
prescriptions that I would like to provide to you. The data consist of the number of prescriptions filled by state for
Opana ER during the third calendar quarter of 2012. However, I just wanted to bring up one potential concern. Endo,
like most companies, considers sales data to be proprietary and confidential. (As a non-pharmaceutical example, think of
the value to Pepsi of territory-by-territory sales data for Coke.) I am required to include the following statement on the
data when I send it:
"Information disclosed herein is proprietary and confidential property of Endo Pharmaceutical Inc. and may not
be disclosed, distributed, or reproduced without the express written permission of Endo Pharmaceuticals Inc."
Thus, for use and analysis within CDC or the Tennessee Department of Health I don't see any problems, but if you were
eventually to publish the information at the level of detail that I have available, there might be an issue on which we

By Brianna Ehley
10/16/2017 12:08 PM EDT
Sen. Joe Manchin (D-W.Va.) is urging President Donald Trump withdraw his nomination of Rep. Torn Marino as
the White House's "drug czar" following media reports that his legislation has effectively weakened the DEA's
oversight of opioid manufacturers and distributors.
A Washington Post/"60 Minutes" investigation published Sunday found that a 2016 law Marino sponsored has
made it harder for the DEA to bring enforcement actions against drug distributors accused of spilling prescription
pain pills outside the legal distribution chain.
The law's language requires the DEA to show that a driigmakers' actions posed a "substantial likelihood of an
immediate threat" of harm, drug abuse or death before the agency could take some actions. Officials at the DEA
and Justice Department told the Post and "60 Minutes" that the new standard makes it nearly impossible for the
agency to stop suspicious shipments.
In a letter to Trump, Manchin says the reports make Marino unfit to lead the White House office tasked with
combating the opioid crisis.
"The legislation that Congressman Marino pushed has tied the hands of the DEA in their efforts to enforce our
nation's laws and ensure that these wholesalers and other industry actors alert authorities to these suspicious
orders instead of simply profiting from them," wrote Manchin, whose home state has the highest drug overdose
death rate in the country. "His advocacy for this legislation demonstrates that Congressman Marino either does
not fully understand the scope and devastation of this epidemic or ties to industry overrode those concerns."
Sen. Claire McCaskill (D-Mo.) today plans to introduce a bill to repeal the 2016 law.

DEA blocks Sanford CVS stores from selling controlled substances
By Amy Pavuk, Orlando Sentinel
7:22 PM EST, February 6, 2012
advertisement
In a measure thought to be the first of its kind against a national retail pharmacy chain, the U.S. Drug
Enforcement Administration has banned two Central Florida CVS stores from selling controlled substances.
Calling the pharmacies an "imminent danger" to the public, DEA served the CVS/pharmacy on Orlando Drive
in Sanford and the other on West First Street in Sanford — stores agents raided on Saturday — with immediate
suspension orders last week.
The actions against the CVS stores were made at roughly the same time that DEA issued a suspension order
against Cardinal Health, one of the nation's largest prescription-drug wholesale distributors with a facility in
Lakeland.
DEA wanted to prevent Cardinal Health from shipping certain drugs — such as the powerful and addictive
painkiller oxycodone — but those efforts were blocked by a federal judge Friday.
Mark Trouville, special agent in charge of DEA's Miami field division, said the actions taken against the two
CVS pharmacies and Cardinal Health are part of the agency's efforts to combat Florida's prescription-drug
epidemic.
Though DEA agents have investigated and taken similar action against locally owned pharmacies, this is
thought to be the first time that a major retailer has been targeted in such a manner.

1

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06826470

 CVS/pharmacy spokesman Michael DeAngelis did not comment on DEA's announcement Monday and instead
referred to a statement he released Saturday, which said the company is "disappointed that the DEA has taken
administrative action to prohibit two CVS/pharmacy stores in Florida from dispensing controlled substances."
An administrative hearing will be held to determine whether DEA's certificates for the two CVS stores and
Cardinal Health will be permanently revoked.
Meanwhile, a hearing will be held Feb. 13 in federal court in the case against Cardinal Health.
In a statement released Monday, Cardinal Health said company officials "strongly disagree with the allegations
the DEA has made against our Lakeland facility and are vigorously challenging this action in court."
Sanford CVS was top customer
Calling the CVS suspension orders a "wake-up call," DEA's Trouville noted that roughly seven people die each
day in Florida because of prescription-drug overdoses.
"People need to be held accountable for their actions," he said.
The average pharmacy in the United States ordered about 69,000 oxycodone pills last year. The two Sanford
pharmacies, located about five miles apart, ordered more than 3 million pills during the same time, DEA said.
And those two CVS stores are among Cardinal Health's top customers, court documents show.
Cardinal Health, which distributes drugs to more than 2,500 pharmacies in the Southeast, paid a $34 million
civil fine to DEA in September 2008 for failing to report suspicious orders. As part of the settlement, Cardinal
Health agreed to maintain a compliance program designed to detect and prevent illegal drug use.
According to court documents filed by Cardinal Health on Friday in an attempt to contest the DEA suspension
order, federal authorities alleged that four of Cardinal Health's pharmacy customers — including the two in
Sanford — have distributed oxycodone for illegitimate purposes.
The CVS on Orlando Drive is Cardinal Health's top customer, according to DEA documents filed in the
Cardinal case. From January 2008 through December 2011, Cardinal sold more than 5 million dosages of
oxycodone to the pharmacy.
In challenging the DEA order, Cardinal Health maintained it has a "vigorous and robust anti-diversion system,"
and that the company monitored and investigated orders placed by the CVS pharmacies. The company "formed
reasonable conclusions that continued sales to them were appropriate."
"Any diversion of oxycodone by these pharmacies cannot be attributed to a lack of diligence by Cardinal
Health," the company argued.
When Cardinal Health — which also supplies to hospitals, nursing homes and urgent-care centers — identified
potentially unusual oxycodone-ordering patterns in the fall of 2010 at the Sanford CVS stores, it asked the
pharmacy company to investigate the orders, according to the court documents.
On Friday, a judge blocked DEA's order and granted Cardinal Health a temporary restraining order against the
federal agency. On Monday, the prescription-drug distributor defended its practices.

2

 "We are committed to helping fight prescription drug abuse and doing our part as a responsible participant in
the drug supply chain," Cardinal Health said in a statement released Monday. "We want to ensure legitimate
patients receive critical medicines without interruption, while at the same time helping to prevent those
medicines from falling in the wrong hands."

Texas to get part of $34 million fine from drug distributor
By RUTH RENDON
Cardinal Health Inc., a pharmaceutical drug distributor with offices in
Houston, has agreed to pay $34 million in civil penalties for its
handling of distributing the painkiller hydrocodone, the U.S.
Department of Justice announced this morning.
part of the settlement, the Southern District of Texas, which
includes Houston, will collect $8 million. Nearly half of the penalty,
$16 million, will go to the Middle District of Florida. Five other U.S.
Attorney's Offices will also collect penalties.

Cardinal Health, which operates 27 distribution facilities, failed to
report to to the Drug Enforcement Administration suspicious orders of
hydrocodone that it then distributed to pharmacies that filled
illegitimate prescriptions originating from rogue Internet pharmacy Web
sites, federal authorities said.
Representatives of Dublin, Ohio-based Cardinal Health could not be
reached for comment this morning.
Cardinal's conduct allowed the "diversion" of millions of dosage units

 of hydrocodone from legitimate to non-legitimate channels, federal
authorities said. DEA regulations require all manufacturers and

more specifically, to "design and operate a system to disclose to the

Date:

Wednesday, June 27 2012 01:34 PM

Subject:

W.Va. AG sues 14 pain drug distributors

From:

Becker, Geoffrey

To:

Phipps, Candice <Phipps.Candice@endo.com >;

CC:

Thomas, Greg <Thomas.Greg@endo.com>; Byrne, Timothy <Byrne.Timothy@endo.com >;

Attachments: image002.png
I didn't know if you sawthis news...

Updated 03:08 p.m., Tuesday, June 26, 2012
CHARLESTON, W.Va. (AP) — West Virginia Attorney General Darrell McGraw announced lawsuits Tuesday against 14 pharmaceutical
drug distributors, alleging their negligent practices have helped fuel the state's pain pill abuse epidemic.
The complaints in Boone County Circuit Court seek to ensure the companies halt all shipments to West Virginia state that aren't for
legitimate medical purposes. They also ask a judge to require that they flag suspicious drug orders to the state Board of Pharmacy.
The lawsuits also request a court-ordered program to monitor the health of prescription drug users, alleging the negligence has exposed
these people to addiction and misuse. Alleging various consumer protection and antitrust violations as well, the filings seek damage
awards to compensate West Virginia for costs to its health and public safety systems from prescription drug abuse, overdoses and related
crimes.
West Virginia suffers the nation's highest drug overdose death rate, with most of those cases involving prescription drugs, the lawsuits
note. Fatal prescription drug-related overdoses quadrupled between 2001 and 2008 in West Virginia to 21.5 deaths per 100,000 residents,
the filings said. Ongoing federal probes centered on southern West Virginia have shut down suspected "pill mills" that unlawfully provide
pain drugs or prescriptions, and have led to the criminal convictions of physicians, pharmacists and their staffers.
"Prescription drug abuse costs West Virginians over $430 million a year, devastates families, and hangs enormous burdens on our
hospitals, courts, law enforcement, and communities," McGrawsaid in a Tuesday statement. "With today's filing, we are seeking to make
major drug distributors that have substantially (benefited) from prescription drug abuse accept responsibility and pay for their illicit
actions."
A spokesman for the parent company of one defendant, Anda Inc. of Florida, said it does not comment on pending lawsuits but that it seeks
to avoid the sort of practices alleged by McGraw.
The official, Charlie Mayr of Watson Pharmaceuticals, said the company's safeguards include sophisticated monitoring that allows the
company to halt and investigate suspicious ordering patterns. The company also doesn't ship directly to physician offices or to clinics or
other places labeled "pill mills" by authorities.
Mayr also noted statistics suggesting that more than 70 percent of young pain pill abusers obtain their drugs through friends and relatives,
at least sometimes through theft. Both state and federal officials in West Virginia sponsor events to allow people to hand in unused
prescription drugs so they can be safely destroyed.
"We do recognize this and we do everything in our power to avoid the diversion of these products," Mayr said, adding that the industry takes
a similar position.
The other defendant companies did not respond to requests for comment Tuesday. At least two were recently targeted by the U.S. Drug
Enforcement Administration for their distribution practices.
A Florida facility of defendant Cardinal Health Inc. of Ohio cannot ship controlled substances for two years as part of a settlement reached
last month after the DEA alleged it distributed amounts of the powerful pain drug oxycodone far in excess oflegitimate medical needs.
The company earlier paid $34 million after DEA cited that same Lakeland, Fla., facility for allegedly failing to flag suspicious orders for
hydrocodone, the main ingredient in painkillers like Vicodin. Cardinal Health is the sole defendant in one of McGraw's lawsuits.
The DEA also barred defendant Harvard Drug Group of Michigan from distributing oxycodone in 2010, alleging the company should have
known that some Florida customers in were trafficking in painkillers. The federal agency relented on a proposed ban ofless-potent
painkillers such as hydrocodone supplied bythat company.
McGraw's lawsuits allege the 14 companies have contributed to an abuse epidemic that has Charleston Area Medical Center reporting that
narcotic abuse plays a role in the injuries of 20 percent of its hospital trauma patients. The filings also cited how the Mingo County town of
Kermit, with 300 residents, has a pharmacy that received 3.1million dosage units of hydrocodone in 2006.

Press Release
DEA Serves Order To Show Cause to Three Walgreens Pharmacies

NOV 28 — (MIAMI, FL) — Mark R. Trouville, Special Agent in Charge of the Miami Field Division, Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA),
announced today the issuance of Orders to Show Cause (OSC) to three Walgreens Florida pharmacies: Walgreens #04727 located at
4950 S. US Highway 1, Fort Piece, FL; Walgreens #03629 located at 12028 Majestic Boulevard, Hudson, FL; and Walgreens #06997
located at 785 Lockwood Boulevard, Oviedo, FL (hereafter "Registrants"). An OSC is served as a notice to a DEA registrant to provide it an
opportunity to show cause as to why the DEA should not revoke its DEA registration because its registration is deemed inconsistent with the
public interest. These administrative actions do not immediately suspend a registrant's ability to handle or distribute under its current DEA
registration medications containing controlled substances such as oxycodone, hydrocodone or others listed in Schedules II — V.
"The diversion of pharmaceutical controlled substances continues to be a great concern for the DEA," Trouville said. "A DEA registration is
a privilege and not a license for bad behavior. These Registrants have a responsibility to their customers, as well as to the community, to
be an advocate against prescription drug abuse that has plagued Florida since 2009, and not contribute to the epidemic. The Miami Field
Division will continue to work with our local and state partners to assure that all prescription drugs are getting into the hands of legitimate
patients for legitimate medical needs."
On April 4, 2012, the DEA Miami Diversion Office served an Administrative Inspection Warrant (AIW) on the Registrants, as well as on three
other Walgreens pharmacies in Florida and its Walgreens Distribution Center in Jupiter. The AIW at the Walgreens Distribution Center was
served to determine if the distribution center maintained a system in place that detects and reports suspicious orders to the DEA and to
prevent the diversion of control substances as governed by federal laws and the Control Substance Act relating to the proper distribution of
control substances. The AIWs served at the six Walgreens retail pharmacies were done so to determine if the pharmacies were dispensing
prescriptions issued for legitimate medical purposes and in the course of professional practice.
On September 14, 2012, the Walgreens Distribution Center was served an Immediate Suspension of Registration. An administrative
hearing is scheduled to begin on that matter on January 7, 2013, in Washington, DC.
These actions are part of the DEA Miami Field Division's continuing efforts to combat the state's prescription drug abuse epidemic and its
role as a major source to other states of diverted pharmaceutical drugs. On average, seven people die every day in Florida due to
prescription drug abuse, according to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. The efforts in recent years have gone beyond arrests
and criminal actions against Florida doctors, pain clinic personnel, and individually owned pharmacies that operated outside the scope of
legitimate medical purposes. The DEA has utilized numerous resources to educate and work with its registrants and the public to battle this

FYI...

UPDATE 2-US judge allows DEA to suspend
Cardinal license
Wed Feb 29, 2012 7:04pm EST

* DEA wins a round in prescription drug abuse battle
* Cardinal says it already cut off pharmacy supplies
* Appeals decision on Florida license to appeals court
* DEA judge due to begin hearings April 3
By Toni Clarke and Anna Yukhananov
Feb 29 (Reuters) - A federal judge allowed the government to suspend Cardinal Health Inc's license to distribute
potentially addictive drugs from a Florida facility, part of the Drug Enforcement Administration's battle against
prescription drug abuse.
The ruling on Wednesday was an initial victory for government efforts to force drug wholesalers to play a bigger role
in fighting drug abuse, and may crimp Cardinal's business for the next 12 months.
Judge Reggie Walton of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia had previously given Cardinal a temporary
restraining order to block the suspension of the Lakeland facility, which serves about 2,700 drug stores or hospitals,
while it pleads its case to a judge within the DEA.
Cardinal said it was appealing Wednesday's decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.
"We want to be part of a new, more effective solution to stop prescription drug abuse, without disrupting legitimate
use," the company said in a statement.
The DEA ordered the current suspension on Feb. 3, saying Cardinal knew, or should have known, that four of its
customers, including two CVS Caremark Corp pharmacies, were inappropriately filling prescriptions for the painkiller
oxycodone.
Cardinal, one of the country's largest drug distributors, said it had already cut off supplies to two of the pharmacies
before the DEA's suspension order. It cut supplies to the remaining two pharmacies as soon as the DEA issued its
order.
Walton said on Wednesday that after getting more information from the DEA, he agreed with the decision to suspend
Cardinal's license.
"I think DEA is correct that companies have an obligation to police themselves... and to be proactive in assessing
whether diversion (of controlled substances) is taking place," Walton said during a court hearing.
Morningstar analyst Matthew Coffina said Walton's ruling could cause Cardinal to lose some market share, at least in
the short run, to competitors such as McKesson Corp and AmerisourceBergen Corp.
Coffina said it is also likely to force all distributors to invest more money in policing the pharmacies they serve.
"It's a negative for the distributors more broadly to the extent that they are going to be held accountable for the
actions of pharmacies," he said.
Shares of Cardinal closed 1.3 percent lower, while McKesson gained 1.2 percent and AmerisourceBergen slipped 0.9

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_PA_00211473

 percent.
The judge said he did not believe Cardinal would suffer 'irreparable harm' because of the suspension, as it had
recovered its business after a previous suspension of Lakeland in 2007.
An administrative hearing of Cardinal's Lakeland license is scheduled to begin at the DEA on April 3. That process
could take as long as a year to play out as both sides present their cases.
The DEA judge will then make a recommendation to the DEA's administrator, Michele Leonhart, who will make a ruling.
Leonhart signed the initial order to suspend Cardinal's license.
FIGHTING ABUSE
The case comes as prescription drug abuse has surged in the United States, eclipsing the abuse of most illicit drugs,
including heroin and cocaine.
Distributors such as Cardinal argue they are unfairly targeted because it is easier for the DEA to attack a distributor
than the thousands of doctors who write the prescriptions.
"DEA does not regulate the practice of medicine. And if anything, a wholesaler is in even less of a position to do so,"
said Randolph Moss, the attorney arguing on behalf of Cardinal.
"It doesn't regulate doctors, and it doesn't regulate patients," he said, adding that the company was doing its best to
prevent prescription drug abuse.
For its part, the DEA argues distributors have an obligation to ensure none of the controlled drugs that go out their
doors land in the wrong hands.
"Cardinal ... is facilitating diversion when it does not take adequate measures to prevent diversion," said Lee
Reeves, an attorney with the U.S. Department of Justice, who argued on behalf of the DEA.
Every entity that handles controlled narcotics, from physician to pharmacy to manufacturer, must register with the
DEA and the agency says each entity must monitor the next.
The DEA said distributors are required to design systems that detect suspicious orders, and Cardinal failed to do so.
Cardinal says it took significant steps to rebuild its systems and hire new personnel after DEA suspended the license
at the same Lakeland facility in 2007.
It also argues there is no "imminent danger" to the public as the affected pharmacies are no longer allowed to
dispense controlled drugs.
The case is Cardinal Health Inc. V. Holder, U.S. District Court, District of Columbia, No. 12-185.

From: Hernandez, Tracey

To: Propst, Charles V. (Trey); Cupero, Phil
Subject: CII orders handled by Memphis
Trey/PhilI may not be able to attend Monday's distribution meeting since I'll be flying to Boca. However, I wanted you both to
have my concerns related to the idea of outsourcing CII distribution to UPS. This will really create some challenges,
both from a regulatory and a customer service perspective. For example:
Customers would need to place orders for CII products separately from all other products. CII orders would
have to be made using Memphis' DEA number since they would ship from there. All other controlled products
would need to be made using Qualitest's DEA number. If a customer made a mistake and used the wrong
DEA number, the order would not be able to be filled until the correct paperwork is received.
CII products would fall under UPS' suspicious order monitoring program. As part of the upgrade to our own
program, we reviewed UPS' program. It is extremely basic. They have no capability to know our customers'
customers as they have no chargeback data and they currently do not perform customer due diligence visits. If
they were to implement this, have we factored in the cost of them doing our chargebacks or the additional
audits? Do we really want UPS auditing our customers?
We would still need to conduct due diligence visits for CIII-V customers so we would again be duplicating
efforts.
With cargo thefts on the increase, do we really want our most desirable products under control by a 3rd party?
They would have to file the paperwork with DEA if a theft/loss occurs and they would be the point of contact
with DEA since it would be their license. What is UPS' experience in shipping large quantities of CII products?
UPS was recently fined heavily by DEA; how will DEA perceive our giving them additional business at this
stage?
What will we do with the vault at our DC in Huntsville? It will be costly to destroy it due to the
construction/concrete walls w/steel reinforcements. If we don't utilize, it's a lot of wasted space.
Have we looked at the duplication — two entities checking customer DEA licenses for example? Is that cost
effective? Two separate places for damages or customer returns?
DEA may require that we modify our DEA license for Distribution; they do not like you to maintain a schedule
on your license if you are not actively utilizing it.
If we are seeking to minimize risk, why would we utilize a distribution location so close to Huntsville?
UPS does not weigh each shipper once it comes from the manufacturing site like our Qualitest DC does. This
effort allows us to discover around 50-75 count discrepancies before the shipper gets to the customer level.
The number of customer complaints and shortages that need to be reported to DEA will increase.
This effort appears to be of interest as it reduces storage cost for brand products by spreading the expense
across all businesses. Based on the volume of product Qualitest has versus the Brand, this does not truly
appear to be cost effective when all factors are considered (transportation, storage, additional personnel
needed at UPS, additional regulatory risk, duplication of efforts, inconvenience to customers, etc.). I would
think that there are better options to pursue.
Lastly, we were told that we must allow the Brand team to develop their own suspicious order monitoring
program, rather than help them by incorporating the shipments into Qualitest's program. This was conveyed by
Margaret and was due to the Corporate Integrity Agreement that they are under. Why would mixing distribution
be any different?
Hope this helps!

Reminder: DSCSA Annual Licensure Reporting by Prescription
Drug Wholesale Distributors Due Today
HDMA distributor members are reminded that the draft guidance implementing state licensure
reporting provisions of the Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA), calls for wholesale distributor
licensure reporting to be completed by Tuesday, March 31. Further information can be found in the
Federal Register published on December 9, 2014 and in the draft guidance "DSCSA
Implementation: Annual Reporting by Prescription Drug Wholesale Distributors and Third-Party
Logistics Providers." Additionally, FDA's webpage for wholesale distributors and third-party

HDMA Publishes Version 2.0 of HDMA Qs and As for the Drug
Supply Chain Security Act
HDMA has released Version 2.0 of the HDMA Qs and As on the Druq Supply Chain Security Act
(DSCSA). The latest update provides changes based on the FDA guidance "DSCSA
Implementation: Product Tracing Requirements — Compliance Policy" released on
December 31, 2014. The latest version also includes new questions addressing Advance Ship
Notices (ASNs) and additional frequently asked questions that HDMA has received.
Some of the questions included in the Qs and As are:
Q: Can you use more than one YNQ segment in the ASN to provide the transaction statement?
A: HDMA recommends that trading partners use one YNQ segment for the TS.
Q: Are items distributed for emergency medical reasons subject to TI/TH/TS requirements?
A: The distribution of product for emergency medical reasons (which does not include a drug
shortage) is exempt from the definition of "transaction" (§ 581(24)(B)(iii)), and thus exempt from
the requirements to pass TI/TH/TS.
For more information, contact Allison Tuszynski.
