Congressional Hearing on State and Local Perspectives on
Prescription Drug Abuse and Heroin Abuse
The House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations held a hearing
on March 26 entitled "Examining the Growing Problems of Prescription Drug and Heroin Abuse:
State and Local Perspectives." The hearing focused on local and state efforts to combat drug
abuse and addiction and included testimony from a number of witnesses from academia, hospitals
and police departments, among others.Further details, including witness testimonies and a video
of the hearing, is available on the committee website.
For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

Medical Device Tax Repeal Introduced

ENDO_TXMDL_00512793

 Senator Ed Markey (D-Mass.) introduced legislation to repeal the medical device tax (S.844). The
legislation would be paid for by a repeal of LIFO for major oil and gas companies and would require
the companies to pay royalties to drill offshore in the Gulf of Mexico. The bill was referred to the
Senate Committee on Finance.
For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

GAO Releases Updated Report on 340B
On March 24, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) released a report entitled, "Drug
Discount Program: Status of GAO Recommendations to Improve 340B Drug Pricing Program
Oversight, GAO-15-455T." The release is an update of a 2011 report on the Health Resources and
Services Administration's (HRSA) oversight practices on the 340B Program. The report is
available on the GAO website.
For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

Virginia Governor Signs Suspicious Orders Legislation
Virginia Governor McAuliffe signed into law HB 1736 on March 17, 2015. The bill requires
wholesale distributors to report to the Virginia Board of Pharmacy when it has ceased distribution
of Schedules II through V drugs to a customer based on suspicious orders. Wholesale distributors
have five days to report the cessation to the Board.
The language was originally introduced at a Va. Board of Pharmacy meeting and approved by the
board members. HDMA provided input during that meeting and continued conversations with the
board on making changes to the language. As the bill moved to the Legislature, HDMA worked
with other interested stakeholders, including the pharmacists and retailers, to improve upon and
secure amended language for the final bill.
The law will go into effect on July 1, 2015.
For more information, contact Devin Boerm.

Download the Revised HDMA Standard Pharmaceutical Product
Form
HDMA members are reminded that the Association's Standard Rx Product Information Form,
revised to support implementation of the DSCSA, may be downloaded from the HDMA website.
The form contains a series of questions about new products; although not all information on the
form is required by each distributor trading partner, it represents the most frequently requested
data points by a majority of HDMA members for item setup.
For questions about specific data fields, check with your trading partners for their requirements.
HDMA does not receive copies of these forms or store any product information.
Download the form and instructions. For more information, contact Marione DePuy.

Legal and Regulatory Guide to EU's New Pharmacovigilance Regulations, Tuesday, March
20, 2012 • 11:00 a.m. - 12:30 p.m. — On July 2, 2012, the European pharmaceutical industry will
change forever. The EU has published what was been described as the largest transformation
covering pharmacovigilance in more than a decade. If you're a marketing authorization holder (MAH)
you'll need to comply. Will you be ready? Register today.
In this issue...
• FDA Touts PDUFA IV Successes as Reauthorization Hearings Continue
• Sandoz's Canadian Plant Stops Work to Correct Duality Control Issues
• Final Guidance Lays Out Bead Size Requirements for Sprinkled Drugs
• Drug World Daily
• Pharma Blo_g Watch

FDA Touts PDUFA IV Successes as Reauthorization Hearings Continue
As Congress gears up to tackle reauthorization of the Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA), the FDA
continues to tout its performance goal record as the current five-year plan draws to a close. A new
agency report outlines 2011 PDUFA reviews, showing the FDA met all but one of its target dates for
NMEs approved last year. It expects average approval times for NMEs in 2011 to fall around 10
months, which is on par with 2010 and continues a trend the FDA has seen since 2002.
Druq Industry Daily
Sandoz's Canadian Plant Stops Work to Correct Quality Control Issues
Three months after the FDA flagged three manufacturing plants operated by Sandoz for quality control
issues, the Novartis subsidiary has temporarily suspended generic-drug production and discontinued
some products at its Boucherville, Quebec, facility to address the agency's concerns. In a recent pair
of letters to customers, Sandoz Canada President and General Manager Michel Robidoux said
remediation at Boucherville is affecting all production processes, significantly reducing the plant's
output, and is likely to result in temporary supply disruptions.
Generic Line
Final Guidance Lays Out Bead Size Requirements for Sprinkled Drugs
The FDA has set a target and maximum "bead size" for drug products that are administered via
sprinkling onto food, according to a final guidance. The agency recommends a target bead size of up
to 2.5 mm with no more than 10 percent variation over this size, to a maximum size of 2.8 mm, the
Feb. 29 guidance states.
Washington Drug Letter

Analysis are key to providing quality practices within the clinical research process. A solid CAPA
system will not only identify problem trends, but help drive the highest quality of research. Learn
how. Download today.

FDA Import Holds addresses your specific concerns about PREDICT and the new FDA import
processes. Why expose your company to unnecessary holds, impoundments, warning letters — or
worse? This management report tells you what to do to get your imported products through
customs as quickly as possible. Order today.

Cheng Yi Liang, a former FDA chemist from Gaithersburg, Md., was sentenced to 60 months in prison
for engaging in insider trading on multiple occasions based on material, non-public information he
obtained in his capacity as an FDA scientist.
Here Is The City
DC Circuit Lifts Shipping Ban on Cardinal Health
The DC Circuit has lifted the ban blocking Cardinal Health prescription drug shipments brought on by
allegations it filled suspicious orders for oxycodone, and on Monday gave the U.S. Department of
Justice until week's end to oppose the company's emergency injunction request.
Law360
Qnasltm Phase III Data Indicate Investigational Therapy With New Mode of Delivery Has
Positive Safety and Efficacy Profile
Teva Pharmaceutical announced positive findings from four Phase III clinical studies that examined the
efficacy and safety profile as well as impact on quality of life of Qnasltm (beclomethasone
dipropionate) nasal aerosol.
Sun Herald
Merck Says Tablet Reduces Ragweed Symptoms
Merck said results from a Phase III clinical study showed its investigational allergy immunotherapy
tablet reduced ragweed allergy symptoms in adults.
The Wall Street Journal
Experts Seek Alternatives to Excluding Drug Companies
Katrice Bridges Copeland used to defend pharmaceutical company executives when their companies
were accused of fraud. But when she saw that Pfizer, after being accused of fraud, had entered a third
corporate integrity agreement with the government and paid $2.3 billion in fines to avoid being
excluded from doing business with Medicare, Copeland said she was infuriated.
USA Today
Mylan Brovana Patent Trial Against Sunovion Set for May 21
Mylan's patent infringement trial against Sunovion Pharmaceuticals over the bronchitis and
emphysema drug Brovana is set for May 21. U.S. District Judge John Koeltl set the date at a hearing in
Manhattan, saying he would also refer the case to a magistrate judge for settlement talks.

Contributing to the Dumbing Down of Healthcare (Drug Wonks Blog)
"I shouldn't have to waste my time writing a response to Ezra Klein's latest blog about the high cost of
medical procedures in the U.S. compared to other countries," blogger Peter Pitts writes. "I won't waste
yours by summarizing it either." Pitts describes Klein's comparisons as a "textbook case of how most

of the "higher cost" they pay that U.S. patients do not.

From: Moody, David

Geoffrey; Munroe, Brian; Fisk, Brent; Bush, Elizabeth

Subject: A New Painkiller Crackdown Targets Drug Distributors
From today's NY Times — Dave

A New Painkiller Crackdown Targets Drug Distributors

Patiaitich's phariii,.

in New ort Beach,

a big portion of its painkiller supplies after a federal crackdown.

BARRY MEIER

A local druggist in Newport Beach, Calif., never expected that the federal government's recent
crackdown on distributors of prescription painkillers would ensnare him.
But in June, Cardinal Health, a major distributor, abruptly cut off his supplies of narcotics like
OxyContin and Percocet. A few months earlier, the Drug Enforcement Administration had accused
1

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_FLAG-00529296

 Cardinal of ignoring signs that some pharmacies in Florida that it supplied with such drugs might be
feeding street demand for them.
Cardinal told the druggist, Michael Pavlovich, that the volume of pain drugs and other controlled
medications he was dispensing was too high, a situation he said was explainable. His pharmacy
specializes in pain patients, he said. Still, it took weeks for Cardinal to start supplying him again, and
even then, it limited its shipments to about 15 percent of his previous orders. As a result, Mr. Pavlovich
said, many of his patients had to go elsewhere to get prescriptions filled.
"We have to convince them that our dispensing is legitimate," he said of his dealings with Cardinal.
Cardinal's crackdown on Mr. Pavlovich was a sign of a new approach by the D.E.A. to stem the growing
misuse and abuse of painkillers. In the last decade, the agency has tried a variety of tactics with limited
success, from arresting hundreds of doctors to closing scores of pharmacies. Now, it and other agencies
are moving up the pharmaceutical food chain, putting pressure on distributors like Cardinal, which act
as middlemen between drug makers and the pharmacies and doctors that dispense painkillers.
In response, the distributors are scrambling to limit their liability by more closely monitoring their
distribution pipelines and cutting off some customers.
Since January, for example, Cardinal has cut ties with a dozen pharmacies in states including Arizona,
California, Nevada and Oklahoma, interviews and court records show. In doing so, the wholesaler,
which is based in Columbus, Ohio, cited audits suggesting that people seeking to buy prescription drugs
illegally might have targeted the store in question.
Several of the affected drugstores sued Cardinal unsuccessfully to resume supplies, but documents filed
in those actions show that until recently, the wholesaler shipped large volumes of pain pills to the stores
for months, if not years.
George S. Barrett, Cardinal's chairman and chief executive, said the company had tightened the criteria
it used in determining whether to sell narcotics to a pharmacy. In May, Cardinal settled the action
brought by the D.E.A. in connection with its Florida sales by agreeing to suspend shipments of
controlled drugs, like narcotics, from a facility in that state for two years. It could also face a significant
fine.
"We had a strong antidiversion system in place, but no system is perfect," Mr. Barrett said. Among
other steps, the company said it had created a special committee to regularly evaluate pharmacies that
order high volumes of narcotic drugs.
Another major distributor, AmerisourceBergen, recently disclosed that it faces a federal criminal
inquiry into its oversight of painkiller sales. And in June, West Virginia officials filed a lawsuit against
14 drug distributors, including Cardinal and AmerisourceBergen, charging that they had fed illicit
painkiller use in that state. The companies have denied wrongdoing.
2

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_FLAG-00529297

 D.E.A. officials have heralded the Cardinal action as the forerunner of a more aggressive approach to
the painkiller problem. But critics say that for years, the agency did little to scrutinize distributors who
were making tens of millions of dollars from the prescriptions generated by pain clinics in Florida, Ohio
and other states. These facilities, often described as "pill mills," employed doctors who wrote narcotics
prescriptions after cursory examinations of patients.
"In the case of West Virginia, they have done nothing," said a lawyer in Charleston, James M. Cagle,
who is working on the state's action against distributors.
The drug distribution system is a sprawling one that involves about 800 companies, which range in size
from a few giants like Cardinal to hundreds of small firms. For wholesalers, the markup on medications
can be small, sometimes a few pennies a pill. But with billions of pills sold annually, the profits can be
big. Narcotic painkillers are now the most widely prescribed drugs in the United States, with sales last
year of $8.5 billion.
This is not the first time the industry has faced scrutiny. In 2008, Cardinal paid $34 million to settle
charges that it failed to alert the D.E.A. to suspicious orders for millions of pain pills that it was
shipping to Internet pharmacies — operations that for years supplied the illicit market. The same year,
another big distributor, McKesson, paid $13 million to settle similar charges. As part of the agreements,
both companies denied wrongdoing.
Executives like Mr. Barrett of Cardinal say that it is often difficult for a distributor to tell whether a
pharmacy or a doctor is serving legitimate pain patients or supplying illicit drug demand. And
distributors have long complained that the D.E.A. has never issued specific guidelines for when they
should stop shipping to a customer.
But agency officials say that wholesalers know about the red flags. For example, the agency charged that
Cardinal was selling 5o times the amount of pain pills containing the narcotic oxycodone, the active
ingredient in OxyContin and other drugs, to its four top pharmacy customers in Florida than it was
supplying to the average drugstore in that state.
Cardinal failed to scrutinize such sales, the agency said, even violating the safeguards it promised to put
in place when it agreed to settle the government charges in connection with its supplying of Internet
pharmacies. "Everyone is making a large amount of money on these drugs," said Joseph T. Rannazzisi,
a deputy assistant administrator of the D.E.A. division that oversees legal drugs, like painkillers.
The D.E.A. is able to track where painkillers are going because distributors regularly file reports
detailing their shipments to customers. But just how aggressively the agency uses that data is anyone's
guess.
An agency employee, Michelle Cooper, testified last year that she had attended a training session at
which instructors described how investigators like her could use the database to identify suspicious
3

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_FLAG-00529298

 distributors. In doing so, they pointed to data showing that a distributor had suddenly started shipping
large and growing volumes of pain pills to Florida drugstores.
It was only later that Ms. Cooper discovered that the case involved a real distributor, not a hypothetical
one, and that the company was still making those shipments despite the agency's apparent awareness of
them.
"I didn't believe the numbers they were showing us were real," she said. "I thought it was for training
purposes."
Ms. Cooper subsequently investigated the company, Keysource Medical, which agreed last year to give
up its license to distribute narcotic drugs.
Faced with Congressional pressure, agency officials like Mr. Rannazzisi have said that they are
increasing the ranks of investigators like Ms. Cooper, and that they provide distribution data to state
officials when local authorities request it as part of an investigation.
But state officials say it would be more helpful to get that data routinely so they can act more quickly
against rogue clinics and pharmacies. For years, Ohio law enforcement authorities did not know which
distributors were supplying the many pill mills operating in the state, one official said. If the D.E.A. had
supplied that information, "we would have known about the number of shipments going into Ohio and
where they were going," said Aaron Haslam, an assistant state attorney general.
Also, while the D.E.A. brings actions against distributors like Cardinal for failing to notify the agency of
a "suspicious order" from a pharmacy or other customer, it does not share those reports with officials in
the state where the pharmacy is based.
In response to a request from The New York Times, the agency even declined to disclose the number of
such reports it received annually. A spokeswoman, Barbara Carreno, said in a statement that the agency
considered such statistics "law enforcement sensitive" information, but she did not elaborate.
The Times has filed a Freedom of Information Act request seeking that data.

Moodv.clovidaendo.corn

Trey/PhilI may not be able to attend Monday's distribution meeting since I'll be flying to Boca. However, I wanted you both to have my

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_ANK_CHI_0953654

 concerns related to the idea of outsourcing CII distribution to UPS. This will really create some challenges, both from a
regulatory and a customer service perspective. For example:
• Customers would need to place orders for CII products separately from all other products. CII orders would have
to be made using Memphis' DEA number since they would ship from there. All other controlled products would need
to be made using Qualitest's DEA number. If a customer made a mistake and used the wrong DEA number, the order
would not be able to be filled until the correct paperwork is received.
All customers send in CII orders separately from other products. Endo EDI currently handles all CSOS Orders for
Brands and Generics so there is no change to our customers.

Redacted - Trade Secret
All CII orders for broth Brands and Generic will come into SAP and fall under the SAP SOM Program. Qtest will have
the same opportunity as they do today to review and release orders before they are sent to the warehouse.
Chargeback data still comes into play. All Order to Cash functions will still be in SAP.
• We would still need to conduct due diligence visits for CIII-V customers so we would again be duplicating efforts.
Qtest still own the Getting to know you customer audits.
• With cargo thefts on the increase, do we really want our most desirable products under control by a 3rd party?
They would have to file the paperwork with DEA if a theft/loss occurs and they would be the point of contact with DEA
since it would be their license. What is UPS' experience in shipping large quantities of CH products?
UPS has handled all of Endo CII products since 2000 and this included the shipment of large Controlled products when
the Generic were under the Brand Company. UPS has a very extensive HV/HR program for ALL shipments, not just
CI Is. UPS's clients included other large generic companies that have high volume of CII products.
• UPS was recently fined heavily by DEA; how will DEA perceive our giving them additional business at this stage?
Tracey needs to provide information on this, so we can research with UPS.
• What will we do with the vault at our DC in Huntsville? It will be costly to destroy it due to the
construction/concrete wails w/steei reinforcements. If we don't utilize, it's a lot of wasted space. This will be used for
safety stock for both Brands and Generic
• Have we looked at the duplication — two entities checking customer DEA licenses for example? Is that cost
effective? Two separate places for damages or customer returns? The Checking of the DEA license is already done
today in SAP for brands and going forward it will be a shared Customer Master, so there is no additional work and
UPS will continue to check DEA License for all customers they shipped. Endo and Qtest shared a large amount of the
same customers, so they would not be duplication.
• DEA may require that we modify our DEA license for Distribution; they do not like you to maintain a schedule on
your license if you are not actively utilizing it.
• if we are seeking to minimize risk, why would we utilize a distribution location so close to Huntsville? An extensive
study was completed and it was a business decision to have Memphis as the 2nd DC for Qtest.
• UPS does not weigh each shipper once it comes from the manufacturing site like our Qualitest DC does. This
effort allows us to discover around 50-75 count discrepancies before the shipper gets to the customer level. The
number of customer complaints and shortages that need to be reported to DEA will increase. This should be a process
conducted at the manufacturing site. And we have a process in place in Memphis to report any shortages and there is
a process in place
• This effort appears to be of interest as it reduces storage cost for brand products by spreading the expense across
all businesses. Based on the volume of product Qualitest has versus the Brand, this does not truly appear to be cost
effective when all factors are considered (transportation, storage, additional personnel needed at UPS, additional
regulatory risk, duplication of efforts, inconvenience to customers, etc.). I would think that there are better options
to pursue. There has been an extensive project over the 2 years to developed the best strategy and cost savings
opportunities for both Brands and Generics. UPS brings a significant freight savings to Qtest
• Lastly, we were told that we must allow the Brand team to develop theft own suspicious order monitoring
program, rather than help them by incorporating the shipments into Qualitest's program. This was conveyed by
Margaret and was due to the Corporate Integrity Agreement that they are under. Why would mixing distribution be
any different? The Endo SOM program is the same for both brands and Generics, when the new SAP system is
implemented in May for Brands and July for Generics. Both business units will be able to review and release their
orders.

company distribution center in Florida was not the result of a technology breakdown or glitch.
The Drug Enforcement Agency on Sept. 14 shut down shipments of oxycodone, a controlled
substance, at a Walgreens facility in Florida after detecting suspiciously high sales of the pain-killer at
a half-dozen Walgreen stores in the state. The move is part of a broader government crackdown
targeting Walgreens CVS Caremark Cardinal Health and other large pharmacy chains regarding the
diversion of oxycodone and other drugs for illegal sale, as the DEA would like these firms to review
their sales records proactively for indications of drugs being diverted to addicts.
Theriault, who oversees technology for over 7,900 retail stores, didn't elaborate on exactly how the
diversion occurred, or how the company's order management and software systems work. But one
expert said vulnerability in the supply chain management system and technology may have created
an opportunity to divert oxycodone from one of the pharmacy chain's distribution centers to the black
market, triggering the federal investigation.
The illegal diversion of oxycodone was likely the result of a person or persons trying to "game the
system with fake orders," said Brian Kilcourse, a managing partner for retail consultant RSR Research
who served as CIO for Longs' Drugs for 9 years until 2002.
"We take this issue very seriously and we'll invest heavily into making sure the meds that are being
prescribed are legitimate and that they are being done for the best intentions of peoples' healthcare,"
Theriault told CIO Journal. Theriault also said the nation's largest pharmacy chain has the capability
to safely and accurately provide controlled substances.
A Walgreens spokesman told CIO Journal that the company reduced the number of oxycodone
tablets dispensed by Walgreens pharmacies in Florida between June 2011 and March 2012 by 35%,
thanks to a series of changes that the company made. In 2011, he said, it implemented new ordering
and inventory reporting requirements with quantity limits for several controlled substances that have
high abuse potential. The company also improved monthly store reporting based on a variety of
factors, including the number of oxycodone prescriptions, the percent of oxycodone prescriptions and
the quantity of oxycodone pills dispensed. It also augmented store procedures and training for the
handling of controlled substances.
Kilcourse said it would take some familiarity with the pharmacy's controlled substance distribution
processes to pull off such a diversion because customer order management is a high priority for
pharmacy retail stores and is closely watched by each store's pharmacist and his or her managers.
When pills or other prescription medicines go missing, the pharmacist must report it to their manager,
CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_AAC_00072555

 who takes it to supervisors at the company for resolution in an audit control process. "Pharmacy
management companies really take this seriously," Kilcourse said. "These aren't just order
management systems, they're health management systems."
Pharmacies are reluctant to detail their order fulfillment and risk management processes to protect
against exploits and preserve competitive differentiation. A CVS Caremark spokesperson told CIO
Journal it "monitors ordering of controlled substances through a combination of internal and external
systems, including working with wholesalers in their monitoring of orders delivered directly to our
individual retail locations." A Cardinal Health spokesperson told CIO Journal it uses a system to
monitor suspicious orders. It reviews customer order history and flags orders that exceed controlled
substance thresholds, and uses investigative practices, when necessary.
Kilcourse said pharmacies have for many years built and used order management software that flags
anomalies, such as when customers come back after two weeks to refill a 30-day prescription, or
order two prescriptions from two different doctors. Such systems also monitor patient information,
such as allergy states and disease states, to ensure that customers are safely being prescribed
medicine. In the physical order fulfillment, pharmacists either literally count each pill they dispense to
customers by hand or use closely calibrated vats to count pills before they put them in bottles.
At distribution centers, which centralize the execution of sales, robotic machines are used to carefully
count medications and are stored by lot number before they ship them to retail stores. Sometimes,
when customers order refills, the prescriptions are counted and filled at the distribution centers before
they are shipped to the retail store. "Those machines are monitored closely," Kilcourse said. "They're
not allowed to be one pill off. The federal government is extremely intolerant" of missing pills. Such
closely choreographed order fulfillment leads Kilcourse to conclude that "somebody is" exploiting the
Walgreens distribution center by "putting orders in for fake people."
Kilcourse said Walgreens likely was warned by the DEA before the news broke earlier this month and
that it looked into the issue to confirm that its computers systems were controlling dispensation and
fulfillment they way they are regulated to do so.

---Original Message---From: Kan, Sarah
Sent: Monday, October 17, 2011 3:22 PM
To: Thomas, Greg; Byrne, Timothy; Becker, Geoffrey; Trzaskawka, Catharine; Phipps, Candice; Michelin, Brett; Moody,
David; Fontana, Josi; Bush, Elizabeth; Munroe, Brian; Fisk, Brent
Subject: FYI: Critics want drug makers to help curb abuse

> Critics want drug makers to help curb abuse

> Pharmaceutical companies say they try but misuse not east to stop
>
> 12:49 AM, Oct. 16, 2011 I
>
> Written by

> Laura Ungar <mailto:lungar@courier-journal.com>

> Zoom <javascript:void(null);>
> (Click the Zoom button to view the chart at full size.)

> They make the painkillers that are being abused by an increasing number of Americans, and critics say it's time drug
manufacturers take responsibility for their role in the nation's fastest growing drug addiction.
> "Nobody is reaching out to the pharmaceutical companies that are causing this problem," said Kristin Jacobs, a
commissioner in Broward County, Fla., where thousands of Kentuckians get the prescription drugs that help fuel their
addictions
> But officials from drug companies and law enforcement say it's not easy for drug makers to stop people from misusing their
products to get high.
> Sharon Brigner, deputy vice president for the trade group Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, said
drug companies are cooperating with law-enforcement efforts to root out wrongdoers and taking such steps as educating
consumers and physicians.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07129554

 > They're also reformulating their drugs to make them harder to snort or inject.
> Kevin Wiggins of Endo Pharmaceuticals in Newark, Del., which makes the painkiller Opana, said the rampant abuse is
giving narcotic painkillers a bad name and is distracting from the mission to help legitimate patients.
> "As a drug company, our first priority is patient safety and that products are used as prescribed," Wiggins said. "We take very
seriously" legal drugs being used for illegal purposes.

> Safeguards, loopholes

> Although they're not foolproof, safeguards exist along the drug supply chain to curb abuse.
> Manufacturers and any entity that distributes controlled substances, such as the painkiller oxycodone, must register with the
federal Drug Enforcement Administration.
> Each year, after getting applications from drug makers, the DEA sets production quotas based on the expected need. For
example, this year's production quota for oxycodone manufactured for sale is 105.5 million kilograms, up from 94 million in
2009 and 70 million in 2008.
> DEA-registered companies must keep records of their controlled-substance transactions. More than 1,000 manufacturers
and distributors report to a DEA database, which tracks drugs from manufacturer to retailer.
> (Page 2 of 3)

> Those statistics show that 4.3 billion oxycodone pills were purchased nationally by dispensing practitioners and pharmacies
in 2010. Purchasers in Florida, considered to be the nation's foremost supplier of illicit pills, ordered 611 million oxycodone
pills — more than any other state.
> In April, DEA Administrator Michele Leonhart described her agency's efforts to curb the illicit prescription drug trade before a
Congressional subcommittee. She said the agency has beefed up oversight of DEA-registered companies, hiring more
investigators and increasing inspections of manufacturers, distributors and others.
> John Coster, senior vice president of government affairs for the Generic Pharmaceutical Association, also testified,
describing drug companies' requirements under DEA rules: having steel vaults and special cages in manufacturing facilities
to protect against theft, using GPS tracking to monitor delivery of controlled substances and developing a system to identify
suspicious orders .
> "Manufacturers typically ship to wholesalers or distributors, who in turn sell the drugs to all kinds of health care outlets ...," he
told the panel. "Addressing the abuse and diversion issue will require cooperation of all these parties in the supply chain."
> Perry Fri, a senior vice president at the Healthcare Distribution Management Association, said the wholesale distributors
represented by his trade organization are aware of their responsibilities.
> "We take safety and security very seriously as far as our business practices," Fri said in an interview, adding that members
of his trade group use technology to monitor customers' ordering practices.
> Distributors can sometimes spot diversion by noticing large increases in the amounts of painkillers purchased by retailers,
which Burke called "a huge red flag." Such changes, however, can be legitimate, such as a new arrangement with a hospice
organization.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07129555

 > Burke said rogue retailers often avoid scrutiny by buying controlled substances from several distributors. That way, he said,
they can remain under the law-enforcement radar.
> (Page 3 of 3)

> "That's something we're constantly vigilant against," Fri said.

> Finger of blame

> But some Kentucky leaders argue that pharmaceutical companies have had a hand in creating the prescription-drug abuse
problem.
> U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers, a Kentucky Republican whose 5th District includes hard-hit southeastern Kentucky, has pointed the
finger at OxyContin maker Purdue Pharma.
> Court records have documented how the company sought out doctors who prescribed high numbers of pain pills, sometimes
with limited training in treating serious pain —which made Appalachia a target for abuse of prescription drugs. Court records
also say the company misled doctors and patients by claiming the drug was less likely to be abused than traditional narcotics.
> Through a federal case brought by the Justice Department, a company affiliated with Purdue Pharma and three top Purdue
executives pleaded guilty in 2007, paid millions in fines in a plea deal and acknowledged misleading physicians.
> But Alan Must, vice president for state government and public affairs at Purdue Pharma, denied his company had a part in
fueling prescription-drug abuse.
> "There are some federal politicians out of Kentucky that seem to hold us responsible for all this," he said. "But we're
committed to being part of the solution. We don't want people misusing our meds."
> Must pointed to an OxyContin reformulation, approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration last year, which makes it
harder for addicts to cut, chew, crush or dissolve the pills — although they can still be abused if the patient exceeds the

FDLI's Drug Quality Security Act Conference
Posted: 22 Oct 2O17 O6:52 PM PDT
The Food and Drug Law Institute's ("FDLI") Drug Quality and Security Act ("DQSA") conference is just a few
weeks away, and spaces are going fast! The conference will be held on November 15, 2O17, in Washington, D.C.
Hyman, Phelps & McNamara, P.C.'s Karla L. Palmer will be chairing the conference.
Panels of key government regulators and industry experts will explore current issues surrounding the DQSA's
Title I (Compounding Quality Act) and Title II (Drug Supply Chain Security Act) four years after
implementation. Title I has had a significant impact in compounding pharmaceutical products by outsourcing
facilities and traditional pharmacies. Conference speakers will review the changes in the law, FDA's current
guidance, regulatory responses, and related state actions involving compounding. Title II has and will continue
to have a significant impact on drug manufacturers, wholesalers and pharmacies, especially as they implement
the next phases of the Drug Supply Chain Security Act and await additional FDA guidance.
You can learn more about and register for the conference here. Use discount code "DQSA-Savelif to save

scheduled to take place in Washington, D.C. from January 29-31, 2O18.

FDA, representatives from State Attorney General and U.S. Attorney Offices, as well as high-level in-house
executives, and top outside counsel. Conference speakers will provide their insights into the most pressing
topics affecting the space such as:

Requirements

Hi Brian,
I hope you're well. I previously reached out to you when I was a counsel on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on
Investigations to set up a briefing on Endo's opioid products. I've since followed Sen. McCaskill over to the Homeland Security
and Governmental Affairs Committee, and I'm hoping you can assist with another briefing on a similar issue—Endo's efforts to
combat opioid diversion. The recent Washington Post article on the DEA investigation into Mallinckrodt has raised concerns
about the level of cooperation between manufacturers, distributors, and pharmacies in monitoring and reporting suspicious
opioid orders, and it would be helpful to hear about Endo's efforts in this area. Specifically, it would be great if Endo's
representatives could cover these topics during a call:

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_ANK_CHI_0093334

 • Efforts by Endo to monitor, investigate, or report suspicious opioid orders, including transactions between distributors and
pharmacies (through a review of chargebacks, for example);

monitor and review these efforts;
• Efforts Endo undertakes to audit or investigate specific pharmacies that receive its products and the standards/analysis
Endo uses to determine when an audit or investigation is necessary;
• Endo communications with DEA, and whether DEA officials have provided clear standards concerning suspicious order
monitoring and the company's anti-diversion obligations generally.
Would it be possible to schedule a briefing for some time in the next few weeks? As with our inquiry last fall, a phone briefing
would be fine. Happy to discuss further at your convenience.

Special Offer for Past Attendees

There are now about 200 unique REMS and four classwide REMS. And big changes are coming.
PDUFA V moves REMS discussions earlier in the review process for sponsors of new molecular
entity NDAs and original BLAs. With REMS discussions commencing as early as pre-NDA meetings,
the agency is determining how to create a more predictable system for requiring REMS and deciding
what tools a REMS should involve.
CDER (in conjunction with CBER) plans to issue new guidance to determine when a REMS is
required, both preapproval and postapproval. The guidance must be released in September 2013.
Plus, the FDA is planning to hold a series of public meetings to determine the best methods for
assessing the effectiveness of REMS.

* DEA wins a round in prescription drug abuse battle
* Cardinal says it already cut off pharmacy supplies
*Appeals decision on Florida license to appeals court
* DEA judge due to begin hearings April 3
By Toni Clarke and Anna Yukhananov
Feb 29 (Reuters) - A federal judge allowed the government to suspend Cardinal Health Inc's license to distribute potentially addictive
drugs from a Florida facility, part of the Drug Enforcement Administration's battle against prescription drug abuse.
The ruling on Wednesday was an initial victory for government efforts to force drug wholesalers to play a bigger role in fighting drug
abuse, and may crimp Cardinal's business for the next 12 months.
Judge Reggie Walton of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia had previously given Cardinal a temporary restraining order
to block the suspension of the Lakeland facility, which serves about 2,700 drug stores or hospitals, while it pleads its case to a judge
within the DEA.
Cardinal said it was appealing Wednesday's decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.
"We want to be part of a new, more effective solution to stop prescription drug abuse, without disrupting legitimate use," the company
said in a statement.
The DEA ordered the current suspension on Feb. 3, saying Cardinal knew, or should have known, that four of its customers, including

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_ANK_CHI_0184801

 two CVS Caremark Corp pharmacies, were inappropriately filling prescriptions for the painkiller oxycodone.
Cardinal, one of the country's largest drug distributors, said it had already cut off supplies to two of the pharmacies before the DEA's
suspension order. It cut supplies to the remaining two pharmacies as soon as the DEA issued its order.
Walton said on Wednesday that after getting more information from the DEA, he agreed with the decision to suspend Cardinal's license.
"I think DEA is correct that companies have an obligation to police themselves... and to be proactive in assessing whether diversion (of
controlled substances) is taking place," Walton said during a court hearing.
Morningstar analyst Matthew Coffina said Walton's ruling could cause Cardinal to lose some market share, at least in the short run, to
competitors such as McKesson Corp and AmerisourceBergen Corp.
Coffina said it is also likely to force all distributors to invest more money in policing the pharmacies they serve.
"It's a negative for the distributors more broadly to the extent that they are going to be held accountable for the actions of pharmacies,"
he said.
Shares of Cardinal closed 1.3 percent lower, while McKesson gained 1.2 percent and AmerisourceBergen slipped 0.9 percent.
The judge said he did not believe Cardinal would suffer 'irreparable harm' because of the suspension, as it had recovered its business
after a previous suspension of Lakeland in 2007.
An administrative hearing of Cardinal's Lakeland license is scheduled to begin at the DEA on April 3. That process could take as long as
a year to play out as both sides present their cases.
The DEA judge will then make a recommendation to the DEA's administrator, Michele Leonhart, who will make a ruling. Leonhart signed
the initial order to suspend Cardinal's license.
FIGHTING ABUSE
The case comes as prescription drug abuse has surged in the United States, eclipsing the abuse of most illicit drugs, including heroin
and cocaine.
Distributors such as Cardinal argue they are unfairly targeted because it is easier for the DEA to attack a distributor than the thousands
of doctors who write the prescriptions.
"DEA does not regulate the practice of medicine. And if anything, a wholesaler is in even less of a position to do so," said Randolph
Moss, the attorney arguing on behalf of Cardinal.
"It doesn't regulate doctors, and it doesn't regulate patients," he said, adding that the company was doing its best to prevent prescription
drug abuse.
For its part, the DEA argues distributors have an obligation to ensure none of the controlled drugs that go out their doors land in the
wrong hands.
"Cardinal ... is facilitating diversion when it does not take adequate measures to prevent diversion," said Lee Reeves, an attorney with
the U.S. Department of Justice, who argued on behalf of the DEA.
Every entity that handles controlled narcotics, from physician to pharmacy to manufacturer, must register with the DEA and the agency
says each entity must monitor the next.
The DEA said distributors are required to design systems that detect suspicious orders, and Cardinal failed to do so.
Cardinal says it took significant steps to rebuild its systems and hire new personnel after DEA suspended the license at the same
Lakeland facility in 2007.
It also argues there is no "imminent danger" to the public as the affected pharmacies are no longer allowed to dispense controlled drugs.
The case is Cardinal Health Inc. V. Holder, U.S. District Court, District of Columbia, No. 12-185.

A New Painkiller Crackdown Targets Drug Distributors

Miunaell F 'Orch s pharmacy in Newport Beach, Calif., lost a big portion of its painkiller supplies after a federal crackdown.
By BARRY MEIER

A local druggist in Newport Beach, Calif., never expected that the federal government's recent crackdown on
distributors of prescription painkillers would ensnare him.
But in June, Cardinal Health, a major distributor, abruptly cut off his supplies of narcotics like OxyContin
and Percocet. A few months earlier, the Drug Enforcement Administration had accused Cardinal of ignoring
CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-03410797

 signs that some pharmacies in Florida that it supplied with such drugs might be feeding street demand for
them.
Cardinal told the druggist, Michael Pavlovich, that the volume of pain drugs and other controlled
medications he was dispensing was too high, a situation he said was explainable. His pharmacy specializes
in pain patients, he said. Still, it took weeks for Cardinal to start supplying him again, and even then, it
limited its shipments to about 15 percent of his previous orders. As a result, Mr. Pavlovich said, many of his
patients had to go elsewhere to get prescriptions filled.
"We have to convince them that our dispensing is legitimate," he said of his dealings with Cardinal.
Cardinal's crackdown on Mr. Pavlovich was a sign of a new approach by the D.E.A. to stem the growing
misuse and abuse of painkillers. In the last decade, the agency has tried a variety of tactics with limited
success, from arresting hundreds of doctors to closing scores of pharmacies. Now, it and other agencies are
moving up the pharmaceutical food chain, putting pressure on distributors like Cardinal, which act as
middlemen between drug makers and the pharmacies and doctors that dispense painkillers.
In response, the distributors are scrambling to limit their liability by more closely monitoring their
distribution pipelines and cutting off some customers.
Since January, for example, Cardinal has cut ties with a dozen pharmacies in states including Arizona,
California, Nevada and Oklahoma, interviews and court records show. In doing so, the wholesaler, which is
based in Columbus, Ohio, cited audits suggesting that people seeking to buy prescription drugs illegally
might have targeted the store in question.
Several of the affected drugstores sued Cardinal unsuccessfully to resume supplies, but documents filed in
those actions show that until recently, the wholesaler shipped large volumes of pain pills to the stores for
months, if not years.
George S. Barrett, Cardinal's chairman and chief executive, said the company had tightened the criteria it
used in determining whether to sell narcotics to a pharmacy. In May, Cardinal settled the action brought by
the D.E.A. in connection with its Florida sales by agreeing to suspend shipments of controlled drugs, like
narcotics, from a facility in that state for two years. It could also face a significant fine.
"We had a strong antidiversion system in place, but no system is perfect," Mr. Barrett said. Among other
steps, the company said it had created a special committee to regularly evaluate pharmacies that order high
volumes of narcotic drugs.
Another major distributor, AmerisourceBergen, recently disclosed that it faces a federal criminal inquiry
into its oversight of painkiller sales. And in June, West Virginia officials filed a lawsuit against 14 drug
distributors, including Cardinal and AmerisourceBergen, charging that they had fed illicit painkiller use in
that state. The companies have denied wrongdoing.
D.E.A. officials have heralded the Cardinal action as the forerunner of a more aggressive approach to the
painkiller problem. But critics say that for years, the agency did little to scrutinize distributors who were
making tens of millions of dollars from the prescriptions generated by pain clinics in Florida, Ohio and
CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-03410798

 other states. These facilities, often described as "pill mills," employed doctors who wrote narcotics
prescriptions after cursory examinations of patients.
"In the case of West Virginia, they have done nothing," said a lawyer in Charleston, James M. Cagle, who is
working on the state's action against distributors.
The drug distribution system is a sprawling one that involves about 800 companies, which range in size
from a few giants like Cardinal to hundreds of small firms. For wholesalers, the markup on medications can
be small, sometimes a few pennies a pill. But with billions of pills sold annually, the profits can be big.
Narcotic painkillers are now the most widely prescribed drugs in the United States, with sales last year of
$8.5 billion.
This is not the first time the industry has faced scrutiny. In 2008, Cardinal paid $34 million to settle
charges that it failed to alert the D.E.A. to suspicious orders for millions of pain pills that it was shipping to
Internet pharmacies — operations that for years supplied the illicit market. The same year, another big
distributor, McKesson, paid $13 million to settle similar charges. As part of the agreements, both companies
denied wrongdoing.
Executives like Mr. Barrett of Cardinal say that it is often difficult for a distributor to tell whether a
pharmacy or a doctor is serving legitimate pain patients or supplying illicit drug demand. And distributors
have long complained that the D.E.A. has never issued specific guidelines for when they should stop
shipping to a customer.
But agency officials say that wholesalers know about the red flags. For example, the agency charged that
Cardinal was selling 5o times the amount of pain pills containing the narcotic oxycodone, the active
ingredient in OxyContin and other drugs, to its four top pharmacy customers in Florida than it was
supplying to the average drugstore in that state.
Cardinal failed to scrutinize such sales, the agency said, even violating the safeguards it promised to put in
place when it agreed to settle the government charges in connection with its supplying of Internet
pharmacies. "Everyone is making a large amount of money on these drugs," said Joseph T. Rannazzisi, a
deputy assistant administrator of the D.E.A. division that oversees legal drugs, like painkillers.
The D.E.A. is able to track where painkillers are going because distributors regularly file reports detailing
their shipments to customers. But just how aggressively the agency uses that data is anyone's guess.
An agency employee, Michelle Cooper, testified last year that she had attended a training session at which
instructors described how investigators like her could use the database to identify suspicious distributors. In
doing so, they pointed to data showing that a distributor had suddenly started shipping large and growing
volumes of pain pills to Florida drugstores.
It was only later that Ms. Cooper discovered that the case involved a real distributor, not a hypothetical one,
and that the company was still making those shipments despite the agency's apparent awareness of them.
"I didn't believe the numbers they were showing us were real," she said. "I thought it was for training

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-03410799

 purposes."
Ms. Cooper subsequently investigated the company, Keysource Medical, which agreed last year to give up its
license to distribute narcotic drugs.
Faced with Congressional pressure, agency officials like Mr. Rannazzisi have said that they are increasing
the ranks of investigators like Ms. Cooper, and that they provide distribution data to state officials when
local authorities request it as part of an investigation.
But state officials say it would be more helpful to get that data routinely so they can act more quickly
against rogue clinics and pharmacies. For years, Ohio law enforcement authorities did not know which
distributors were supplying the many pill mills operating in the state, one official said. If the D.E.A. had
supplied that information, "we would have known about the number of shipments going into Ohio and
where they were going," said Aaron Haslam, an assistant state attorney general.
Also, while the D.E.A. brings actions against distributors like Cardinal for failing to notify the agency of a
"suspicious order" from a pharmacy or other customer, it does not share those reports with officials in the
state where the pharmacy is based.
In response to a request from The New York Times, the agency even declined to disclose the number of such
reports it received annually. A spokeswoman, Barbara Carreno, said in a statement that the agency
considered such statistics "law enforcement sensitive" information, but she did not elaborate.
The Times has filed a Freedom of Information Act request seeking that data.

https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/to- your-health/wp/2017/01/18/mckesson- nations-largest-drug-distributor-to-pay150-million-in-fines-in-opioid-settlement/?utm term=.940a8c4c6467

McKesson, nation's largest drug distributor, to pay $150 million in fines in opioid settlement

By Lenny Bernstein
January 18 at 1:33 PM
McKesson's headquarters in San Francisco. (Paul Sakuma/Associated Press)
McKesson, the largest drug distributor in the United States, has agreed to pay a record $150 million in fines and to suspend
sales of controlled substances from four distribution centers to settle allegations that the company violated federal law, the
Justice Department announced Tuesday.
The settlement is the second for the giant drug distributor. In 2008, McKesson paid a $13.25 million fine over similar
allegations.
In the current case, the government accused McKesson — the fifth-largest company in the United States — of failing to design
and use an effective system to detect "suspicious orders" from pharmacies for powerful painkillers such as oxycodone, as
required by the Controlled Substances Act. In Colorado, for example, McKesson filled more than 1.6 million orders for
controlled substances from June 2008 through May 2013, but it reported just 16 of them from a single customer as suspicious,
the Justice Department said.
The company had previously acknowledged in Securities and Exchange Commission filings that it would have to pay the fine.
Tuesday's announcement adds that the company will have to employ an independent monitor to assess its compliance with
the law in the future and will shutter warehouses in Colorado, Ohio, Michigan and Florida on a staggered basis for unspecified
numbers of years.
[DEA slowed enforcement as the opioid epidemic grew out of control]
In a statement on its website, McKesson said it settled "in the interest of moving beyond disagreements about whether
McKesson was complying with the controlled substance regulations ... and to instead focus on the company's partnership with
regulators and others to help stem the opioid epidemic in this country."

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_ANK_CHI_0950512

 In October, The Washington Post reported that the Drug Enforcement Administration slowed an enforcement campaign
against major wholesale drug distributors like McKesson in the face of pressure from the pharmaceutical industry.
In December, Cardinal Health, another member of the "Big Three" drug distributors, agreed to pay $44 million in penalties to
resolve allegations that it failed to notify the DEA of suspicious narcotic orders.
More than 16,000 Americans died of overdoses of prescription opioids, including methadone, last year. Since 2000, the toll has
been about 180,000 people.
[How drugs intended for pain patients ended up on the black market]
In 2013, the DEA began investigating reports that McKesson was failing to maintain proper controls to prevent the diversion of
opioids. Six years earlier, the DEA had accused it of failing to report hundreds of suspicious orders from online pharmacies.
The company settled those claims, agreeing to a $13.25 million fine and promising to set up a monitoring system.
The Justice Department said in documents made public Tuesday that McKesson continued to fail to report suspicious orders
between 2008 and 2012 and did not fully implement or follow the monitoring program. In 2014, federal prosecutors told
McKesson it faced civil sanctions based on the results of the investigation.

TOP NEWS
Senator expands opioid investigation to more drug manufacturers, distributors

Senator expands opioid investigation to more drug manufacturers, distributors (back)
By Sarah Karlin-Smith
Sen. Claire McCaskill is expanding her investigation into the causes of the opioid epidemic to four additional
drug companies and three opioid distributors, seeking information about their efforts to monitor, report and
investigate the diversion of opioids for illicit use.
McCaskill sent letters to opioid manufacturers Mallinckrodt, Endo, Teva and Allergan and opioid distributors
McKesson Corporation, AmerisourceBergen Corporation and Cardinal Health.
"We've seen numerous reports that potentially hundreds of millions of opioid pills wound up on the black
market, fueling a nationwide epidemic — we need a better understanding of how committed these companies
are to preventing this type of drug diversion or whether they are turning a blind eye," the Missouri Democrat
said in a statement today.
McCaskill asked drug manufacturers for documentation of suspicious order notifications provided to the Drug
Enforcement Agency originating from Missouri. And she wants details of any effort to audit or investigate
Missouri-based pharmacies, distributors or other customers.

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06989129

 She also asked drug distributors for suspicious order notifications provided to the DEA and details of opioid
shipments to any Missouri pharmacy or other customers. She wants to know whether the companies provided
any commission or incentives to employees that derived from revenue or profitability targets for sales of opioid
products.
In March, McCaskill asked for a Justice Department investigation into the DEA's ability to hold major drug
distributors accountable for opioid diversion, raising concerns that fines levied against companies were
inadequate. That month she also launched an investigation into whether the sales and marketing practices of the
country's five largest manufacturers contributed to the over-utilization of the drugs and the resulting addiction
epidemic.
To view online click here.

'Skinny' Obamacare repeal getting slimmer, sources say (back)
By Jennifer Haberkorn, Seung Min Kim and Rachana Pradhan
Republican leaders are making the Senate's so-called skinny Obamacare repeal bill even slimmer.
Sources on and off Capitol Hill have described a new outline that would do the following:
- Repeal the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate.
- Partially repeal the ACA's employer mandate.
- Defund Planned Parenthood for one year and transfer the funding to community health centers.
-

Give states new authority in Section 1332 waivers.

-

Significantly cut the ACA's Prevention and Public Health Fund.

The slimmed-down package would no longer repeal the ACA's medical device tax, or other taxes created by the
health law.
The bill is likely to go through further changes as Republicans try to pass a repeal plan at the end of an all-night
Senate "vote-a-rama" anticipated to begin this evening.
To view online click here.

FDA opens up digital health pre-certification pilot program (back)
By Darius Tahir
FDA announced it would seek applicants for a pilot program allowing digital health developers to be precertified as quality coders, allowing eased submission requirements for their products. The move is the first of
an anticipated wave of regulatory reorganizations targeting the digital health sector.
2

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06989130

 Under terms of the pilot, the agency will accept applications from developers beginning Aug. 1 and pick nine on
Sept. 1. The agency's announcement anticipates a diverse group ranging from non-traditional medical device
manufacturers to large and small software developers.
"Can we identify excellence that [works for] the small two-person company, and the large organization?" asked
Bakul Patel, the agency's digital health director. "Those are the goals."
The pilot is intended to suss out what makes a high-quality developer, in order to decide how much scrutiny to
apply to low-risk software or updates to code.
Patel said specific programmatic elements will evolve as the agency work with the developers it selects.
Questions such as how or whether or de-certify previously certified developers in the event of quality slippage
will be addressed as the process evolves.
The agency is looking to "build a program with a happy path ... and then we'll figure out the guardrails," Patel
said.
The pilot is the first in a series of digital health rollouts. In an accompanying report, the agency set timelines for
a series of anticipated regulatory actions. It's targeting the first quarter of 2018 for both its long-awaited clinical
decision support software guidance and guidance on "multi-functional" software whose workings impact
multiple areas of FDA regulation. The agency is also looking to bring on entrepreneurs-in-residence to help
with the design of its digital health goals.
To view online click here.

No layoff notices at FDA with user fee reauthorization expected (back)
By David Pittman
The FDA doesn't intend to send layoff notices to employees who could be sidelined if the agency's authority to
collect user fees for product evaluations expires, Commissioner Scott Gottlieb wrote in an agency-wide email
this afternoon.
Instead, Gottlieb expects the Senate to pass the FDA Reauthorization Act, H.R. 2430 (115), before Sept. 30,
when the current authorization expires.
"I have been in regular communication with members of Congress, many of whom have expressed their high
degree of confidence that FDARA will be enacted before the authorizations lapse," Gottlieb wrote. "There is
strong support for the FDA, our public health mission and recognition of the importance of FDARA."
He added he is working with senior FDA officials on contingency plans if Congress doesn't pass a bill by Sept.
30.
More than 40 percent of the FDA's $5.1 billion budget comes from industry user fees. More than $1 billion of
that sum comes from the prescription drug and medical device industries. The agency normally would give
employees whose salaries are supported by the fees a 60-day layoff notice.
To view online click here.
3

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06989131

 Democrats' Better Deal' would penalize drug price hikes (back)
By Sarah Karlin-Smith
Democrats are going straight at one of the top concerns of voters, using the rising cost of drugs to strike a more
populist tone and counter President Donald Trump, who campaigned hard against the power of the drug
industry, but took a friendlier stance after taking office.
Congressional Democrats today laid out a three-pronged approach to lower the cost of prescription drugs in the
United States that aims to stop large price increases and give the federal government more power to influence
what Medicare pays for medicines.
The announcement comes as polls have increasingly found that drug pricing — not Obamacare — is the No. 1
health policy concern of both Democratic and Republican voters, and as expectations dimmed that the Trump
administration would follow through on his own plans to lower drug pricing by calling for government
negotiations or importation of medicines from overseas.
The Trump team is working on an executive order on drug pricing that is expected to have little impact on costs
and be embraced by the industry he once vilified as "getting away with murder."
In contrast, the Democrats' plan, part of party leadership's new economic agenda launched ahead of the 2018
elections, would create an independent, Senate-confirmed "price gouging" enforcer to identify medicines with
"unconscionable" price increases and impose fines on manufacturers that are proportional to the size of the price
hike. Money paid will be given to NIH to further its work on new drug development.
The proposal takes aim at highly publicized incidents, including former pharma executive Martin Shkreli hiking
the price of a drug often used by AIDS patients by more than 5,000 percent when he led Turing
Pharmaceuticals, and Mylan Pharmaceuticals raising the price of the lifesaving allergy drug EpiPen by $500.
"Right now, there is nothing to stop vulture capitalists from egregiously raising the price of lifesaving drugs
without justification. We're going to fight for rules to stop prescription drug price gouging and demand that
drug companies justify price increases to the public," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote in an op-ed
Monday morning.
Drugmakers would have to justify what are deemed excessive price increases to HHS at least 30 days before the
boosts take effect.
The justification to HHS would be made public and include information such as how much federal funding
factored into developing the drug and the total cost of marketing the product.
The last part of the Democratic proposal would allow the government negotiate the cost of prescription drugs
covered by Medicare Part D. This policy has long been pushed by Democrats, though they failed to get it into
law when they controlled Congress in the early years of the Obama administration. The nonpartisan CBO has
also cautioned that to achieve significant savings, such a proposal would need to be paired with a new Medicare
drug formulary that could create some restrictions on access to some medicines.

Tracey
You have outlined many good issues. My recommendation is to take each one and work with Cesar Penaherrera and Tony
Mason to come up with solutions on how we would overcome each issue if we would implement the UPS solution. It is
important for you and Tony Martinez to feel comfortable on how Qualitest would overcome them with a second source
distribution center. Once you have a plan in place on how to best solve for these issues present it to Tony Martinez and the
Distribution Team to see if it makes sense before we move forward.
Thanks
From: Hernandez, Tracey
Sent: Sunday, March 09, 2014 6:08 PM
To: Propst, Charles V. (Trey); Cupero, Phil
Subject: CII orders handled by Memphis
Trey/PhilI may not be able to attend Monday's distribution meeting since I'll be flying to Boca. However, I wanted you both to have my
concerns related to the idea of outsourcing CII distribution to UPS. This will really create some challenges, both from a
regulatory and a customer service perspective. For example:
• Customers would need to place orders for CII products separately from all other products. CII orders would have
to be made using Memphis' DEA number since they would ship from there. All other controlled products would need
to be made using Qualitest's DEA number. If a customer made a mistake and used the wrong DEA number, the order
would not be able to be filled until the correct paperwork is received.
All customers send in CII orders separately from other products. Endo EDI currently handles all CSOS Orders for
Brands and Generics so there is no chanAg to our customers.

Redacted - Trade Secret
HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_ANK_CHI_0953652

 Redacted - Trade Secret
All CH orders for broth Brands and Generic will come into SAP and fall under the SAP SOM Program. Qtest will have
the same opportunity as they do today to review and release orders before they are sent to the warehouse.
Chargeback data still comes into play. All Order to Cash functions will still be in SAP.
• We would still need to conduct due diligence visits for CIII-V customers so we would again be duplicating efforts.
Qtest still own the Getting to know you customer audits.
• With cargo thefts on the increase, do we really want our most desirable products under control by a 3rd party?
They would have to file the paperwork with DEA if a theft/loss occurs and they would be the point of contact with DEA
since it would be their license. What is UPS' experience in shipping large quantities of CII products?
UPS has handled all of Endo CII products since 2000 and this included the shipment of large Controlled products when
the Generic were under the Brand Company. UPS has a very extensive HV/HR program for ALL shipments, not just
CI Is. UPS's clients included other large generic companies that have high volume of CII products.
• UPS was recently fined heavily by DEA; how will DEA perceive our giving them additional business at this stage?
Tracey needs to provide information on this, so we can research with UPS.
• What will we do with the vault at our DC in Huntsville? It will be costly to destroy it due to the
construction/concrete wails w/steel reinforcements. If we don't utilize, it's a lot of wasted space. This will be used for
safety stock for both Brands and Generic
• Have we looked at the duplication — two entities checking customer DEA licenses for example? is that cost
effective? Two separate places for damages or customer returns? The Checking of the DEA license is already done
today in SAP for brands and going forward it will be a shared Customer Master, so there is no additional work and
UPS will continue to check DEA License for all customers they shipped. Endo and Qtest shared a large amount of the
same customers, so they would not be duplication.
• DEA may require that we modify our DEA license for Distribution; they do not like you to maintain a schedule on
your license if you are not actively utilizing it.
• If we are seeking to minimize risk, why would we utilize a distribution location so close to Huntsville? An extensive
study was completed and it was a business decision to have Memphis as the 2nd DC for Qtest.
• UPS does not weigh each shipper once it comes from the manufacturing site like our Qualitest DC does. This
effort allows us to discover around 50-75 count discrepancies before the shipper gets to the customer level. The
number of customer complaints and shortages that need to be reported to DEA will increase. This should be a process
conducted at the manufacturing site. And we have a process in place in Memphis to report any shortages and there is
a process in place
• This effort appears to be of interest as it reduces storage cost for brand products by spreading the expense across
all businesses. Based on the volume of product Qualitest has versus the Brand, this does not truly appear to be cost
effective when all factors are considered (transportation, storage, additional personnel needed at UPS, additional
regulatory risk, duplication of efforts, inconvenience to customers, etc.). I would think that there are better options
to pursue. There has been an extensive project over the 2 years to developed the best strategy and cost savings
opportunities for both Brands and Generics. UPS brings a significant freight savings to Qtest
• Lastly, we were told that we must allow the Brand team to develop their own suspicious order monitoring
program, rather than help them by incorporating the shipments into Qualitest's program. This was conveyed by
Margaret and was due to the Corporate Integrity Agreement that they are under. Why would mixing distribution be
any different? The Endo SOM program is the same for both brands and Generics, when the new SAP system is
implemented in May for Brands and July for Generics. Both business units will be able to review and release their
orders.
Hope this helps!

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

 I hope you're well. I previously reached out to you when I was a counsel on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee
on Investigations to set up a briefing on Endo's opioid products. I've since followed Sen. McCaskill over to the
Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and I'm hoping you can assist with another briefing on a
similar issue—Endo's efforts to combat opioid diversion. The recent Washington Post article on the DEA
investigation into Mallinckrodt has raised concerns about the level of cooperation between manufacturers,
distributors, and pharmacies in monitoring and reporting suspicious opioid orders, and it would be helpful to hear
about Endo's efforts in this area. Specifically, it would be great if Endo's representatives could cover these topics
during a call:

• Efforts by Endo to monitor, investigate, or report suspicious opioid orders, including transactions between
distributors and pharmacies (through a review of chargebacks, for example);
• Any requirements Endo imposes on its distributor partners in terms of their anti-diversion efforts, and methods
Endo uses to monitor and review these efforts;
• Efforts Endo undertakes to audit or investigate specific pharmacies that receive its products and the
standards/analysis Endo uses to determine when an audit or investigation is necessary;
• Endo communications with DEA, and whether DEA officials have provided clear standards concerning
suspicious order monitoring and the company's anti-diversion obligations generally.
Would it be possible to schedule a briefing for some time in the next few weeks? As with our inquiry last fall, a
phone briefing would be fine. Happy to discuss further at your convenience.
Thanks,
Brandon

submit your request through your state identification bureau", which in Nevada's case requires those original fingerprint
cards.

From: Reavis, Brandon (HSGAC) [mailto:Brandon_Reavis©hsgac.senate.gov]
Sent: Friday, June 16, 2017 12:49 PM
To: Munroe, Brian
Subject: [EXTERNAL] Briefing from Endo re: anti-diversion efforts
ATTENTION: This email came from an external source. Do not open attachments or click on links from unknown senders or
unexpected emails. Click the "Report Phishing" button in Outlook if it is suspicious.

Hi Brian,
I hope you're well. I previously reached out to you when I was a counsel on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on
Investigations to set up a briefing on Endo's opioid products. I've since followed Sen. McCaskill over to the
Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and I'm hoping you can assist with another briefing on a
similar issue—Endo's efforts to combat opioid diversion. The recent Washington Post article on the DEA
investigation into Mallinckrodt has raised concerns about the level of cooperation between manufacturers, distributors,
and pharmacies in monitoring and reporting suspicious opioid orders, and it would be helpful to hear about Endo's
efforts in this area. Specifically, it would be great if Endo's representatives could cover these topics during a call:
n Efforts by Endo to monitor, investigate, or report suspicious opioid orders, including transactions between

distributors and pharmacies (through a review of chargebacks, for example);
n Any requirements Endo imposes on its distributor partners in terms of their anti-diversion efforts, and methods
Endo uses to monitor and review these efforts;

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06210010

 n Efforts Endo undertakes to audit or investigate specific pharmacies that receive its products and the
standards/analysis Endo uses to determine when an audit or investigation is necessary;
n Endo communications with DEA, and whether DEA officials have provided clear standards concerning
suspicious order monitoring and the company's anti-diversion obligations generally.
Would it be possible to schedule a briefing for some time in the next few weeks? As with our inquiry last fall, a phone
briefing would be fine. Happy to discuss further at your convenience.
Thanks,
Brandon

Date:

Subject: How to Design an Effective ETASU with Integrated Digital Elements
From:

FDAnews <enewsletters@fdanews.com>

To:

Craven, Colleen <craven.colleen@endo.com>;

Illerc ❑re now about 200 unique REMS and four classwide REMS. And big changes are coming.
PDUFA V moves REMS discussions earlier in the review process for sponsors of new molecular entity NDAs
and original BLAs. With REMS discussions commencing as early as pre-NDA meetings, the agency is
determining how to create a more predictable system for requiring REMS and deciding what tools a REMS
should involve.
