F.D.A. Rejects Mandatory Training in Painkillers for Doctors
By BARRY IMEIER (NYT)

The Food and Drug Administration decided doctors did not need extra instruction on prescribing some strong painkillers,
despite a growing problem of abuse.
***************************

http://www.painmedicinenews.com/NiewArticle.aspx?ses=ogst&d=Web+Exclusives&d id=244&
i=ISSU E°/o3a+June+2012&i id=858&a id=21258
POSTED: JULY 10, 2012
printer friendly I email this article I
Comment(s)
Years in the Making, REMS Approved for Long-acting, Extended-Release Opioids
More than three years after it was first promised, the other shoe has finally dropped on the FDA-mandated risk
evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) for all extended-release (ER) and long-acting (LA) opioid analgesics.
Announced on July 9, the new REMS will require the manufacturers of ER and LA opioid analgesics to provide
training for health care professionals who prescribe these agents. The companies also must provide educational
materials to the health care professionals and to their patients that explain how to safely use the agents. The new
REMS affect more than 20 drug companies and involves in excess of 30 products, according to the FDA. Both
trade-named and generic agents will now fall under the ER/LA opioid REMS.
Although it is mandatory for the drug companies to provide educational training and resources, undergoing the
training is voluntary on the part of prescribers. This represents a departure from a planned mandatory component of
the REMS discussed when two FDA committees' reviewed an initial proposal in July 2010.
"Such a requirement [mandatory prescriber training] would require the establishment of a new system for registering
prescribers of ER/LA opioid analgesics . . . that would duplicate the existing Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA)
registration system. This would be potentially burdensome . . ." wrote the FDA in a press release announcing the new
REMS.
The REMS is being billed as a part of the Obama administration's 2011 national prescription drug abuse plan.
"The new ER/LA opioid analgesic REMS advances the Agency's goal of improving the safe use of ER/LA opioid
CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06204826

 analgesics while ensuring continued access to these medications for patients who need them," the FDA said in the
press release.
Components and Timeline
According to the FDA, more than 320,000 individuals prescribe ER/LA opioids annually. The agency announced a
goal of 25% of prescribers trained one year following implementation of the program, 40% at two years and 60%
within three years. The FDA expects the first company-provided educational materials to be available by March
2013. An approved patient-counseling document is available immediately.
The prescriber education resources will include information on assessing patient need for opioid treatment; starting,
modifying, managing and discontinuing opioid therapy; monitoring patients; and counseling patients and caregivers
about opioid safety.
Stating that it understands how important continued access to ER/LA opioid analgesics is to chronic pain patients, the
FDA vowed to monitor patient access and to communicate with patients "to ensure that patients get proper pain
management." The FDA also plans to conduct follow-up surveys to gauge the effectiveness of the REMS and
whether it is hampering access.
"If FDA determines that the REMS is not meeting its goals, the Agency will re-evaluate the program," the FDA
wrote.
Magnified Risk
In explaining why only ER and LA opioids are being required to carry REMS, and not immediate-release (IR) agents,
the FDA stated, "The FDA has concluded that there is a disproportionate safety problem associated with these
products that must be addressed. . . . The amount of opioid analgesic contained in an ER tablet can be much more
than the amount of opioid analgesic contained in an IR tablet because ER tablets are designed to release the opioid
analgesic over a longer period of time. Improper use of any opioid can result in serious side effects, including,
overdose and death, and this risk is magnified with ER/LA analgesics. "
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there were 14,800 deaths related to the use of opioid
pain relievers in the United States in 2008. That number rose to 15,597 in 2009.
In January2012, the FDA approved a single, shared REMS for transmucosal IR fentanyl products. All of these
products are opioid analgesics indicated for breakthrough pain in cancer patientswho are already receiving and who
are tolerant to opioid therapy for underlying persistent cancer pain. Called the TIRF (transmucosal immediate-release
fentanyl) REMS Access Program, the new, shared system began in March.
A Checkered History
According to the FDA, REMS "go beyond requirements in the drug prescribing information to manage serious risks
associated with a drug." The Food and Drug Administration Amendments Act of 2007 allows the FDA to require
drugs to carry REMS "when further measures are needed to ensure that the drug's benefit outweigh it's risk." The
FDA first acknowledged in February 2009 that it would ask 24 manufacturers of LA and ER opioids to develop such
risk management plans for their products. Each of these agents was formulated with one of the following active
ingredients: fentanyl, hydromorphone, methadone, morphine, oxycodone and oxymorphone.
"For perhaps the first time in the history of U.S. food and drug laws, the definition of an adverse drug experience was
broadened to include drug abuse and overdose," wrote a group of pain experts, led by John J. Coleman, PhD,
president of the Prescription Drug Research Center in Fairfax, Va. ("A Brief Overview and Critique of the Proposed
Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy for Opioid Medications,"Pain Medicine News, April 2010, page 30) about
the FDA Amendments Act of 2007.
The FDA held a series of meetings with stakeholders, including large public meetings, and also solicited written
public comments to hear more about how to develop an opioid REMS, yet still managed to frustrate groups like the
American Pain Society (APS). When the first opioid REMS was announced in July 2009, APS president Charles E.
Inturrisi, PhD, wrote in a letter to the FDA stating that the group was "surprised and disappointed" that the REMS
was "in stark contrast to many of the stakeholder suggestions made." Chief among these was the fact that the
proposed REMS covered only LA agents, sparking concern that physicians would simply decide not to register and
be trained to use these drugs, whether or not they were the best treatment option.
Then in October 2009, the FDA announced that it would postpone REMS implementation for one year, and continue
to solicit feedback from stakeholders, "perhaps recognizing that a classwide opioid REMS program may be more
difficult than envisioned," wrote Dr. Coleman and colleagues. At the time, several companies introducing opioids to
the market voluntarily developed REMS for their products, adding restricted distribution programs under which
prescribers, pharmacies and patients would have to register in order to prescribe, dispense and receive the agent,
respectively. In these cases, the drug would be delivered directly to the patient's home and restricted in physician
CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06204827

 offices and hospitals in order to reduce the risk for diversion.
The FDA's Anesthetic and Life Support Drugs Advisory Committee and the Drug Safety and Risk Management
Advisory Committee voted overwhelmingly on July 23, 2010 to scrap the initial ER/LA opioid REMS initiative and
start over toward a more stringent version. At the time, it was believed the new REMS would make training
mandatory for opioid prescribers—a component the FDA ultimately chose to leave out.

Seven Doctors 7 "';'7.ind in Puerto Rico
Those Arrested Sold $3.3 114iIlioti vic, Li. of Illegal Prescriptions over Internet
JAN 29--(SAN JUAN) —Jerome Michael Harris, Special Agent in Charge, Caribbean Division, Drug Enforcement
Administration (DEA), Rosa Emilia Rodriguez-Velez, United States Attorney for the District of Puerto Rico, and Ralph Culkin,
Resident Agent in Charge, Food and Drug Administration, Office of Criminal Investigations (FDA/OCI), today announced the
indictment of seven doctors licensed to practice medicine in Puerto Rico. Charges include conspiracy to distribute controlled
substances, wire fraud, and money laundering. In addition, a forfeiture allegation in the amount of $3.3 million dollars was also
included in the indictment.
Those arrested (location of arrest) as part of DEA's Operation Click4Drugs are:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

Dr. Alfred VALDIVIESO- Rodriguez (Tampa, Florida)
Dr. Juan A. TOSADO-Polanco (Santa Isabel, PR)
Blanca I. PLAZA-Rodriguez (Dorado, PR)
Maileen LUGO-Torres (Cabo Rojo, PR)
Abelardo E. LECOMPTE-Torres (Ponce, PR)
Norberto J. SEDA-Olmo (Parma Heights, Ohio)
Juan M. RAMOS-Gonzalez (Houston, Texas )

Operation Click 4 Drugs targeted an organization which distributed large quantities of Schedule III and Schedule IV
controlled substances via the internet. These doctors issued thousands of illegal prescriptions through the internet for drugs
such as Hydrocodone, Phentermine and Diazepam. The physicians were involved with Internet Facilitation Centers and
Internet pharmacies that solicited customers throughout the United States who were seeking controlled substances. These
centers would then refer the customers to these physicians using numerous web sites and e-mail addresses. The doctors
would review on-line questionnaires and electronically approve a prescription via the internet. Then pharmacies in the United
States would ship the controlled substances via private carriers to customers in numerous jurisdictions within the 50 states.
These physicians prescribed controlled substances and dangerous drugs to internet customers without establishing patient
history, performing a mental or physical exam, using appropriate diagnostic or laboratory testing, or providing a means to
monitor medication response. The prescriptions were issued after only an alleged internet consultation and without a
legitimate medical purpose.
These physicians issued prescriptions in states where they did not possess a license to practice medicine or a DEA
registration to lawfully handle controlled substances which is in violation of the Controlled Substance Act.
The indictment was issued by a federal grand jury on January 26, 2007 and is the culmination of a two- year joint investigation
led by the DEA San Juan Diversion Tactical Group and the FDA/OCI San Juan Resident Office with the assistance of the
National Drug Intelligence Center, Document Exploitation Unit.
The public is reminded that they can report suspicious internet pharmacies activities through the toll- free line 1-800-RXABUSE [ Redacted _Privacy

DEA ATTACKS INDIANA OPANA PAINKILLER EPIDEMIC
10 Arrests target R/x and meth trafficking network in HIV-infected area
INDIANAPOLIS —The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) today announced 10 arrests for drug trafficking charges related to
Opana and methamphetamine in southern Indiana. Launched last year, this operation involved state, local and federal law
enforcement in attacking the opioid and recent HIV epidemic Scott and Clark Counties.
In April of 2015, DEA Indianapolis became aware of an outbreak of HIV cases, due in part to intravenous drug use occurring in
Indiana. The abuse of meth, heroin, Opana, and other opioids is dramatically on the rise and has caused a public health crisis.
Typically Scott County would report less than 10 cases of HIV annually, but in the last 13 months has reported 188 cases.
In June 2015, agents from DEA Indianapolis launched a joint investigation with the Indiana State Police and Scott County law
enforcement officials to target the source of these powerful drugs so prevalent in the region. DEA and its partners quickly
uncovered a large-scale distribution network led by Bennito L. Rodriguez and his wife Brooklynn G. Mack, both of Scottsburg.
They obtained their drug supply from sources in Louisville, Kentucky, Indianapolis and Detroit, Michigan and oversaw a trafficking
network that included those arrested below:
Bennito L Rodriguez, a/k/a Benny, 38, Scottsburg, IN.
Brooklynn G. Mack, 29, Scottsburg, IN.
Rashawn A Vaughn, a/k/a Ray, 41, Louisville, KY.
Eric L. Gude, 36, a/k/a Bubba, Indianapolis
Rashaan S. Perkins, a/k/a Phil, a/k/a D, 21, Detroit, MI.
Anthony L. Hardy, 39, Indianapolis
James D. Haney, 56, Austin, IN.
Justin M. Roberts, a/k/a Booger, 38, Austin, IN.

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-01107420

 Travis D. Brock, 34, Scottsburg, IN.
Michael A. Doyle, 38, Scottsburg, IN.
"Scott County is one of the many great communities in our nation that is experiencing the pharmaceutical drug and
methamphetamine epidemic that is turning Americans into drug addicts," said DEA Associate Special Agent in Charge Karen I.
Flowers. "DEA will always stand with our local and state partners to fight this epidemic. Today's work is the beginning of a safer,
stronger and healthier Scott County."
DEA's efforts to address this epidemic will not stop with the arrest of these drug traffickers. DEA and its partners are also
investigating potential excessive writing or filling of opiate-based prescription medications, while also providing continued
community outreach to pharmacy employees. Part of this outreach involves educating pharmacies on potential drugs that are
diverted and sold on the illicit market.
"Scott County has been plagued with prescription drug abuse for many years and authorities there asked for federal assistance
with their problem" said Josh Minkler, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Indiana. "We were happy to assist but it is
not a problem which can be cured overnight and requires a comprehensive approach. Arresting drug dealers and reducing the
flow of illegal drugs into Scott County is a start but only one aspect of the bigger solution."
Scott County Sheriff Dan McClain said: "I am grateful for the participation of our state and federal partners in this operation. This
should be an indication to drug dealers throughout the county that our law enforcement agencies are working together to get
drugs off our streets."
"The DEA and the US Attorney have tools in their toolbox that are not available in state prosecutions, which make these types of
outcomes difficult for us to pursue with local resources alone," said Scott County Prosecutor, Jason Mount. "As one can see,
these investigations can be long-term and intensive. We appreciate their joint efforts in this matter, and look forward to continuing
to work together in both federal and state prosecutions."
"For those that are addicted, we want to point them to the services they need to end their addiction," said Indiana State Police
Superintendent Doug Carter. "But for those who are trafficking and profiting from those suffering the misery of addiction, we will
work tirelessly with our local and federal partners to put them in prison for a long, long time.
This case was jointly investigated by the Drug Enforcement Administration offices from Indianapolis, Louisville, Detroit, and
Atlanta, Scott and Clark County, Indiana Prosecutor's Office, Bureau of Acohol Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Internal
Revenue Service Criminal Investigation, U. S. Postal Inspection Service, United States Marshal's Service, Indiana State Police,
and the Sheriff's Department of Hendricks and Scott County, Indiana.
Parents and children are encouraged to educate themselves about the dangers of drugs by visiting DEA's interactive websites
at www.JustThinkTwice.com,vmv.GetSmartAboutDrugs.com and www.dea.gov.

High-Level Integrated Timeline (Updates on attachment in green)

You will note a common theme in the update. We are encountering great difficulty moving these studies
along for a variety of reasons. The EN3202-037 (Opana ER) and EN3310-302 (Opana immediate release
liquid in ages 2-12) studies needed additional protocol amendments to change inclusion/exclusion
requirements that were deemed show-stoppers by clinical sites. We have also just learned that there are
potentially irreconcilable contract issues with the site most likely to produce FPI for EN3202-037. The
EN3319-303 protocol is being revised with the help of Premier Research and will not be submitted to FDA
until mid-September. Using the current patient enrollment assumptions, this could push the sNDA
submission for Opana immediate release to December 2016.

Opana ER (EN3202-037) 7-17 yrs
Amendment 4 was drafted to address a number of issues that were resulting in sites declining to
participate in the study. It was sent for R&D Management approval on July 25, with the aim to submit to
FDA by end of next week. Due to the difficulty in recruiting pediatric patients who will be on an opioid for
3 months, the criteria for "chronic" use have been changed. Sites are being asked to recruit patients who
are candidates for chronic opioid therapy (minimum 2 week treatment) with an extended release product
instead of insisting on 3 months of dosing. The team believes that this will help with site recruitment and
patient enrollment. As of now :
o 170+ sites had been contacted, 0 sites qualified. The team is in the process of re-contacting 30+
sites to inquire if they may be interested based on these new criteria. Development Operations and
Clinical Development are working closely with the CRO to position the study more favorably with potential
sites.
o Same sites are also being used for EN3319-302, causing a bottleneck with IRB submissions and budget
negotiations.
First sites are targeted for initiation in August.
The Team is aiming for first patient in by end of September. Issues with the contract (concerning

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07873001

 risks associated with the study) at the site most likely to produce FPI are jeopardizing this milestone. S.
Schaffer is attempting to mediate, as all other elements are in place for start of study.
Opana IR Liquid (EN3319-302) 2-12 yrs
Amendment 3 was drafted to address issues which were, again, discouraging sites from
participating in the study. It was submitted to FDA on July 25.
o 5 sites up and running on Amendment 1 protocol, all have been shipped drug. 7 additional sites in
process of being initiated with changes from Amendments 2 and 3. 550+ new patients pre-screened and
failed since May. 0 new patients enrolled. Team is discussing how to identify sites that have patients that
meet the criteria of being scheduled to have surgery for which oral opioid to be used for 24/48 hrs and
are expected to be hospitalized for duration of study.
Opana IR Liquid (EN3319-303) 0-2 yrs
Charli Sanders of Premier Research has reviewed the existing protocol and FDA correspondence to
understand what elements are needed to fulfill the PREA requirements. There has been much discussion
between Dr. Sanders and Endo on the likelihood of us being able to fulfill the FDA
requirements. Nevertheless, we have instructed Premier to develop a protocol that allows us to fulfill the
stated requirements (efficacy) in an efficient, but safe manner. A final draft of the protocol is expected
from Premier by August 14 (synopsis by July 27). In parallel, S. Schaeffer is discussing the synopsis with
Chesapeake IRB to determine likelihood of acceptance prior to finalization of the protocol and submission
to FDA. Internal approvals (allowing for Labor Day holiday) should be completed in time to allow for
submission of the protocol to the FDA by mid-September.
Move of manufacturing of IR Liquid from Novartis to Patheon is underway. An acceptable quote
has been submitted. DEA quota is still being sorted out. Drug supply for EN3319-303 (including placebo)
will not be available for shipment to sites until mid/late-December at the earliest.

Opana Pediatric Program Budget

No changes have been made to the budgets for any of the studies since the last update. 2012 LBE
for EN3202-037 and EN3319 is $1.825M and $0.948M respectively (inclusive of clinical drug
supplies). Budget needs for EN3319-303 cannot be fully assessed until a draft protocol is
available. There is currently a placeholder of $0.444M in the 2012 budget for this study.

EXTERNAL: Hydrocodone reclassification harms millions suffering from chronic pain

Today's "The Hill" newspaper.
FYI
Dan
Dan Cohen
Chair - Abuse Deterrent Coalition
1001 Pennsylvania Avenue, NW

abusedeterrent„o

Hydrocodone reclassification harms millions suffering from
chronic pain
By Matt Jeffers
Nearly two years ago, the DEA made the lives of millions of Americans more difficult. On August 22, 2014, the agency moved hydrocodone
combination drugs such as Vicodin from Schedule III to Schedule II. This reclassification created tougher rules, greater bureaucracy, stricter
penalties, and a corrosive doctor-patient atmosphere for millions of Americans who suffer from chronic pain — many of whom are elderly,
financially disadvantaged, or permanently disabled. Chronic pain afflicts more than 25 million Americans according to the National Institutes of
Health. Many of those people take narcotic analgesics, such as hydrocodone, to treat their pain and improve their daily lives. These
prescription drugs bring relief to millions of people by reducing the burden of their pain. For many, the medicine means enjoying activities that
would otherwise be excruciating. For others, it means being able to work a full-time job or being able to take care of loved ones. For all, it
makes an otherwise painful existence a bit more bearable.

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-02803029

 According to the DEA, the reclassification was aimed at "curbing this [opioid] misuse and abuse." The Agency cited CDC reports indicating
that in 2010 "seventy-five percent of the prescription drug overdose deaths (16,651 people) were due to opioid drugs primarily containing
oxycodone, hydrocodone, or methadone." However, these numbers do not distinguish between medical and recreational users. Many of those
who died due to prescription drug overdose were not medically prescribed these drugs, but rather obtained them through theft or illegal
purchase. The DEA believes that they are only targeting pill mills and drug abusers, but these strict rules create artificial barriers for chronic
pain patients and distort incentives for doctors and pharmacies. Under the new rules, prescriptions cannot be refilled, meaning that chronic
pain patients must continuously return to the doctor for new prescriptions. The rules also place .greater restrictions on distributors, which in
turn reduces the total supply that pharmacies have available. This reduction in supply, coupled with the fact that pharmacies are often not
allowed to tell patients over the phone if drugs are available, forces patients to drive to numerous locations before finding a facility that has
their medicine in stock. The new rules also generated a lot of alarm among pharmacists and doctors who fear investigation from the DEA.
This can push doctors away from prescribing medication in favor of more expensive and risky physical procedures. Additionally, other
guidelines foster medical environments to treat patients with suspicion. It is now routine for doctors to have patients with a recorded history of
chronic pain urinate in a cup to prove that they are taking the medication and not selling it.
When the drug rescheduling was originally proposed, the American Medical Association came out strongly against it arguing that "the change
may limit legitimate patient access to this medication." They were right. Bureaucratic and administrative rules have serious costs. Every time a
federal agency implements a new rule, it should ask itself if it's doing more harm than good. Is the DEA protecting drug addicts or does it
mainly serve as an impediment to those who are trying to find relief? In the case of the hydrocone regulation, the answer is clearly the latter.
Pain cannot be externally measured, but the number of deaths prevented can. It is much easier for the government to point to the statistical
drop in the number of deaths caused by overdoses than it is to point to the amount of physical pain that has been relieved. There will always
be a tendency to favor what can be externally measured over what is internally experienced, since the former can be seen by all and the latter
cannot. Pain, however, is only directly observed by those it afflicts and is difficult to transport its gravity through language. In simple terms, it is
easy to count bodies, and it is almost impossible to measure pain. However, that fact does not make the pain any less real.
The DEA does a great disservice to the millions of Americans who suffer from chronic pain when it ignores the barriers to pain relief that drug
rescheduling creates. Regardless of the agency's commitment to waging a War on Drugs, people who suffer from chronic pain should not
have to suffer even more because of the combined actions of addicts and bureaucrats. Due to the negative effects that this policy has on
millions of Americans, the DEA ought to reverse its scheduling decision on hydrocodone combination drugs.

Matt Jeffers is a graduate from the University of Wisconsin, Madison holding a Bachelor's degree in Economics and Philosophy. He is
currently a Masters in Philosophy candidate at Georgia State University.

Subject: From today's Pink Sheet: Opana Safety Review Will Set Tone For Opioid Regulation Under Trump

Opana Safety Review Will Set Tone For Opioid
Regulation Under Trump
Executive Summary
FDA's 2017 advisory committee calendar is extremely light, but the one product focused review on the
schedule should be a doozy: a two-day look at safety issues with Endo's Opana ER as well as generic
versions of oxymorphone. The topic is likely to resonate with the Trump Administration and especially
Vice President Pence.

A March review of Endo Pharmaceuticals Inc.'s Opana ER formulation and other versions of
oxymorphone will provide an early read on the future of opioid pain drug regulation in the Trump
Administration.

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-01354182

 By accident or design, FDA has chosen a particularly resonant case study for its first opioid
formulation review of 2017, one that illustrates the pitfalls for betting too heavily on "abuse-deterrent"
formulation technology to combat the epidemic, with consequences that flared into controversy for the
new Vice President when he was governor of Indiana.
At this point, Endo's attempt an abuse-deterrent formulation of its extended-release oxymorphone
looks like a failure. While the product is intended to be crush-resistant and therefore more difficult to
snort, FDA rejected an explicit labeling claim in 2013. (Also see "FDA Crushes Endo's Hopes, Allows
Original Opana Generics To Remain On Market" - Pink Sheet, 10 May, 2013.)
One key element of FDA's rejection was that it appeared that the new formulation might be easier to
inject than the original formulation — raising the question of whether the result was a net positive or
negative for the public health.
Then injectable Opana abuse was cited as a key factor in an outbreak of HIV in Indiana, which became
a high profile public health crisis for Pence when he was the state's governor. Pence ultimately
implemented a policy to allow needle exchange programs in the country most affected by the outbreak.

Best-Case Scenario: Public Humiliation
Endo resubmitted an application to seek an explicit abuse deterrent claim, but withdrew it in 2016 after
"discussions with FDA.- (Also see "Keeping Track: Opana ER Abuse Deterrence Claim Withdrawn.,
Third Neulasta Biosimilar Submitted., Keytruda Cleared In Head And Neck Cancer" - Pink Sheet, 12
Aug, 2016.)
The company had previously announced that the review would be delayed to allow for an advisory
committee in the fall. At the time, that did not seem unduly ominous, given FDA's new policy of taking
all opioid formulations to committee prior to approval. When Endo subsequently pulled the
application, however, that signaled the end to attempts to re-establish the brand as a major growth
product.
The company now no longer cites Opana as a core brand as its sales erode in the face of competition
from generics approved as equivalent to the original formulation. In addition, Endo divested its newest
entrant in the opioid category, returning rights to the recently approved buprenhorphine formulation
Belbuca to developer BioDelivery Sciences International Inc.
In a best-case scenario for Endo, the March meeting will simply be a chance for FDA to register
publicly the concerns about the formulation that it has already raised in the context of the review of the
withdrawn application. However, the framing of the meeting does leave open some other, even worse
outcomes — including potentially the removal of the new formulation in the belief that the original was
in fact safer. Given the tone of past advisory committee discussions and FDA's intention to look at all
formulation of oxymorphone — including IR forms — may lead to broader calls to withdraw the
ingredient altogether.
FDA's announcement of the meeting makes clear that this is not a typical new formulation review, but
rather an assessment of "safety issues." The two-day meeting, March 13-14, will involve the Drug
Safety & Risk Management and Anesthetic & Analgesic advisory committees in a discussion of "pre-

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-01354183

 and post-marketing data about the abuse of OPANA ER, and the overall risk-benefit of this product.
The committees will also discuss abuse of generic oxymorphone ER and oxymorphone immediaterelease (1R) products." (Also see "Endo's Opana ER, Generic Oxymorphone Safety Get US FDA Panel
Review" - Pink Sheet, 10 Jan, 2017.)

Agency Actions Vs Industry Actions
How those issues play out will be an important marker of how FDA's continued review of the opioid
pain reliever class plays out in the Trump Administration — and potentially for how other government
agencies move to address abuse.
On the campaign trail, the opioid abuse issue was one area where candidate Trump outlined a detailed
series of policy proposals. During an October campaign stop in New Hampshire (a state he ultimately
lost by a very narrow margin), Trump repeated a pledge from the GOP primaries at the start of 2016 to
make the issue a high priority. (Also see "Drug Abuse And US Presidential Politics: Surprising
Bipartisan Agreement" - Pink Sheet, 1 Nov, 2016.)
Among his list of policy prescriptions, he called out FDA for moving too slowly to approve abusedeterrent formulations. On the other hand, he also called for sharp reductions in production quotas by
DEA to help curb over-prescribing of opioids in general.
The Opana ER experience seems like a case study in why FDA is smart to apply high standards to
proposed abuse deterrent formulations — and perhaps for taking a closer look at industry practices
rather than agency decisions. Endo is under investigation by at least five different state and local
agencies, including the New Hampshire attorney general, for its marketing of the new formulation.

Date:

Monday, January 13 2014 03:43 PM

Subject: EXTERNAL: [The Pain Community] Medscape: CMS Proposes New Rules to Combat Prescription Drug Abuse
From:

pain-community@googlegroups.com

To:

pain-community@googlegroups.com;

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has proposed new rules to combat fraud and abuse in the federal Medicare
Advantage and Part D prescription drug program.
"Prescription drug abuse is a serious and growing problem nationwide. Unfortunately, the Medicare Part D prescription drug program
(Part D) is not immune from the abuses associated with this nationwide epidemic," CMS said in a statement issued January 6.
CMS takes this problem "seriously and is taking steps to protect Medicare beneficiaries and the Medicare Trust fund from the harm and
damaging effects associated with prescription drug abuse," the statement reads.
Dual Targets
CMS says a centerpiece of the antifraud strategy that focuses on protecting beneficiaries is identifying Part D enrollees who have
"potential opioid or acetaminophen over utilization issues that indicate the need to implement appropriate controls on these drugs for the
identified beneficiaries."
In addition, the agency will employ data analysis to identify prescribers and pharmacies that may be engaged in fraudulent or abusive
activities.
"We are leveraging CMS' access to all PDE [Prescription Drug Event] data and using it to guide our anti-fraud efforts and share the results
of our analysis with Part D plan sponsors, law enforcement agencies and pharmacy and physician licensing boards, as appropriate, so this
information can assist our joint efforts to combat fraud and abuse," CMS says.
A key provision of the proposed rules is to require prescribers of Part D drugs to enroll in Medicare. This will ensure that Part D drugs are
prescribed only by qualified individuals, CMS explains.
CMS is also seeking authority to revoke a physician's or eligible professional's Medicare enrollment if:
• CMS determines that he or she has a pattern or practice of prescribing Part D drugs that is abusive and represents a threat to the
health and safety of Medicare beneficiaries or otherwise fails to meet Medicare requirements; or
• His or her Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Certificate of Registration is suspended or revoked; or
• The applicable licensing or administrative body for any state in which a physician or eligible professional practices has suspended
or revoked the physician or eligible professional's ability to prescribe drugs.
"Providing CMS the authority to revoke such prescribers' Medicare enrollment would help protect beneficiaries and the Medicare Trust
Fund from fraud, waste and abuse," the agency says.
Another proposed rule would provide CMS, its antifraud contractors, and other oversight agencies the ability to request and collect
information directly from pharmacy benefit managers, pharmacies, and other downstream entities that contract or subcontract with Part D
sponsors to administer the Medicare prescription drug benefit.
This provision would streamline CMS's and its antifraud contractors' investigative processes, the agency says.
"Currently, it can take a long time for CMS' contractors who are often assisting law enforcement to obtain important documents like
invoices and prescriptions directly from pharmacies, because they must work through the Part D plan sponsor to obtain this information,"
they explain in a statement. "This proposal is designed to provide more timely access to records, including for investigations of Part D
fraud and abuse, and responds to recommendations from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office of Inspector
General."

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07446652

 Overutilization Monitoring System Working
The CMS is also targeting payment accuracy by proposing that Medicare Advantage plans and Part D sponsors report and return
identified Medicare over payments.
The proposed CMS regulations to combat fraud and abuse in Medicare Advantage and Part D prescription drug plan are scheduled for
official publication in the Federal Register on January 10, 2014. CMS will accept comments on them until March 7, 2014, and then issue a
final version of the regulations.
Last summer, CMS implemented the Overutilization Monitoring System (OMS) to combat Part D fraud and abuse, and it's paying off, the
agency reports. "An initial comparison with 2011 PDE data pre-dating the implementation of OMS shows there has already been a
substantial reduction in the number of acetaminophen and opioid overutilizers in Medicare Part D," CMS reports.

<munroe.brian@endo.com>; 'Paul.Romness@boehringer- in .elheim.com' <Paul.Romness@boehringerin selheim.com>: 'Patrick Flues' <pplues@cephalon.com>;

Irizarry' <sinzarry@caphillgrp.com >; 'Tom.Long@watson.com' <Tom.Long@watson.com >;

You have asked us whether the Drug Enforcement Administration ("DEA") registration process could be used
as a vehicle to collect and document practitioner compliance with the Food and Drug Administration's ("FDA's
") opioid class-wide Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies ("REMS") certification and training
requirements. This memorandum discusses the legal and practical issues involved if DEA were to require
applicants for a DEA practitioner registration to provide such information in lieu of requiring affected opioid
manufacturers to monitor practitioners' compliance with FDA's REMS certification requirement.
In summary, there is no statutory or regulatory mandate that would compel DEA to require this certification.
However, it would not be inconsistent under either the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or the Controlled
Substances Act ("CSA") for DEA to request this certification on its practitioner registration application forms.
It would also be consistent with DEA's recent initiatives to combat the increased levels of abuse of controlled
substance prescription medicine.

The FDA has notified a number of companies that certain opioid products will be required to have a REMS to
ensure that "the benefits of the drugs continue to outweigh the risks of: 1) use of certain opioid products in nonopioid-tolerant individuals; 2) abuse; and 3) overdose, both accidental and intentional." FDA, Opioid REMS
Invitation Template (available at: http://www.fda.gov/cder/drug/infopage/opioids/default.html). In relevant
part, Section 505-1 of the Food and Drug Administration Amendments Act of 2008 ("FDAAA"), states that
FDA may require, as an element to assure safe use and access for patients for drugs with know serious risks,
that: "(A) health care providers who prescribe the drug have particular training or experience, or are
specifically certified (. . . ); [and/or] (B) pharmacies, practitioners, or health care settings that dispense drugs
are specially certified." 21 U.S.C. § 355-1(f)(3).
FDA has indicated that a database of all affected health care practitioners, institutions, and pharmacies would
be required to document certifications to monitor and evaluate implementation of the opioid REMS. Sharon
Hertz, M.D., Proposed Opioid REMS, FDA, CDER, March 3, 2009 (available at:
hit p: \\ \\ \\
cciciinfopage/opioids/meeting/20090303.html). Responsibility for creating and
maintaining the REMS training and certification could be assigned to the manufacturers who market the opioid
drugs. This could create a significant burden on manufacturers to collect and maintain such data and subject
the manufacturers to possible penalties for any errors or omissions in this effort.
Therefore, we have reviewed the possibility that DEA could collect and maintain such information.
Specifically, we have looked into whether it might be possible, that DEA could document and maintain this
information as part of the controlled substance application and renewal registration process.
The CSA requires that DEA consider certain factors in determining whether a practitioner, that is, a pharmacy
or physician, should be registered with DEA to dispense, prescribe, or administer controlled substances,
including narcotics. 21 U.S.C. § 823(f). These factors include the practitioner's "[c]ompliance with applicable
State, Federal, or local laws relating to controlled substances." 21 U.S.C. § 823(f)(4). The CSA does not

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-08537766

 further define the scope of these terms or requirements including how it would define "Federal law." The CSA
also provides that DEA may pursue revocation or denial of a DEA registration if a practitioner "has committed
such acts as would render his registration if . . . inconsistent with the public interest" 21 U.S.C. § 824(a)(4).
By reference, this means DEA can revoke a DEA registration or deny a renewal application if it is found that a
DEA registrant has failed to comply with Federal law.
Arguably, if FDA imposes a class-wide opioid REMS under the authority granted by a Federal law like
FDAAA, the requirement will have the force and effect of a "Federal law." Given that the CSA requires
DEA to consider compliance with Federal law, it would not be inconsistent for DEA to require
practitioners who apply for a new or renewed DEA registration (DEA From 224) to certify that they are
familiar and in compliance with FDA's opioid REMS educational requirement. DEA could then use a
practitioner's certification of REMS compliance, or lack thereof, as a factor in deciding whether to issue
a controlled substance registration to the practitioner.
The current DEA application for registration, DEA Form 224, already contains certain "liability" questions
that must be answered by each applicant. These questions require the applicant to respond as to whether the
company, an officer or a director has surrendered a DEA registration, had a professional license suspended or
revoked, or been convicted of a crime related to controlled substances. See Section 5. Thus, it would not be
inconsistent with the CSA or the DEA application process for DEA to require that an applicant state whether it
has complied with the practitioner certification for compliance with FDA's opioid REMS requirements as an
additional liability factor for use in determining the applicant's fitness for controlled substance registrations.
Section 2 of the DEA Form 224 provides practitioners with the option of checking either the "Narcotic" or
"Non-Narcotic" classifications of Schedules II and III controlled substances. This section of the Form 224
could be used, or perhaps modified in some way, in conjunction with new language inserted into Section 5 to
indicate that only those practitioners who intend to prescribe, dispense, or administer the opioids subject to
FDA's REMS requirements need to make the proper certification.
We would suggest the following language for insertion into Section 5 of the current DEA Form 224:
"If the applicant intends to dispense, prescribe, or administer narcotic drugs, does the applicant certify that the
applicant is in compliance with all Food and Drug Administration Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies
(REMS) associated with the narcotic drugs, including but not limited to, knowledge of all educational and
training materials issued by the manufacturers of the narcotic drugs and of the risks associated with and
conditions for safe use of the narcotic drugs? Yes or No"
The proposal outlined above may be subject to some opposition. First, although we have not conducted
extensive research into the case law, we believe there are some administrative law cases that may challenge the
argument that an agency action, like a REMS requirement constitutes a measure that has the full force and
effect of a Federal law. These judicial opinions could be used by opponents of this proposal to argue that it
should not be implemented. DEA itself may oppose the measure because it would add to their administrative
burden. On the other hand, it is consistent with DEA's recent initiatives on regulating prescribing practices for
controlled substances, especially pain medications. Finally, as a practical matter, even if DEA were to elect to
require practitioner REMS certification as part of its controlled substance registration application and renewal
process, there can be no assurance that FDA would agree that this certification mechanism would be sufficient
to relieve opioid manufacturers from any obligation to independently and directly obtain certification of
compliance with FDA's final opioid REMS requirements from each practitioner who intends to prescribe,
dispense, or administer the manufacturers' narcotic drugs. Any effort to persuade DEA to assume
responsibility for obtaining and monitoring practitioners' compliance with FDA's opioid REMS requirement
therefore would have to be conducted in conjunction with an effort to persuade FDA that a DEA-administered
certification program will adequately address its concerns.
In conclusion, there is a good argument that, as a matter of law, the FDA's REMS practitioner certification
requirement can be interpreted as having the full force and effect of a "Federal law" and thus DEA should

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-08537767

 consider compliance with REMS in its review of a practitioner's DEA registration application. Opposition to
DEA adding this to its application form will likely focus on the legal issue of whether the REMS initiative does
have the effect of Federal law and whether DEA's compliance tracking fulfills FDA's mandate. However, in
our opinion, there is nothing that legally precludes DEA from requiring controlled substance registration
applicants to certify their compliance with FDA's opioid REMS requirements, and doing so would advance the
DEA stated mission of further combating the increased levels of controlled substance abuse.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

placed on probation for five years and he must fulfill other obligations such as keeping a "controlled substances log" for

Date:

Thursday, July 6 2006 02:03 PM

Subject:

Re: Digital Pain Expert

From:

Michael Moskowitz <wolfhowl @ix.netcom.com>

To:

Brown,Bobbie-Sue;

Attachments: Post Test Opioid 2 sides.doc; ATT4417541.htm; initialassessment.doc; ATT4417542.htm

Dear Bobbie-Sue,
Here is the other two missing parts. On May 16, the day I returned from my vacation the DEA came to visit me
unannounced. They had not received a complaint and had not investigated me beyond the fact that I prescribed
a lot of opioid medications. They had 12 specific charts they had subpoenaed and they interviewed me for an
hour and one half and then reviewed the charts for an hour. They asked me all of the questions that followed the
Federation of State Medical Board Guidelines, part of the course I teach with Bill and Bobbie, an article I wrote
with Diane for the NIPC newsletter, and a method of documentation I follow religiously. When they came to
the section on informed consent, they asked if I gave any form of informed consent. I was able to give each of
the three agents a shrink wrapped copy of the Digital Expert Pain Expert DVD, the written informed consent
and the evaluation we ask the patient to fill when they see it. They were notably surprised and impressed when I
did so and it seemed a major turning point, when the interview went from interrogation to informal and
educational chat. One of the odd things is that if you google me, you can see that I practice pain medicine, that I
am a nationally known lecturer on the subject of opioid treatment and that I am a member of the AAPM. They
didn't know the name of our practice when they arrived. They spent time in the waiting room, while I was
finishing up with my current patient and took in our patient population, stating at the outset that the people in
our waiting room looked like they had "a lot of pain." The Subpoena is a scary document that states rather
clearly that any evidence found of an incriminating nature could be used against me in a criminal prosecution.
They were not intimidating, but they were thorough and were clearly looking for documentation, including
aberrant behavior and referral patterns to verify that I was taking care. Up until this point everything I've taught
about safety has been theoretical. Now it is quite practical, as they gave me a clean bill of health and said that
the practice was obviously performing a needed service and the documentation was excellent. While I do not
think the DVD protected above the rest, it is clear to me that it was a lynchpin in that documentation. I have
recently set up a series of True False questions to give after the patient views the DVD. These are easy
questions to answer correctly if the DVD is viewed and can be repeated later on if the patient exhibits aberrant
behavior. I will attach these to the email. I'm looking forward to Monday's dinner and I'm excited about the
potential of Opana for a number of our patients. I will also email you some of our other documentation.
Michael

Friday, June 8, 2012
Top Clips
Brand Biologics, Generics Battle Over REMS Provision In User Fee Bill
(6/8 FDA Week) reports "...The Generic Pharmaceutical Association sent a letter this week to top lawmakers on the Senate health and House Energy
and Commerce committees reiterating support for the REMS provision. We believe that this language will expedite access to safe and effective
generic drugs, and provide a more effective method for raising revenue than an alternative provision in the House legislation, which would make a
modest change in the statutory language regarding citizen petitions,' said GPhA President and CEO Ralph Neas in a Thursday (June 7) statement,
explaining the group's concerns. At a time of great budgetary challenges for consumers and for the federal government, it is especially important that
barriers to fair and timely generic drug and biosimilar competition are addressed, and the Senate provision provides the most effective way of
ensuring this is the case,' he adds." Paid Subscription Required
Battle Lines Drawn in Brand vs. Generic Fight Over Cost-Saving Efforts in PDUFA Bills
(6/8 Drug Industry Daily) reports "Generic-drug makers have been rooting for a provision in the Senate's FDA user fee bill that would expand access
to REMS-restricted brand drugs to aid them in developing generic versions. But some proponents are not confident that language will survive the
ongoing reconciliation with the House version. Instead, another cost-saving measure supported by brand drugmakers could be the chosen avenue for
savings....The Generic Pharmaceutical Association wrote a letter Wednesday to congressional leaders voicing its strong support of the REMS
provision." Paid Subscription Required
Generics Industry Pushes Congress On Brand-Name Samples
(6/7, Rachel Slajda, IP Law360) reports "...The generics industry claims that brand-name drug makers are using the restrictions to refuse to provide
samples to generics makers, which need samples for the bioequivalence testing required to win FDA approval. The industry also claims that some
companies have voluntarily taken on REMS as part of a strategy to slow down generic development...GPhA also advised Congress to drop an
amendment to the Senate bill that would reclassify most hydrocodone drugs as Schedule III controlled substances." Paid Subscription Required
Government & Policy
House Committee Joins Senate in Jacking Up Counterfeiting, Drug Theft Penalties
(6/8 Drug Industry Daily) reports "...H.R. 3668, approved by a voice vote, would raise the maximum prison sentence for an individual who
knowingly manufactured, sold or trafficked counterfeit drugs from 10 years to 20 for a first offense and 30 years for a second offense. Fines could
range from $5 million to $30 million, depending on the number of offenses and size of the organization. The new penalties arc in line with the current
repercussions for trafficking in counterfeit military goods or services." Paid Subscription Required
Hydrocodone Gets Advisory Committee Review, Offering Congress A Scheduling Out
(6/7, Martin Berman-Gorvine, The Pink Sheet Daily) reports "...The Drug Enforcement Administration may have created a path for a congressional
truce on the question of how hydrocodone should be scheduled. The occasion is an FDA Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee
meeting Oct. 29-30, convened at the instigation of DEA, which will discuss the abuse potential of hydrocodone-containing drugs combined with
other analgesics or as an antitussive." Paid Subscription Required
Vicodin-Type Pain Pills May Face Stricter U.S. Regulation
(6/7, Anna Edney, Bloomberg) reports "...Advisers to the Food and Drug Administration, which regulates pharmaceutical sales, will meet in October
to discuss the risks and benefits of hydrocodone preparations used as pain relievers or cough suppressants, the agency said in a notice today on its
website. The DEA has been taking a closer look at rules for hydrocodone combinations since 1999." Full
California Track-and-Trace Law Is Good Model, EMD Serono Says
(6/7, Cathy Dombrowski, The Pink Sheet Daily) reports "...While FDA and an alliance of stakeholders debate the best way to implement a track-andtrace system for pharmaceuticals, EMD Serono has in place an electronic pedigree system for its specialty products and says a California
requirement for an e-pedigree to accompany individual drug packages through pharmacy dispensing is reasonable." Paid Subscription Required
FDA Eyes Health Reform Program To Advance Regulatory Science
(6/8 FDA Week) reports "...Jesse Goodman, chief scientist at FDA, said the Cures Acceleration Network, or CAN, program should not mimic
commercial drug development -- where therapies are developed for a narrow purpose -- but should select projects that could have a larger impact on
drug development. Goodman said FDA is looking at CAN as a way to leverage a lot of the agency's interests in drug development, including in
advancing its regulatory science priorities, along with gaining a better understanding of disease mechanisms." Paid Subscription Required

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07367340

 Injectable Boniva Drug in Short Supply - US FDA
(6/7 Reuters) reports "Patients who want an injectable form of Roche Holding AG's bone-strengthening drug Boniva may not be able to get it in the
next few weeks because the company did not accurately forecast demand, federal officials said. A mismatch between company forecasts and actual
demand is one of the many reasons medicines can go into shortage, especially when there is only one company making them." Full
Cancer Drug Shortages 'A Total Nightmare'
(6/8, Sanjena Sathian, Pittsburgh Post-Gazette) reports "...The legislation being pushed in Washington is expected to be sent to President Barack
Obama before Congress takes its August recess. Under the measures, federal officials would have to take steps to `help mitigate or prevent' the
shortages, perhaps by finding other sources of supply, in this country or abroad. Manufacturers would also have to inform the FDA before shutting
down production of certain drugs. Still, the legislation won't do anything to address the current shortages or offer incentives for generic drugmakers
to continue producing older, cheaper drugs." Full
NACDS Appoints Tom O'Donnell as VP Federal Government Affairs
(6/7, Allison Cerra, Drug Store News) reports "The chief of staff for Rep. Steve Rothman, D-N.J., is taking on a new role. The National Association
of Chain Drug Stores announced that Tom O'Donnell is joining the organization as VP federal government affairs, where he will spearhead the
strategic direction for and overall management of NACDS' federal legislative advocacy program, including serving as a resource and advocate on
Capitol Hill and advancing the association's grassroots and political affairs activities, NACDS president and CEO Steve Anderson said." Full
Influence Roundup: BIO Hires New Lobbyist, Gramm Joins AEI, and More
(6/7, Andrew Joseph, National Journal) reports "The Biotechnology Industry Organization has named Derrick White its director of federal
government relations. The onetime aide to Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-Utah) was previously the principal at Derrick White Consulting and a lobbyist at
PhRMA." Full
Blog: Gulp: Antidepressants, Autism & The Water Supply
(6/7, Ed Silverman, Pharmalot) reports "Yet another study suggests that pharmaceuticals finding their way into the water supply may be linked to a
troubling issue. A team of researchers has discovered that fish show autism-like gene expression after exposure to water containing antidepressants,
such as Prozac and Effexor. The results may suggest an environmental trigger for autism, although the researchers caution this may only apply to
genetically predisposed people." Full
Blog: Dear Janet: What Does The FDA Really Do?
(6/7, Ed Silverman, Pharmalot) reports "In its most recent bid to appear attentive and transparent, the FDA has initiated a new program: Ask Janet.
Actually, the effort has a crunchier name — the CDER Director's Mailbag. In any event, the FDA now has an online form on its web site in which each
and every one of you can ask Janet Woodcock, who is the director of the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, a burning question about the drug
or policy of your choice (here it is)." Full
Industry
Medicis Sues To Block Zydus' Generic Acne Treatment
(6/7, Camille DeMere, IP Law360) reports "Medicis Pharmaceutical Corp. hauled Zydus Pharmaceuticals USA Inc. and its parent company to New
Jersey federal court on Tuesday, claiming the drugmakers' proposal to manufacture generic versions of acne drug Solodyn violates three of its
patents." Paid Subscription Required
Bayer Finds Some of Its Global Suppliers Need `Considerable' Quality Upgrades
(6/8 Drug Industry Daily) reports "In a recent assessment of a small sliver of Bayer's vast global network of suppliers, 10 percent were found to
require `considerable' improvement on quality, the company says in a new report." Paid Subscription Required

EU Drug-Scanning Plan to Secure Supply Chain Is Held Up by Repackaging Obstacle
(6/8 Drug Industry Daily) reports "Counterproductive cross-border repackaging requirements in the EU are holding back a group of drug distributors
from approving a drugmaker-backed supply chain security plan to scan all treatments at the point of dispensing." Paid Subscription Required
EMA Urges Quick Communication Among EU States About Drugmaker C MP Failures Found by Outside-EU Sources
(6/8 Drug Industry Daily) reports "The European Medicines Agency (EMA) is stressing the need for timely, coordinated communications between
EU member states when one state finds out about a drugmaker's noncompliance with good manufacturing practices (GMPs) from a non-EU country's
regulators or from an international organization, such as the World Health Organization." Paid Subscription Required

Pharmaceutical Association Release]
(5/7 Canada NewsWire) comments "The release of 2011 Canadian prescription drug sales information by IMS Brogan shows that generic
prescription medicines offer greater value than ever before for Canadians, Jim Keon, President of the Canadian Generic Pharmaceutical Association
(CGPA), said today. Generic prescription medicines were dispensed to fill more than 60 percent of all prescriptions in Canada, yet accounted for less
than 25 percent of the $22-billion Canadians spent on prescription drugs in 2011." Full

text:
Date:

Tuesday, July 27 2010 12:31 PM

Subject: FW: Brief Summary - Opioid REMS Ad Comm
From:

Barto, Bob

To:

Chapman, Tara <chapman.tara@endo.com>;

Bob Barto
VP, Regulatory Affairs
Endo Pharmaceuticals Inc
From: Barto, Bob
Sent: Monday, July 26, 2010 3:45 PM
To: Gergel, Ivan
Cc: Kitlinski, Linda; Clark, Michael
Subject: Brief Summary - Opioid REMS Ad Comm

Ivan,
Below is a high level summary of the opioid REMS Ad Comm meeting:
The committee generally agreed that abuse of prescription ER opioids is a growing problem and a significant
public health issue. This is a societal issue and FDA cannot solve the problem without the cooperation of other
governmental agencies. The data supporting the extent of the problem is less than ideal and the committee
acknowledged that new data streams would need to be developed to determine if the REMS is having any
impact on the problem.
FDA presented their proposed REMS to the panel and the two major criticisms of the FDA's proposal were that
the educational component was voluntary and that immediate-release (IR) opioid formulations were not
included in the REMS. The IWG presented their proposed REMS which is very similar to the FDA REMS with
the major exception being the desire of the IWG to include a Communication Plan. FDA confirmed that if a
Communication Plan exists under a REMS and if an ANDA is approved for the same product, FDA must
assume responsibility for the Communication Plan. FDA admitted that they did not include a Communication
Plan in the proposed REMS due to resource limitations at FDA.
With respect to the educational component of the REMS, the committee expressed opinions that voluntary
education would not work (i.e., education does not change behavior) and that HCPs should receive training, not
education, and it should be mandatory. FDA indicated there were two options available for mandatory training
the first being a registry type system administered by the manufacturers and the second option was to use the
DEA registration system. The committee seemed to be uncomfortable with manufacturers running the registry
system and FDA stated that legislative action was required in order to use the DEA system. FDA viewed the
DEA registration as a long term solution and voluntary education training as an immediate solution.
Regarding IR opioids, committee members weren't convinced by the data presented that the public health issue
could be resolved without including IR opioids in the REMS. Some members stated that IR issues would be
covered by default in the ER training materials whereas FDA indicated that they did not believe they had a
safety signal to require REMS for IR opioids.
The committee voted on only one question — "please vote on whether you agree with the Agency's proposed
REMSfor the extended-release and long-acting opioid analgesics and discuss the rationale for your vote".
Members were instructed prior to voting that a yes vote meant that the Member agrees with every aspect of the
proposed REMS put forth by FDA and a no vote does not mean that the Member disagrees with the principle of
a REMS only that he/she disagrees with all or part of the FDA's proposal. The vote was 25 members against,

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07612569

 10 members in favor. All members of the committee who voted no support the concept of a REMS but felt that
the proposed REMS would fall short of its goals primarily because the educational component was voluntary
and that IR products were not included. Those who voted yes stated that although the proposed REMS fell
short in many aspects FDA needed to start somewhere due to the seriousness of the problem.
The public comment session was fairly balanced and primarily featured spokespersons from professional
organizations that came to voice their support for the proposed REMS and also offer recommendations for
enhancing the REMS. Comments from all professional/patient organizations that Endo and IWG have been
working with were supportive of the FDA proposed REMS and urged the Agency to keep patient
access/avoiding undue burden high on its list of priorities in approving a final REMS. Some stakeholders also
provided suggestions for implementing particular portions of the REMS based upon their respective
expertise/interest (e.g. provider training/education, easy-to-understand patient info sheets, metrics, etc.). One
interesting suggestion by the representative from the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network was
that the FDA be prepared to implement "an exit strategy" from REMS if it resulted in unintended consequences
on patient access.
Another topic discussed by the committee was regarding FDA's control around advertising and promotion of
ER opioids. Some committee members voiced concerns that excessive promotion by manufacturers could
diminish the impact of a REMS whereas others felt industry should apply all their expertise in A&P to get the
word out to the public about REMS and the risks of inappropriate use of ER opioids.
The committee recognized the limitations of REMS and acknowledged that a REMS alone would not solve the
public health problem. The committee encouraged more interagency cooperation to address the problem but
fell short of defining exactly what needs to be done.
Next steps:
FDA will need to consider the committee's recommendations and decide whether or not to proceed with the
program as presented or to make modifications. It appears unlikely that FDA will move at this time point to
include IR opioids as they admitted that they do not have the data necessary to support the requirement of a
REMS. Revising the REMS to make the education/training mandatory is well within the scope of their
regulatory authority at this time. Endo has been actively engaged in discussions with all key educational
stakeholders since the inception of the IWG and has discussed both voluntary and mandatory training/education
options. Professional and patient stakeholders will be submitting specific recommendations to the docket for
the FDA's consideration. Endo's proactive planning/established relationships with the educational stakeholder
will assure we are well-positioned for whatever form the final REMS training/education takes. The opioid
REMS docket is open through October 19, 2010 and traditionally FDA has not taken action when a docket is
open. From a regulatory perspective the next step is for FDA to issue a letter to each sponsor informing them
that a REMS is necessary and a timeline of when it needs to be submitted. It is premature to speculate when
FDA intends on issuing the letter or its contents with respect to the REMS components.

Bob
(with input from Linda Kitlinski and Michael Clark)

From: Utt, James

To: Teat, Roderick; Thomson, Heather; Hartry, Ann; Crawford, Deborah; Lopez, Victoria; Birner, Tim;
Britt, Bonnie; Hill, Peter; Gilbert, John; Thomas, Greg
Cc: Rubino, Mark; Sawyers, Timothy; Owens, Glenda; DeLucia, Michael; Polansky, Paul; Berner, Todd;
Howell, Brian; Logan, Alicia; Wieman, Matthew; Arment, Robert
Subject: Some selected highlights from the East Tennessee Rx Drug Summit (7/26/11 in Knoxville)

On Tuesday, July 26th, I attended the East Tennessee Prescription Drug Summit held in Knoxville at the
UT Conference Center. I was one of about 250 attendees present. Most were law enforcement personnel
from local police departments and sheriffs' offices, parole officers, drug diversion investigators, district
attorneys' offices, as well as several present from various state and federal law enforcement agencies and
judicial districts. Others in attendance included drug abuse counselors, social workers, psychologists,
school counselors, educators, physicians, nurse practitioners, pharmacists, pharmaceutical manufacturers,
nurses, elected and appointed local, state, and federal government officials, and members of the press.
The Summit was organized by the staff of US Attorney for Eastern Tennessee, William Killian and is one of
many similar conferences being sponsored at key locations across the nation by other Justice Dept.
officials. The principal guest speakers at the Summit were Regina LaBelle, Policy Advisor in the White
House Office of National Drug Control Policy, Joe Rannazzisi, Deputy Assistant Administrator at the Drug
Enforcement Administration, and John Eadie of the Brandeis University Prescription Monitoring Program
Center of Excellence. Other speakers included drug diversion invesigators, prosecuting attorneys,
providers involved in patient care (MD, PharmD, LCSW, DDS), a recovering addict, elected officials. Each
shared a number of meaningful statistics documenting aspects of the prescription drug abuse problem as
well as perspectives from their own professional points of view. Here are some of the many interesting
comments from the various speakers throughout the day.

Joe Rannazzisi of DEA briefly cited OpanaER as a product that is surfacing more and more as a drug
of diversion. (When he mentioned this, there was an audible murmur of "yes", "that's right", etc. from
several members of the audience.)
> 6,000 persons per day [> 2 million persons per year] are initiating non-medical use of pain
2

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06835765

 relievers (of these, 2,500 per day are teens, with 60% of those < 15 yo)
The Vaults of Erowid [www.erowid.org] is a website that contains lots of information - some
scientific, some not scientific - about drugs and other substances used for recreational purposes; it's
frequently accessed by teenagers and young adults seeking information on psychoactive drugs and other
mind-altering substances.
Immediate-release oxycodone 30 mg tablets (Roxicodone) have grown in popularity since the
reformulation of Oxycontin. Many Rx's for it are being generated in Florida.
Florida pill mill explosion came after legislation shut off hundreds of internet pharmacies.
As FL laws banned dispensing of drugs from pain clinics, applications for new pharmacies (located
next to the clinics) have risen sharply. Amazing who some of these proposed pharmacy owners are (e.g.
truck drivers, exotic dancers, etc.). (DEA reviewing these applications.)
There are 7+ Rx drug overdose deaths per day in Florida.
In Tennessee, there are five deaths due to prescription drug overdoses for every death due to
methamphetamine or cocaine overdose.
Nationally, in 2009, 6.8% of admissions to drug treatment facilities were for abuse of opioids
In Tennessee in 2009, 23% of admissions to drug treatment facilities were for abuse of opioids
In eastern Tennessee in 2009, 42% of admissions to drug treatment facilities were for abuse of
opioids
Median age of persons admitted to drug treatment facilities in Tennessee is approx. 30 yo (slight
surplus of women over men)
In the aggregate, prescription drug misuse has surpassed marijuana as the gateway drug for new
users of drugs susceptible to abuse.
In Florida and Washington (perhaps other states too), there's been a quadrupling of the rate of
newborns who are physically dependent on opioids.
The prevalence of opioid prescriptions written for adolescents is growing steadily (largely driven by
prescriptions from dentists and oral surgeons)
"Doctor shopping" is most common in patients in their 20's and 30's (younger age groups than
usually predicted).
The source of the explosion of opioid use in part goes to the time in the mid-1990s when risks of
opioids were often described as not being as great as previously thought (though subsequent evidence
documents that the risks are indeed greater than was being described in the mid-1990s). This period
coincided with the increase in focus on pain as a prominent assessment factor in patient care.
There needs to be better and wider access to prescription drug monitoring programs in the states
so that appropriate analyses can be done with information dissemination to public health and other
appropriate authorities. Need laws passed to enable Veterans Health facilities and DOD health facilities to
share controlled substance prescribing and prescription filling data to prescription drug monitoring
programs.
•
In 2010, Knoxville, Tennessee had the 2nd greatest number of pharmacy robberies in the nation
(#46).
The task of prosecuting prescribing providers (for inappropriate prescribing of controlled
3

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06835766

 substances) is difficult - mounds of evidence have to be accumulated to have a good chance of proving
guilt beyond a reasonable doubt (juries often tend to sympathize with providers who "are just trying to
take care of very sick patients as best they can"). When investigations are underway, it's often useful to
get IRS investigators involved. Unscrupulous prescribers almost always run afoul of laws pertaining to tax
reporting, money-laundering, etc. That's often a successful avenue for convictions.
Can buy blank tamper-resistant Rx paper over the internet, get DEA #'s and NPI #'s, prescriber
addresses via the internet; diverters can print very authentic looking fake Rx's, then take to other
geographic areas to get filled.
Pain Management Clinics (ie. "pill mills") are moving north out of Florida as new laws take effect in
Florida to curb these businesses. Many setting up shop in Georgia and Tennessee.
Thefts are becoming more brazen. In addition to more pharmacy robberies, recently there was
nearly a successful attempt to hijack a drug wholesaler's courier van (used to deliver controlled
substances to pharmacies that had ordered them).
In middle Tennessee, growing demand for Suboxone, high-dose immediate-release oxycodone,
Adderall, alprazolam, OpanaER.
Law enforcement has to pay more attention opioid diversion (don't keep focus on meth, marijuana,
and heroin)
Need closer regulatory oversight of physicians who are "supervising" physician assistants/nurse
practitioners. (e.g. There's one DO in middle Tennessee who "supervises" more than 40 NP's (at $1K per
week for each))
Need standard of practice (perhaps rules) in pharmacies that persons picking-up prescriptions for
controlled substances have to provide positive ID that they are the patient or a person authorized by the
patient to pick-up medicines for them.
We "cannot arrest our way out of the problem of misuse of prescription drugs". Better and more
comprehensive prevention efforts have to be brought to bear.

Subject: NJ Department of Law & Public Safety Release: Project Medicine Drop
From:

Kan, Sarah

To:

Mendez DeTore, Janett <MendezDeTore.Janett@endo.com >; Yuen, Frank <yuen.frank@Endo.com>; Thomson,
Heather <Thomson.Heather@Endo.com >; Thomas, Greg <Thomas.Greg@endo.com>; Byrne, Timothy
