FDA Approves EXALGO(TM) (Hydromorphone HCL) Extended-Release Tablets
Covidien, CombinatoRx Collaboration Achieves Significant Milestone in Effort to Deliver the Only Extended-Release Formulation of
Hydromorphone
ST LOUIS, Mar 02, 2010 (BUSINESS WIRE) -- Covidien (NYSE:COV) today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has
approved the New Drug Application 21-217 for EXALGO(TM) (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets, (CII).
The indication for EXALGO is once daily administration for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid-tolerant patients requiring
continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.
Currently, many people suffer from moderate to severe chronic pain such as low-back pain, even with the medications that are already
available. In fact, physicians frequently try many types of opioids before finding a regimen that provides adequate pain relief for a patient.
EXALGO tablets provide a well known therapy in hydromorphone HCI, which has been used in the treatment of chronic pain for more than 80
years - now in an extended-release formulation. FDA approval of EXALGO tablets offers an important new treatment for physicians treating
opioid-tolerant patients for moderate to severe chronic pain.
EXALGO utilizes the OROS(R) Push-Pull(TM) osmotic delivery system designed to release the opioid at a controlled rate. By providing a steady
release of hydromorphone throughout the day, the drug is formulated to help minimize the peaks and troughs that are sometimes experienced by
chronic pain patients who rely on products that are dosed at more frequent intervals.
Covidien is the largest supplier of controlled pain medications in the United States based on number of prescriptions. Its development partner,
CombinatoRx, Incorporated, develops novel drug candidates with a focus on the treatment of pain and inflammation.
"We are excited that our collaboration with CombinatoRx provides physicians and patients with the only extended-release hydromorphone
treatment that will be available for this type of pain relief," said Timothy R. Wright, President, Pharmaceuticals, Covidien. "Building on more than
a century of pain treatment experience, Covidien is focused on providing patients with access to advanced medications that expand the limits of
pain therapy by combining proven drugs with innovative delivery systems.

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - ATTORNEYS EYES ONLY INFORMATION

ENDO-NY-00109648

 In June 2009, the companies announced that Mallinckrodt Inc., a Covidien company, had entered into an asset purchase agreement with
Neuromed for the U.S. commercialization rights to EXALGO. Under the agreement Covidien is responsible for all commercialization activities
for EXALGO, including marketing, sales and all post-approval FDA regulatory filings.
"Reflecting our commitment to pain management, we will be significantly increasing our branded pharmaceutical sales force in 2010 as a result
of the approval of EXALGO," said Wright.
The launch of EXALGO tablets, which Covidien anticipates in the first half of calendar year 2010, will include a comprehensive Risk Evaluation
and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) that is designed to ensure that the benefits of EXALGO outweigh the potential risks. The REMS for EXALGO
includes a medication guide and a robust set of educational programs and materials as part of the company's focused effort to help ensure that
prescribers, pharmacists and patients have the needed information regarding appropriate prescribing, dispensing and use of EXALGO tablets.
Under the program, healthcare provider education is required as an important element to assure safe use with a focus on appropriate patient
selection and dosing. As part of Covidien's ongoing commitment to be a responsible advocate for patients, the company has also voluntarily
developed a broad range of safe use tools for EXALGO that will be provided to healthcare professionals, pharmacists, patients and caregivers
and will be continually reviewed for improvement.
PLEASE SEE IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION, INCLUDING BOXED WARNING BELOW
EXALGO is contraindicated in opioid non-tolerant patients, in management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist, in patients with
compromised respiratory function or in patients with narrowed or obstructed gastrointestinal tract or with known hypersensitivity to any
components including hydromorphone hydrochloride and sulfites. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol,
increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. Not recommended in
patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.
See full package insert for full prescribing information.
WARNING: POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, IMPORTANCE OF PROPER PATIENT
SELECTION AND LIMITATIONS OF USE
Potential for Abuse
EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid analgesics. EXALGO can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid
agonists, legal or illicit. These risks should be considered when administering, prescribing, or dispensing EXALGO in situations where the healthcare professional is concerned about increased risk of misuse,
abuse, or diversion. Schedule II opioid substances which include hydromorphone, morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, oxymorphone and methadone have the highest potential for abuse and risk of fatal overdose due to
respiratory depression [see Drug Abuse and Dependence (9))
Proper Patient Selection
EXALGO is an extended-release formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients when a continuous around-the-clock opioid
analgesic is needed for an extended period of time. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morpltine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg of oral
oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg of oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer [see Indications and Usage (1) and Dosage and Administration (2)1
EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only [see Indications and Usage (1) and
Dosage and Administration (2)1
Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.
Accidental constrnption of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone [see Warnings and Precautions (5.13
Limitations of Use
EXALGO is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain [see Indications and Usage (1)1
EXALGO is not intended for use as an as needed analgesic [see Indications and Usage (1)1
EXALGO tablets are to be swallowed whole and are not to be broken, chewed, dissolved,
crushed or injected. Taking broken, chewed, dissolved or crushed EXALGO or its contents leads to rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone (seeWarnings and Precautions (5)}

Hi Cassie, See update below. Again, I copied Michael in case he had anything additional to add.

Overall Class-Wide Opioid REMS update:
•
FDA held an advisory committee meeting in July 2010 where they discussed their version of the class-wide
opioid REMS. Two major criticisms of the FDA's proposal were that the educational component was voluntary
and that immediate-release (IR) opioid formulations were not included in the REMS.
The Industry Working Group, which is a consortium of the companies (brand and generic) that currently have
on the market or pending approval a long-acting opioid analgesic with the specific compounds FDA has noted
to be included in the class-wide REMS, also presented a version of the class-wide opioid REMS. The biggest
difference from what the FDA presented was that a communication plan was included. FDA indicated they did
not include a communication plan because of resource constraints.
The committee voted on one question "please vote on whether you agree with the Agency's proposed REMS
for the extended-release and long-acting opioid analgesics and discuss the rationale for your vote". The vote
was 25 members against, 10 members in favor.
FDA has not released any further iterations of the class-wide opioid REMS since the meeting in July 2010.
The IWG consortium of companies awaits further communication from FDA.
FDA has approved several "interim" REMS programs, including several for products designed to be abuse
deterrent.
EN3288 REMS update:
•
An interim REMS was submitted as part of the NDA. We agreed to comply with the final class-wide opioid
REMS program, when it becomes available.
The EN3288 REMS will include a Med Guide, Healthcare Professional Training Guide, Education
Confirmation Form, and Assessment Plan.
No mandatory training will be included. The HCP Training Guide is a voluntary program we included at FDAs
request during the review.
We received several rounds of comments during the first review cycle, we are close to a final REMS program.
Current OPANA ER Formulation Update:
•
The current formulation of OPANA ER remains under the RiskMAP.
•
As noted above, no official letter has been received regarding REMS requirements for OPANA ER.

Hi Cassie,

upcoming oxymorphone situation analysis workshop.
Overall Class-Wide Opioid REMS update:
FDA is planning to hold an advisory committee meeting in July 2010 where they will discuss their version of
the class-wide opioid REMS.
The Industry Working Group, which is a consortium of the companies (brand and generic) that currently have
on the market or pending approval a long-acting opioid analgesic with the specific compounds FDA has noted
to be included in the class-wide REMS, continues to work to prepare a version of the class-wide opioid REMS
program for FDA consideration.
FDA has approved 3 "interim" opioid REMS programs — the 3 compounds are: Embeda, OxyContin, Exalgo.
The later 2 REMS (OxyContin and Exalgo) have a voluntary form physicians can fill out to indicate that they
have read and understood the training material provided as part of the REMS program. There is no
mandatory training or certification.
FDA has not released any specific details, there have been suggestions that it will include mandatory training,
but that is not confirmed.
EN3288 REMS update:
An interim REMS will be submitted as part of the NDA. We will agree to comply with the final class-wide
opioid REMS program, when it becomes available.
The EN3288 REMS will include a Med Guide, Healthcare Professional Education Plan, and Assessment Plan.
No mandatory training will be included.
The final REMS will be negotiated during the review period.

Subject: Opioid formulation change

Good morning!

Attached is a "Letter to the Editor" from the New England Journal of Medicine. The article discusses data
collected over the past three years focused specifically on the impact of the Oxycontin formulation change.

Two data points of note:

the selection of Oxy-Contin as a primary drug of abuse decreased from 35.6% of respondents before the
release of the abuse-deterrent formulation to just 12.8% 21 months later (P<0.001).

for other opioids, including high-potency fentanyl and hydromorphone, selection rose markedly, from
20.1% to 32.3% (P = 0.005).

Dr. Cicero's conclusion:

Our data show that an abuse-deterrent formulation successfully reduced abuse of a specific drug but also
generated an unanticipated outcome: replacement of the abuse-deterrent formulation with alternative
opioid medications and heroin, a drug that may pose a much greater overall risk to public health than
OxyContin. Thus, abuse-deterrent formulations may not be the "magic bullets" that many hoped they would
be in solving the growing problem of opioid abuse.

Subject: Congratulations!
Importance: High
I wanted to congratulate all of you on the approval of Opana today. It was no small feat to have the FDA grant approval to the
first new branded opioid in many years.
We at Inflexxion have had several contacts with the FDA in the past few months regarding risk management work that we are
doing with you and others. They have made clear that for them, moving forward, risk management and surveillance, pre- and
post-launch is and will remain pivotal in the approval and continued marketing of prescription opioids.
We feel privileged to have worked with Endo so closely over these past six years and hope to continue this wonderful and
important partnership into the future.
I also wanted to let you know that the NAVIPPRO program has already begun to gather data and will have major impact as the
standard in the field for scientifically-based, surveillance and signal detection. Our PainEdu and PainAction sites have significant
momentum. (PainEdu has been around for 4+ years and now has about 500 healthcare professionals visiting per day and over
7000 registered users.)
The SOAPP scale, developed with Endo and National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) support, has already become the standard
screening tools used by clinicians to differentiate those who are likely to use opioids appropriately, from those who are likely to
misuse them. The Massachusetts Department of Public Health recently decided to incorporate the SOAPP into an information
packet that they will be sending to every health provider in Massachusetts. Today, San Diego Department of Public Health
asked permission to distribute SOAPP to their healthcare providers as well.
We are also about to begin work on MyStudentBody: Drugs (MSB: Drugs). Components of MSB, a comprehensive suite of
health programs for college students (including Alcohol, Tobacco, Stress, Nutrition, Stress and now Drugs) are being used
around the country by colleges and universities that subscribe for their entire student population. This year over 100 colleges will
be using MSB, and therefore MSB: Drugs and we will have exposure to over 700,000 college students.
Endo had the vision and willingness to take a chance on some of these programs and tools at a very early point and for that we
feel most grateful
I would also like to commend the great work that is being done by Linda Kitlinski and Marie Pinizzotto. They are terrific,
thoughtful and forward looking people and have contributed to the strong ties between our companies. Both have championed

Hi, just a reminder that you're receiving this email because you have expressed an interest in American Association for
the Treatment of Opioid Dependence, Inc.. Don't forget to add info@aatod.org to your address book so we'll be sure to
land in your inbox!
You may unsubscribe if you no longer wish to receive our emails.

x

Dear Friends and Colleagues,
We have just concluded one of our most successful conferences in the history of AATOD. Roland
Lamb did a magnificent job in Chairing the conference and organizing incredible content with all of the
organizing committees and policy planning partners. Many people approached me during the course
of the conference to tell me how much they were getting out of the plenary sessions, workshops, preconference sessions, hot topic roundtables, and posters. It was very rich in content, being specifically
designed to help guide our field for the challenges that are coming in 2014 as Health Care Reform is
fully implemented and as programs work more closely with the Criminal Justice System.
There was a brilliant policy discussion during the Policymakers Luncheon in how OTPs can best
engage Drug Court representatives, probation and parole officers, and correctional facility managers.
It will lead to specific training opportunities for OTP staff in providing best methods to increase
referrals to our treatment programs.
We are also beginning the planning of our next conference, which will convene at the Hyatt Regency
Hotel in Atlanta between March 28-April 3, 2015. You will receive more information about this in the
coming months.
As is our tradition at this time of year, the AATOD Board of Directors wishes all of our planning
partners and friends throughout the United States and other nations a joyous holiday season. I am
forwarding a donation request for 2013 to support our continued work in the New Year. Many people
from our field have been generous in the past and we are hoping that you will continue to provide
support for our activities, which were certainly in evidence during our recent conference in
Philadelphia.

• We are working with our policy partners in the Legal Action Center and the Coalition for Whole
Health as we prepare for Health Care Reform and its impact on our patients and treatment
system. We understand that there will be many challenges in the states but have been
encouraged by recent changes, such as the approval in California to have the health insurance
exchange reimburse OTPs for the use of medications to treat chronic opioid addiction. This was
a major breakthrough and I commend our colleagues in California for persevering.

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_ANK_CHI_0492561

 • We are also working with our policy partners to expand access to Medication Assisted
Treatment in the Criminal Justice System, and will continue to work with our federal agency
partners and Criminal Justice representatives during the course of 2014. There were two
important publications moving this forward in 2013. The Department of Justice through its
subsidiary agency published a groundbreaking training manual on treating the offender
population with Medication Assisted Treatment for opioid addiction. The second publication
was from the National Association of Drug Court Professionals when they released their new
Best Practice Guidelines for Adult Drug Courts during July 2013. This publication provides
excellent guidance to its members on the use of Medication Assisted Treatment for opioid
addiction, including all three federally approved medications (methadone, buprenorphine, and
NaltrexoneNivitrol).
• We are continuing our work with our partners in the World Federation under the Special
Consultative Status an as NGO through the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs.
Our conference had several presentations on advances in treatment in Europe, Vietnam, and
Africa. The work of the World Federation is expanding, and I am pleased to report that the
Scottish Ministry of Health made the decision to continue providing access to Medication
Assisted Treatment for opioid addiction, reversing the call to end all such care in Scotland. The
World Federation sent correspondence to Minister Cunningham and will be convening its next
conference in Glasgow during May 2014.
I am asking you to make a contribution to AATOD as a way to continue our critical work in organizing

hope that you will consider joining AATOD's President's Club, which has been an opportunity for the

As indicated on our website, you can also elect to be listed as a donor to AATOD in a special section.

Maria,
I would love to share the information about Drs. Stocking and Murphy. They were pleased to know you took notice of
them. I had lunch with the office on Tuesday. I should give you a brief description of their practice first. In addition to
doctors Murphy and Stocking there are two NPs, Michael Aines and Karen Doggett. Dr Murphy is boarded in addiction
medicine and Michael specializes in the area. Both are trained speakers and have had excellent reviews on their
programs. Dr Murphy likes doing medical management (a rarity these days) and enjoys his patients (some more than
others :)
With some exceptions, the doctors follow our guidelines regarding dosing. They quickly realized our first guideline was too
conservative and adjusted their protocol by adding in Opana IR and determining the total daily dosage. In most cases they
will titrate, if needed after 7 to 10 days. They have become very comfortable with Opana ER
and their expectations of efficacy. They require that the patients stay on Opana ER for one month. They want the patients
to reach steady state and adjust to the feeling of pain relief without euphoria. Dr Murphy spoke to me about a patient that
he started on 5 mg of Opana ER who had been on high doses of another product. I asked him why he chose 5 mg and
how the patient was doing. He said because the patient is an educated gentleman with realistic expectations of pain
control. He went on to say that many patients expect to feel like they did before pain became a part of their lives. Dr
Stocking told me they are all happy with Opana ER and Michael said they have moved it up in their rotation. They do not
like to use Oxycontin and will take most patients off of it if they come to their practice on Oxycontin. They do this not

Subject: Webinar: Impact of Clinical Trial Design on Outcomes of Chronic Pain Studies
From:

McConkey, Ian <McConkey.lan@Endo.com >;

WEBINAR: The Impact of Clinical Trial Design on
Outcomes of Chronic Pain Studies
PIZESFATI.:D BY:

Organizers of the Annual Pain Therapeutics
Summit, now going into its 8th Year!

The epidemic of failed clinical trials of analgesics known to be efficacious
has prompted first a soul searching, then a search for evidence, on how
specific aspects of clinical trial design and conduct can influence outcomes.
Nathaniel Katz, MD, MS, President, Analgesic Solutions will present
emerging data on:
► The relationship between the patients' ability to report pain accurately and
study outcome
► The impact of a specific program to reduce placebo effects on patient
expectation of treatment benefit (which is the main driver of the placebo
response)
► The impact of the number of clinical research sites on the study outcome
► A bedside method for subtyping patients based on putative pain
mechanism
► A new approach to differentiating analgesics based on an integrated riskbenefit composite measure
The presentation will conclude with recommendations on what research
sponsors can do to take advantage of these findings to reduce risk of failure
of analgesic studies, followed by a question and answer session.

DETAILS:
February 12, 2014
1:30 - 3:00 PM EST
Price: USD$95

REGISTER NOW

ABOUT THE PRESENTER:
Dr. Katz is President of Analgesic Solutions, a consulting firm focused on
analgesics. Dr. Katz is also Adjunct Assistant Professor of Anesthesia at
Tufts University School of Medicine. After completing his neurology
residency at Tufts-New England Medical Center he entered a Pain
Management fellowship in the Department of Anesthesia at Brigham &
Women's Hospital in 1990. After which Dr. Katz was appointed Staff
Neurologist in the Pain Management Center of Brigham & Women's
Hospital. Subsequently, he founded the Pain & Symptom Management
Program at Dana Farber Cancer institute, and the Pain Trials Center (a
clinical analgesics research unit) at Brigham & Women's Hospital. He
remained Director of both until 2001. From 2000-2004 Dr. Katz served as
Chair of the Advisory Committee, Anesthesia, Critical Care, and Addiction
Products Division, United States Food and Drug Administration, during
which time he completed a Master of Science degree in Biostatistics at
Columbia University.
Dr. Katz's interests include clinical research methods, analgesic clinical
trials, opioids for chronic pain, opioids and addiction, neuropathic pain, and
cancer pain. He has completed numerous clinical trials of treatments for
pain, both industry-initiated and investigator-initiated, involving

conducted studies related to opioids, pain, addiction, and other issues
related to opioid therapy. Dr. Katz is active on many publications and was

(Pain) for the Encyclopedia of Neurological Sciences, and has overseen

CC:

Tribou, Scott <Tribou.Scott@Endo.com >;

Hi Rianne,
I have a few of the same comments/questions that you shared below, particularly about opportunities for advancement without moving to
Chadds Ford and really appreciating the Bend the Trend contest (the team concept was great because we were all pulling for each other to
succeed).
Here's something else:
1. Act with Integrity
A. I understand why we cannot dispose of Lidoderm or Opana marketing materials. Can we setup a date where we can ship what we
have accumulated in our storage facilities back to a central holding location in Chadds Ford or somewhere else?
B. I really appreciate the books from Lynn Webster about Avoiding Abuse while Managing Pain. I believe they help us become
partners with our physicians and demonstrate pure intent, rather than just selling Opana ER to them.
2. Value All Contributions
It would be great to see the minimum thresholds for incentive payouts to be lowered a bit. It can be difficult to keep momentum
going on all 3 products simultaneously and it's unfortunate to be penalized when a product grows slightly from one semester to the next,
but does not qualify for compensation.
2 & 3 Value All Contributions & Respect Each Other
At Takeda, they have a program called "Home Team", where once a year each district has a weekend team outing. The company
budgeted approximately $1000 per team member and the district decided what they'd do together. There were things like a ski weekend,
boating. wine tours, etc. They were simply a way for the team and spouses, sometimes children too, to get together, get to know each
other better as individuals rather than as representatives and therefore build team unity. It was also a reward for our spouses/families for
the sacrifices they make when we travel away from home for POA's, trainings, or just working our territories. Many people would
comment that it was worth more than another $1000 in their annual salary because they felt valued and appreciated. I would really enjoy
seeing Endo adopt something similar into their culture.
4. Reward and Celebrate Success
While this hasn't affected me directly, early success could potentially lead to reduce motivation. What I mean by this is that if you
compare two territories' goals, one that performed above goal last semester and one that performed below goal, the representative whose
territory performed above goal, now has a much higher goal to reach and with Opana ER, we may be talking about one territory that needs
to achieve 600 Rx's vs. another that only needs to reach 75. This is a lot of disparity between territory goals to reach the same incentive
payout.
Michael

Sent: Wed 4/16/2008 7:33 AM

Hi everyone,

 • Act with Integrity

Chadds Ford.
• Respect Each Other
• Reward and Celebrate Success
**Really liked the "Bend the Trend" because it was a district/team contest and one that was within our
ability to do and we were quickly compensated...run it again!
**Qualifying for "Bend the Trend" was interesting—the Opana market is variable and you may have "up"

then go through a slump.. just in time not to qualify or not enough to qualify even though you are still
contributing...kinda a "downer"...maybe "tweeking" the rules would help????—(value all contributions)???

clinics don't allow me to leave literature and thus it begins to pile up. Plus, is it necessary for my samples

FYI.
Fentanyl Buccal Film Now Available for the Management of Breakthrough Pain in Cancer
SOMERSET, N.J., Oct. 13 /PRNewswire/

Meda Pharmaceuticals Inc. today announced the launch of Onsolis (fentanyl buccal soluble film) in the

U.S. for the management of breakthrough pain (BTP) in patients with cancer, eighteen years of age and older, who are already receiving and who are
tolerant to opioid therapy for their underlying persistent cancer pain. Onsolis uses an innovative drug delivery technology called BioErodible
MucoAdhesive (BEMA(TM)), developed by BioDelivery Sciences International, Inc. (BDSI). Onsolis consists of a small, dissolvable, polymer
film, formulated with fentanyl, for application to the inner lining of the cheek.
Onsolis is available through a controlled distribution program called FOCUS(TM) (Full Ongoing Commitment to User Safety), the first opioid Risk
Evaluation and Management Strategy (REMS) program that provides for prescriber, pharmacy, and patient enrollment for the integrated,
coordinated safe use of Onsolis. The FOCUS Program was designed to meet requirements by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to help
ensure appropriate use of Onsolis.
"The launch of Onsolis represents a significant achievement for Meda and an innovative pain management option for physicians to offer their
patients with cancer who are experiencing breakthrough pain. The Onsolis technology differs from existing products used in these patients by virtue
of its physical characteristics that enable patients to obtain the pain relief they need in a convenient delivery system," said Sharon Clarke, President,
Meda Pharmaceuticals Inc. "We are proud of our work with the FDA on the development of FOCUS, a program that is designed to facilitate the
appropriate use of Onsolis and to provide healthcare practitioners, patients, and caregivers with comprehensive training and information."
The goal of the FOCUS Program for Onsolis is to lessen the risk of Onsolis overdose, abuse, addiction, and serious complications due to medication
errors by:

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_OPIOID_OHAG-00270660

 • Helping to assure proper patient selection, including avoidance of the use of Onsolis in opioid non-tolerant patients;
•

Reducing the risk of exposure to Onsolis in persons for whom it was not prescribed, including accidental exposure in children; and

• Training prescribers, pharmacists, and patients about proper dosing and administration.
Under the FOCUS Program, only prescribers, pharmacies, and patients registered with the program are able to prescribe, dispense, and receive
Onsolis. This program provides educational materials, patient counseling and managed distribution of the drug. Healthcare practitioners who wish to
enroll in the FOCUS Program may call

Redacted - PrivasiD (1-877-4ONSOLIS)

or visit http://www.OnsolisFocus.com.

Clinical Study
The efficacy of Onsolis was investigated in a clinical trial in opioid tolerant adult patients experiencing breakthrough cancer pain. Breakthrough
cancer pain was defined as a transient flare of moderate-to-severe pain occurring in patients with cancer experiencing persistent cancer pain
otherwise controlled with maintenance doses of opioid medications including at least 60 mg morphine/day, 50 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, or an
equianalgesic dose of another opioid for one week or longer. All patients were on stable doses of either long-acting oral opioids or transdermal
fentanyl for their persistent cancer pain.
A double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study was performed in patients with cancer to evaluate the effectiveness of Onsolis for the treatment
of breakthrough cancer pain. Open-label titration identified a successful dose of Onsolis, within the range of 200 to 1200 mcg. A "successful" dose
was defined as a dose in which a patient obtained adequate analgesia with tolerable side effects. In the double-blind portion of the study, patients who
identified a successful dose were randomized to a sequence of nine treatments; six with the successful dose of Onsolis and three with placebo. Of the
patients who entered the study, 54 percent achieved a successful dose during the titration phase and 4 percent withdrew for lack of effective pain
relief. The final titrated dose of Onsolis for breakthrough cancer pain was not predicted from the daily maintenance dose of opioid used to manage
the persistent cancer pain and, therefore, the dose was determined by titration starting at 200 mcg. The primary outcome measure, the mean sum of
pain intensity differences at 30 minutes (SPID30) for Onsolis-treated episodes was statistically significantly higher than for placebo-treated
episodes.
About Onsolis
Onsolis is a small, dissolvable, polymer film, formulated with the opioid fentanyl for application to the buccal mucosa (inner lining of the cheek) that
is designed to deliver a dose of drug across the oral mucous membranes. Fentanyl belongs to the group of medicines called narcotic analgesics,
which are used to relieve pain. Onsolis was evaluated in over 300 patients; over 90,000 doses were administered in clinical trials. Onsolis adheres to
the buccal mucosa in 5 seconds, starts to dissolve in 15 to 30 minutes and delivers fentanyl across the mucosa. In clinical trials, following buccal
application of Onsolis in healthy volunteers, the absolute bioavailability of fentanyl was 71%.
About Breakthrough Pain in Cancer
Breakthrough Pain (BTP) in cancer is a transitory, severe, or excruciating pain flare-up that "breaks through" the relief provided by around-the-clock
analgesics. Unlike persistent cancer pain, BTP is generally rapid in onset (within three minutes) and lasts up to two hours. A large multicenter survey
conducted by pain specialists in twenty-four countries found that 65% of 1,095 cancer patients had BTP. It is estimated that over a half-million
people in the U.S. with cancer suffer from breakthrough pain, however, only about twenty thousand receive a treatment approved for the condition.

 The organization to consider are:
Academy of Integrative Pain Management (AIPM)
(formerly American Academy of Pain Management)
The Academy is widely recognized as the nation's foremost voice in proposing and advocating for public policy that
allows its members and other healthcare practitioners to provide optimal pain care.
AIPM's mission is to improve the lives of people with Pain by advancing a person centered, integrative model of pain
care through evidence-guided education, credentialing, and advocacy.
The advocacy arm of AIPM communicates with its members through bi-monthly meetings, policy updates, and action
alerts. Their resources include: bi-monthly teleconferences, electronic newsletters, a comprehensive website with
resource links, policy statements, a state policy analysis grid, draft legislative and regulatory language, and training and
networking opportunities.
American Society for Pain Management Nursing
The American Society for Pain Management Nursing's mission is to advance and promote optimal nursing care for
people affected by pain by promoting best nursing practices. This is accomplished through education, standards,
advocacy and research.
Nurses are members of the society and as such are provided access to current, best practices, evidence-based
resources.
U.S. Pain Foundation
The U.S. Pain Foundation was established by a person of pain with the goal to connect, inform, educate and empower
those living with pain while advocating on behalf of the entire pain community.
Because chronic pain is still widely underfunded, misunderstood and undertreated, the U.S. Pain Foundation sponsors
local and online support groups and pain events so caregivers as well as those living with pain can connect.
Additionally, they provide information to help patients navigate governmental matters such as state-level advocacy
legislation pertaining to unfair practices against people with pain, Worker's Compensation issues and Social Security
Disability Insurance.
American Cancer Society
The Cancer Action Network (CAN) ACS CAN encourages states and the federal government to carefully balance
considerations of prescription drug monitoring programs, public education efforts and policies governing the
prescribing of opioid pain medicines. Many recently enacted policies have focused solely on preventing illicit drug
abuse — however they risk jeopardizing legitimate patient access to pain relief.
Additionally, ACS CAN has been actively involved in working with governors and state legislators to establish evaluation
mechanisms for pain policies to ensure they are achieving the desired abuse mitigation goals without detrimental
impact to patients with pain.
Center for Lawful Access & Abuse Deterrence (CLAAD)
The Center for Lawful Access and Abuse Deterrence coordinates a comprehensive national effort to prevent
prescription drug fraud, diversion, misuse, and abuse while advancing patient access to high-quality health care.
CLAAD gathers information and research on prescription drug abuse, misuse, and diversion. CLAAD makes policy
recommendations on prescription drug abuse with the goal of improving the public health.
CLAAD's policy positions are established through a consensus process, in which at least 80 percent of the participants
must represent not-for-profit organizations. This rule of governance ensures that the public interest drives CLAAD's
priorities, as opposed to the interests of individual stakeholders.
Alliance for Patient Access
The Alliance for Patient Access is a national network of physicians dedicated to ensuring patient access to approved
therapies and appropriate clinical care. AfPA accomplishes this mission by recruiting, training and mobilizing policyminded physicians to be effective advocates for patient access.
AfPA Physician Working Groups serve as a means to bring together physicians who share a common therapeutic
interest or access challenge so that they might work collaboratively in the development of education resources that are
used to promote informed policymaking.
National Fibromyalgia & Chronic Pain Association
The National Fibromyalgia & Chronic Pain Association unites patients, policy makers, and healthcare, medical and

The Washington Post:

Aetna is notifying some doctors about their drugdispensing habits
By Lenny Bernstein
To Your Health
rust 3 at

(Toby Talbot/AP)
Many experts say the prescription painkiller epidemicstarted when physicians began over-prescribing powerful opioid
medications, a well-meaning attempt to more aggressively treat patients' pain. With addiction to those pills at crisis levels,
they argue, a good part of the solution would be for doctors to rein in use of the drugs.
The giant health insurer Aetna is now actively encouraging change. Using the vast amount of data it collects from insurance
claims by pharmacies, it has begun contacting doctors whose prescribing habits are far outside the norm.
"You have been identified as falling within the top i percent of opioid prescribers within your specialty," Aetna wrote to 931
physicians across the country last week. The not-so-subtle reminder was aimed at doctors who refill opioid prescriptions at
very high rates compared to their peers. Only doctors who prescribed the painkillers at least 12 times were included in the
data examined, which represented more than 8.6 million claims. Physicians such as oncologists, who are likely to dispense
large amounts of opioids as part of their practices, were excluded.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

EN DO-OPIOID_MDL-07063009

 INearlu six in 10 Americans have leftover narcotics at home]
ADVERTISING
Harold Paz, Aetna's chief medical officer, said his experience has convinced him that the best way to change doctors' behavior
is to provide them with the numbers. "By nature, doctors are data-driven," he said. "It's one of the skills required to get
through medical school and residency and training. It's unemotional.
"If you show them how they're doing, they'll want to do better," he said.
At the same time, Paz cautioned, Aetna can't-- and shouldn't -- assess a physician's clinical judgments with each patient.
There may be legitimate reasons for a high refill rate in some cases but not others. So Aetna is urging physicians to check.
"We're asking you to look at your practice...and identify if the way you're prescribing narcotics is best practice," Paz said. "And
if it's not, here's an opportunity to improve."
In 2014, U.S. physicians wrote 24o million prescriptions for narcotic painkillers, according to the Centers for Disease Control
and Prevention. About 2.1 million people are addicted to legal narcotics, and 14,838 died of overdoses from opioid
medications that year.
'Pfizer agrees to truth in opioid marketing!
Insurers routinely send physicians data on the quality of care, which can include the number of prescriptions written, an
Aetna spokesman said. But generally they do not supply the refill-to-prescription ratio, he said.
Paz said that if the 931 doctors brought their refill rate in line with the average for all physicians who prescribe opioids, 1.4
million fewer pills would be dispensed annually. The physicians receiving the letter had an average refill rate of 4.5 for each
prescription written; the overall average was o.3 refills per prescription.
A survey published in June in the journal JAMA Internal Medicine showed that nearly 60 percent of Americans have leftover
narcotics at home and 20 percent have shared them with someone.
In March, the CDC issued new guidelines for physicians who dispense opioids that encouraged them to maximize the use of
non-opioid therapies, set specific criteria for stopping or continuing the use of opioids and assess a medication's effectiveness
in controlling pain versus its potential harm before refilling a prescription at that dose.
The Aetna data showed that family medicine doctors (58 percent) and internists (31 percent) were by far the top refill
prescribers, trailed by obstetricians (4 percent), surgeons (3 percent), neurologists (2 percent) and rheurnatologists (2
percent). Pennsylvania, where the opioid epidemic has hit hard, was home to 136 "superprescribers," followed by Missouri
(87), Florida (78), North Carolina (52) and Utah (45)•
None of those doctors turned up on Aetna's list of doctors suspected of fraud or abuse in opioid prescribing, Paz said.

 Andrew Kolodny, executive director of the advocacy group Physicians for Responsible Opioid Prescribing, said Aetna's
experiment "sounds worthwhile" though probably less effective than a similar message from a
department or law enforcement agency.
The same message should be sent to other "risky prescribers," such as physicians who authorize large doses of opioids,
Kolodny said. Insurers could help more by requiring prior authorization before a doctor can order a narcotics refill, as

The Wall Street Journal:

Teva to Buy Generics Distributor Anda From
Allergan for $500 Million
Aug. 3, 2016 8:12 a.m. ET
By Austen Hufford
Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. said it would purchase Allergan PLC's generic pharmaceuticals distributor for $500
million, just a day after Teva closed its much larger deal to buy Allergan's generics business.
Teva is buying Allergan's Anda Inc., the fourth-largest distributor of generic pharmaceuticals in the U.S.
Tuesday, Teva closed its $40.5 billion deal for Allergan's generics business. They first struck that deal last July but it was
delayed due to regulatory hurdles. Teva ended up having to divest 75 drugs to rivals to win Federal Trade Commission
approval.
Anda distributes drugs from more than 300 manufacturers to pharmacies across the U.S. In 2016 Anda is expected to
generate more than $i billion in third-party net revenue.
As part of the deal, Teva will acquire distribution centers in Olive Branch, Miss., Weston, Fla., and Groveport, Ohio. Anda will
operate as a stand-alone business. The deal is subject to regulatory approval and other closing conditions and is expected to
close in the second half of the year.

Big Pharma's Biogen Dilemma
Landing Biogen in a deal will require a big risk from major drug makers
Created with Highstock 2.1.5In Sickness and in HealthBiogen's price/forward earnings ratio201520161015202530
By
Charley Grant
Aug. 3, 201611:57 a.m. ET
After a recent lull, health-care megadeals are once again percolating. But any suitors for Biogen BIIB -1.13 % will need to take

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07063011

 a risk.
Biogen shares rose 9% Tuesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that the biotechnology giant has fielded preliminary
interest in a takeover from at least two other drugmakers.
There certainly are reasons to believe Biogen, a leader in central nervous system drugs, would make an attractive target.
Growth among the largest pharmaceutical companies is scarce and Biogen can certainly help on that front. Revenue grew by
12% in the second quarter from a year earlier. At a market value of $70 billion, Biogen is large enough to move the needle on
the top line at even the largest of pharma companies.

Biotechnology giant Biogen Inc. has drawn takeover interest from drug companies including Merck & Co. and Al lergan PLC, The Wall
Street Journal reported on Tuesday. PHOTO: BLOOMBERG NEU'S/SCOTT EISEN
Buyers would need to absorb less than $3 billion of net debt—a sum easily within big pharma's reach. And the timing could be
right for Biogen. Chief Executive and Chairman George Scangos announced plans to step down last month once a successor is
named. Meanwhile, any breakthrough from Biogen's pipeline of experimental drugs—focused on highly risky but potentially
lucrative treatment areas such as Alzheimer's disease—would offer a major bonus.
Nevertheless, any would-be buyer won't be getting that growth for a song. Shares trade above 15 times forward earnings,
according to FactSet. As recently as June that multiple was just 11.5 times. Add in a takeover premium above today's price and
a buyer might depend on a clinical breakthrough to earn a suitable return on its investment.
True, Biogen traded as high as 27 times forward earnings a year and a half ago. But that was fueled by excitement over an
early stage Alzheimer's study amid a euphoric market for biotech stocks. The market has since cooled off significantly, and the
outcome of Biogen's program won't be known any time soon.
A true Alzheimer's breakthrough would make any deal a home run. But swinging for the fences at a full price raises the risk of
a strikeout.

FDA Safety Changes: Opana and Sodium Chloride Saline Irrigation Solution
The FDA has approved revisions to the safety labeling for oxymorphone HCI injection (Opana) and 0.9%
sodium chloride solution in a plastic irrigation container.
Medscape Medical News 2007

January 18, 2007 — The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved safety labeling
revisions to advise of the risk for respiratory depression associated with use of oxymorphone injection
and the risk for circulatory overload associated with absorption of normal saline irrigation solution.
Oxymorphone HCI Injection (Opana) Linked to Risk for Respiratory Depression
In October 2006, the FDA approved safety labeling revisions for oxymorphone HCI injection (Opana,
made by Endo Pharmaceuticals Holdings, Inc) to warn that respiratory depression is the chief hazard
associated with its use.
Schedule II substances, such as oxymorphone, morphine, hydromorphone, methadone, oxycodone,
and fentanyl, have the highest potential for abuse and associated risk for fatal overdose due to
respiratory depression. Concomitant use of oxymorphone with alcohol or other central nervous system
depressants can further increase the risk for respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation,
and coma.
Oxymorphone should therefore be initiated at one third to one half the usual dose and titrated slowly in
patients receiving concomitant treatment with sedative/hypnotics, general anesthetics, phenothiazines,
tranquilizers, and alcohol. Significant dose reductions might also be required for the coadministered
agent.
The FDA notes that respiratory depression is more likely to occur in elderly or debilitated patients and in
those who have conditions accompanied by hypoxia or hypercapnia when even moderate therapeutic
doses can dangerously decrease pulmonary ventilation.
Oxymorphone should therefore be used with extreme caution under careful supervision and at the
lowest effective dose in patients with asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or cor pulmonary,
severe obesity, sleep apnea syndrome, myxedema, kyphoscoliosis, central nervous system depression,

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07471750

 or coma. Use of alternative nonopioid analgesics should be considered in these patients.
Also, the respiratory depressant effects of oxymorphone and their potential to elevate cerebrospinal fluid
pressure can be markedly exaggerated in the presence of head injury, other intracranial lesions, or
preexisting increases in intracranial pressure. Opioid analgesics, such as oxymorphone, can produce
effects on pupillary response and consciousness that can obscure neurologic signs related to further
intracranial-pressure increases in patients with head injuries.
The FDA also warned that because concomitant use of agonist-antagonist analgesics (eg, pentazocine,
nalbuphine, butorphanol, and buprenorphine) can reduce the analgesic effects of pure opioids and/or
precipitate withdrawal symptoms, they should be used with caution in patients who have received or are
receiving a course of therapy with oxymorphone.
As with all opioid analgesics, oxymorphone can cause severe hypotension in patients whose ability to
maintain blood pressure has been compromised by blood volume depletion or concurrent use of other
drugs that compromise vasomotor tone (eg, phenothiazines). Caution is advised when treating patients
in circulatory shock because oxymorphone-related vasodilatation can further reduce cardiac output and
blood pressure.
Although the effects of oxymorphone on hepatic impairment have not been studied, studies of
oxymorphone extended-release tablets (Opana ER, made by Endo Pharms) have revealed increased
plasma concentrations in patients with hepatic disease compared with those with normal hepatic
function. Caution is therefore advised when administering oxymorphone injection in patients with mild
impairment. Treatment should be initiated at the lowest dose and titrated slowly while carefully
monitoring for adverse events. Use of oxymorphone injection is contraindicated in patients with
moderate or severe hepatic impairment.
Oxymorphone injection is indicated for the relief of moderate to severe pain, preoperative medication,
support of anesthesia, obstetrical analgesia, and for the relief of anxiety in patients with dyspnea
associated with pulmonary edema secondary to acute left ventricular dysfunction.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07471751

Digital Marketing Visual Aid and other key field sales tactics and programs.

seeing/hearing in the field. Anything you feel would be key information for the marketing team, be it
negative or positive information, is greatly appreciated. I will compile and save for the next conference
call. Additionally, you can expect me to inform you about what was discussed on our calls. I will keep
the summary brief, with bullet points for easy read and ready to forward to your respective teams as

"Trigger" of switching from short-acting opioids to Belbuca should be discussed in lesser pills per
day. In other words, instead of discussing 6-7 Vicodin/day, discuss the patient on 4-5
Vicodin/day. At 5mg/500APAP per tab, this is closer to the 30mg MSE and therefore Taper &
Transition is seamless.
Talk Patient-Type with clinician. A "30mg Vicodin" patient resonates more with MDs for
conversion than just saying chronic pain patient.
When promoting to Family Practice, some feel the term "Around-the Clock" therapy is
preferable to "Long Acting Opioid" therapy. "Dr, at what point do you feel a chronic pain
patient on short-acting opioids like Vicodin/Percocet is ready for "Around the Clock" opioid
therapy?" Less stigma than Long-Acting opioid.

"farming" out your patients to Pain Specialists, keep track of your patients with Belbuca as it is a
CIII"
Total office call very important for the "Tolerability" benefit of Belbuca. The Nurses receive the
most calls for side effects, not the doctor. Be sure to discuss Belbuca's excellent side effect
profile comparable to placebo with all the RNs.
If Belbuca having a lack of "abuse deterrent component" comes up, bring it back to the product
being a CIII and compare to definition of CII to clarify with clinician. Stick to PI and discuss
"appropriate pain patient".

Timeline:
February 2015 Governor Baker establishes a working group to develop a plan to reduce opioid deaths in the Commonwealth
June 2015 the working group releases 65 recommendations to reduce opiate deaths & addiction
November 2015 Senate Bill 2020 and Governor Baker's House Bill 3817 were introduced and included the provisions below.
Endo Government Affairs worked with our partners in the region to prevent either both SB 2020 and HB 3817 from passing its
chamber of origin.
• SB 2020 would require each manufacturer of CII and CIII to pay an assessment into the Prescription Drug
Awareness Trust Fund based on a sliding scale not less than $10,000 per year but not to exceed $100,000 per year.
This would fund pharmaceutical take-back & disposal. While funded by CII and CIII manufacturers, the collection
system may accept any covered drug and any other prescription drug in a pill formulation regardless of its schedule.
Given the history of many of these types of programs, we anticipated this assessment to increase significantly
following enactment.
• SB 2020 would direct the Department of Public Health and the licensing boards to annually determine each
practitioner's Schedule II and Schedule III opiate prescribing quantity and volume and their standing in that regard,
expressed as a percentile ranking. Each practitioner whose prescribing exceeds the mean or median shall be sent
notice of the practitioner's ranking; and further, the rankings shall be distributed to the relevant licensing boards.
• HB 3817 would prohibit a practitioner from issuing a prescription for more than a 72-hour supply of an opiate to a
patient the first time the practitioner prescribes an opiate to that patient.
• HB 3817 would mandate that regulations shall require every practitioner to use the prescription monitoring
program prior to prescribing an opiate.
• HB 3817 would define "substance use disorder" in an unworkable and overly broad way.
• HB 3817 would permit involuntary commitment to a substance use disorder treatment program for up to 90
days. If there are no other suitable facilities available for treatment, the person may be committed to a secure facility
for women, if a female; or to the Massachusetts correctional institution at Bridgewater, if a male.
January 2016 MA S 2103 introduced. MA S 2103 was a 2nd take on the blocked bills of 2015 and became MA H 4056 in March
2016.
March 14, 2016 MA HB 4056 Signed into law by Governor Charlie Baker

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07089268

 This final version, as passed, includes the following provisions:
• Establishing that a to an adult patient for outpatient use for the first time, a practitioner shall not issue a
prescription for more than a 7-day supply (increased from 3-days)
n EXCEPTION: If, in the professional medical judgment of a practitioner, more than a 7-day supply of an
opiate is required to treat the adult or minor patient's acute medical condition or is necessary for the
treatment of chronic pain management, pain associated with a cancer diagnoses or for palliative care, then
the practitioner may issue a prescription for the quantity needed to treat such acute medical condition,
chronic pain, pain associated with a cancer diagnosis or pain experienced while the patient is in palliative
care.
O Subsequent prescriptions, as we read the legislation, are not bound by the 7-day rule. Just first time
outpatient prescriptions
o While final rules remain to be promulgated, physicians shall utilize the prescription monitoring
program each time a prescription for a narcotic drug that is contained in Schedule II or III is issued
• Establishment of a drug stewardship program for all controlled substances as defined by the Food and Drug
Administration.
n In previous legislation this was an assessment the state would charge in an amount they deemed
appropriate to only CII and CIII manufacturers to collect ALL pharmaceuticals. In the enacted version, all
controlled substance manufacturers as defined by the FDA would need to develop their own program or
jointly fund a program they design which meets certain parameters. Endo will likely follow the continuation of
participation in the Pharmaceutical Product Stewardship Work Group as we have done previously for
stewardship programs such as Alameda county.)
O Also worth noting, section 77 of the bill automatically repeals the pharmaceutical stewardship program on
December 31, 2021if not extended in the interim by legislative action.
• Pharmacists may provide a lesser quantity of requested by the patient, but must notify the physician within 7 days
of doing so
• Practitioners renewing their license must receive opiate training which includes identifying those at risk for
substance abuse disorders
• Elementary & secondary school education with guidance from the Department of Health on prevention and
abuse education policies.

As a recap, I'm resending the jobs in question as well as the rationale for the Escalation (below), provided by Brian
Williams. Per the SOP, this meeting should include Senior Leadership Representation consisting of ELT members or a
designee. I've included ELT members as well as those involved in the MARC. If you cannot attend, please send a
designee in your place. Also, MARC team members are encouraged to debrief their corresponding Executive Committee
member on the issues.

Regulatory Concerns:
1. Use of the word "alternate/alternative" in our messaging is seen as constituting a comparative claim, insinuating
that OPANA ER is a superior alternative to other options
• Example: "Consider OPANA ER for appropriate patients who need an alternative to their current longacting opioid therapy" — utilized on almost every OER piece
2. Other messages utilized (specific instances for particular pieces) are felt to imply comparative superiority
• Example: "When your patients' current long-acting opioid does not provide sufficient analgesia and
tolerability" — from the Patient Profile Tool (OP-04654)
1

 3. The notion of switching to OPANA ER from another LAO is a concern due to our Limitations of Use statement,
which states:
"Because of the risks of addiction, abuse, and misuse with opioids, even at recommended doses, and
because of the greater risks of overdose and death with extended-release opioid formulations, reserve
OPANA ER for use in patients for whom alternative treatment options [e.g. non-opioid analgesics or
immediate-release opioids] are ineffective, not tolerated, or would be otherwise inadequate to provide
sufficient management of pain"
• Example: dialogue in both Sales Video scripts (OP-04707a and OP-04719a) where reps discuss with HCPs
their triggers and behaviors around LAO switching/rotation
Note: all of these concerns have implications to the overall OER brand strategy, which is why they're being escalated.
Additionally, concerns # 1 & 2 were raised after prior approval were rec'd on existing pieces currently in use — which
opens up a larger brand concern around ensuring consistency in MARC guidance across all pieces to avoid similar
situations in the future.

To ensure receipt of this email, please add edigest@gphaonline.org to your address book.

Wednesday, February 17, 2016

Government & Policy
Couple to Give $7.2 Million Toward Efforts to Lower Drug Prices; the Laura and John Arnold Foundation Will Fund Four Organizations
to Find Ways to Rein in Drug Costs
(2/16, Peter Loftus, The Wall Street Journal Online) reports "...The money will fund efforts to expand payment arrangements in which health
insurers and government health programs pay drug companies based on how well a treatment works in patients—sometimes called spay-forperformance'—rather than payments based solely on volume of medicine sold." Paid Subscription Required
A New Class of Drugs Could Save the US Billions of Dollars — but We're Way Behind in Adopting Them
(2/17, Lydia Ramsey, Business Insider) reports "Last week, a US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory committee gave a critical
recommendation for a version of an expensive, branded drug used to treat a class of painful diseases...The panel's recommendation isn't the final
word on the drug; the FDA is expected to either approve or reject it in April. An approval could be a huge deal. The US is getting hit with more costly
— and typically more innovative — new drugs. To make up for the rising costs, something needs to change. Biosimilars could be that change, since
they have the potential to compete with older, more expensive biologic drugs." Full
Can BIO's Heartfelt Image Campaign Win Hearts and Minds? Pharma Skeptics Aren't Convinced
(2/16, Beth Snyder Bulik, FiercePharma Marketing) reports "...Created by trade association BIO, the one-minute TV ad and companion website ask
viewers to consider the value of the extra time that biopharma drugs can offer." Full
Doctors Call for Fight Against Generic Drug Price Increases
(2/16, Dan Cook, BenefitsPro.com) reports "A state medical association is calling on similar organizations across the nation to rise up and take action
against spiraling generic drug price increases. The Pennsylvania Medical Society issued a statement alleging that increases in certain key generics
were likely the result of anti-competitive behavior on the part of pharmaceutical firms." Full
GAO Report on the Safety of Drugs Approved Using Expedited Programs Finds Shortcomings in FDA's Postmarket Oversight, Reviews
Use of Expedited Programs Instead
(2/16, James E. Valentine, FDA Law Blog) reports "...The report sought to examine the status of postmarket safety oversight of drugs approved using
one or more of FDA's expedited programs, which are programs to facilitate and expedite the development and review of new drugs. This would have
allowed GAO to determine the validity of Congresswoman DeLaura and consumer advocates' concern that the use of expedited programs increases
the risk of unforeseen safety issues once marketed (e.g., because there is less information due to fewer, smaller, or shorter clinical trials). However,
because `FDA lacks reliable, readily accessible data on tracked safety issues and postmarket studies needed to...conduct systematic oversight,' there
was not reliable data to allow GAO to test this hypothesis." Full
Medicare and Insurance Industry Officials Agree on Quality Metrics
(2/16, Andrew Siddons, CQ Roll Call) reports "Public and private health insurance providers on Tuesday announced a new set of quality
measurements meant to make reporting requirements for doctors and care providers more consistent and efficient. By easing the reporting
complexity for clinicians, insurers are also hoping to bring down costs for themselves and consumers." Paid Subscription Required
Pfizer to Pay $784m to Settle Claims it Overcharged Medicaid
(2/16, Ed Silverman, Stat: Pharmalot) reports "After a long-running government investigation, Pfizer has agreed to pay more than $784 million to
settle al legations that its Wyeth unit overcharged state Medicaid programs for the Protonix heartburn drug." Full
Ads for Costly Drugs Get Airtime
(2/17, Peter Loftus, The Wall Street Journal) reports "...The shift reflects a big change in the industry: as drugs for many common conditions lose
patent protection and face generic competition, branded drug companies increasingly are relying on revenue from drugs for serious and sometimes
rare conditions, a class of medicines known as `specialty drugs.'" Paid Subscription Required
Governor Takes Issue With Super Bowl Drug Ad as New House Bill Looks to Restrict DTC Pharma Advertising
(2/16, Zachary Brennan, Regulatory Focus) reports "Vermont Gov. Peter Shumlin (D) has sent a letter to pharmaceutical companies AstraZeneca
and Daiichi Sankyo calling on them to pull their advertisement that aired during the Super Bowl. The ad promoted a drug to treat opioid-induced
constipation. `Like many Americans, I was baffled by the commercial your companies paid an estimated $10 million to air during the Super Bowl. In
the midst of America's opiate and heroin addiction crisis the advertisement was not only poorly timed, it was a shameful attempt to exploit that crisis
to boost your companies' profits,' Shumlin said in the letter." Full

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07078747

 Senator Aims To Add Opioid Responsibility To FDA Mission Statement
(2/16 InsideHealthPolicy.com) reports "Senator Joe Manchin (D-WV) introduced legislation to amend FDA's mission statement to hold the agency
responsible for protecting the public health from prescription opioid medications." Paid Subscription Required
12) an Raises Possibility TPP Will Never Pass Congress; Details Objections
(2/16 Inside U.S. Trade) reports "House Speaker Paul Ryan (R-WI) over the weekend held open the possibility that Congress will never pass the
Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) by saying he does not know if and when there will be enough votes to pass it. He also publicly spelled out his
problems with the agreement for the first time, citing provisions on cross-border data flows, dairy and biologic drugs." Paid Subscription Required

Stop Wasting Money on Brand-name Drugs
(2/16, Julia Belluz, Vox) reports "...In order to bring costs down, at both the population and individual level, many experts have encouraged a switch
to generic drugs wherever possible. Here's what you need to know." Full
Video: This Is How One Company Is Bringing Down Costs of Generic Drugs

Subject: Some selected highlights from the East Tennessee Rx Drug Summit (7/26/11 in Knoxville)
On Tuesday, July 26th, I attended the East Tennessee Prescription Drug Summit held in Knoxville at the UT Conference Center. I
was one of about 250 attendees present. Most were law enforcement personnel from local police departments and sheriffs'
offices, parole officers, drug diversion investigators, district attorneys' offices, as well as several present from various state
and federal law enforcement agencies and judicial districts. Others in attendance included drug abuse counselors, social
workers, psychologists, school counselors, educators, physicians, nurse practitioners, pharmacists, pharmaceutical
manufacturers, nurses, elected and appointed local, state, and federal government officials, and members of the press. The
Summit was organized by the staff of US Attorney for Eastern Tennessee, William Killian and is one of many similar
conferences being sponsored at key locations across the nation by other Justice Dept. officials. The principal guest speakers at
the Summit were Regina LaBelle, Policy Advisor in the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy, Joe Rannazzisi,
Deputy Assistant Administrator at the Drug Enforcement Administration, and John Eadie of the Brandeis University
Prescription Monitoring Program Center of Excellence. Other speakers included drug diversion invesigators, prosecuting
attorneys, providers involved in patient care (MD, PharmD, LCSW, DDS), a recovering addict, elected officials. Each shared a
number of meaningful statistics documenting aspects of the prescription drug abuse problem as well as perspectives from
their own professional points of view. Here are some of the many interesting comments from the various speakers
throughout the day.
• Joe Rannazzisi of DEA briefly cited OpanaER as a product that is surfacing more and more as a drug of diversion.
(When he mentioned this, there was an audible murmur of "yes", "that's right", etc. from several members of the
audience.)
• > 6,000 persons per day [> 2 million persons per year] are initiating non-medical use of pain relievers (of these,
2,500 per day are teens, with 60% of those < 15 yo)
• The Vaults of Erowid [www.erowid.org] is a website that contains lots of information — some scientific, some not
scientific — about drugs and other substances used for recreational purposes; it's frequently accessed by teenagers
and young adults seeking information on psychoactive drugs and other mind-altering substances.
• Immediate-release oxycodone 30 mg tablets (Roxicodone) have grown in popularity since the reformulation of
Oxycontin. Many Rx's for it are being generated in Florida.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07171380

 • Florida pill mill explosion came after legislation shut off hundreds of internet pharmacies.
• As FL laws banned dispensing of drugs from pain clinics, applications for new pharmacies (located next to the
clinics) have risen sharply. Amazing who some of these proposed pharmacy owners are (e.g. truck drivers, exotic
dancers, etc.). (DEA reviewing these applications.)
• There are 7+ Rx drug overdose deaths per day in Florida.
• In Tennessee, there are five deaths due to prescription drug overdoses for every death due to
methamphetamine or cocaine overdose.
• Nationally, in 2009, 6.8% of admissions to drug treatment facilities were for abuse of opioids
• In Tennessee in 2009, 23% of admissions to drug treatment facilities were for abuse of opioids
• In eastern Tennessee in 2009, 42% of admissions to drug treatment facilities were for abuse of opioids
• Median age of persons admitted to drug treatment facilities in Tennessee is approx. 30 yo (slight surplus of
women over men)
• In the aggregate, prescription drug misuse has surpassed marijuana as the gateway drug for new users of drugs
susceptible to abuse.
• In Florida and Washington (perhaps other states too), there's been a quadrupling of the rate of newborns who are
physically dependent on opioids.
• The prevalence of opioid prescriptions written for adolescents is growing steadily (largely driven by prescriptions
from dentists and oral surgeons)
• "Doctor shopping" is most common in patients in their 20's and 30's (younger age groups than usually predicted).
• The source of the explosion of opioid use in part goes to the time in the mid-1990s when risks of opioids were
often described as not being as great as previously thought (though subsequent evidence documents that the risks
are indeed greater than was being described in the mid-1990s). This period coincided with the increase in focus on
pain as a prominent assessment factor in patient care.
• There needs to be better and wider access to prescription drug monitoring programs in the states so that
appropriate analyses can be done with information dissemination to public health and other appropriate authorities.
Need laws passed to enable Veterans Health facilities and DOD health facilities to share controlled substance
prescribing and prescription filling data to prescription drug monitoring programs.
• In 2010, Knoxville, Tennessee had the 2nd greatest number of pharmacy robberies in the nation (#46).
• The task of prosecuting prescribing providers (for inappropriate prescribing of controlled substances) is difficult —
mounds of evidence have to be accumulated to have a good chance of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt (juries
often tend to sympathize with providers who "are just trying to take care of very sick patients as best they can").
When investigations are underway, it's often useful to get IRS investigators involved. Unscrupulous prescribers
almost always run afoul of laws pertaining to tax reporting, money-laundering, etc. That's often a successful avenue
for convictions.
• Can buy blank tamper-resistant Rx paper over the internet, get DEA It's and NPI It's, prescriber addresses via the
Internet; diverters can print very authentic looking fake Rx's, then take to other geographic areas to get filled.
• Pain Management Clinics (ie. "pill mills") are moving north out of Florida as new laws take effect in Florida to curb
these businesses. Many setting up shop in Georgia and Tennessee.
• Thefts are becoming more brazen. In addition to more pharmacy robberies, recently there was nearly a
successful attempt to hijack a drug wholesaler's courier van (used to deliver controlled substances to pharmacies that
had ordered them).
• In middle Tennessee, growing demand for Suboxone, high-dose immediate-release oxycodone, Adderall,
alprazolam, OpanaER.
• Law enforcement has to pay more attention opioid diversion (don't keep focus on meth, marijuana, and heroin)
• Need closer regulatory oversight of physicians who are "supervising" physician assistants/nurse practitioners.
(e.g. There's one DO in middle Tennessee who "supervises" more than 40 NP's (at $1K per week for each))
• Need standard of practice (perhaps rules) in pharmacies that persons picking-up prescriptions for controlled
substances have to provide positive ID that they are the patient or a person authorized by the patient to pick-up
medicines for them.
• We "cannot arrest our way out of the problem of misuse of prescription drugs". Better and more comprehensive
prevention efforts have to be brought to bear.

Speaking Faculty Stephen Arneric, Ph.D., Senior Research Fellow, Pain & Migraine Drug Hunting Team, Neuroscience Discovery, Eli Lilly & Co. Travis Mickle, Ph.D., President, CEO, KemPharm, Inc. MORE to be announced soon... Featured Presentations ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07478654 The G Protein Biased Mu-opioid Liga lid TRV130: A Developmental-stage Analgesic with an Improved Tolerability Profile TRV130 is a potent, selective G protein biased ligand at the mu-opioid receptor. The compound is active in several preclinical models of pain with an improved tolerability profile compared to morphine. TRV130 was dosed intravenously to normal volunteers and has doseproportional levels of exposure. Subjects dosed with TRV130, experienced a dose dependent increase in pupil constriction, a classical effect of mu opioid receptor activation. The compound was well tolerated and plans are now being made to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of TRV130 compared to morphine in an experimental medicine study in healthy volunteers. Michael Lark, Ph.D., Chief Scientific Officer & Senior Vice President, Research, Trevena, Inc. Pain Models and Methods to Reduce Experimental Error in Analgesic Clinical Trials Falsely negative analgesic clinical trials are not only a squandered societal burden, but also are a waste of precious time and resources. Pharmaceutical companies spend large amounts of time perfecting their protocol and selecting quality sites so that the efficacy of their drug can be statistically demonstrated. However, an equal amount of effort is rarely placed on other aspects of clinical trials that may lead to optimizing their success such as patient education and analgesic model manipulations. This talk will discuss techniques for site education, subject placebo response training, and other mechanisms to mitigate variability in analgesic clinical trials. Neil Singla, MD, Founder & Chief Scientific Officer, Lotus Clinical Research, LLC New Approaches for Preclinical Assessment of Analgesic Efficacy and Side Effects The treatment of acute and chronic pain continues to present an enormous challenge to physicians and other healthcare professionals. In many cases, current pharmacotherapies offer incomplete efficacy and/or produce self limiting side effects. Development of new (novel) analgesics has been limited and disappointing from the patient, practitioner and pharmaceutical perspectives. Assessment of analgesic efficacy in preclinical animal models is one area that needed careful reevaluation and change to help address the overall lack of progress. This talk will present some of the latest approaches in inducing nociceptive (pain) states in animals, measuring the consequences of the pain on behavior and other relevant endpoints, and assessing analgesic candidates as part of the drug development process. The presentation will include new methods for measuring spontaneous and affective components of pain, as well as pain suppressed behaviors. Dear PAIN/CREO Business Units,
Some information came through today-this week regarding class labeling for opioids. Note the FDA is requiring
updated labeling for the entire class of all opioids (both ER/LA and IR products) pain medicines to include safety
information about potentially harmful drug interactions with other medicines that can result in a serious central nervous
system condition reaction called serotonin syndrome. Updated labeling will also include information about opioid
effects on the endocrine system, including a rare but serious disorder of the adrenal glands (called adrenal
insufficiency) and decreased sex hormone levels (androgen deficiency). These labeling changes will also make it clear
that these negative outcomes can occur whether a patient is taking an opioid to treat pain or if the product is being
used for medication assisted treatment (MAT). On March 22nd, the FDA issued a Drug Safety Communication
outlining these risks.
For IR Opioids, in a continuing effort to educate prescribers and patients about the potential risks related to opioid
use, the FDA today announced required class-wide safety labeling changes for immediate-release (IR) opioid pain
medications. Among the changes, the FDA is requiring a new boxed warning about the serious risks of misuse, abuse,
addiction, overdose and death.
The updated indication clarifies that because of these risks, IR opioids should be reserved for pain severe enough to
require opioid treatment and for which alternative treatment options (e.g., non-opioid analgesics or opioid combination
products, as appropriate) are inadequate or not tolerated. The dosing information also provides clearer instructions
regarding patient monitoring and drug administration, including initial dosage, dosage changes during therapy, and a
warning not to abruptly stop treatment in a physically dependent patient.
As part of the boxed warning on IR opioid analgesics, the FDA now requires a precaution that chronic maternal use of
opioids during pregnancy can result in neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS), which may be life-threatening if
not recognized and treated using protocols developed by neonatology experts. NOWS may occur in a newborn
exposed to opioid drugs for a prolonged period while in utero.
