Zogenix Appoints Chief Medical Officer and Expands Medical
Leadership Team
December 17th, 2013
Additional Clinical and Medical Affairs Leaders Join Zogenix to Support Zohydro(TM) ER Launch
SAN DIEGO, Dec. 17, 2013 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Zogenix, Inc. (Nasdaq:ZGNX), a pharmaceutical company developing and
commercializing products for the treatment of central nervous system disorders and pain, announced today the expansion of its
senior leadership team in support of the planned launch of Zohydro TM ER (hydrocodone bitartrate) extended-release capsules in
March 2014. This includes the appointment of a Chief Medical Officer, Vice President of Medical and Scientific Affairs, and
Executive Director of Medical Affairs, effective immediately.
The new- senior appointments are all distinguished leaders in the fields of pain management and analgesic drug development and will
play key roles in the launch and post marketing support of Zohydro ER, as well as building the company's product pipeline targeting
CNS disorders and pain management. The new hires include the following:

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06227716

 Bradley S. Galer, M.D., Executive Vice President and Chief Medical Officer - Prior to joining Zogenix, Dr. Galer
served as President of the Pain Group at Nuvo Research, a specialty pharmaceutical company with three
commercialized topically delivered pain products. In this position, he oversaw the strategy and operations of the Pain
Group, including its commercialization, drug development activities, business development and licensing opportunities
and liaising with partners. Prior to joining Nuvo, Dr. Galer was employed at Endo Pharmaceuticals as Senior Medical
Officer and Group Vice President, Scientific Affairs, where he was responsible for the departments of Clinical and
Biostatistics, Medical Affairs, Pharmacovigilance, Medical Liaison and Medical Information. He and his team provided
clinical and scientific leadership for the development and marketing of analgesic and migraine products, including
Lidoderm, Percocet, Opana, Opana ER and Frova. Dr. Galer has also held numerous other industry positions, along
with academic and clinical appointments. He has published over 200 articles on pain management in peer review
journals and textbooks. Dr. Galer received his medical doctorate and a neurology residency from Albert Einstein in
New York and two Pain Fellowships, at Memorial Sloane-Kettering in New York and University of California San
Francisco, as well as headache training at Montefiore Headache Clinic in New York and University of California San
Francisco.
Arnold R. Gammaitoni, Pharm.D., Vice President, Medical and Scientific Affairs - Prior to joining Zogenix, Dr.
Gammaitoni served as Vice President of Scientific Affairs of the Pain Group at Nuvo Research. Prior to joining Nuvo,
Dr. Gammaitoni was Global Director of Scientific Affairs for Analgesia, Immunology, and Anesthesia at Merck & Co.
Previous to Merck, he served as Senior Director of Medical Affairs at Endo Pharmaceuticals. Dr Gammaitoni has
also been a clinical practitioner with a focus on pain management and has authored or co-authored over 50 articles.
He received his doctoral degree in pharmacy from the Philadelphia College of Pharmacy.
Marsha R. Stanton, Ph.D., RN, Executive Director, Medical Affairs - Dr. Stanton is nationally known for her work
in pain management including clinical practice, public policy and patient education. Prior to joining Zogenix, Dr.
Stanton served as Executive Director of Program Development, External Affairs, Medical Affairs at Horizon Pharma,
a specialty pharmaceutical company with three commercialized products focused on arthritis, pain and inflammatory
diseases. She held similar positions representing pain products and organizations at Pfizer, King Pharmaceuticals,
Alpharma Pharmaceuticals and Purdue. Prior to joining the pharmaceutical industry, Dr. Stanton practiced as a nurse
responsible for the provision of acute and chronic pain services in a variety of hospital and outpatient settings. In
addition to being a registered nurse, she holds a Ph.D. in health education from Glendale University, NM.
"We are v-ery pleased to welcome Drs. Galer, Gammaitoni and Stanton to the Zogenix team," said Stephen Farr, Ph.D., President of
Zogenix. "They all have a proven track record of successful accomplishments in the development and commercialization of opioid
analgesics and other drug products. Under Brad's leadership we are building a strong clinical and medical affairs organization that
will be immediately focused on our programs to assure the appropriate use of Zohydro ER, be active participants in the design and
execution of the class-wide post marketing requirements for ER opioid analgesics, and advance our development pipeline that
includes an abuse deterrent formulation of Zohydro ER."
Dr. Galer commented, "I am very excited to be joining Zogenix, with an outstanding team passionate about helping patients
suffering from chronic pain and migraine. Zogenix has made significant strides in building a company focused on improving
treatment options for central nervous system disorders and pain. I believe Zohydro ER will fulfill a significant need for severe
chronic pain patients by providing the first extended-release hydrocodone product and the first hydrocodone product without
acetaminophen. In addition, Zogenix's pipeline products could provide needed new treatments for many patients."

June 24, 2013 — 6:00 a.m.
Lawmakers Probe Painkiller Abuse in Medicare
By Emily Ethridge, CQ Roll Call
A Senate committee is investigating prescription drug abuse in Medicare, following a report that found more than 700 Medicare
physicians had questionable patterns of prescribing painkillers and other risky drugs.
Several congressional committees have held hearings on prescription drug abuse, and lawmakers have introduced legislation
dealing with different aspects of the issue. But Congress has yet to coalesce around an approach for fighting the "pill mill"
problem, including in federal programs, while ensuring that medications are available for patients in chronic pain.
Witnesses at the Monday hearing will include two deputy inspectors general from the Department ofHealth and Human
Services' Office of Inspector General, which conducted the Medicare report .
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention classifies prescription drug abuse as a growing epidemic, and concerns about
Medicare fraud have grown as the abuse has become more widespread. In 2010, approximately 7 million people in the United
States were misusing prescription drugs, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse.
There is bipartisan legislation (S 621, FIR 1285) to put more limitations on hydrocodone-containing drugs by moving them to
schedule II. Rep. William Keating, D-Mass., has introduced a bill (HR 486) encouraging companies to create tamper-resistant
formulations for commonly abused painkillers. And West Virginia Democrats Rep. Nick J. Rahall II and Sen. Jay Rockefeller
also have legislation (HR 672, S 348) to set training requirements for prescribers of methadone and other opioids, and to give
grants to states for consumer education about opioid abuse. But none of the measures has progressed yet beyond bill
introductions.
The Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee will be looking into how to combat prescription drug fraud
in Medicare, as part of its investigation to limit waste, fraud and abuse in the program.
The OIG report made several recommendations for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, including expanding
analysis of prescribers, giving additional guidance on how to monitor prescribing patterns and following up with providers with
questionable prescribing patterns.
The report noted that some physicians defraud Medicare by writing large numbers of prescriptions for controlled substances that
are not medically necessary. They also might take kickback payments for writing unnecessary prescriptions, which are then
billed to Medicare. In addition, providers might have their prescription pads or identification numbers stolen or sold.
Of the more than 86,000 general-care physicians reviewed, the OIG found 736 who were extreme outliers in terms of drug
prescribing patterns. More than half of those physicians ordered extremely high percentages ofschedule II or III drugs, which
have a high or moderate risk for abuse. For example, the report noted one California physician who ordered 115 schedule 11 drugs
for one Medicare beneficiary in 2009.
Some physicians prescribed an extremely high number of prescriptions per beneficiary, including an Ohio physician who
ordered more than 400 drugs each for 13 of his Medicare patients.
The report also noted that Medicare paid $9.7 million — 151 times higher than the average — for the prescriptions of one
California physician. Most of those prescriptions were filled by two independent pharmacies that the OIG identified as having
questionable billing practices.
Also testifying at the committee hearing will be Joseph T. Rannazzisi, the deputy assistant administrator for the Drug
Enforcement Administration's Office of Diversion Control, and Jonathan Blum, the deputy administrator and director of
Medicare at CMS.
In addition, Alanna Lavelle, director of special investigations at WellPoint, will discuss how her company fights fraud inside its
health care plans. Testifying at a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing last year, Lavelle noted that WellPoint has
a dedicated fraud and abuse prevention team and a data analysis team, and was working on predictive modeling to find patterns
of fraud and abuse.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07017222

 WellPoint also has a restricted recipient program for its Medicaid plans, in which certain members who are at risk for abuse are
restricted to using only one primary care physician as a prescriber, one retail pharmacy and one hospital for non-emergency care.

The health subcommittee of Energy and Commerce also has launched a fresh series of hearings this year looking at prescription
drug abuse.

Drug-drug interactions between opioid medications used to treat opioid dependence, such as

pharmacokinetic and/or pharmacodynamics interactions. This presentation will also review
drug-drug interactions and clinical consequences using a series of case studies that address

VOLUME 103, NUMBER 4
PainEDU is an educational resource for clinicians who treat patients with chronic pain.

This week's features:
Spotlight Interview: Andrew Kolodny, MD, Physicians for Responsible Opioid Prescribing
The dilemma of opioid prescribing -- finding the right balance between the needs of patients with
chronic pain for effective analgesia and the public health risks of addiction and misuse -- has recently
been the subject of increased scrutiny, as government and medical organizations investigate the
possible connections between the availability of opioids and their potential misuse.
Among the voices calling for a reassessment of opioid prescribing practices are Physicians for
Responsible Opioid Prescribing (PROP), and its president, Andrew Kolodny, M.D., Chairman of the
Department of Psychiatry at Maimonides Medical Center in Brooklyn, N.Y. In July, PROP petitioned
the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to remove chronic non-cancer pain from the labeled indications
for opioid analgesics. In this interview, Dr. Kolodny discusses the specifics of the petition with
PainEDU's Kevin Zacharoff, M.D.
Course-in-a-Box - Teaching Chronic Pain Patients about Medication-Related Adverse Effects
Patient education is essential to successfully managing chronic pain with opioid analgesics. This "
Course-in-a-Box" reviews the best current practices for communicating effectively with chronic pain
patients about their role in identifying and managing the possible adverse effects of opioid medication.
Each PainEDU "Course-in-a-Box" is a downloadable, print-ready PowerPointTM presentation, complete
with speaker notes, designed for use in classrooms, grand rounds, conferences, and for in-service
education. You will need to register or login to download this tool. It's halfway down the page, under
"Non-Interactive Tools".)
painACTION ACTIONSteps: 12 Medication Safety Resources for Your Patients
ACTIONSteps are concise, single-sheet handouts designed to teach your patients about managing
their medications safely; these handouts can also prompt increased physician-patient dialogue and
reinforce patient education.
Each of these valuable clinical tools discusses a different aspect of medication safety. Topics include
dealing with side effects, proper storage and disposal of medications, and traveling with opioids.
Download ACTIONStep #7: How to manage opioid side effects or, download the entire set of 12
ACTIONSteps.
News and Resources
Remember to check this page on our website to find the latest pain news, as well as links to other
resources.

WARNING: POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, IMPORTANCE OF PROPER PATIENT SELECTION AND LIMITATIONS OF USE

Potential for Abuse
OPANA ER containsoxymorphone, which is a morphine-like opioid agonistand a Schedule II controlled substance, with an abuse liability similar to other
opioid analgesics.

Oxymorphonecan be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. This should be considered when prescribingor dispensing OPANA ER

 in situations wherethe physician or pharmacist is concerned about an increased risk of misuse, abuse, or diversion.

Proper Patient Selection
OPANA ER is an extended-release oral formulation of oxymorphone indicated for the management of moderateto severe pain when a continuous,
around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extended period of time.

Limitations of Use
OPANA ER is NOT intended for use as an as needed analgesic.

OPANA ER tablets are to be swallowed whole and are not to be cut, broken,chewed, dissolved, or crushed.

Taking cut, broken, chewed,dissolved, or crushed OPANA ER tablets leads to rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of oxymorphone.

Patients must not consume alcoholic beverages,or prescription or non-prescription med ications containing alcohol, while on OPANA ER therapy. The
co-ingestion of alcohol with OPANA ER may result in increased plasma levels and a potentially fatal overdose of oxymorphone.

CONTRAINDICATIONS
•

OPANA® ER is contraindicated in patients with a known hypersensitivity to oxymorphone hydrochloride, morphine analogs such as codeine, orany

of the other ingredients of OPANA ER; in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment or in any situation where opioids are contraindicated such
as: patients with respiratory depression (in the absence of resuscitative equipment or in unmonitored settings), acute or severe bronchial asthma,
hypercarbia, and in any patient who has or is suspected of having paralytic ileus.
•

OPANA ER is not indicated for pain in the immediate post-operative period or if the pain is mild, or not expected to persist for an extended period of

time. OPANA ER is only indicated for post-operative use if the patient is already receiving the drug prior tosurgeryor if the post-operative pain is expected
to be moderate or severe and persist for an extended period of time. Physicians should individualize treatment, moving from parenteral to oral analgesics
as appropriate (see American Pain Society guidelines). OPANA ER is not indicated for pre-emptive analgesia (administration pre-operatively for the
management of post- operative pain).

WARNINGS
Respiratory depression is the chief hazard of OPANA ER, particularlyin elderly or debilitated patients.
OPANA ER should be administered with extreme caution to patients with conditions accompanied by hypoxia, hypercapnia, or decreased
respiratory reserve.
•

Patients receiving other opioid analgesics, general anesthetics, phenothiazines or othertranquilizers, sedatives, hypnotics,orotherCNS

depressants (including alcohol) may experience additive effects resulting in respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma and death.
•

In the presence of head injury, the respiratory depressant effects of OPANA ER and the potential to elevate cerebrospinal fluid pressure maybe

markedly exaggerated.
•

OPANA ER may ca use severe hypotension in patients with compromised ability to maintain blood pressure. Administer with caution to patients in

circulatory shock.
•

Prolonged gastric obstruction may occur in patients with gastrointestinal obstruction, especially paralytic ileus.

•

Use with caution in patients with biliary tract disease, as it may cause spasm of the sphincterof oddi.

•

Opioid analgesics, including OPANA ER, may impair the mental and physical abilities needed to perform potentially hazardous activities such as

driving a car oroperating machinery.
•

OPANA ER is not recommended during labor and delivery, pregnancy, or nursing.

•

OPANA ER should be used with caution in elderly and debilitated patients and in patients who are known to be sensitive to CNS depressa nts, such as

those with cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal, or hepatic disease. OPANA ER should be used with caution in patients with mild hepatic impa irment and in
patients with moderate tosevere renal impairment. These patients should be started cautiously with lower doses of OPANA ER while carefully monitoring
for side effects.
•

OPANA ER tablets should be taken one tablet at a time, with enough water to ensure complete swallowing immediatelyafter placing in the mouth.

•

Advise patients that OPANA ER tablets should be taken one at a time.

•

Advise patients not to pre-soak, lick, or otherwise wet tablet prior to placing in the mouth.

•

Advise patients to take each tablet with enough water to ensure complete swallowing immediately after placing in mouth.

•

Patients and their families should be instructed toflush any OPANA ER tablets that are no longer needed.

ADVERSE REACTIONS

 •

Adverse reactions reported at (≥2%) in placebo-controlled trials were: nausea, constipation, dizziness, somnolence, vomiting, pruritus, headache,

sweating increased, dry mouth, sedation, diarrhea, insomnia, fatigue, appetite decreased, and abdominal pain.
•

In clinical trials there were several adverse events that were more frequently observed in subjects 65 and over compared to younger subjects. These

adverse events included dizziness, somnolence,confusion, and nausea.

DRUG INTERACTIONS
•

CNS depressants: Increased risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma and death. When combined therapy with CNS

depressant is contemplated, the dose of one or both agents should be reduced. Mixed agonist/antagonistopioids (i.e., pentazocine, nalbuphine, and
butorphanol): May reduce analgesic effect and/or precipitate withdrawal symptoms. Cimetidine: Combination use may precipitate confusion,
disorientation, respiratory depression, apnea, seizures. Anticholinergics: May result in urinary retention and/or severe constipation, which may lead to
paralytic ileus. Monoa mine oxidase inhibitors (TVIAO1s): Potentiate the action of opioids. OPANA ER should not be used in patients taking M AOI s orwithin
14 days of stopping such treatment.

VOLUME 102, NUMBER 5
PainEDU is an educational resource for clinicians who treat patients with chronic pain.

This week's features:
Spotlight Interview: Thomas Clark on the Prescription Drug Monitoring Program Center of
Excellence
Every state in the U.S. but one has passed legislation creating a prescription drug monitoring program
(PDMP); 41 are operational, collecting data from pharmacies and practitioners who dispense
medications and reporting that data to authorized users. The PDMP Center of Excellence (COE) at
Brandeis Univesity was founded in 2010 to evaluate, identify, and share best practices for PDMPs.
Thomas Clark, senior research associate at Brandeis' Heller School for Social Policy and
Management, is also manager of the COE's resource clearinghouse. In this Spotlight interview, he
talks about the COE's mission to "end the prescription drug abuse epidemic in the United States
without compromising accepted standards of pain management or the legitimate prescribing of
controlled substances."
PAINWeek 2012: The Pharmacist's Role in Palliative Care
Rebecca Maxson, PharmD, BCPS, is clinical pharmacy specialist in nephrology and palliative care at a
teaching hospital in Birmingham, Alabama. When her hospital formed its palliative care team in 2010,
she was thrilled to be appointed its clinical pharmacist. In that role, she teaches and mentors
pharmacists and physicians in training, and is confronting the need to educate her hospital colleagues
in the appropriate use of palliative care. In her essay, which earned a PainEDU scholarship to
PAINWeek 2012, she writes that attending PAINWeek will provide "opportunities for improving the care
of the patients we serve, and enhancing the education and pain management skills of the present and
future pharmacists and physicians that I instruct and mentor."
PainEDU.org at PAINWeek 2012
PainEDU.org will be at PAINWeek 2012 next week (September 5 - 8) at the Cosmopolitan hotel in Las
Vegas. As part of the award ceremony and keynote presentation on Wednesday, September 5, at 6:30
p.m., we'll recognize the 10 pain management clinicians whose essays earned PainEDU.org
scholarships to attend PAINWeek. Immediately after the ceremony, at 7:30 p.m., we will introduce the
second edition of Your Guide to Pain Management: A Road Map for painACT1ON.com. Lead author
Kevin L. Zacharoff, M.D., FACPE, FACIP, FAAP, will sign complimentary copies of the guide from
7:30-9:30 p.m. in the exhibit hall. Unsigned copies will be available at booth 105 throughout the
conference. Inflexxion, Inc./PainEDU researchers will present two posters at PainWEEK; they will be
available to discuss the data at the poster session and reception, Thursday, September 6, from 6:308:30 p.m. Dr. Zacharoff will speak about his survey on prescriber acceptance of opioid REMS
education at Friday's Poster/Podium Presentations, 8:10-10:10 a.m.
painACTION ACTIONSteps: 12 Medication Safety Resources for Your Patients
ACTIONSteps are concise, single-sheet handouts designed to teach your patients about managing
their medications safely; these handouts can also prompt increased physician-patient dialogue and
reinforce patient education.
Each of these valuable clinical tools discusses a different aspect of medication safety. Topics include
dealing with side effects, proper storage and disposal of medications, and traveling with opioids.

WOMA 2012 Spring Seminar - Chronic Pain Management for Primary Care - Saturday April 21, 2012

Rich,
Here's a top level round-up of the WOMA Pain Update for Primary Care.
Primary speaker was Scott M. Fishman, MD who was well received by attendees. Dr. Fishman is author of
"Responsible Opioid Prescribing," the book we've used in the past for key accounts. Dr. Fishman is currently Chief of
Pain Medicine at the UC Davis School of Medicine in Sacramento, CA. He is regarded by many as THE expert in all
matters opioid.
Take home points: I've highlighted key points for a quick read. See agenda below for particular topics.
Methadone can be dangerous. One physician described a situation where an hospitalized patient was given 100mg
of methadone instead of 10mg. The physician quickly assessed the patient vital signs which were all fine but as a
precaution put the patient in the ICU. Two days later while still in the ICU the patient experienced life-threatening
respiratory depression. Patient was given NArcan drip to stabilize. The physician said this patient would've died if she
had been discharged out of the hospital the day she first took the 100mg methadone even though her vital signs were
normal!
Dr. Fishman explained how methadone's Alpha and Beta elimination phases can account for patient overdose. The
Alpha elimination phase is the therapeutic stage when patients experience pain relief (analgesia). This analgesia lasts
for about 4-8 hours. However methadone remains active in the body for up to 60 hours total. The Beta elimination
phase can last 20-60 hours. So if a patient takes too much as the above story shows, the methadone levels can over
just a few days lead to respiratory depression. This would be a particular concern if a patient were to take more
methadone than prescribed per day thinking that more would control pain better.
Methadone is a long-acting opioid, not a long-acting analgesic, Fishman said. He commented methadone could be
better categorized as a short-acting opioid due to its short therapeutic effect.
Opioid insensitivity is how Dr. Fishman characterized some patients not responding to higher and higher levels of
opioids. This was his response to Phillip Matthews, DO asking about Dr. Fishman's opinion on the existence and
validity of hyperalgesia — that higher doses of opioids can cause patients to feel more pain rather than less. Fishman
said he has not seen evidence of hyperalgesia in his patients. "Hyperalgesia is a lab term," he said.
Feeling better is not enough to warrant receiving continued opioid therapy, Fishman said. He wants improved
function and asks patients to prove they are doing more ADLs because of therapy.
Fishman recommended doctors become enrolled and use the Prescription Monitoring Program installed by WA
State. He said this resource allows physicians to quickly see where patients are filling prescriptions and when the
prescriptions are filled. The link to sign up is here: http://www.wapmp.org/practitioner/pharmacist/
Opana ER did not come up by name in discussions from the podium.
Marijuana is a Schedule I substance according to the DEA. Fishman said DEA officials he knows say patients
receiving any Schedule I substances should not be taking any other scheduled products.
Paul Brown, MD Rheumatology said he is an advocate for early and aggressive use of opioids in appropriate
patients suffering from rheumatological diseases.
In summary, the mood of doctors was not as alarmed as last year but there's still significant hesitation to treating pain
using opioids. Dr. Fishman's clarification of the legal issues of marijuana and clinical statements about methadone

minimal. Dr. Brown's exhortation to use opioids in patients with rheumatic ailments may calm some doctors as Dr.
Brown is well-regarded specialist. Dr. Brown practices in Seattle.

Subject: National DEC e-Update: April 2012 - DEC Awareness Day is April 25!
From:

National DEC <info@nationaldec.ccsend.com>

To:

Crawford, Deborah <Chilcote-Crawford.Deborah@endo.com >;

Dear Deborah,

Ai

Ii

&JO

As many of you know, April means Child Abuse Prevention Month (see the
presidential proclamation HERE) and National Rx Drug Takeback Day (click
HERE to find a collection site near you).

But did you also know that April means
DEC Awareness Day, too?
That's right! On April 25, 2012, state DEC alliances around the nation will
be celebrating the second annual DEC Awareness Day. DEC alliances in
Colorado, Missouri, and Iowa are commemorating the day with small
events in their local communities. In Kansas, volunteers will be
remembering the 274 substances exposed babies born in Shawnee County
this year. They'll be in front of the capitol building holding a rope with 274
baby onesies. The onesies were donated by a local charity called Cocktails
for a Cause. Kansas DEC members will also be giving out micro-grants to
assist communities hosting local events and handing out resource cards
and posters on the dangers of prenatal exposure.
For information on other DEC Awareness events around the country, or to
get started planning DEC Awareness Day 2013, contact your state DEC
alliance coordinator. Don't have a DEC alliance in your state? Contact
National DEC's DEC Network Services Director Susannah Carroll for more
information on how to get involved!

And while we have you, be sure to check out some of the latest uploads to
our Online Library, learn about our new partnership with Lamar
Associates to protect Native children, get information about the 2012
national conference (registration opens in May!), and see what upcoming
trainings and events are happening in YOUR neck of the woods.

Updates to A to Z Resources
National DEC Partnering to Serve Native
Children
2012 Conference Registration Opens in May

Your Neck of the Woods

National DEC Home

*Recently updated*

As always, if you've got a question or need information, please contact us
at info®nationaldec.org. We'll get right back to you.
Warmly,

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

Join our Mailing List!

ENDO_ANK_CHI_1007794

 National DEC Staff

Updates to Online A to Z Resources Library
National DEC's A to Z Resources Library now has more than 950 resources to help you in your work, including articles, research
reports, protocols, collateral materials, and more!
Here are just a few of the more than two dozen new resources we've added this month:
• Marijuana legalization: The issues (Gorman, T. J.)
• Working with drug-abusing families: Reference guide (The R.U.R.A.L. Project; California Institute on Human Services at
Sonoma State University)
• Polyvictimization: Children's exposure to multiple types of violence, crime, and abuse (Finkelhor, D., Turner, H.,
Hamby, S., and Ormrod, R.)
• Preventing FASD: Healthy women, healthy babies (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Substance Abuse
and Mental Health Services Administration, Center for Substance Abuse Prevention)
• Interpersonal violence and illicit drugs (Atkinson, A., Anderson, Z., Hughes, K., et al.)
As a reminder, we also post the recordings of our popular monthly webinar series on our website as well, on the Training
Downloads page.

National DEC Announces Partnership with Lamar Associates to Serve Native Children
Statistics on child welfare in Indian Country, although far from complete, paint a troubling picture of too many children being
neglected and even abused, with substance abuse emerging as the most common contributing factor. For this reason, Lamar
Associates-Indian Country Training and the National Alliance for Drug Endangered Children (National DEC) have formed a
partnership to develop a specific curriculum for service providers who work with children in tribal communities. The collective
goal is to improve early detection and intervention so that Native families get the help they need before a tragedy occurs.
"Our mission is to promote prevention education for our tribal communities because we know firsthand the drug threat in our
tribal lands is significant," said Steven Juneau, Chief Executive Officer of Indian Country Training. "Children are primarily at risk
of neglect as a result of their caregivers involvement in substance abuse. We want our children safe and we want parents to get
well. To accomplish this, our partnership with the National DEC will strengthen our capacity to provide training and technical
assistance in early identification and intervention, along with substance abuse awareness on drugs that plague our communities.
Adds National DEC president Chuck Noerenberg, "Drug endangered children need our help.This partnership between National
DEC and Lamar Associates-Indian Country Training will greatly strengthen our efforts to protect and serve children wherever they
live and whatever their circumstances."
For the complete press release, click HERE.

I',112 National DEC Conference Registration Opens in May
National DEC is pleased to announce that registration for our 2012 annual national conference, "Collaborating for Healthier
Children, Stronger Families, and Safer Communities," will open in May! Keep your eyes out for an email with information about
how to register and details about the conference schedule including our annual silent auction and our inaugural Healthy
Families Fun Run/Walk!
We'll have information about you can increase your organization's visibility by sponsoring or exhibiting at the conference!
"Collaborating for Healthier Children, Stronger Families, and Safer Communities"

 Federal Perspectives on Bath Salts and Other Synthetics
Date: Wednesday, April 25,2012
Time: 11:30am - 12.30pm (mountain)
Speakers: Representatives from ONDCP, DEA, and COPS
[REGISTRATION OPENS 4/18]
About:
Some questions to be addressed include the following:
What is happening nationally with bath salts and other synthetics, including synthetic marijuana? What are the stats and trends?
How is the Federal government reacting to this challenge? How can the states weigh in to help? What do local practitioners need
to know to deal with this challenge - whether law enforcement, child protection, prosecutors, teachers, medical personnel, etc.

*****

Opioids During Pregnancy and Beyond to Baby
Date: Wednesday, June 13,2012
Time: 11:30am - 12.30pm (mountain)
Speakers: Dr. Jacquelyn Starer and Dr. Marcia VanVleet, American Society of Addiction Medicine
[REGISTRATION OPENS 5/30]
About:
The management of opioid dependence during pregnancy will be reviewed, including treatment with methadone and
buprenorphine. Data from the MOTHERS study will be presented. Drug selection will be discussed along with dosing issues during
the pregnancy, labor and post partum periods. Recommendations and strategies for detoxification will be identified. Breast
feeding recommendations will be reviewed. Opiate withdrawal in the newborn will also be reviewed including issues concerning
observation for symptoms and how long to observe, environmental treatment with the utilization of occupational therapy and
massage, and the management of neonatal withdrawal symptoms with medications.
Check our website for announcements about other National DEC webinars.

National DEC provides these webinars at no charge to you and your colleagues working to improve the lives of children living in drug environments. We are
dependent upon the generosity of individuals like you in order to offer these exceptional learning opportunities. Please consider how your gift will help us

Subject: Update on REMS from NCCN
Dear REMS Work Group,
Below is a summary of recent news and ongoings on the topic of REMS. If you have any comments or questions, please
let me know.
Best,
Jess DeMartino
Most significantly, the FDA is seeking to remove Medication Guides from the REMS process because of the substantial
burden Medication Guide-only REMS impose on manufacturers, providers, and the FDA ("The Pink Sheet," June 21,
2010). The FDA is investigating ways to streamline this process and to reduce the workload in this area.
The work that we have done with the REMS Oncology Summit and White paper may have contributed to these
events. The FDA is revising its policies and approaches to REMS based on public feedback. Participants at the NCCN
REMS Oncology Summit, held on May 7, 2010, expressed concern over the issues related to the Medication Guides, and
an FDA representative publicly acknowledged the limitations of Medication Guides at this meeting. Additionally, some key
discussions at the Oncology Summit:
• presented data regarding how prescribers will avoid utilizing drugs with complex REMS.
• emphasized the need to better assess whether REMS are effective in mitigating risk.
• highlighted the need to focus on patient and provider education.
In other news, on June 28, 2010, the FDA informed manufacturers of long-acting opioids that the REMS for their products
will not require provider or patient registration. Originally, in February 2009, the FDA informed manufacturers of certain
opioid products that their product would require a REMS, citing safety concerns related to the improper selection of
patients treated with opioids, misuse, abuse, and overdose (intentional and accidental). It was expected that the classwide REMS for opioids would include elements to assure safe use (ETASU), which would require that physicians enroll in
a program and that pharmacies verify prescriber training. However, the FDA recently acknowledged concerns that
pharmacies and physicians would utilize other options that did not require registration, thus decreasing
access. Additionally, public input suggested that creating a patient registry would hinder the useful prescribing of these
drugs; patients may forgo treatment to avoid the stigma associated with being on an opioid. Therefore, the FDA narrowed
its approach to opioid REMS. The current focus is now on prescriber and patient education. Physician education would
be voluntary, and the manufacturers would provide prescribers with FDA-approved patient education materials to be used
1

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-CHI_LIT-01026671

 during patient counseling sessions. Assessing the effectiveness of the REMS will also be emphasized, and
manufacturers are working with the FDA to identify and collect baseline metrics in prescriber/patient knowledge,
behaviors, and health outcomes so that improvement can be measured.
As the FDA considers the future of Medication Guides and opioid REMS, please keep in mind these future events:
• The revised opioid REMS proposal will be presented at a joint meeting of the Anesthetic and Life Support Drugs
Advisory Committee and the Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee of the FDA on July 22-23.
• The FDA is holding a 2-day public meeting on July 27-28 to obtain input on the issues and challenges in the
development and implementation of REMS. NCCN will submit comments based on the Work Group
recommendations and Trends data
• The comment period for opioid REMS ends on October 19, 2010.
• After the comment period, the FDA will make a final decision regarding opioid REMS.

OPANA° ER has been approved by the FDA. The approval of this new formulation, designed to be crush-resistant, is an

called OPANA ER with the same dosage strengths. However, it has not been established that this new formulation of OPANA

Using Medication Assisted Treatment with Veterans
for Opioid, Alcohol, and Tobacco Use Disorders
Free Webinar Tomorrow- February 11, 2014 (Noon-1prn) - Offering CME

The Center for Substance Abuse Treatment/Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration
has awarded the American Academy of Addiction Psychiatry (AAAP) a three-year grant, Providers' Clinical
Support System for Medication Assisted Treatment (PCSS-MAT). As the lead organization, AAAP has
formed a collaborative effort for this project in partnership with other professional organizations involved in
care of patients with addiction: the American Osteopathic Academy of Addiction Medicine (AOAAM),
American Psychiatric Association (APA) and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM). Collectively
these organizations bring together a wealth of experience and expertise that will enhance and extend our
work in addressing this public health priority. The Association for Medical Education and Research in
Substance Abuse (AMERSA), an affiliated partner, will expand our reach to nurses, social workers and
pharmacists.
PCSS-MAT intends to provide free, evidence-based resources to train clinicians and the public about the
effectiveness of medications used for treating opioid addiction, including buprenorphine, naltrexone and
methadone, in order to more effectively address this public health crisis.

Free APA Webinar - Offering CME!
Using Medication Assisted Treatment with Veterans for Opioid, Alcohol,
and Tobacco Use Disorders

Andrew J. Saxon, M.D.
Professor, Department of Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences
Director, Addiction Psychiatry Residency Program
University of Washington
Director, Center of Excellence in Substance Abuse Treatment and Education (CESATE)
VA Puget Sound Health Care System

ENDO_SF-00104362

 Date: Tuesday, February 11, 2014 (Noon-1pm)
Webinar Description:
The presentation will cover the epidemiology of substance use among active duty military and
veterans and will address the common co-occurring disorders (e.g. posttraumatic stress disorder,
traumatic brain injury) that may complicate medication assisted treatment for veterans. Additionally,
the session will (1) present data on veterans receiving opioid maintenance therapy (methadone or
buprenorphine) for opioid use disorder, (2) address the treat-ment gap, and (3) discuss some of the
outcomes seen. Dr. Saxon will review medication assisted treatments for alcohol use and tobacco
use disorders and discuss how useful these treatments can be when delivered in conjunction with
behavioral interventions.

My fellow Pain Warriors,

also like to thank the Assembly Speaker Sheila Oliver for putting it on

eliminate the ability of health insurers in New Jersey to unnecessarily
limit access to pain medication.
Step Therapy (also referred to as fail-first) is one of the many tools
employed by health care payers to manage utilization of health care
services. In the case of medications, the process usually requires a
patient to try medications for his or her conditions in a series of steps.

New Presentations Announced (plus many more to be announced soon)
Tri-Institutional Pain Registry and Discovery of New Therapeutic Targets
This presentation will describe the Tri-Institutional Pain Registry that goes beyond current databases and includes patients in outpatient
pain clinics at Weill Cornell Medical College, the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, and the Hospital for Special Surgery (all in
NYC). The objective of the Tri-Institutional Pain Registry is to use the Practice Based Evidence Model (PBE) to define standardized data
elements and collect and analyze data that will identify patient characteristics associated with better or worse outcomes from standard pain
treatments administered to real-world cancer and non-cancer chronic pain patients.
The data collected include Patient Variables (e.g., demographics, diagnosis codes, and comorbidities), Process Variables (e.g., current and
past medications and treatments including drug and nondrug interventions), a Comprehensive Severity Index (CSI®) score at each visit,
and Patient Outcome Surveys that measure pain intensity, pain interference with activities of daily living, patient reported health status,
adverse effects of treatments, and aberrant drug behaviors for those receiving opioids. We will present and compare by clinic site and
diagnosis our data on treatments and outcomes for 1700 clinic patients. We also will discuss how one can apply these observations to
evidence-based new medication development to provide effective relief to real-world patients.
Susan Horn, Ph.D., Senior Scientist, Institute for Clinical Outcomes Research, Vice President, Research, International Severity
Information Systems, Inc.
Charles Inturrisi, Ph.D., Professor of Pharmacology, Weill Cornell Medical College
Clinical Development of EMA401 as a Potential First in Class Oral Treatment for Chronic Pain Without CNS Side Effects
Over half the patients suffering from neuropathic pain do not receive adequate pain relief from current medicines and/or cannot tolerate
their CNS side-effects. New treatment options are also required for patients suffering from nociceptive pain and visceral pain. As a result,
there is a tremendous unmet medical need and research and development activities are focused on delivering new treatment approaches
for chronic pain patients.
Spinifex Pharmaceuticals is focused on the discovery and development of angiotensin II type 2 (AT2) receptor antagonists to treat chronic
pain. This presentation will describe the underlying biological rationale and mechanism of action studies behind the development of AT2
receptor antagonists to treat pain, including results of human tissue pharmacology studies. It will also describe the results from a 183
patient Phase 2 clinical trial of EMA401 in postherpetic neuralgia patients, a painful condition that develops in some patients following
shingles and that represents a "sentinel" neuropathic pain indication.
Tom McCarthy, Ph.D., Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, Spinifex Pharmaceuticals
Development of Lasmiditan, a Selective 5-HT1F Receptor Agonist, as a Novel Acute Therapy for Migraine
The development of triptans in the 1980s provided the first specific therapies that transformed the acute treatment of migraine. However,
due to their inherent vasoconstrictor mechanism of action (a direct effect on vascular 5-HT1B receptors), their use is contraindicated in
patients with cardiovascular disease and warnings limit their use in patients with cardiovascular risk factors. Hence, there is an unmet
need for development of therapies with a non-vascular mechanism of action. Lasmiditan was developed as a CNS penetrant, neurally
acting anti-migraine agent that lacks vasoconstrictor activity. Due to its distinct mechanism of action from triptans, lasmiditan also offers
an alternative therapy for the high proportion of patients who fail to achieve adequate migraine pain relief after using triptans. The
development of lasmiditan will be reviewed, including its preclinical profile, data from Phase 2 clinical trials and plans for Phase 3.
Nadia M.J. Rupniak, Ph.D., Vice President of Research & Development, CoLucid Pharmaceuticals Inc.
Pain Models and Methods to Reduce Experimental Error in Analgesic Clinical Trials
Falsely negative analgesic clinical trials are not only a squandered societal burden, but also are a waste of precious time and resources.
Pharmaceutical companies spend large amounts of time perfecting their protocol and selecting quality sites so that the efficacy of their
drug can be statistically demonstrated. However, an equal amount of effort is rarely placed on other aspects of clinical trials that may lead
to optimizing their success such as patient education and analgesic model manipulations. This talk will discuss techniques for site
education, subject placebo response training, and other mechanisms to mitigate variability in analgesic clinical trials.
Neil Singla, MD, Founder & Chief Scientific Officer, Lotus Clinical Research, LLC

 KP201: A Novel Opioid Pain Therapy with Reduced Abuse Potential and Improved Safety
Although a small number of pain drugs with abuse deterrent features has been introduced in recent years, the common method to reduce
the abuse potential of opioids thus far has been through special formulations. This approach, however, has drawbacks and offers only a
partial answer to alleviate the problem.
The inherent physicochemical and pharmacological properties of KP201, a prodrug of hydrocodone, provide a differential and superior
approach to address narcotic abuse. Preclinical studies suggest that 1O201 exhibits unique abuse deterrent properties by significantly
limiting the narcotic exposure upon intranasal administration and being resistant to chemical and physical extraction methods. The poor
solubility of KP201 in aqueous media also makes it less suitable for intravenous injection. In this presentation, Dr. Mickle will cover the
following:
• Description of the chemical structure and pharmacology of 1O201
• Clinical data regarding the phannacokinetic properties of 1O201
• Preclinical data regarding abuse-deterrent properties of KP201
• Preclinical data regarding the prevention of opioid-induced constipation with KP201
• The first disclosure of the tamper resistant properties of KP201

A Systematic Approach to the Use of Opioids in the Treatment of Chronic Pain
12/10/2008
Many primary care clinicians have reluctance to prescribe opioids for patients in pain outside of the most controlled of situations (i.e., when the patient is a
hospital inpatient). This phenomenon is fairly well accepted by clinicians and patients, and is often the result of a combination of a variety of factors:
•

Clinicians who are not experts in the field of pain management may have had little training in the area of pain management beyond treatment of the
short-term management of acute pain.
• Patients may have fears about becoming addicted or dependent to opioids, and have questions about these issues that go unanswered and further
propagate those fears and concerns.
• Negative media coverage about high profile opioid overdoses fuels additional public uncertainty at both the prescriber and patient level.
• Clinicians have fear of regulatory scrutiny and investigation if they prescribe these medications on a regular basis.
The easiest solution for the primary care clinician might seem to be to avoid the use of opioids when treating chronic pain altogether, and utilize alternative
measures that exclude their use. In reality, that solution is likely an unrealistic and untenable solution as the incidence of chronic pain is seemingly rising
on an annual basis, and opioids remain the hallmark, if not an important component of a pain treatment plan. In fact, there is an outcry for more effective
management of chronic pain than we currently achieve today, including a patient's right to demand it.
Despite concerns about opioid prescribing, primary healthcare providers remain the frontline practitioners faced with treating the most common kinds of
chronic pain, such as back pain, arthritis pain, headache pain, and other common types of musculoskeletal pain. Beyond education directed towards
primary healthcare providers about the pathophysiology of these common types of pain, and its appropriate treatment, there have been many valuable
contributions made by experts about the issue surrounding the responsible, safe and effective use of opioids when appropriate.
Experts in the field of pain management have suggested using common medical approaches and paradigms, similar those used as part of routine clinical

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-02774389

 practices for other medical conditions. This can help allay some fears and concerns on both sides of the "opiophobic fence". It has the potential to improve
the confidence level for clinicians to use opioids when they are the appropriate choice for the treatment of patients in chronic pain.
The term "universal precautions" originated from an infectious disease model that addressed an approach to patients when there was a deficiency of
significant risk assessment information. Past behavior or practices were not reliable indicators of safe and reasonable approaches, especially with at-risk
patients. In 2005, Gourlay, Heit, et al., proposed a universal precautionsl approach to the use of opioids in the pain patient. The intention of the authors
was to offer a structured rational approach to pain patients and serve "as a guide to start a discussion within the pain management and addictions
communities. They are not proposed as complete but rather as a good starting point for those treating chronic pain. As with universal precautions in
infectious diseases. by applying the following recommendations, patient care is improved, stigma is reduced, and overall risk is contained."
These universal precautions for opioid use include the following 10 steps:
1.
Make a Diagnosis with Appropriate Differential - Along with other steps to arrive at a diagnosis for the cause of the patient's pain, address
any comorbid conditions, including probable substance use disorders and other psychiatric illness.
2.
Psychological Assessment Including Risk of Addictive Disorders - A complete inquiry into past personal and family history of substance
misuse is essential to adequately assess any patient. A sensitive and respectful assessment of risk should be done with available tools, and
should not be seen in any way as diminishing a patient's complaint of pain or reliability. Patient-centered urine drug testing (UDT) should be
discussed with all patients regardless of what medications they are currently taking. Those found to be using illicit or un-prescribed licit drugs
should be offered further assessment for possible substance use disorders. Those refusing such assessment should be considered unsuitable for
pain management using controlled substances.
3.
Informed Consent - The health care professional needs to educate the patient about the proposed treatment plan with opioids including
anticipated benefits, foreseeable risks, and concerns at a level appropriate to the individual patient
4.
Treatment Agreement - The expectations and obligations of both the patient and the treating practitioner need to be clearly understood. The
format of this agreement can be verbal or written. Along with the informed consent should clearly identify responsibilities of both the clinician and
the patient, monitoring for compliance plans, and any other important information that needs to be discussed.
5.
Pre- and Post-Intervention Assessment of Pain Level and Function - Initiation of opioid therapy for patients in this setting should be
considered a 'friar of therapy by both the clinician and patient. Without prior assessment of pain level and function, it would be impossible to
measure progress.
6.
Appropriate Trial of Opioid Therapy +/- Adjunctive Medication - Opioids may or may not be the first treatment of choice, and will most likely
be used with other adjunctive medications. At this point, it is important to monitor the success or failure of the therapeutic trial with opioids.
7.
Reassessment of Pain Score and Level of Function - Regular reassessment of the patient is critical to support continuation or
discontinuation of the therapy.
8.
Regularly Assess the Four "A"s2of Pain Medicine - Routine assessment of analgesia. activity. adverse effects. and aberrant behavior will
help to direct therapy and support pharmacologic options taken.
9.
Periodically Review Pain Diagnosis and Comorbid Conditions, Including Addictive Disorders - It is important to assess for changes in the
patient's condition, or behavior time. These need to be considered dynamically.
10. Documentation - Careful and complete documenting of the initial evaluation and each follow-up is both medico-legally indicated, and in the best
interest of patients and clinicians. Thorough documentation can reduce medico-legal exposure and risk of regulatory sanction. A rule of thumb to
remember is: if you do not document it, it did not happen.
Utilizing an approach like universal precautions for all patients who are appropriate candidates for opioid therapy has the potential to unify treatment plans,
allow for unbiased application of treatment standards and monitoring, and can reduce the under-treatment of pain when opioids are part of the indicated
solution.
References
1.
Gourlay DL, Heit HA, Almahrezi A. Universal precautions in pain medicine: a rational approach to the treatment of chronic pain. Pain Med. 2005
Mar-Apr;6(2):107-12.
2.
Passik SD, Weinreb HJ. Managing chronic nonmalignant pain: Overcoming obstacles to the use of opioids. Adv Ther. 2000;17(2):70-83.

A new national survey has revealed that both U.S. adults and primary
care physicians hold various misperceptions and stereotypes about
opioid dependence that may impact the way the disease — and those
living with it — are treated. Harris Interactive conducted the survey online
and commissioned Reckitt Benckiser Pharmaceuticals Inc. to
understand U.S. attitudes about opioid dependence, also known as
prescription painkiller and heroin addiction, and treatment for the
disease. The survey involved more than 1,000 adults aged between 26
to 49 years, and 200 non-Drug Addiction Treatment Act 2000 certified
primary care doctors.
The survey pointed out some key facts:

"Opiate dependence is an equal opportunity disease," says Mark I.
Kraus, M.D., FASAM, assistant clinical professor of medicine at Yale
University School of Medicine and fellow of the American Society of
Addiction Medicine. "It affects the sexes the same, men and women, it
affects all ages the same. Race has no barrier. It affects all of the
races. So gender, race, religious, socioeconomic, they all basically have
the same incidence. I think that it needs to be portrayed that there is no
cure. You don't just go into a rehab and walk out a cured person. You
need to be treated and that treatment plan has to be put together by the
doctor, the nurses, the counselors, and psychiatrists."
According to the survey, nearly half of all adults surveyed reported having
a personal connection with addiction and almost one in eight personally
struggled with addiction, more than diabetes or cancer. Sixty-eight
percent of adults and 87 percent of doctors agreed that opioid
dependence affects millions of Americans. Three-quarters of adults and
96 percent doctors are aware that misuse or abuse of opioid prescription
painkillers poses a significant burden on the U.S. healthcare system.
Although nearly 9 in 10 doctors recognize addiction as a disease, only
about 6 in 10 adults agree. More than two thirds of adults and 8 in 10
doctors said that they saw that opioid dependence represents a mental
health problem. Forty-five percent of adults and 30 percent of doctors
believe that opioid dependence is more of a psychological problem rather
than a physical illness.
Stigma may pose a barrier to treatment. More than three fourths of adults
and 93 percent of doctors mention shame or embarrassment, fear that
others will find out, and the fear of putting life on hold as reasons why
those suffering from addiction would refrain from seeking treatment.
"What we need to do is eradicate that stigma because it prohibits people
from getting help," Dr. Kraus told Med Ad News. "It creates a stigma and
that is not good. I think that we need to address that, and that is public
perception and physician perception. I think that it is really incumbent of
us all to paint the right picture."
Regarding relapse, 67 percent of adults and 65 percent of doctors
believe that opioid dependence can be cured. Ninety-two percent of
adults and 98 percent of doctors say that the disease is treatable. Only
35 percent of adults and 21 percent of doctors agreed that staying at
rehab clinics are very effective. More than half of adults and 69 percent
of doctors believe that the vast majority of people living with opioid
dependence will experience a relapse.
"Relapse is prevented by the commitment that the patient makes and the
disease that they accept," Dr. Kraus told Med Ad News. "The patient has
to take ownership of the disease themselves. You can't be a diabetic and
not make a commitment to the diet and the way of life and doing what
you have to do to stay well. The self-help groups that are available are
very helpful and have been part of the addiction plan."
Dr. Kraus also mentions that counseling or spirituality may help some
patients. "The point is that it has to work for the patient," he says.
Pharmacists have also played an important role in the medical treatment
plan for opioid dependence. "Having a relationship with pharmacy and
pharmacists within a person's neighborhood are very important," says
Dr. Kraus. "Doctors have available to them the prescription monitoring
programs, which are also very helpful. Also patients can turn to
itrzttollelp cont. It is an educational website where patients can become
informed of what opiates are; how they affect the brain; the risk of
3

 developing the disease and even at that website, they can take a screen
test to see if there is a risk of opiate dependence and if they have
it. There is also a doctor locator on that website that can help them find
a physician who is knowledgeable about opiate dependence and can
help treat them. There are a lot of things out there that people need to
know."
"The survey sheds light on barriers beyond the commonly perceived lack
of patient recognition of the disease and motivation to seek treatment,"
said Richard Simkin, president of Reckitt Benckiser Pharmaceuticals. "As
a pioneer in office-based treatment for opioid dependence, Reckitt
Benckiser Pharmaceuticals is committed to doing everything we can to
raise awareness about this disease and help reduce the misperceptions,
stigma and stereotypes surrounding it. Finding new ways to reach those
suffering in silence and help them overcome their addiction is at the
forefront of everything we do, and the information we've garnered from
this survey will serve as a strong cornerstone for our future educational
efforts among both the U.S. public and doctors."

On May 2, 2014, at 12:06 PM, "Manser, James" <Manser.James@endo.com > wrote:

Here ya go....
Pennsylvania Controlled Substance Coalition
As background, previously Government Affairs had defeated a measure calling on the Attorney General to "recover
damages to the Commonwealth from drug manufacturers and distributors", placing blame on manufacturers for
prescription drug abuse. This legislation and media coverage surrounding it demonstrated a lack of understanding of
the REMS process and associated safety measures. Had it passed, the previous legislation would do little to address the
issue it sought to impact.
HR 659 was then introduced to create a Prescription Drug Task Force to study the issue of diversion. The initial
legislation created a committee which encompassed extensive background from the punitive side of diversion, but did
not adequately represent patients and prescribers who use and prescribe medications appropriately.
After meeting with the prime sponsor, Representative Heffley, and subsequent meetings with the Executive Director of
the Human Services Committee, Endo Government Affairs was able to draft an amendment to broaden the
representation on the committee. The amendment was inclusive of our external affairs partners, was accepted by
Representative Heffley and ultimately the legislation passed unanimously.
Endo was asked to provide recommendations for the newly created Task Force. Rather than act in a vacuum, we have
created a Pennsylvania Controlled Substance Coalition which has already met with members of the Opiate Task force
to provide information on some of the regulations already in place which differentiate controlled substances from
other prescriptions.
Alabama R&D Tax Credit Coalition
While 38 states have some form of a Research & Development Tax Credit, Alabama is does not.
In the 30 days of Alabama's 2014 legislative session, a bill was introduced late to establish the first R&D tax credit in
Alabama. With a short calendar to enact such legislation and the looming indictments of several legislators, including
the Speaker of the House for breaking ethics commission law, the tax credit bill fell short of passing.
Given the potential impact to Endo's tax liability in Alabama, Government Affairs is in the process of organizing a
coalition to help advance this legislation when the legislature reconvenes in 2015. To date, we have received favorable
responses from many influential stakeholders including the Alabama Department of Commerce, Economic
Development Partnership of Alabama, Economic Developers Association of Alabama, the Huntsville Chamber and the

** MANDATORY READING **
Questions have been received from the field regarding discussions with customers relating to the abuse potential of
OPANA® ER. This communication responds to these questions and reinforces the training you have received in regard to
the abuse potential of CII opioid analgesics.
You may not make statements or inferences regarding potential differences in the abuse potential for OPANA ER compared
to any other CII medication. No adequate evidence currently exists that demonstrates any differences between the abuse
potential of OPANA ER and any CII opioids. This prohibition includes discussion of any differences in the molecular
structures, delivery systems, or pharmacokinetic profiles of products and relating these differences to abuse potential. In all
customer details, the features and benefits of OPANA ER must be balanced with limitations and safety information relevant
to the topics discussed. In addition, comparisons of the prescribing Information for OPANA, OPANA ER and any other
products are prohibited. Comparative statements may only be communicated if provided in approved promotional materials.
Please review the examples below of approved and prohibited messaging relating to the abuse potential of OPANA ER.
Examples of some approved promotional messages that may be used in promotional discussions
Abuse Potential
OPANA ER contains oxymorphone, which is a morphine-like opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance, with an abuse
liability similar to other opioid agonists.
OPANA ER can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal, or illicit. This should be considered when
prescribing or dispensing OPANA ER in situations where the physician or pharmacist is concerned about an increased risk of
misuse, abuse, or diversion.
OPANA ER tablets are to be swallowed whole and are not to be broken, chewed, dissolved, or crushed. Taking broken, chewed,
dissolved, or crushed OPANA ER tablets leads to a rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of oxymorphone.
Delivery System
Only OPANA ER has a true matrix for every 12-hour dosing.
Patented TIMERx®-N oral delivery system precisely and predictably controls the release of oxymorphone into the patient's
system for proven every 12-hour dosing.
Examples of unapproved promotional messages that may not be used in a promotional discussion. These and similar
messages are also prohibited from use in responding to unsolicited questions.
Abuse Potential
OPANA ER has a lower abuse potential than other long-acting opioids.

The majority of physicians initially try Opana ER for patients after failure of several other extended-release

The treatment of chronic pain is challenging with some patients failing to achieve adequate relief of their
symptoms while others experience adverse outcomes (addiction, unintended overdose, and death) related to
inappropriate prescribing, abuse, and misuse. For this reason, the FDA has required the makers of extendedrelease (ER) and long-acting (LA) opioids to participate in a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) and
support the provision of education to the prescribers of these medications.
Sixteen AHME-member hospitals have been providing this education to theirfaculty and residents during the past
six months through live activities. A number of these institutions have also developed enduring activities that they
are now making available to otherAHME-member hospitals. These webinars are free, available at the learner's
convenience via the internet, and eligible forAMA PRA Category 1CreditsTM.
On behalf of these institutions, we invite youto encourage yourfaculty and consider requiring your residents in
relevant specialties to become a part of this national effort to reduce the incidence of adverse outcomes related
to inappropriate prescribing, abuse, and misuse of long-acting opioids.
Further details and access to these educational activities (that residents can complete on their own time) are
available through the following link, ER/LA Opioid REMS Educational Activities.

"These educational activities are supported by an independent educational grant from the ER/LA Opioid

Ohio Senate passes bill targeting 'pill mills'; federal agents crack down on doctors

Published: Tuesday, May 17, 2011, 7:45 PM

Updated: Wednesday, May 18, 2011, 8:14 AM

Joe Guillen, The Plain Dealer <http://media.cleveland.com//avatars/joe- guillen-sig-cropped.JPG> By Joe Guillen, The Plain
Dealer The Plain Dealer
COLUMBUS, Ohio A The Ohio Senate, federal drug agents and the Ohio attorney generalOs office sent a message on
Tuesday that they are working to stem the abuse of prescription drugs in Ohio, a problem many say is nearing epidemic
proportions.
The Senate unanimously approved legislation targeting pain-management clinics that supply the drugs. Separately, the U.S.
Drug Enforcement Agency suspended a handful of Ohio doctors and a pharmacy from prescribing and distributing opiate
painkillers and other controlled substances.
Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWineAs office was involved with the DEAOs efforts, which included a raid of a doctorOs
office and pharmacy in Scioto County, a region in the southern part of the state plagued by prescription drug abuse.
DeWineAs office would not disclose specific locations involved in the raid because search warrants remain sealed.
"Today's action reinforces our commitment to putting an end to the prescription drug abuse problem in Ohio," DeWine said in a
statement. "We are serious about this fight, and we aren't going to relent."
Addiction to prescription drugs has become so widespread that unintentional drug overdoses have been the stateAs leading
cause of accidental death since 2007, according to the governorOs office.

A growing number of addicts hooked on OxyContin and other prescription drugs in Ohio have died from overdoses, committed
crimes to support their addiction and flooded treatment centers.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07386432

 Users crush and snort the pills or dilute them with water for injection for a heroinlike rush.
The bill passed in the Senate would increase accountability for the pain management clinics that distribute prescription drugs
and limit the quantity of controlled substances a doctor could provide within given timeframes. It also would establish a takeback program to collect unused drugs and prevent them from being sold on the street.
The House of Representatives, which already passed an earlier version of the bill, will approve the Senate As version later this
week and send the bill to Gov. John Kasich, said Mike Dittoe, spokesman for House Speaker William G. Batchelder.
Kasich will sign the bill, a spokesman said.
Meanwhile, the DEA on Tuesday cracked down on four doctors and a pharmacy that were involved in distributing prescription
drugs that are commonly abused.
The DEA suspended the licenses to prescribe certain controlled substances belonging to Margy Temponeras, John
Temponeras, Mark Fantazuzzi, Michael Dawes and Prime Pharmacy in Portsmouth. The licenses were suspended because
the DEA decided the situation "constitutes an imminent danger to public health and safety," according to a DEA news release.
The doctors will not be allowed to prescribe drugs until a federal investigation is resolved.
Margy Temponeras defended her work in an interview with The Plain Dealer earlier this year.
scioto-2.jpg <http://media.cleveland.com/open_impact/photo/9328597- large.jpg> View full size
"Some doctors are trying to help patients in a lot of pain --we aren Ot drug dealers, and we aren Ot bad people," she said in
February. "We are being vilified by the press and the fanatics who have had only negative experiences"
She could not be reached for comment Tuesday.
Under current state law, pain management clinics are exempt from a requirement that certain businesses be licensed with the
Ohio State Board of Pharmacy to distribute controlled substances.
The bill approved in the Senate on Tuesday would require that pain management clinics also must obtain a license. Pain
management clinic operators would have to prove the facility is owned and operated by an authorized physician. Workers at
the clinics also would be subject to criminal background checks.
Senate President Tom Niehaus, a Republican from the Cincinnati area, said the bill strikes an appropriate balance between
addressing a growing problem and ensuring those who need medication have continued access.

R.I. Health Department suspends license of Lincoln doctor

Published: August 31, 2013 11:26 AM
Comments
2

10 148+12 1 0 2
By Lynn Arditi
Lynn Arditi Providence Journal
Published: August 31 2013 11:26
The Health Department suspended a Rhode Island physician's license to practice medicine after a review of
six patients' deaths showed that he had inappropriately prescribed them narcotics.
Fathalla Mashali, an anesthesiologist whose practice includes pain management, was barred from practicing
until further notice, according to an order signed Thursday by state Health Department Director Michael D.
Fine.
Concerns about Mashali, who has an office at 6 Blackstone Valley Place, Lincoln, were raised after the Office
of the State Medical Examiners observed a pattern of fatal overdoses of prescription pain medication in
Mashali's patients and reported their findings to the state Board of Medical Licensure and Discipline.
The suspension order says that while the board did not necessarily find Mashali responsible for the deaths
of the six patients, a review of their medical records showed that he had prescribed opioids (painkillers) to
patients with a history of drug abuse and failed to properly monitor them.
The report describes one case in which Mashali continued to prescribe a month's worth of opioids to a
female patient even after he had evidence that suggested she was not taking them as prescribed. In
another case, he gave a male patient who had tested positive for amphetamine and cocaine a month's
worth of narcotics.
Mashali dispensed "vast amounts of opioids and Benzodiazepines to a patient with multiple urine toxicology
screens suggesting that he was not taking the medication as prescribed..." the report states.
In a third case, he gave a female patient who repeatedly tested positive for Ecstasy, an illegal drug, was
given a month's supply of opioids. A reviewer who analyzed Mashali's medical records stated in the report
that his prescribing habits in the case as as "lavish" and his physical exam as "cursory."
The Health Department has advised patients who need copies of their medical records to contact Mashali's

is interesting their opinion on the risk of opioid abuse and addiction. We do not want to downplay the issue of

The Risk of Opioid Abuse in Primary Care Patients with Chronic Pain
8/7/2007
There are many factors that influence the primary care clinician with respect to prescribing opioid's for chronic pain. Although it would seem that
since chronic pain affects more than 50 million people in the United States, (Brookoff, D.; Chronic Pain: A New Disease? Hosp. Prac.
(Minneapolis) 35:45-52, 2000) comfort levels with prescribing opioids for its treatment is sometimes approached with concern for a variety of
reasons, including:
Lack of education with respect to treating chronic pain
Lack of education about appropriate use of opioids
Insufficient resources to provide assistance for logical pain management
Fear of legislative and enforcement policies with respect to prescription of controlled substances, especially opioids
Fear of addiction
Fear of abuse or diversion
Negative press in the media also continues to fuel more controversy and confusion specifically towards the issue of opioid use disorders in
patients on long-term opioids therapy. Although the pain management experts have the experience and expertise to evaluate and monitor
patients for these types of conditions, there seems to be a need for more translation of information into practical logic to allay some of this
controversy and confusion.
A recent article appeared in the Journal of Pain, Vol.8, No. 7 (July), 2007:pp 573-582, entitled Substance Use Disorders in a Primary Care
Sample Receiving Daily Opioid Therapy. This article details a study that had the following goals:
Primarily to present a comprehensive picture of substance use disorders in patients receiving opioids therapy prescribed by their
primary care physician
Secondarily to determine the relation of positive urine screens of illicit drugs and aberrant drug behavior to opioid use disorders
For the purposes of this particular study, the definition of "substance use disorders" referred to patients that met the DSM-IV criteria for abuse
or addiction. The study is the largest primary care study to date that reports the frequency of substance/opioid abuse disorders in a primary
care sample of patients. The participants were 801 adults receiving daily opioids therapy, prescribed by 235 primary care practices, consisting
of family physicians and internists in Wisconsin.
The 5 most common pain diagnoses of the participants were:
Degenerative arthritis

Low back pain
Migraine headaches

Fibromyalgia

Since this study was focused on patients already taking opioids, it was not possible to determine the relationship between current therapy and
development of use disorder — patients may have been opioid dependent prior to initiation of the current course of therapy.
The study found that the frequency of opioids use disorders was four times higher in patients who were prescribed opioids by their primary care
physician than that of the general population (3.8% vs. 0.9% respectively). Even with this increased risk, the authors concluded that in patients
with chronic pain who require daily opioid therapy, a 3.8% rate of addiction is relatively small compared to the pain and suffering that would
exist without this important medication. This important article supports the thinking that when a primary care practitioner deems that an opioid is
necessary as an essential part of a pain treatment regimen, fear of abuse and addiction risk should not be a reason to preclude its appropriate
use.
Indeed, there is a need for more education and resources that the primary care clinician can utilize for assistance with regard to these and all of
the other issues surrounding treatment of chronic pain, a prevalent condition that is likely to present itself to the healthcare provider on a regular
basis.
