Rick Scott's top doc declares pill-mill health emergency St. Pete Times BuzzBlog July 1, 2011 Gov. Rick Scott's surgeon
general, Frank Farmer, has declared a public-health emergency regarding pill mills. The headline-grabbing decision
comes just before Scott is scheduled to host a ceremonial bill signing of a pack of healthcare bills.
But the subject of this declaration, HB7095, isn't one of them. The new law seeks to crack down on physicians who
prescribe inordinate amounts of pills such as oxycodone and Xanax. Some physicians are banned from dispensing them
and so, under the order, "practitioners who are no longer authorized to dispense controlled substances in listed in
Schedule II and Schedule III of Section 893.03, Florida Statutes, to dispose of any inventory and cooperate fully with the
Florida Department of Health (DOH), Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE) and local law enforcement
personnel," according to a press release.
The order to seize the drugs from the docs was issued today because its 30 days after the signing of the bill, giving some
physicians little reason to have the meds, said Scott spokesman Brian Hughes.
What's unclear from the state of emergency declaration at the moment, though, is what other powers Farmer is able to
exercise as a result of the
declaration<http://leg.state.fl.us/Statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&Search_String=&URL=03000399/0381/Sections/0381.00315.html>.

CD&E Educational Initiatives Supporting the Responsible Use of Opioids for Moderate-to-Severe Pain:

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-01013401

 Multiple studies confirm the usefulness of opioid analgesics in the tx of moderate-to-severe pain
Like all medications, however, there are risks associated with their use
Responsible use of opioids necessitates a balanced approach including:
Appropriate access to these effective medications
Education on appropriate prescribing principles & safe use
Patient selection, initial & ongoing assessment, documentation, appropriate prescribing principles,
patient/family education, exit strategy if tx not effective or if intolerable side effect
Proactive efforts to safeguard against potential misuse, abuse and diversion
Educational Components of Endo's Commitment to the Responsible Use of Opioids:
■ National Initiative on Pain Control (NIPC)
o a Continuing Education (CE)-accredited educational program for physicians and pharmacists supported by an
educational grant from Endo, which was established to advance clinicians' understanding of pain
assessment/treatment, and to improve outcomes for patients with chronic pain
o A series of CE-accredited educational programs relating to "Advances in Opioid Analgesia: Maximizing Benefit
While Minimizing Risk" are ongoing. These programs are designed to educate clinicians on the practical clinical
prescribing principles and the risk management considerations associated with the use of opioid therapy for chronic
pain patients.
o Multiple media are used to deliver the accredited programs: live case-based evening programs, half day Saturday
symposia, audioconferences, webcasts, and newsletters.
■ Other CE-accredited symposia, web-based CE and enduring materials with professional societies such as:
American Pain Society
American Academy of Pain Medicine
American Academy of Pain Management
American Society of Addiction Medicine
Multi-National Association for Supportive Care in Cancer
American Society of Pain Management Nurses
Oncology Nursing Society
PriMed Primary Care Education Conferences
American College of Physicians
American Academy of Family Physicians
American Society of Health System Pharmacists
■ www.PainEdu.org website — interactive pain education website accredited for physicians, pharmacists, nurses, and other
health care providers. The site features clinical updates on pain assessment and pain management, interactive
case-based learning, practical clinical tools and patient/caregiver educational materials. The website includes substantial
content on appropriate prescribing of opioid analgesics and risk management information/tools which can be integrated
into clinical practice.
SOAPP (Screener & Opioid Assessment for Patients with Pain) patient screening tool - a brief screening, self-report
tool for those chronic pain patients being considered for opioid therapy. The tool, which is supported through grants
from the Nat'l Institute on Drug Abuse and Endo, is designed to assist physicians in determining the relative risk of
aberrant medication related behaviors in chronic pain patients being considered for opioid therapy. It will be easily
completed and scored in less than 10 minutes in the waiting room of a physician's office. The tool is not intended to
"screen in" or "screen out" patients, but rather to help the clinician make an informed assessment of a given patient's
relative risk of developing aberrant medication related behaviors.
Handbooks and copies of clinical guidelines produced by various professional organizations and regulatory bodies
regarding the responsible use of opioid analgesics

Ian;

As I mentioned to you, Judy and I attended Grand Rounds at RIH on Tuesday. Dr. Michael Picchioni,
Associate Program Director, Internal Medicine Residency, Baystate Medical Center/Tufts University School
of Medicine, Assistant Professor of Medicine, Tufts University School of Medicine, Springfield, MA presented
"Long-term Opioid Use in Chronic Non-Malignant Pain". The following is a brief summary and is for your
information only;
According to the Drug Abuse Warning Network:
•

Rate of initiation of prescription drug use/abuse among 18-25 year-olds is on the rise.

•

Visits to the ER due to substance abuse treatment doubled from 1995 to 2000.

• There are 1 million Americans dependent on controlled substances and they account for 22% of
current users.
Dr. Picchioni presented information regarding the efficacy of opioids and the value when treating chronic pain
patients. He showed an interesting slide that, as we are all aware, portrayed the risk/benefits of prescribing
opioids for the patient, but also the risk/benefits to society (the risk being diversion and abuse vs. more

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_ALAG-00485834

 productive members of society) and to the prescriber (the risk od being viewed as a "soft target"-easy to obtain
a prescription and sanctions vs. symptom relief and improvements in patients' functionality).
In order to minimize risk to all involved, Dr. Picchioni outlined a model policy (that he follows) from the
Federation of State Medical Boards.
Patient Selection (used for all controlled substances)•

Prescribing is decided by the PCP only

•

Only after all conservative measures are exhausted

•

Prescription is never written at the first encounter

Protocol
•

Clinical evaluation

•

Informed consent

• Use of a written contract
•

Follow-up

• Documentation (everything!)
• Rx dispensed at 28 day intervals (prescriptions written only on Thursdays-avoids patients "losing"
scripts etc...)
•

Monitoring

•

Case review (with PCP, nursing staff, social worker).

Dr. Picchioni's intent is for residents' to recognize that pain is under treated, but to feel comfortable prescribing
opioids. Interestingly enough he emphasized that he does not prescribe any short-acting drugs as the focus
becomes the pill rather than the overall treatment.
The following statistics are courtesy of Donnah Mathews, M.D., Attending Physician, Division of General
Internal Medicine, Rhode Island Hospital. They are compiled from the residents' medical clinic.
• >60% of the residents did not feel prepared to treat chronic pain patients
•

86% of the patients in the clinic received opioids from another PCP

•

62% are diagnosed with a mood disorder

•

62% have a history of or are active substance abusers

•

75% use tobacco

•

The higher the dose of opioid the less likely the patient is to adhere to the clinic's contract.

Any questions let me know.

Subject: HT's Embeda blog

Sorry if you wish you weren't on this distribution list, but you all knew I would have an interest in Embeda®,
and delete for this e-mail is just a keystroke away at any time. . . Besides, I had a flight from Atlanta to Philly
with a free Delta WiFi promotional code the day after it was approved.
But first, an early entry from the delectable Café Pharma, or whatever that web site is where sales
representatives whine about their companies:
It's not abuse resistant. You can't even say the words to a doc. All opioids have the capacity to be abused. This
will be a tight sell and a guarded one. Hopefully MKTG will not screw up... the you never know' was total BS.
Also the alpharma mktg group is not as saavy [sic] or smart. never were.
I think the PI is a very nice piece of work. FDA made it clear that no one is going to get a direct claim without
long-term epidemiological studies, and that their position is more along the lines of, "It would be nice to avoid
accidental poisonings of small children and dogs who might chew on a dropped tablet."

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-CHI_LIT-00808137

 So the PI is chock-a-block with discussions of risk, examples of drug-seeking behavior, and many references to
abuse, addiction and diversion; the Alpharma representatives can have a field day with this story line right out
of the PI. Then there is a big section of what happens if an Embeda is crushed and what withdrawal looks like.
And then it says that there is no evidence of a reduction in abuse liability with Embeda. But if I were the MSL
for Alpharma and someone asked me why not, I would simply ask them how they would design the study to
satisfy FDA. The Alpharma MSL told me he didn't know what their message was going to be for the drug, but
you can lead a horse to water, tell him not to drink, and then stand back.
Not a lot of efficacy data presented, but let's say it works as well as morphine anyway. What really interests me
is the data from the likeability and euphoria studies. Apparently, a lot of recreational users either can't tell the
difference between straight morphine and that which has been contaminated with naltrexone, or it doesn't
bother them that much. Over 12% of the subjects liked crushed Embeda just as much as regular morphine, and
at worst, they liked it at least half as much. Almost a third of them had no reduction in euphoria and again, had
no less than 50% decrease in buzz from the crushed Embeda. If they shot up morphine mixed with naltrexone
(not a true Embeda, but close enough,) 29% of the recreational user subjects still had no diminution of euphoria.
I find this an intensely interesting research question from two angles: a) what does the distribution curve look
like for how much naltrexone you have to add to morphine to block a euphoric response for everybody and b)
I'm assuming they used the old Addiction Center Research Inventory Morphine-Benzedrine Group subscale,
but they don't say. Anyone who has heard me whine about this knows that I am critical of the uses to which the
ACM has been put, granted in the absence of anything better.
Random observations from the PI:
• There's a nice discussion on conversion from other opioids and other routes of administration of
morphine.
• Embeda should not be dosed more frequently than every 12 hours.
• Don't put it in a gastric tube.
• There is one efficacy study mentioned in the PI of an enriched randomized withdrawal design showing a
significant difference from placebo in weekly average BPI scores over twelve weeks, but not a lot of
detail, including no mention of withdrawal rate from side effects. Over 75% of the subjects were opioidnaive.
• "Morphine can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, licit or illicit. This should be
considered when prescribing or dispensing Embeda in situations where the physician or pharmacist is
concerned about an increased risk of misuse, abuse or diversion." So by virtue of drawing attention to
risk factors, you're obviously supposed to impute the advantage of the sequestered naltrexone. Section
5.4 is "Accidentally Precipitated Withdrawal" and warns of withdrawal symptoms appearing in opioidtolerant patients within five minutes of consuming a tampered Embeda [not "tampered with," but
"tampered by crushing, chewing," etc. I didn't know the word "tampered" could be used that way.]
• Naltrexone will not screw up GC/MS urine drug tests but enzymatic tests may or may not be affected.
• The two pivotal trials were done in OA of the hip and knee.
• Section 9 includes a description of "drug-seeking behavior" which it identifies as either signs of abuse
and addiction or under-treatment of pain.
• The label says that the sequestered naltrexone has no role in treating overdose.
• The study endpoints with recreational drugs users were "drug-liking" and "euphoria." Subjects didn't
like crushed Embeda as much as straight morphine by 87% to 12% but the range of by how much the
subjects didn't like it ranged from 10 to 50%. For euphoria, it was 69% to 31% (nearly a third had no
reduction in euphoria) with a similar range of reduction in euphoria.
• The PI states that there is no evidence that the naltrexone reduces the abuse liability of Embeda.
• If taken with a high-fat meal, the uptake of morphine is enhanced, although total bioavilability is
unaffected. There is no recommendation on when to take it with regards to food, though.
2

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-CHI_LIT-00808138

 •

Naltrexone was detected in 13 of 67 subjects at steady-state. [An early effort at a Duragesic® with
sequestered naltrexone was shot down by FDA for trace amounts in four subjects. How times have
changed.]

I believe this is the first label for an opioid under the new PI format, and I found it amusing that the
likeability/euphoria studies went under 12.2 Pharmacodynamics. I have more opinions, including how they
handled the side effects profile of morphine, but this is already more than you signed up for. CI
Regards,
HT

Manser, James
EXTERNAL: PMP Bills in Many States, More Action in MO

Advocates,
This year has started fast and furiously--SPPAN is already tracking nearly 700 policies
related to pain care. Look for more udpates by topic, like this one, that give you an ata-glance overview of bills we are watching so you can decide if and how you want to
take action. Also, as always, with your networks and "boots on the ground", we
appreciate hearing any local updates you have on any of the policies we're tracking.
Prescription Monitoring Programs:
Highlights:
•

•

Missouri's County-by-County PMP Progress: As the lone state without a statewide
program, advocates in Missouri are actively working to establish PMPs on a countyby-county and city-by-city basis. To date, five counties and the cities of Kansas City,
St. Louis, and Independence have passed local legislation to participate, with two
more counties on the verge of joining the effort. All told, these programs now cover
more than 45% of all Missourians. The next hearings in this effort will be on 2/4 and
2/6, for Boone County and its county seat, the city of Columbia. To get engaged and

stay up to date, consider joining the MO PDMP Now coalition, if you haven't
already.
SPPAN is already tracking 88 PMP bills across 26 states and Puerto Rico.
See more details below, and stay up to date with daily changes by checking
SPPAN's tracker.

Prescription Monitoring Programs

Missouri SB 74 would establish a PMP unique among PMPs in that it would disallow
all prescribers and dispensers from having access to the information contained within
the PMP. Position: Oppose; read AIPM's letter of opposition.
Missouri SB 231/314/340 / HB 90 would establish a traditional PMP in
Missouri. Position: Support; read AIPM's letter of support.
Hawaii HB 1164 would require the annual determination of the mean and median
prescription quantities and volumes within categories of practitioners of a similar

1

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07087266

 specialty or practice type, express each practitioner's standing as a confidential
percentile ranking, and notify all practitioners of their ranking.
Indiana SB 151 requires the ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and controlled substance
prescription monitoring program to include an entry for a dispenser to indicate, when
applicable, if a patient has entered into a pain management contract with a designated
practitioner.
Indiana SB 157 requires the establishment of a multidisciplinary workgroup for the
purpose of evaluating the cost and feasibility of cataloging: (1) each administration of
an overdose intervention drug by an emergency medical services provider; and (2) data
related to certain controlled substance investigations by law enforcement; in the PMP.
Indiana SB 408 requires information to be transmitted to the PMP on a real time
basis. Further, requires a practitioner to obtain PMP information about a patient before
prescribing ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, or a controlled substance.
Mississippi FIB 1032 requires all licensed health care providers that are authorized by
law to diagnose and prescribe drugs to register as users with the PMP.
New Jersey A 4440 / S 2795 would provide all insurers, private and public, access to
the PMP for the purpose of identifying whether a covered individual is obtaining a
prescription in a manner that may be indicative of misuse, abuse, or diversion of a
controlled dangerous substance or a violation of law or regulation or a breach of
standards of practice.
New York AB 2810 requires the inclusion of information regarding the administration
of overdose reversal agents on the PMP. Position: Support.
South Dakota SB 4 requires an annual report on the monitoring and use of
prescription opioids. This report shall include the number of opioid prescriptions from
the prior three years and an update to any changes or advances made to the
PMP. Position: Amend.
Utah FIB 50 would require a prescriber to check the PMP before an initial prescription
of a Schedule II or III opioid and periodically thereafter. A prescriber is not required
to the check the PMP if the prescription is for three days or fewer or the prescriber has
prior knowledge of the patient's history. Position: Amend.
Washington FIB 1426 / SB 5248 makes changes relating to persons to whom the
Department of Health may provide PMP data. SB 5248 is scheduled for hearing on 2/2
by the Senate Committee on Health Care.

DEA quota causes painkiller shortage for
legitimate uses
By Bill Scanlor, Rocky Mountain News (Contact)

 Published February 3, 2009 at 2:53 p.m.

More stories »
Oxycodone is in short supply in some Colorado pharmacies because of a quota imposed on the powerful painkiller, which
is abused by both the sick and the slick.
Good-faith efforts to keep the pills from addicts and pushers are also keeping them from those who desperately need
them, say some pharmacists.
"We have customers who bring in a prescription from a doctor every month . . . and now we can't fill them," said Dennis
Mantas, owner of Wheat Ridge Pharmacy. "It's a big problem."
Jeannine Hawkins, 68, of Littleton, who takes oxycodone to deal with the pain of cancer treatments, nerve damage and
knee surgery, used to be able to get a 30-day supply at a time.
This week, "the doctors today told her they could give her just a 10-day supply because of the shortage," her husband,
Wayne, 69, said. He's worried that next time, there will be no pain pills available for his ailing wife.
The Drug Enforcement Administration limits the amount of oxycodone and Oxycontin (the leading brand name)
manufacturers can produce, said Val Kalnins, executive director of the Colorado Pharmacists Society.
Each year, the DEA estimates how much Oxycontin is needed to meet the "legitimate medical, scientific, research and
industrial needs of the United States," then sets the quota accordingly.
Oxycodone is an opioid, as is heroin, codeine, fentanyl and morphine. Too much inventory heightens the chance of its
diversion to illegal uses, the DEA says.
But Mantas says the DEA must not have taken into account that the population is getting older, and that means more
aches and pains and cancer treatments that need to be treated by Oxycontin and other pain medications.
A recall by drug maker Mallinckrodt and cutbacks by Ethex have exacerbated the shortage, which started about
December, say pharmacists.
Oxycontin, also called "Oxy" or "hillbilly heroin," contains the active ingredient oxycodone and first was made in 1996. By
2001, its use had increased twentyfold.
Doctors are prescribing more pain medication, mostly because people legitimately need it, says Mantas.
Certainly, thieves try to steal from the supply, and there are some doctor shoppers who may get a 30-day supply three
times for the same injury, say pharmacists. "But you know your regular customers, and you know their issues," Mantas
said.

3

 "We have customers who go to their doctor once a month, and stay right on time, right on task," he said. "We can't fill
them. They try to switch to something else, but sometimes it's not covered by insurance.
"We're not going to fill prescriptions willy-nilly for anyone who walks in from the street. The DEA's intentions are good, but
they're hitting the wrong end of it," Mantas said.

The state of Maine recently passed legislation aimed to address opioid abuse. The Government Affairs team is

governments...legislatures enacting increasingly restrictive measures in both duration and potency of pain

Aspects of this enacted legislation include:
A. Strengthening the prescription drug monitoring program by requiring prescribers to check the
state's prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) when first prescribing an opioid or
benzodiazepine—prescribers must also check the PDMP every 90 days thereafter for as long as the

prescription written by an out-of-state provider, or if an individual is paying cash despite having
insurance information on file
C. Limits new scripts to 7-day supplies beginning in 2017
D. Limits chronic pain scripts to 30-day supplies beginning in 2017
E. The daily supply is limited to 100 morphine milligram equivalents (MME) of medication per day,
which is an aggregated total in cases where an individual receives a combination of opioids.
a. The law also includes a provision allowing individuals currently receiving more than 100
MME of opioid medication per day to continue to receive up to 300 MME until July 1, 2017, at
which time the 100 MME limitation will apply.
b. The law allows a number of exceptions, including cancer pain, palliative care, end-of-life
and hospice care, medication assisted treatment for substance use disorder, and other
circumstances determined through rulemaking by the state's Department of Health and
Human Services.
F. Requires prescribers to receive 3 hours of opioid training every two years
G. Requires prescribers to submit opioid and benzodiazepine scripts to pharmacies electronically by
July 1, 2017 in an effort to prevent diversion. (waivers may be granted by the Maine Department of

CVS Pharmacy does not allow its pharmacists to check customers' prescription histories using
prescription monitoring program (PMP) databases, according to TheFix.com. A CVS spokesman said
the company's pharmacists are sufficiently "trained and prepared" to recognize inappropriate drug use
without consulting the PMP, and that the proper role of pharmacies is to provide dispensing information
to the PMP. Full story.

Drug-distribution companies must police themselves to keep controlled substances from finding their

distributors the DEA determines not to be doing enough to prevent the diversion and abuse of the

U.S. Representatives Harold "Hal" Rogers (KY-05) and Frank Wolf (VA-10), along with Senators Rob
Portman (OH) and Sheldon Whitehouse (RI), introduced legislation to facilitate the sharing of
prescription monitoring program (PMP) data. The Interstate Drug Monitoring Efficiency and Data Sharing
(ID MEDS) Act, H.R. 4292, would create a nationally standardized system that would enable states to
exchange PMP data without havinato develop multiple interfaces. Fi story/ News release„

Schumer Bill Targets Prescription Drug Thefts
U.S. Sen. Charles Schumer (NY) has proposed the SAFE DOSES Act to address prescription drug
theft. The bill would give law enforcement the ability to use wiretaps and other tools to investigate
criminal prescription drug rings. The SAFE DOSES Act has 32 Senate co-sponsors. Full story. Related
stork. Bill text.

New North Carolina Law Requires ID for Certain
Medications
A new law that took effect March 1 in North Carolina requires pharmacies to check photo identification
before filling prescriptions for all Schedule II and certain Schedule III medications. The law aims to
address fraudulent activity related to prescription drug diversion and abuse, such as doctor shopping
under various names. Full story.

Oklahoma Bill Would Mandate PMP Data Checks
Legislation approved by the Oklahoma House of Representatives would require prescribers to check the
prescription history of new patients. House Bill 2574 would require Oklahoma physicians to check the
state's prescription monitoring program (PMP) when first prescribing a controlled substance to a new
patient and annually thereafter. The bill would implement one of the policy recommendations set forth in
the National' Prescryption Druci Abuse Prevention Strategy. News release. Bill summarl.

role in preventing prescription drug abuse. The meeting will be a first step toward greater resourcesharing and collaboration among multiple stakeholders. Full stor/.

CLAAD To Co-Host National Dialogue on DrugImpaired Driving
A Florida judge recently declared that he will suspend defendants' drivers' licenses if he finds that the
individuals are using oxycodone -- unless they produce a letter from their prescriber stating that they are
capable of driving safely. This approach could put health care practitioners at greater risk for liability. To
address the complex policy issues related to drug-impaired driving, CLAAD will co-host a national
dialogue on April 12, 2012, in Orlando, Florida. Fuii story.

 NUCYNTAT" is indicated for the relief of moderate to severe acute pain in patients 18 years of age or
older.
IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION
•

Like other drugs with mu-opioid agonist activity, NUCYNTAT" is contraindicated in patients with
significant respiratory depression, acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercapnia in
unmonitored settings or in the absence of resuscitative equipment. NUCYNTAT" is
contraindicated in patients who have or are suspected to have paralytic ileus. NUCYNTAT" is also
contraindicated in patients currently using or within 14 days of using monoamine oxidase
inhibitors (MAOIs) due to potential additive effects on norepinephrine levels, which may result in
adverse cardiovascular events.

•

Respiratory depression is the primary risk of mu-opioid agonists. Respiratory depression occurs
more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients and in those suffering from conditions
accompanied by hypoxia, hypercapnia, or upper airway obstruction, in whom even moderate
therapeutic doses may significantly decrease pulmonary ventilation. NUCYNTATm should be
administered with caution to the elderly, debilitated patients, and patients with conditions
accompanied by hypoxia, hypercapnia or decreased respiratory reserve such as: asthma,
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or cor pulmonale, severe obesity, sleep apnea syndrome,
myxedema, kyphoscoliosis, CNS depression, or coma. In such patients, even usual therapeutic
doses of NUCYNTATm may increase airway resistance and decrease respiratory drive to the point
of apnea. Alternative non-mu-opioid agonist analgesics should be considered and NUCYNTATm
should be employed only under careful medical supervision at the lowest effective dose in such
patients. If respiratory depression occurs, it should be treated as any mu-opioid agonist-induced
respiratory depression.

•

Patients receiving other mu-opioid agonist analgesics, general anesthetics, phenothiazines, other
tranquilizers, sedatives, hypnotics, or other CNS depressants (including alcohol) concomitantly
with NUCYNTATm may exhibit additive CNS depression. Interactive effects resulting in respiratory
depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma or death may result if these drugs are taken
in combination with NUCYNTATm. When such combined therapy is contemplated, a dose
reduction of one or both agents should be considered.

•

Opioid analgesics can raise cerebrospinal fluid pressure as a result of respiratory depression with
carbon dioxide retention. Therefore, NUCYNTATm should not be used in patients susceptible to
the effects of raised cerebrospinal fluid pressure such as those with head injury and increased
intracranial pressure. Opioid analgesics may obscure the clinical course of patients with head
injury due to effects on pupillary response and consciousness. NUCYNTATm should be used with
caution in patients with head injury, intracranial lesions, or other sources of preexisting
increased intracranial pressure.

•

NUCYNTATm is a mu-opioid agonist and is a Schedule II controlled substance. Such drugs are
sought by drug abusers and people with addiction disorders. Diversion of Schedule II products is
an act subject to criminal penalty. NUCYNTATm can be abused in a manner similar to other muopioid agonists, legal or illicit. This should be considered when prescribing or dispensing
NUCYNTATm in situations where the physician or pharmacist is concerned about an increased risk
of misuse and abuse. All patients treated with mu-opioid agonists require careful monitoring for
signs of abuse and addiction. NUCYNTATm may be abused by crushing, chewing, snorting or
injecting the product. These practices pose a significant risk to the abuser that could result in
overdose and death.

•

Experience with NUCYNTATm overdose is very limited. Management of overdose should be
focused on treating symptoms of mu-opioid agonism. Primary attention should be given to
reestablishment of a patent airway and institution of assisted or controlled ventilation when
overdose of NUCYNTATm is suspected. Supportive measures (including oxygen and vasopressors)
should be employed in the management of circulatory shock and pulmonary edema
accompanying overdose as indicated. Cardiac arrest or arrhythmias may require cardiac
massage or defibrillation.

•

Patients should be cautioned that NUCYNTATm may impair the mental and/or physical abilities
required for the performance of potentially hazardous tasks such as driving a car or operating
machinery. This is to be expected especially at the beginning of treatment, at any change of
dosage as well as in combination with alcohol or tranquilizers.

•

NUCYNTATm has not been systematically evaluated in patients with a seizure disorder, and such
patients were excluded from clinical studies. NUCYNTATm should be prescribed with care in
patients with a history of a seizure disorder or any condition that would put the patient at risk of
seizures.

3

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_TXMDL_00305437

 •

The development of a potentially life-threatening serotonin syndrome may occur with use of
SNRI products, including NUCYNTAT", particularly with concomitant use of serotonergic drugs
such as SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, MAOIs and triptans, and with drugs which impair metabolism of
serotonin (including MAOIs). Serotonin syndrome may include mental-status changes (eg,
agitation, hallucinations, coma), autonomic instability (eg, tachycardia, labile blood pressure,
hyperthermia), neuromuscular aberrations (eg, hyperreflexia, incoordination) and/or
gastrointestinal symptoms (eg nausea, vomiting, diarrhea).

•

Withdrawal symptoms may occur if NUCYNTATm is discontinued abruptly. These symptoms may
include: anxiety, sweating, insomnia, rigors, pain, nausea, tremors, diarrhea, upper respiratory
symptoms, piloerection, and rarely, hallucinations. Withdrawal symptoms may be reduced by
tapering NUCYNTATm.

•

Pregnancy Category C. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of NUCYNTATm in
pregnant women. NUCYNTATm should be used during pregnancy ONLY if the potential benefit
justifies the potential risk to the fetus. NUCYNTATm is not recommended for use in women during
and immediately prior to labor and delivery. Neonates whose mothers have been taking
NUCYNTATm should be monitored for respiratory depression. NUCYNTATm should not be used
during breastfeeding.

•

NUCYNTATm is not recommended in patients with severe renal or hepatic impairment.
NUCYNTATm should be used with caution in patients with moderate hepatic impairment. Like
other drugs with mu-opioid agonist activity, NUCYNTATm may cause spasm of the sphincter of
Oddi and should be used with caution in patients with biliary tract disease, including acute
pancreatitis.

•

The most common adverse events are nausea, dizziness, vomiting, somnolence and headache.

Date:

Tuesday, November 5 2013 02:05 PM

Subject: DeWine champions Scioto County fight against drugs
From:

Mike DeWine <info@mikedewine.com>

To:

Moody, David <Moody.David@endo.com >;

bc

Friend,
Last week, I traveled for three days along the Ohio River, meeting with local law
enforcement and community members to discuss crime and drug issues. We had a very
informative public forum in Portsmouth, focusing on the prescription drug problem and the
heroin problem. At least five Ohioans die each day to accidental drug deaths. This is tragic.
We are fighting back and have closed many pill mills and taken the licenses of 35 bad
doctors who were illegally prescribing drugs. Portsmouth has had a huge drug problem and
the community has fought back! Other communities can learn a lot from the way
Portsmouth citizens have come together as a community. We are scheduling more of these
meetings soon throughout Ohio.
I wanted to share the article from the Portsmouth Daily Times about our forum.
Very respectfully yours,
Mike DeWine

DeWine champions Scioto County fight against drugs
By Frank Lewis
Portsmouth Daily Times
Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine says he wants to use the success Scioto County has
had in dealing with the drug epidemic as a springboard for his statewide program.
Portsmouth was DeWine's first stop in what will be his planned Attorney General's Drug
Abuse Community Forum series, and he spoke exclusively with the Daily Times about what
he hoped to take away from that forum held Wednesday at The Counseling Center on Court
Street.
"I think Scioto County is really a model of a community that was devastated, and continues
to be hit hard by drugs," DeWine said. "But it is fighting back. And what we heard today is
the comment - `we all came together. We worked together. We broke down this old way of
looking at things.' One department would deal with one problem and another department
would deal with another problem, and no one talked to each other. We broke that down."
Several people spoke at the event including State Representative Terry Johnson (RMcDermott), Ed Hughes, CEO of Compass Community Health, Lisa Roberts RN of the
Portsmouth Health Department, and anti-prescription drug activist, Jo Anna Krohn, founder
of SOLACE (Surviving Our Losses And Continuing Everyday), Portsmouth Police Chief
Robert Ware, Scioto County Sheriff Marty V. Donini and Deputy Scioto County Coroner

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_ANK_CHI_0577699

 Dr. Wayne Wheeler, who drew a large applause when he said - "I make a point when I first
see a patient, at the very first encounter I say - 'you are worth something. You are not trash.
You are not garbage. You are a human being and are deserving of self respect, and
deserving of community respect, and our problem is to try to help you earn that back in your
own heart'
Wheeler said the first job of the community is to change the attitude toward drug addiction.
He said - "Then you can start working on the problem."
DeWine talked with guarded optimism about the successes of the last several years
including the shutting down of pain clinics in Scioto County, telling those in attendance "We have taken the licenses of 38 doctors. That's a lot. They were just pill pushers."
But he also called attention to the changeover that has occurred since a lot of the opiate
availability has gone away.
"Today we have heroin in every county," DeWine said. "And we have communities in this
state that will not admit they have a drug problem."
Johnson told the audience the root of the problem has to be addressed holistically, telling
them it takes the whole community working together.
"People ask me, how did you come together?" Johnson said. "I tell them we did, but we're
not done."
Johnson said the drug epidemic crosses every economic strata.
"We've got a lot more to do, but we've come a long way," Johnson said. "I couldn't be
prouder of the efforts of the people here in southern Ohio."
In another exclusive interview, Hughes told the Daily Times - "We were contacted by the
Attorney General's office, stating that Mike DeWine was going to be going around the state
and going to local communities trying to get input from these local communities in terms of
the role their office could play in our prevention and intervention services, and how to try
and address especially this transition we're seeing between prescription drugs and heroin, so
this is the first of those events that the Attorney General has set up, and we were really
happy to host it"
Hughes said DeWine is not new to the drug epidemic.
"He (DeWine) has a long history of interest in treatments and prevention services around
drug and alcohol abuse," Hughes told the Daily Times. "And I think he's trying to get some
input from the local community with the idea that somewhere this is going to lead to him
trying to look at what kind of a contribution his office makes in helping us locally to try and
address these problems."
According to the Ohio Department of Health, drug overdose deaths increased 440 percent in
Ohio from 1999 to 2011, with Scioto County having the highest drug overdose rate per
capita from 2007 to 2011. More recent statistics from the Scioto County Coroner's Office
show a 30 percent decrease in direct drug deaths from 2011 to 2012, and a 32 percent
decrease in indirect drug deaths during the same time period. DeWine credited the
grassroots efforts of the health, law enforcement, court, and community segments all
coming together to bring about success.

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

 "I think other communities need to do the same thing," DeWine said. "Because this is not a
Scioto County problem. This is a problem that is across the state of Ohio. Every county has
it. Every county has these issues."
DeWine will return to southern Ohio Thursday hosting several events. First, DeWine will
tour McGinnis, Inc. at 740 County Road 1 in South Point, including a barge being restored
by the company. That visit will begin at 9 a.m. Second, at 11:30 a.m., DeWine will tour
Serenity House, a domestic violence shelter at 11 Hickory Lane in Gallipolis. Serenity
House received a Victims of Crime grant from the Attorney General's Office. Lastly,
DeWine will host a roundtable for area law enforcement at the Wild Horse Cafe, 251 West
Main Street in Pomeroy, in Meigs County at 1:30 p.m.

FYI, in case any of you hear about this in your territory. Tapentadol has launched under the brand
name Nucynta.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-CHI_LIT-00947058

 Nucynta is a mu-opioid agonist and is a Schedule II controlled substance for acute pain.

•

Dosing is one tablet of 50 mg, 75 mg, or 100 mg every 4 to 6 hours depending on pain intensity
•

Patients can receive a second dose of NUCYNTATm as early as one hour after initial dose, if
needed on Day 1

Maximum 24-hour dose of NUCYNTATm on Day 1 is 700 mg and on subsequent days is 600 mg.
Higher doses have not been studied and are therefore not recommended

NUCYNTAT" is indicated for the relief of moderate to severe acute pain in patients 18 years of age or
older.
IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION
•

Like other drugs with mu-opioid agonist activity, NUCYNTAT" is contraindicated in patients with
significant respiratory depression, acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercapnia in
unmonitored settings or in the absence of resuscitative equipment. NUCYNTAT" is
contraindicated in patients who have or are suspected to have paralytic ileus. NUCYNTAT" is also
contraindicated in patients currently using or within 14 days of using monoamine oxidase
inhibitors (MAOIs) due to potential additive effects on norepinephrine levels, which may result in
adverse cardiovascular events.

•

Respiratory depression is the primary risk of mu-opioid agonists. Respiratory depression occurs
more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients and in those suffering from conditions
accompanied by hypoxia, hypercapnia, or upper airway obstruction, in whom even moderate
therapeutic doses may significantly decrease pulmonary ventilation. NUCYNTATm should be
administered with caution to the elderly, debilitated patients, and patients with conditions
accompanied by hypoxia, hypercapnia or decreased respiratory reserve such as: asthma,
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or cor pulmonale, severe obesity, sleep apnea syndrome,
myxedema, kyphoscoliosis, CNS depression, or coma. In such patients, even usual therapeutic
doses of NUCYNTATm may increase airway resistance and decrease respiratory drive to the point
of apnea. Alternative non-mu-opioid agonist analgesics should be considered and NUCYNTATm
should be employed only under careful medical supervision at the lowest effective dose in such
patients. If respiratory depression occurs, it should be treated as any mu-opioid agonist-induced
respiratory depression.

•

Patients receiving other mu-opioid agonist analgesics, general anesthetics, phenothiazines, other
tranquilizers, sedatives, hypnotics, or other CNS depressants (including alcohol) concomitantly
with NUCYNTATm may exhibit additive CNS depression. Interactive effects resulting in respiratory
depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma or death may result if these drugs are taken
in combination with NUCYNTATm. When such combined therapy is contemplated, a dose
reduction of one or both agents should be considered.

•

Opioid analgesics can raise cerebrospinal fluid pressure as a result of respiratory depression with
carbon dioxide retention. Therefore, NUCYNTATm should not be used in patients susceptible to
the effects of raised cerebrospinal fluid pressure such as those with head injury and increased
intracranial pressure. Opioid analgesics may obscure the clinical course of patients with head
injury due to effects on pupillary response and consciousness. NUCYNTATm should be used with
caution in patients with head injury, intracranial lesions, or other sources of preexisting
increased intracranial pressure.

•

NUCYNTATm is a mu-opioid agonist and is a Schedule II controlled substance. Such drugs are
sought by drug abusers and people with addiction disorders. Diversion of Schedule II products is
an act subject to criminal penalty. NUCYNTATm can be abused in a manner similar to other muopioid agonists, legal or illicit. This should be considered when prescribing or dispensing
NUCYNTATm in situations where the physician or pharmacist is concerned about an increased risk
of misuse and abuse. All patients treated with mu-opioid agonists require careful monitoring for

2

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-CHI_LIT-00947059

 signs of abuse and addiction. NUCYNTATm may be abused by crushing, chewing, snorting or
injecting the product. These practices pose a significant risk to the abuser that could result in
overdose and death.
•

Experience with NUCYNTAT" overdose is very limited. Management of overdose should be
focused on treating symptoms of mu-opioid agonism. Primary attention should be given to
reestablishment of a patent airway and institution of assisted or controlled ventilation when
overdose of NUCYNTATm is suspected. Supportive measures (including oxygen and vasopressors)
should be employed in the management of circulatory shock and pulmonary edema
accompanying overdose as indicated. Cardiac arrest or arrhythmias may require cardiac
massage or defibrillation.

•

Patients should be cautioned that NUCYNTATm may impair the mental and/or physical abilities
required for the performance of potentially hazardous tasks such as driving a car or operating
machinery. This is to be expected especially at the beginning of treatment, at any change of
dosage as well as in combination with alcohol or tranquilizers.

•

NUCYNTATm has not been systematically evaluated in patients with a seizure disorder, and such
patients were excluded from clinical studies. NUCYNTATm should be prescribed with care in
patients with a history of a seizure disorder or any condition that would put the patient at risk of
seizures.

•

The development of a potentially life-threatening serotonin syndrome may occur with use of
SNRI products, including NUCYNTATm, particularly with concomitant use of serotonergic drugs
such as SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, MAOIs and triptans, and with drugs which impair metabolism of
serotonin (including MAOIs). Serotonin syndrome may include mental-status changes (eg,
agitation, hallucinations, coma), autonomic instability (eg, tachycardia, labile blood pressure,
hyperthermia), neuromuscular aberrations (eg, hyperreflexia, incoordination) and/or
gastrointestinal symptoms (eg nausea, vomiting, diarrhea).

•

Withdrawal symptoms may occur if NUCYNTATm is discontinued abruptly. These symptoms may
include: anxiety, sweating, insomnia, rigors, pain, nausea, tremors, diarrhea, upper respiratory
symptoms, piloerection, and rarely, hallucinations. Withdrawal symptoms may be reduced by
tapering NUCYNTATm.

•

Pregnancy Category C. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of NUCYNTATm in
pregnant women. NUCYNTATm should be used during pregnancy ONLY if the potential benefit
justifies the potential risk to the fetus. NUCYNTATm is not recommended for use in women during
and immediately prior to labor and delivery. Neonates whose mothers have been taking
NUCYNTATm should be monitored for respiratory depression. NUCYNTATm should not be used
during breastfeeding.

•

NUCYNTATm is not recommended in patients with severe renal or hepatic impairment.
NUCYNTATm should be used with caution in patients with moderate hepatic impairment. Like
other drugs with mu-opioid agonist activity, NUCYNTATm may cause spasm of the sphincter of
Oddi and should be used with caution in patients with biliary tract disease, including acute
pancreatitis.

•
The most common adverse events are nausea, dizziness, vomiting, somnolence and headache.

Good morning Warren,
What a great CCCBI event last night. Thank you for attending and your support of the Chamber. Per our discussion on opioids
and those designed to be "abuse deterrent" Steve Barrar's co-sponsorship memo is below. As shared we think this is good
public policy and one way of addressing prescription drug abuse. I appreciate your willingness to review the intent of Steve's
legislation and the possibility of you signing on as a co-sponsor.
Please call if I you need any additional information.
Best regards,
Greg

January 31, 2013 03:54 PM
Rep. Stephen Barrar
•
Prescription Drug Abuse (Prior HB 1635)
•
In the near future, I plan to reintroduce H.B. 1635 (with two minor,
•
non-controversial changes). This bill deals with the prevention of
•
prescription drug abuse, which has become a growing and alarming
•
epidemic in the U.S. Opioids, which are used to treat pain, are at
•
high risk of abuse. Through innovative research and development,
•
prescription drug manufacturers are now able to produce opioids with
•
properties that are designed to prevent and deter abuse. The new
•
formulations are designed to prevent abusers, including children and
youth who steal pills from medicine cabinets, from being able to chew
•
or grind and then snort or inject the active ingredient for a quick
•
high. Studies indicate these new formulations are working as intended
•
and have dramatically reduced abuse.
*
•
•
•
•
•
•
*

When a physician or other prescriber determines a patient should have
a product designed to prevent abuse, there are two situations that
might prevent the patient from getting the product. First, we have a
mandatory generic substitution law that requires pharmacists to
automatically substitute with a generic and, second, some insurance
companies require substitution.

•
•
•
•
•
•
•
*

My legislation does not require health care providers to prescribe
abuse deterrent formulations. However, when a prescriber believes an
abuse deterrent drug is the best option for the patient, the bill will
prevent the pharmacist from automatically substituting without first
notifying the prescriber. It does allow pharmacists to substitute an
abuse deterrent opioid with another abuse deterrent opioid, without
notifying the prescriber.

•
•

Prescription drugs have become an entranceway into the world of drug
abuse and this legislation will help reduce those situations where the

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07204086

 pills are ground and injected or snorted. The bill will not eliminate
all types of abuse, but it is one step in the prevention of abuse.
Last session, this bill was supported by: National Association of
Drug Diversion Investigators, Inc., Center for Lawful Access and Abuse
Deterrence, American Academy of Pain Management, American Society for
Pain Management Nursing, US Pain Foundation, American Chronic Pain
Association, and the Kidney Cancer Association.

 Bill/Heather — for the OxyM approval Press Release text on Endo's commitment to Responsible Pain Management, there's some
good stuff in here that's taken from the current article on Endo's own Intranet site... I have highlighted some that I think we can
draw from... . I will send you a some additional material on PROMISE to add. Thanks. Let me know your thoughts.... DEK

Oxymorphone Risk Management
In December 2005, Endo submitted New Drug Applications (NDAs) to the FDA for immediate-release (IR) and
extended-release (ER) oxymorphone tablets. If approved, oxymorphone IR and ER will provide patients suffering
with moderate to severe chronic pain their first new extended release treatment option since 1995.
As with all opioids, there is an inherent risk with oxymorphone for misuse, abuse, or diversion, even when prescribed
properly to the appropriate patient population. Therefore, in addition to reviewing Endo's NDA submissions, the FDA
will also be assessing Endo's oxymorphone Risk Minimization Action Plan (RiskMap).
Endo is committed to making oxymorphone available to the patients who need it and will benefit from a new option
for pain relief. At the same time, Endo is equally committed to working with the FDA and other government
agencies to help prevent potential misuse and abuse of the product. Establishing the balance between these two
objectives is both challenging and critical.
As David Kerr, Vice President for Business Development and oxymorphone launch team leader explains, "Endo
takes its responsibilities very seriously, not only to commercialize oxymorphone but also to help manage the risk
inherently associated with these products. We will work closely with the FDA and in collaboration with outside
groups to do everything we can to see the drug is used safely and appropriately."
The oxymorphone RiskMap focuses on proper labeling, education, sales force training, safety surveillance, tight
control of the distribution chain and, if it is necessary, intervention. In addition, the plan includes a self-evaluation
and amendment process to ensure it remains effective over time.
As with any drug on the market, the oxymorphone label has specific prescribing and patient-use information based on
proven clinical data. This label sets the boundaries and FDA-approved prescribing guidelines for proper use. "Endo
is committed to adhering to the label and promoting the product only within the label's specifications," Kerr says.
Education and training for health-care professionals are a major element of the plan. It is critical for health-care
professionals to consider the risks and benefits of any opioid before prescribing it to patients. Physicians need to
know how to screen patients for risk factors that may predict the potential for abuse prior to prescribing the drug and
to monitor patients after the medication is taken. Through grants to patient advocacy and education groups,
educational information for patients and caregivers regarding the risks of opioids and other analgesics is available
from a number of resources.
The education and training aspect of the plan also extends to Endo's sales force. Sales team members must be aware
of the drug's risks as well as the benefits so they can help inform physicians. In addition, if physicians report any
incidents of misuse to a sales representative, the rep is obligated to formally report it to Endo's Pharmacovigilance
and Risk Management Group, who will investigate the event and report it to the FDA if warranted.
Safety surveillance of events is another aspect of the risk management plan. "A multidisciplinary team led by the
Pharmacovigilance and Risk Management Department meets on a regular basis to assess the data obtained by safety
surveillance to evaluate safety signals or trends," says Dr. Marie Pinizzotto, Senior Director, Global Safety and
Pharmacovigilance.
In addition to the reports that come to Endo directly, the Pharmacovigilance Department will review reports and data
generated from national databases. As Kerr explains, "Endo will work closely with outside groups to communicate
and intervene if there is a problem."
There is an evaluation process built into the plan to help ensure it is making an impact. "The data obtained from
CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-00850102

 surveillance will be reviewed on a regular basis to identify safety signals or trends in a specific area or population. If
a trend is noted, we will investigate and attempt to identify its etiology. Intervention through various means will be
initiated to the particular area or population. One such intervention would be increased educational initiatives," says
Pinizzotto.

In order to make oxymorphone available to the patients who will benefit from it, there is, unfortunately, no way to
prevent abuse. Endo can try, however, to reduce the potential for these products to be misused by collaborating with
the FDA and other government agencies to see that the drug is used safely and appropriately.

Stephenson Murder Case
follow upl tried to explain to the caller that there was often DNA analysis done for different reasons; i.e.
paternity, id etc. and that in my limited knowledge those test would take less time and that the in depth
analysis required for a murder investigation requires an extensive standard, multiple profiles and methodical
testing... because the evidence would be under great degrees of scrutiny as it can provide the proof to arrest
and prosecute. AND in a court case the evidence has not only the power to identify but, convict a
person/persons who if convicted may receive the death penalty. ( hope that sounded correct)

As always, thank you for your help. As you understand and are more than aware, not having answers is so
difficult for the family.

H B 377 Tamper Resistant or Abuse Resistant/Deterrent Opioids - My take on the proposed bill, is another
tool to combat prescription narcotic drug abuse that is taking a toll on Kentucky families. In a nutshell- when the
physician feels it is in the best interest of the patient to write a prescription for the tamper resistant form of the
pain medication, pharmacists would be required to "fill as written" no substitution. The cost of tamper resistant is
the same as the non tamper resistant form of the medication. No one pharmaceutical company holds the patent,
so generic forms of the tamper resistant medications are also in the pipeline. Most importantly, this is about
saving lives. Too many l ives lost, too many futures destroyed and too many children suffer from the destructive
effect on their young lives. Family court judges report that 85% of their abuse, neglect and dependency cases are

CONFIDENTIAL

EPI001073259

 the result of substance abuse.

HB 377 is on the agenda for the House Health and Welfare Committee for next Thursday, Feb 23 and noon.
Testifying on the bill
A mother's story I have a mother who has lost two adult children to Opana over doses. They began
popping pills, the progressed to snorting and then IV.
(Some of the pharmacist say, " it doesn't stop abuse . because they can still take the pills by mouth".
My response is that as users progress and spiral in their addiction, the go for a more intense high,
that is why they crush pills etc.)

I do not call Tamper Resistant Opioids Formulations (TRF) the end all, but another tool in the tool box
to combat this scourge on Kentucky.

•

Michael Barnes, Interim Executive Director, Center for Lawful Access and Abuse Deterrence (he will be
here to testify and has sent a letter of support see a quote from Michael below)

•

but is clearing it with AOC. Judge Roberts will speak on the extremely high amount of cases related to

Troopers in the room

number of brands TRF (5 currently approved and 12 in development) and generics TRF are still forth coming. There is no difference
in the cost of brand narcotic TRF or the same brand in the non TRF.

•

(my response, the physician prescribes TRF - tamper resistant formulas for opioids, i.e. OxyContin, morphine,
oxymorphone, at his/her discretion., not routinely for every patient. )

 (there are no patent restrictions or ownership any company can obtain the patent to manufacture TRF.)
(personally, I am really not for cheap narcotics.... I really do not want a market flooded with $4 generic OxyContin and
Opana)
I want medication to be affordable but, the toll substance abuse is taking on this Commonwealth, we need tools to assist in
addressing the issue.

As always, thank you for your assistance with Thursday's testimony. I look forward to receiving your statement for our fact sheet.
Please see a few of the other quotes below.

Please do not hesitate to call me if you have any questions or concerns.

Warmest Regards,

Addia

P.S. CASA event last Friday- thank you and KSP for helping us. We are just going over the post conference surveys and "Examining

Quotes for fact sheet

Since 2009, CLAAD's National Prescription Drug Abuse Prevention Strategy has called for the adoption of technologies to impede
the intentional abuse of prescription medications.
The use of abuse-deterrent opioids is the new standard of care in pain treatment.
Abuse-deterrent medications are the new equivalent of child-proof medicine caps.
Please heed the recommendations of the 30 organizations endorsing the National Prescription Drug Abuse Prevention Strategy, and
act in accordance with federal policy, by shepherding safe prescribing and dispensing legislation through the Kentucky Legislature.
Michael C. Barnes
Interim Executive Director
Center for Lawful Access and Abuse Deterrence

Due to ongoing problems with drug diversion in the United States, NADDI is strong proponent of new tamper resistant medicines
that make it more difficult for an abuser and more helpful for law enforcement, yet still provide quality relief to the patient. NADDI
has a strong belief that the diversion of prescription medication, can many times ultimately negatively affect legitimate patients, the
vast majority of those who use controlled substances.
Charles F. Cichon

CONFIDENTIAL

National Association of Drug Diversion Investigators, Inc. (NADDI)

The poll also showed more than 3 in 10 adults in Northern Kentucky and statewide reported that they have friends or family
members who have experienced problems as a result of misusing prescription pain relievers. — "The Kentucky Health Poll"

Stephen J. Pasierb, President and CEO, The Partnership at Druqfree.orq:
The Partnership at DruRfree.org believes that tamper resistant formulation can be one important piece of an overall effort to deter
the abuse of prescription medications.
While it is by no means a silver bullet, the prescribing and dispensing of tamper resistant formulations is an important part of
reducing the behavior of prescription drug abuse. That means that if more prescribers substitute TRF for non-TRF opioid analgesics,

Tim and Brian,
Has there been any status change on the federal legislation identified several months ago that impact opioids?
Current Federal Legislation Regarding Prescription Drug Abuse H.R. 1065 — "The Pill Mill Crackdown Act" by Representative
Buchanan
- What it does: This bill increases the penalty for pill mills and re-schedules Vicodin from a schedule Ill controlled substance to a
schedule II controlled substance.
- Endo's Position: Support on the general premise of increasing penalties for pill mills but Endo is not speaking on the
re-scheduling of Vicodin.
H.R. 1266 — "The Fraudulent Prescription Prevention Act" by Representative Grimm
- What it does: This bill is intended to prevent the fraudulent abuse of certain prescriptions by creating a new registration and
reporting requirements relating to schedule II and III controlled substances.
- Endo's Position: No position taken by Endo. Though we support efforts that address fraudulent prescriptions, the method by
which this bill addresses the issue could impact appropriate access to pain management medicines.
H.R. 1316 — "The Stop Oxy Abuse Act" by Representative Bono Mack
- What it does: This bill is intended to modify eAsting approvals and limit subsequent approvals of drugs containing controlledrelease oxycodone hydrochloride. It would do this by directing the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to take actions to restrict
the indications of such drugs to "severe-only" pain as opposed to "moderate-to-severe pain."
- Endo's Position: Endo joins the entire pain management community (including providers and physicians) in opposition of this bill.
H.R. 2119 — "The Ryan Creedon Act" by Representative Bono Mack
- What it does: The "Ryan Creedon Act" requires practitioners to obtain training or certification on addiction to and abuse of
controlled substances and appropriate and safe use of these controlled substances.
- Endo's Position: Support requirements for a DEA certification check-off.
S. 507 — "The Prescription Drug Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act" by Senator Rockefeller
- What it does: The bill would create an additional training for practitioners who dispense narcotic drugs, restrict 40 mg
methadone diskettes, establish a Controlled Substances Clinical Standards Commission (and new dosing guidelines), and require
reporting and tracking of opioid mortality statistics.
- Endo's Position: Neutral except for concerns regarding specifics of training requirements that single out Opiods and Methadone
rather than all pain management medicines. Endo also has concerns about language that establishes a commission that would
create clinical standards, dosing and benchmarking guidelines for controlled substances which could affect access to appropriate
pain management medicines.
S. 882 — "The STOP Act" by Senator Brown (OH)
- What it does: S. 882 would require each State Medicaid plan to develop and implement a restricted recipient program for
individuals identified as high-risk prescription drug users and require the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) to
establish a similar program for individuals enrolled in a voluntary prescription drug benefit program under Medicare Part D.
- Endo's Position: Oppose this legislation as it could unnecessarily inhibit access to appropriate
White House: Vice President Biden, through PhRMA, aggressively solicited information on industry efforts to address prescription
drug abuse for prescription medications. PhRMA met with VP staff and Endo provided information related to our efforts and
programs.

Area ERs tightening policies on pain med dispensing
HDH, Adena work to balance legit prescriptions with growing abuse issues

By GARY ABERNATHY
Publisher
Area hospitals are cracking down on dispensing pain medications in their emergency departments in an
ongoing effort to thwart those who abuse or sell prescriptions like oxycodone or other narcotics.
The issue has increasingly been in the spotlight in recent months across southern Ohio, particularly in Adams
and Scioto counties, where so-called "pill mills" have been targeted by legislation designed to shut down pain
clinics whose purposes are suspected to be little more than to funnel heavy duty narcotics to abusers or drug
pushers.
But law enforcement officials in neighboring counties like Highland County have also expressed a growing
concern about the trafficking in prescribed narcotics locally.
At Highland District Hospital, officials say they recognize that accidental deaths by prescription drugs and
abuse of prescription drugs are on the rise.
"For these reasons, our emergency department physicians closely monitor and screen patients for narcoticseeking behavior," said Tracey Coss, emergency department manager. "We have a patient-first mindset. We
do all we can to assure that patients with pain are properly diagnosed and treated."
But under Highland District's policy, if a narcotic prescription is given for the care of an acute painful
condition, the prescription will be only for a small number of pills to last only long enough until the patient can
follow up with a primary care provider or specialist.
Highland District Hospital's emergency department does not prescribe refills for narcotic medications,
officials say. If the condition is determined to be chronic in nature, the patient may be referred to Dr. Amol
Soin, a non-narcotic pain management specialist at HDH.
Patients identified with narcotic abuse issues in the emergency department may also be referred to an
addiction specialist.
Adena Health System, headquartered in Chillicothe, with a facility in Greenfield, announced this week that at
its facilities, emergency department doctors will limit the number of prescribed narcotics and controlled
substances given to patients as part of a new patient safety policy beginning April 2.
As part of the new initiative, patients who visit the emergency department for non-emergency chronic pain
conditions will be given an alternative medication.
"The medical providers at Adena have become very concerned about the use of narcotics and controlled
substances in our society," said Dr. Brad S. Goldman, assistant medical director of emergency services and
EMS director at Adena.
"We discourage their use except when absolutely medically necessary."
Dr. Kort Gronbach, an anesthesiologist who specializes in pain medicine at Adena, said in a press release that
he applauded the new policy. "In Ohio, accidental deaths by prescription drugs rank number one and are
responsible for an average of four deaths a day," said Gronbach, who is one of 3o members of the Ohio
Prescription Drug Abuse Task Force.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-08368289

 Similar to Highland District Hospital's policy, patients with acute pain who an attending physician at Adena's
emergency department believes have symptoms that warrant narcotic treatment will be given only a limited
number of pills until they can seek treatment with their personal physician, said Goldman.
The patient is also required to have valid photo identification before receiving such prescriptions, and is
required to have a responsible driver physically present in the emergency department before the medication
is given.
Last October, nearby Adams and Scioto counties were designated as federal High Intensity Drug Trafficking
Areas in an announcement by White House drug czar Gil Kerlikowske. Gaining that designation had been a
top priority for U.S. Sen. Rob Portman, who worked with federal and state officials, including Gov. John
Kasich and Attorney General Mike DeWine, in making the goal a reality.
Under the designation, those counties will be able to receive federal resources to assist in drug control efforts
among federal, state, and local law enforcement officers in southeast Ohio.
Highland County Sheriff Ron Ward said at the time that he welcomed the news, noting that HIDTA
designation helps free up additional federal grant dollars for the drug fight. It also allows existing drug task
forces in the region to tap into HIDTA assistance, said Ward.
Even though Highland was not specifically part of the HIDTA designation, drug trafficking "doesn't stop at
the county line. In time, this reaps benefits for neighboring counties too," said Ward.
Scioto County's "pill mill" problem was the target of a bill introduced by State Rep. Terry Johnson (RMcDermott) and signed into law last year. The bill has been effective in helping shut down several pain clinics
in Portsmouth, but some clinics simply moved across the river into Kentucky. The federal HIDTA designation
helps law enforcement agencies work more effectively across state lines.
Adams and Scioto Counties joined ii other Ohio counties including Cuyahoga, Fairfield, Franklin, Greene,
Hamilton, Lucas, Mahoning, Montgomery, Stark, Summit, and Warren Counties as part of the Ohio HIDTA.

explaining we need to add up all the pain medications he was on and
multiply by .5 to get a more accurate starting dose, that way we at least have a fair comparison. The patient then said he
pops the Vicodin like candy for his pain. I looked at Dr. Stamelos, and trying to remain
professional, said it sounds like his pain in not controlled. At this point I was feeling a little uncomfortable being that the
patient was in the room during the conversation with Dr. Stamelos. The patient was
asked to leave and Dr. Stamelos said he was a Cancer patient in remission. I offered the explanation that maybe the disease
was causing the lack of effectiveness with the opioids. Dr. Stamelos then shook his
head and said treating pain with these kinds of drugs is a sleazy business. I was not sure where that came from, maybe
frustration. We both stood and I tried to leave on a positive note saying this was

a difficult first patient to try Opana ER on, he agreed.
I contacted my counterpart Ben Manibog and discussed the situation with him; we both agreed that it might be a
smart idea if we contacted our DM Bill Kellens just in case.

News in Pain Management

ENDO_SF-00103909

 CDC Director on Prescribing Guidelines for Opioids
In a recent press briefing on a CDC report on women and opioid overdoses (story below) Centers for Disease Control and
Prevention director Thomas Friedan, MD, called for a more thorough understanding of risks and benefits of opioids and urged
caution in their use as chronic non-cancer pain therapy. Read a news report here.

CDC: Opioid Prescribing Trends, Attendant Risks Rising Sharply for Women
The recent holiday weekend saw widespread media coverage of a new Vital Signs report from the CDC documenting a 400
percent increase in opioid overdose fatalities among American women over the past decade. The corresponding figure for men
was 265 percent. Among the reasons cited by the report: Women are more likely to suffer from chronic pain, are prescribed
opioid painkillers at higher rates and higher doses, and are more likely to use them longer. Read a news report here.

Resistance Training and Chronic Low Back Pain
Research reported online in the July 1 edition of Spine compared full range of motion and limited range of motion exercise and
found that both produced clinically meaningful improvement in perceived pain and disability from CLBP. Read the study abstract
here.

Investigating Antibiotic Therapy for Back Pain
Two studies published recently in the European Spine Journal focus respectively on the coincidence of bacterial infection and
lumbar disk inflammation, and on the effectiveness of a standard 100-day course of antibiotics in relieving bone swelling and
attendant back pain. Read abstracts of the first and second studies here.

New Report on Efficacy of State Pain Policies
The Pain Policy and Study Group at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health has released a new report,
Achieving Balance in State Pain Policy- A Progress Report Card. The report, available here, assesses current regulatory policy in
each of the states with respect to the government's dual obligation to prevent the abuse and diversion of controlled medicines
while maintaining their legitimate availability. Recommendations for improvement in low scoring states are also offered by the
study group.

PAINWeek News
PAINWeek 2013 Session Spotlight
"The Madwoman in the Attic": Chronic Pain and Borderline Personality
Disorder
Patients with chronic pain, and who also suffer from Borderline Personality Disorder present special
challenges to the practicing clinician. In his course presentation, "The Madwoman in the Attic", veteran
PAINWeek faculty member Michael R. Clark, MD, MPH, MBA, will explore the ways in which patients with
personality disorders evoke a variety of feelings in clinicians. While some may seize the challenge, others are
more likely to decide these patients are at least difficult and at most not worth the trouble. "Certainly, they are difficult cases,
but practical strategies for management will be presented." said Dr. Clark. "When successfully engaged, the care of these
patients can be remarkably rewarding."

ENDO_SF-00103910

 You'll find dozens of course topics in all aspects of pain management spanning some 14 different tracks at PAINWeek 2013.
Register today and save $200 off the onsite conference cost. Get even larger discounts if you attend with your group! Save the
date (September 4-7, 2013) and we'll see you in Las Vegas for PAINWeek 2013!

PAINWeek: Meeting the Needs of Primary Care
Ilene R. Robeck, MD, is a physician with the Veterans Health Administration, Bay Pines VA Health Care
System. She is also a member of PAINWeek faculty, and offers these observations on PAINWeek and its
particular attention to the needs of the primary care practitioner.
At PAINWeek, we educate frontline practitioners like you about pain management. And we learn from each
other. This year, join your colleagues, and be part of the discussion. Register NOW for PAINWeek 2013!

ORDER NOW: The PAINWeek Online Content Package!
PAINWeek offers over 100 hours of CE/CME content—but since you can only attend 1 course at a time, we offer the PAINWeek
Online Content Package. The package enables you to access the majority of concurrent sessions online, with audio and
synced slides. You can also download MP3 files to listen to on your iPod or MP3 player. The cost of the package is $100 before
August 20. Package price increases to $149 at the conference, and $249 after the conference. Place your order now and save!
NOTE: Online content becomes available in early October and is not certified for credit.

NOW AVAILABLE: The PAINWeek Journal!
The Premier Issue of our new publication, the PAINWeek Journal is now available!
As a new component in the PAINWeek outreach to frontline practitioners, the PAINWeek Journal is the multidisciplinary
publication that will provide timely coverage of the panoply of issues in pain management—assessment and diagnosis, legal,
policy, R&D, and medication regulatory concerns. Among the content in our first issue are features on behavioral risk
assessment; the challenge of centralized pain; topical and transdermal pain relievers; the epidemiology and pathophysiology of
migraine, and commentary on governmental intervention in prescribing. Targeted specifically to frontline practitioners, the
PAINWeek Journal will be a valuable resource for your clinical practice. Download a preview of the premier issue, and get your
FREE subscription to future issues here!

Accommodations at PAINWeek: Great Rates, Great Choices!
We've contracted a special room rate of just $135 per night, plus tax for PAINWeek attendees. This year, you can also extend
your stay at the resort for up to 3 days before and/or after the conference, AND we've made a variety of accommodation
upgrades available at discounted prices. Find out more here and then book your room during registration.
Make the most of your stay in Las Vegas, while getting the most from your learning experience—only at PAINWeek 2013!

PAINWeek to Feature Opioid Safety Day
In response to increasing concern over misuse and abuse of prescription medications, and opioids in particular, PAINWeek 2013
will be designating Day 3 (Friday, September 6) of the 2013 conference as Opioid Safety Day. The day will feature multiple
course offerings, symposia, and special sessions designed to provide the latest information on prescribing safety for opioids, as
well as on the increasingly stringent and complex regulatory environment surrounding them. Commercially supported activities
will also be offered to PAINWeek attendees. The objective is to better prepare frontline practitioners in the appropriate use of

ENDO_SF-00103911

 opioid analgesics as an element of multidisciplinary pain therapy.
The world of opioid prescribing is changing fast. Register today for PAINWeek 2013, and be fully briefed on this critical topic in
pain management!

PAINWeek 2013 Schedule at a Glance Now Available!
The PAINWeek 2013 Schedule at a Glance is now available here. This year's program agenda will offer more
than 100 hours of continuing medical education courses and master classes, special interest sessions and
satellite symposia. We will also feature full-day programs sponsored by the American Pain Society, the
American Society of Pain Educators, the National Association of Drug Diversion Investigators, the
American Academy of Pain Medicine, and the Veterans Health Administration.
For more information on PAINWeek 2013, and to register for the conference at discounted early-bird rates, visit painweek.orq.

Friday, November 16201201:02 PM

Sent:
