WARNING: P TENTIAL FO AEA SE, IMPORTANCE OF
PROPER PATIENT SELECTION AND LIMITATIONS OF
USE

Potential for Abuse
OPANA® ER contains oxymorphone, which is a morphine-like opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled
substance, with an abuse liability similar to other opioid analgesics.
Oxymorphone can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. This should be considered
when prescribing or dispensing OPANA® ER in situations where the physician or pharmacist is concerned about an
increased risk of misuse, abuse, or diversion.

Proper Patient Selection

(R)
OPANA • ER is an extended-release oral formulation of oxymorphone indicated for the management of moderate to
severe pain when a continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extended period of time.

Limitations of Use
OPANA

ER is NOT intended for use as an as needed analgesic.

OPANA® ER tablets are to be swallowed whole and are not to be cut, broken, chewed, dissolved, or crushed. Taking
cut, broken, chewed, dissolved, or crushed OPANA® ER tablets leads to rapid release and absorption of a
potentially fatal dose of oxymorphone.
Patients must not consume alcoholic beverages, or prescription or non-prescription medications containing alcohol,
while on OPANA® ER therapy. The co-ingestion of alcohol with OPANA® ER may result in increased plasma
levels and a potentially fatal overdose of oxymorphone.

CONTRAINDICATIONS
• OPANA® ER is contraindicated in patients with a known hypersensitivity to oxymorphone hydrochloride,
morphine analogs such as codeine, or any of the other ingredients of OPANA ER; in patients with moderate
or severe hepatic impairment or in any situation where opioids are contraindicated such as: patients with
respiratory depression (in the absence of resuscitative equipment or in unmonitored settings), acute or severe
bronchial asthma, hypercarbia, and in any patient who has or is suspected of having paralytic ileus.
• OPANA ER is not indicated for pain in the immediate post-operative period or if the pain is mild, or not
expected to persist for an extended period of time. OPANA ER is only indicated for post-operative use if the
patient is already receiving the drug prior to surgery or if the post-operative pain is expected to be moderate

All,
I have heard of multiple ER opioids being used but the practice is not documented in any guidelines. I believe that it has to do
with emerging basic science surrounding the variability of opioid receptors (and their subreceptors), and the differences in how
actually activate the receptor.
I have not specifically heard about oxymorphone and oxycodone. From an anecdotal perspective, this can be mentioned but your
reply is appropriate. I think the only thing that needs to be emphasized are the CNS depressant warnings...
This approach will at least allow the pharmacist understand that it is not unheard of, particularly if he or she is not well versed in
pain medicine and also allows us to look like we are aware of what is going on in the environment. However, we do not make any
recommendations as you have noted and it is up to the MD to determine what is best clinically and also to advocate to a third
party payor, should one be involved.
Let me know how this works out (or if you have any questions).
Thanks.
Nancy
From: Robin Reap [mailto:Robin.Reapkv,ppdi.com]
Sent: Friday, June 26, 2009 1:14 PM
To: Alvarez, Nancy
Cc: Terleckyj, Oksana; Tania Vila; Nora Tu; Tamara Murry; Robin Reap
Subject: Out of Scope: Opana ER Use with Oxycontin
Hi Nancy,
We received the following inquiry from the PCC: "This pharmacist has a doctor who is using Opana ER & OxyContin together in treating
some of his patients. She could not find anything that would suggest that this could be done and wants to know if we are aware of any data
along these lines?"
We conducted a search of the internal (including SRLs/old ad hoes for Opana IR/ER and other pain products) and external (medline,
American Pain Society website; reviewing some of the pain guidelines) literature (see attached for lit search results). No relevant studies
or data were identified. Guidelines included studies that were either non-opioid + Opana ER vs. another agent or Opana ER vs. longacting agent (such as sustained release oxycodone), but never in combination.
Unless you are aware of additional information, below (in blue text) is our current proposed response:
Endo Pharmaceuticals Inc is not aware of any studies evaluating the efficacy or safety of Opana ER in combination with OxyContin (or

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07590001

 any other long-acting opioid analgesic).
The prescribing information cautions that the concomitant use of other CNS depressants, including other opioids, may produce additive
CNS depressant effects. These effects may include respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, or comaJPPDIIIPPDII.
If inadequate analgesia is achieved, a supplemental dose of OPANA, another immediate-release opioid, or a non-opioid analgesic may be
administered. There is no information in the prescribing information to suggest adding another long-acting opioid analgesic for
inadequate analgesia; therefore, Endo Pharmaceuticals Inc cannot recommend the concomitant use of Opana ER and OxyContin.
Below are sections from the PI that may be also considered for the response:
Misuse, Abuse and Diversion
Oxymorphone can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. This should be considered when prescribing or
dispensing OPANA ER in situations where the physician or pharmacist is concerned about an increased risk of misuse, abuse, or
diversion.
Interactions with Alcohol and Drugs of Abuse
Healthcare professionals should contact their State Professional Licensing Board, or State Controlled Substances Authority for
information on how to prevent and detect abuse or diversion of this product.
Oxymorphone may be expected to have additive effects when used in conjunction with alcohol, other opioids, or illicit drugs that cause
central nervous system depression because respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation or coma may result[PPD21
JPPD21.
Drug Abuse and Addiction
OPANA ER, like other opioids, may be diverted for non-medical use. Careful record-keeping of prescribing information, including
quantity, frequency, and renewal requests is strongly advisedITPD3] JPPD.31.
Proper assessment of the patient, proper prescribing practices, periodic re-evaluation of therapy, and proper dispensing and storage are
appropriate measures that help to limit abuse of opioid drugs.
Use With CNS Depressants
JPPD41 [PPD4JThe concomitant use of other CNS depressants including sedatives, hypnotics, tranquilizers, general anesthetics,
phenothiazines, other opioids, and alcohol may produce additive CNS depressant effects. OPANA ER, like all opioid analgesics, should
be started at 1/3 to 1/2 of the usual dose in patients who are concurrently receiving other central nervous system depressants including
sedatives or hypnotics, general anesthetics, phenothiazines, tranquilizers, and alcohol because respiratory depression, hypotension, and
profound sedation or coma may result, and titrated slowly as necessary for adequate pain relief.
Additive effects resulting in respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation or coma may result if these drugs are taken in
combination with the usual doses of OPANA ER.
When combined therapy with any of the above medications is contemplated, the dose of one or both agents should be reduced.

Study Suggests Physician Dispensing of Opioids in
Florida Led to Overorescribing
Physician dispensing may have contributed to the unnecessary prescribing of strong opioids by some physicians in
Florida, a recent study suggested.
The Workers' Compensation Research Institute (WCRI), an independent, not-for-profit research organization,
analyzed 46,192 claims from injured workers to gauge the effect of Florida's anti-pill mill bill (HB 7095) on prescribing
behavior. The ban, which went into effect on July 1, 2011, established standards of care for doctors who prescribe
narcotics and restricted physician dispensing of strong opioids (prescriptions for these drugs can be filled at
pharmacies).
Claims were separated into two groups: pre-reform, for injuries dating from Jan. 1, 2010 to June 30, 2010, and post-

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07088825

 reform, for injuries from July 12011 to Dec. 30, 2011. There were 24,567 pre-reform claims with 59,564 prescriptions
and 21,625 post-reform claims with 52,747 prescriptions included in this study.
The WCRI found a high rate of compliance with the ban by physician-dispensers. The number of workers receiving
physician-dispensed strong opioids during the first six months for new injuries decreased from 3.9% to 0.5% after the
ban. The WRCI also found an increase in physician-dispensed pain medications such as nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (from 24.1% to 25.8%) and nonbanned opioids (from 9.1% to 10.1%). The researchers noted that
only 2% of workers who received weaker physician-dispensed pain medication in the first six months required strong
opioids in the next six months.
"When we compare pre- and post-reform prescribing practices, it appears that physician-dispensers not only reduced
their dispensing of strong opioids, but also reduced prescribing of strong opioids. This raises concerns that a
significant proportion of pre-reform physician-dispensed strong opioids were not necessary, which means injured
workers in Florida were put at greater risk for addiction, disability or work loss, and even death," said Richard Victor,
WCRI's executive director, in a press release. "Since Florida has banned physician dispensing of strong opioids, the
lessons of this study are relevant for the other states concerned about eliminating unnecessary costs in their system
while protecting injured workers from unnecessary medical care."
Lynn Webster, MD, past president of the American Academy of Pain Medicine, said dispensing from a physician's
office is typical of a problematic opioid-prescribing business and that Florida in particular has had a problem with pill
mills. He noted that there have been a lot of changes in Florida besides the pill mill ban that could have affected the
amount of opioids prescribed.
"Increasingly physicians are reluctant to prescribe schedule II opioids due to fear of regulatory sanctions. Some
pharmacies are not stocking schedule II like they had before the new laws so less is available," said Dr. Webster. "So I
would suggest caution in interpreting the reduction in prescribing as all due to the change laws."
Dr. Webster advised to ensure that efforts to protect patients and the public do not abandon patients in pain.
"At the same time public policymakers are working toward protecting patients, they should also ensure access and
coverage for comprehensive pain programs that include behavioral and physical therapies along with medication
management when necessary," he said.
—PMN Staff

Matt —
Are you certain this change needs to be made? Gruenenthal's data show that EN3288 is crush resistant compared with
the old OPANA ER by objective measures of mechanical resistance—there is no controversy about that. The clinical
relevance of the crush-resistance is what is uncertain, but no claims about that are made in this abstract. Merely saying
"crush resistant" makes no more claim of clinical relevance than saying (for example) that the tablet color is different.
Rob

Hi Ladies,
Let us know if you would prefer to have an MSL/medical lead contact this physician. Otherwise, we have the attached
previous OOS and poster that should help.
Proposed Verbal Response:
Provide general recommendations below (not specific to Opana ER) from American Pain Society (APS) guidelines for use of
opioids for chronic noncancer pain (Chou R, Fanciullo GJ, Fine PG, et al. Clinical guidelines for the use of chronic opioid therapy
in chronic noncancer pain. J Pain 2009;10:113-130.):
"Theoretically, opioids have no maximum or ceiling dose, but there is little evidence to guide safe and effective prescribing at
higher doses and there is no standardized definition for what constitutes a "high" dose. By panel consensus, a reasonable
definition for high dose opioid therapy is >200 mg daily of oral morphine (or equivalent), based on maximum opioid doses studied
in randomized trials and average opioid doses observed in observational studies.
When opioid doses reach 200 mg daily of morphine (or equivalent), more frequent and intense monitoring is often appropriate, to
sufficiently inform the decision to continue therapy or consider additional dose escalations."
Refer the MD to the Conversion Ratios table (sec 2.1) in the Opana ER PI; the oral conversion ratio from morphine to
oxymorphone is 0.333 (e.g., 40 mg oxymorphone/day = 120 mg morphine equivalent dose [MED]). Emphasize that there is
substantial inter-patient variability in the relative potency of different opioid drugs and formulations.

Endo conducted a post hoc analysis to describe the adverse event profile of high-dose oxymorphone
extended release using pooled patient data from 10 clinical trials in which oxymorphone extended release
was administered at doses ≥60 mg/d (equivalent to ≥180 mg/d morphine). Results from this analysis
described that these higher doses of oxymorphone ER did not appear to be associated with a marked
worsening of tolerability. (can provide poster [APS Poster_Opana ER tolerability at high doses.pdf] upon
request)
Let the MD know that "With pure opioid agonist analgesics, there is no defined maximum dose; the ceiling to analgesic
effectiveness is imposed only by side effects, the more serious of which may include somnolence and respiratory
depression." The approach for finding the appropriate dose of Opana ER for a patient is similar to that used for other opioids,
and is ultimately the clinician's decision.

Date:

Tuesday, November 19 2002 05:15 AM

Subject: RE: N1PC program in Minneapolis
From:

Kitlinski, Linda

To:

Shively, Scott <Shively.Scott@Endo.com >; Wickline, Ron <Wickline.Ron@Endo.com >; Ambrefe,
Joseph <Ambrefe.Joseph@Endo.com >;

CC:

Galer, Bradley <Galer.Bradley@Endo.com >; Tormo, Vin <Tormo.Vin@Endo.com >;
Guyz,
Appreciate your input, and I will pass it along to PPS.
A few things to keep in mind — (and two questions for Ron/Joe in paragraphs 4 & 5)
1) As with the promotional speakers bureau, some speakers are more dynamic and "engaging" than others, and
PPS does try to utilize those speakers who can deliver the most effective presentations. As you know, however,
we were asked to broaden and deepen the visiting faculty this year, and as such have had to expand beyond our
former first tier speakers.
As a well-known pain expert, Dr. Raja (who authored the recently published paper documenting the efficacy of
opioids for neuropathic pain vs tricyclics) is someone who will be asked by numerous institutions/organizations to
lecture on neuropathic pain. It therefore behooves us to assure he has access to the most recent information on
Endo's current and future analgesics, and we are working toward that by involving him with NIPC, and also by
considering him as a potential investigator for future studies.
Since this was Dr. Raja's first lecture with NIPC, it may be somewhat understandable that he was not as wellversed with the information as other speakers have become. (I remember attending Charles Argoff's first lecture,
which was far less than stellar, and look what he's become!!) Ill check with PPS to assure this did indeed occur
with Dr. Raja, but they speak with each faculty member after every lecture, to provide constructive feedback
based upon the evaluations received, and to assure that the faculty can continuously improve. (I do appreciate
your input, both on the presentation and the AN, and will relay it to PPS.)
While this in a CME program, and therefore Endo cannot approach Dr. Raja about what Lidoderm information he
presented in his lecture, we can assure that he acquires as much hands-on experience with the patch as possible
outside of the CME setting. Ron, do you know which representative covers Dr. Raja? Perhaps we could be sure
Dr. Raja is being called on regularly and sampled? I will also catch up with him at the Neuropathic Pain meeting if
he attends, but the local representative's ongoing calls will go a long way!!
2) With regards to the level of the information presented, how can we get the word out to the reps and DM's that
the NIPC programs are INTENTIONALLY geared to primary care? I'm not sure who "Betsy" is in the attached
email, but she refers to the program not being "geared enough to specialists." Could we perhaps reiterate with the
reps/DMs that these programs are not intended for specialists? Thanks!

As always, many thanks for your input and feedback — I apologize for the length of this message, but I did want to share the
background info on Dr. Raja so we can have a plan for moving forward with him, as well as with other new additions to the
visiting faculty. We have an excellent vehicle with the NIPC program, and we'll do everything possible to assure the best
outcomes with it! Thanks again, and talk to you soon!
Best,
Linda

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

 Original Message----From: Paige Bookholtz [mailto:paigebookholtz@peoplepc.com]
Sent: Wednesday, October 30, 2002 7:41 AM
To: Weisenberger,Stephanie
Subject: NIPC program
Steph,
Here is some feedback regarding the NIPC program held at the Ritz Carlton on
Thursday, October 24.
The turnout was pretty good, at 35 attendees.
The speaker seemed to be knowledgeable about neuropathic pain; and discussed it's origins, etc.
There was not much discussion about Lidoderm, and the way Dr's are using it to treat their patients neuropathic pain.
The Q&A was virtually non-existant because the Dr's left when the speaker concluded his presentation.
The content of the presentation seemed to be geared to general practitioners and may have seemed "elementary" to
the audience.
There were some AV problems and the speaker's microphone did'nt work well in certain areas of the room.
Thank-you
Paige

Steph,
I attended the NIPC dinner program on October 24th with the speaker from John Hopkins. My observations from the
program were that the speaker failed to engage the audience. One doctor at my table mentioned that he needed
some jokes to make the presentation a little more entertaining. Another mentioned that the speaker needed some
"eye candy". The acoustics in the room were not good. Sometimes the speaker could not be heard.
The program was not geared enough to specialists. The subject material was fairly basic. There were almost no
questions asked during Q & A because the speaker had not engaged the audience. He was sometimes difficult to
understand.

Betsy

Oxymorphone: Third Party Road Show
Oxymorphone Advocacy Recommendations FINAL.doc

All -As you know, we have been busy approaching key third-party groups regarding one-on-one meetings with Endo to further
introduce them to oxymorphone/SOAPP and discuss potential synergies to work together on the PR front. I have re-attached a
memo outlining our goals for the meetings for your reference. Following is an update on our progress, including tentative dates
for the meetings:
• American Pain Foundation (Baltimore, MD): Group is very interested in meeting with Endo and is available on June 9th
for a meeting at their headquarters in Baltimore. As of now, Debbie and Errol have openings on their calendars. Marie
and Marcia, please let us know if June 9th would work for you.
• American Society of Addiction Medicine (Chevy Chase, MD): Given its close proximity to the American Pain
Foundation, we recommend also meeting with this group on June 9th. As of now, the group is holding the day for us.
Debbie and Errol have openings on their calendars for this day. Marie and Frank, please let us know if this would
work for you.
• National Pain Foundation (Denver, CO): NPF is extremely excited to meet with Endo. As of now, we are tentatively
scheduled to meet with the group on June 23. Debbie and Marie currently have openings on their calendars. Carey and
Errol/Arnold, please let us know if this date would work for you.
• American Academy of Pain Medicine (Glenview, IL): The group is very interested in meeting with Endo and has
suggested June 8th for the meeting. The meeting would be at the group's offices in Glenview. So far, we confirmed that
Debbie, Arnold and Marie have openings on their calendars on June 8th. Vin, please let us know if this day would
work for you. (Of note, AAPM and APS share offices. While APS is not one of our target groups for the roadshow,
they are a key organization for us. We recommend also exploring a meeting with APS on June 8th, as we will already be
at their headquarters.)

While we have been working with Avis and team to secure schedules, please confirm these dates work for you, and we will
move forward arranging the meetings. We hope to have a representative from Marketing, Medical Affairs, Global Safety, CD&E
and C&W at all meetings. We look forward to meeting with these groups and identifying possible opportunities to work together
this year and beyond.
As always, please call me with any questions.
Best, Lauren

Hi Team,
Just wanted to let you all know that Endo is now a proud supporter of the State Pain Policy Advocacy Coalition
(SPPAC), a joint effort of the American Academy of Pain Management, the American Pain Foundation, and the
American Society for Pain Management Nursing.
These three national organizations have made a commitment to support State pain policy issues through this coalition,
which will be staffed out of the AAPM.
The mission of SPPAC is to counteract harmful legislation and regulations and effect positive pain policy on the state
level.
Once the coalition is developed more fully, I will share contact information, etc.
We look forward to this being a very productive partnership!
Please let me know if you have any questions.
Sincerely,
Cathy

Jai
Here's some interesting gossip. Medicare has apparently been conducting audits of pain practitioner practices in
Florida, and more recently New York, through consultants who get to keep 20% of the value of any fines they can get levied
against providers, and each violation, that is, each individual billing code error or unnecessary procedure, can be worth
$10,000, so the incentive is definitely there for these companies to go through promising physician records with a fine-toothed
comb. They apparently look for significant increases in Medicare billings or just high levels of reimbursement. In
conversation with someone who defends physicians against these charges, I learned that practitioners who do, for example,
repeated injections with no documentation of improvement in patient status or otherwise continue to charge for therapies with no
demonstrable efficacy are at risk for fines that can accumulate into the hundreds or thousands of dollars. I don't know if these
audits are likely to be common over this way geographically, but they should provide additional incentive for physicians treating
pain to keep careful records with documentation like the four As (analgesia, adverse events, activities of daily living,
adherence to therapy) and not just for opioid therapy but all modalities, so I no longer think that opioid prescribing is putting an
additional burden on prescribers when it comes to record-keeping. And even if the practitioner isn't treating a lot of Medicare
patients, I see that the Internet is full of ads for companies who will conduct these audits for employers providing health
insurance (as well as law firms happy to take on physicians as clients in case of an audit.)
I don't think I mentioned in earlier c-mails that the American Society of Pain and the American Academy of Pain Medicine
have jointly released "Opioid Treatment Guidelines:
Use of Chronic Opioid Therapy in Chronic Non-Cancer Pain." Anyone can go to the APS website and download the publication,
and it is a clearly-written set of about 25 mostly strong recommendations, i.e. the benefit of the practice is felt to clearly outweigh
the risk. However, the evidence supporting most of the statements is weak, i.e. there are not well-conducted studies in each of the
areas discussed, which just emphasizes how thin the pain research is. A valiant effort, in any event.

Heather Thomson, MS
Clinical Affairs Manager

Chronic low back pain is among the most common chronic pain syndromes,

suffering and upset a person's life at home and on the job. The good news is
that a wide range of treatment options are readily available to successfully

Drug Enforcement Administration Rescinds its Endorsement

On October 6, 2004, the Pain and Policy Studies Group (PPSG) of the University
of Wisconsin Comprehensive Cancer Center announced that they had received a
letter, dated October 4, 2004, from the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA)
in which they were informed that the DEA had rescinded its endorsement of the

Decade of Pain Initiatives Improving Awareness of Pain-Care
Issues
After four years, the Decade of Pain Control and Research—mandated by
Congress in late 2000—has made important strides toward improving public
awareness of pain-care issues. Dennis C. Turk, PhD, president of the American
Pain Society, reported that chronic pain is still the nation's leading public health
problem and pain research remains woefully underfunded in the United States.
"Although the Decade of Pain has yielded beneficial achievements thus far, we
have a long way to go to achieve a meaningful level of public awareness about
pain and pain management to help shift the tide toward expanded pain research and
improved access to quality care," said Turk in his keynote address at the annual
convention of Partners for Understanding Pain. He spoke to this national patientadvocacy group on September 18, 2004, in Washington, DC. Jmorel

Management—An Evidence-Based Review." Jmorej

Subject: RE: Nat'l Chronic Pain Soc weekly radio show
Sensitivity: Private
Hi Folks,
Finally got to listen in to one of Helen's broadcasts today and thought I'd give you a "download" - I don't want to say that the
program was "bad" (it did have some redeeming aspects), but I would have some reservations regarding Endo getting involved
at anything more than a very minimal level...
Purdue is now a sponsor - their logo was prominently displayed and Helen read a blurb touting their "pioneering research" as
well as pitching "Partnering" Against Pain - of course, she meant to say Partners Against Pain.
Other sponsors are:
• PhRMA - which Helen specifically mentioned is "spelled p-h-a-r-m-a"(!). Their logo is HUGE and interestingly enough,
the link to their website when you click on their logo (you can't miss it) takes you to the Purdue website by mistake(!)
• Medtronic - logo prominently displayed but they weren't mentioned in the acknowledgments read by Helen at the start
of the show
• Dr. Keepers, MD - a Houston pain specialist (NCPS is based in Houston - if I had to guess, I'd bet that he's Helen's pain
physician)
Helen's definitely not the world's greatest moderator - she sounds a bit nervous, is not super adept at conversationalism, got
her facts wrong a number of times and had to be corrected by her guest.
Her guest today was a woman with chronic LBP, multiple failed back surgeries, and a recent diagnosis of breast cancer - her
story was truly an emotional one and, in addition to a very revealing discussion of how differently the healthcare system
perceived her cancer pain vs her chronic non-malignant pain, was what I considered to be the redeeming aspect of the show.
Commercials are interspersed every 15 min - they are repetitive to the point of being annoying...
• The same NCPS piece aired 3 times
• The same Medtronic piece aired 3 times - it was quite an interesting one - directing you to a "Certified Pain
Management Specialist" who can offer info on "new medical technology options" (gee, I wonder what those might
be?). Here's the kicker - they then give you MEDTRONIC'S phone number and ask you to call to find a pain
management specialist in your area (I wonder if any of them might know anything about interventional modalities?).
It would appear that the regulation of device manufacturer's advertising might be just slightly less rigorous than that
for pharmaceutical manufacturers!

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_SF-00354862

 • VoiceAmerica (the health channel that airs these pieces) did 3 different blurbs for 3 upcoming programs (one was
on "Body-Space Medicine - Alternatives to Expensive Drugs"!)
• VoiceAmerica also got in 6 additional brief self-promotional blurbs
There was some "doctor bashing" during the show (however, in this case it was justified). The "financial pain" of drugs was
also mentioned.
Being a webcast, the signal became "spotty" a number of times (maybe 4-6x) throughout the show - that was with my
broadband cable connection - I don't think I'd want to listen via a dial-up connection.
Over the course of the show Helen literally begged listeners to call in and ask questions of her guest. She only got one caller
(and it turned out that it was a good friend of Helen's!).
So there you have it (wordy and somewhat sarcastic, I know) - but I wanted you to have some background info before
forwarding the LOR on to Marketing.
PS - the website to listen to these programs (and tons of others) is - www.health.voiceamerica.com .

Opioid REMS in Practic_

to Measure Succe__

Class-wide opioid Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS)
are being developed federally to manage escalating prescription opioid
abuse while not hindering the provision of adequate pain control.
REMS endeavors to educate patients, prescribers, and pharmacists
and to implement opioid-prescribing surveillance, proper medication
disposal, and enforcement against any individuals who engage in
diversion or abuse.
This activity is available as a monograph.
x

Case-Based Considerations in Rheumatoid Arthritis Treatment
and Management
This video program features an illuminating interview between a
rheumatologist and his patient that focuses on applications of critical
decision-making factors in managing patients with rheumatoid arthritis
(RA). The captivating patient-clinician interview is followed by a short
evidence-based presentation in which a national leader in managed
care pharmacy summarizes findings from key RA clinical trials.
This activity is available as a multimedia presentation.

Acute Pericarditis (American College of Physicians PIER)
Substernal chest pain associated with acute pericarditis is typically
sudden, sharp or stabbing, radiating along the trapezius ridge, worse
with inspiration and lying flat, and alleviated with sitting and leading
forward. This activity will discuss how to diagnose acute pericarditis
using findings on the patient's history, physical examination, and ECG.

Subject: state pain policy action coalition

May 31, 2011
Dear Cathy Trzaskawka:
State-based public policy issues related to pain management have never been more widely and thoroughly debated than at
the present time. The development and implementation of rules for opioid therapy and the use of implanted devices in
Washington, attempts to control the proliferation of "pill mills" through legislation in Florida and elsewhere, and bills to
eliminate "fail-first" and step therapy protocols in a number of states are only the most recent and visible examples. National
pain management organizations have attempted to influence many of these issues, but often have done so in an ineffective
piecemeal and hit-or-miss fashion, failing to take advantage of opportunities to speak with one voice and achieve desired
outcomes. With the threat to the practice of pain management embodied in the current policy environment, it has never
been more important for advocates to take advantage of the synergy inherent in speaking with a united voice.
To that end, the American Academy of Pain Management, the American Pain Foundation, and the American Society for Pain
Management Nursing invite you to attend a meeting of industry representatives on June 22, 2011 from 2:00 PM to 4:30 PM in
the Marble Room of the Tremont Plaza Hotel in Baltimore, Maryland. The three organizations will present the outline of a
plan to begin creating a state pain policy action coalition involving their members and solicit comments from attendees about
that plan. We believe that such a coalition of our organizations will provide a synergy in terms of influence on state pain
policy, and also may present opportunities for some economies of scale. Your support in this effort is vital, and we welcome
your advice on issues related to the formation of this coalition.
Please respond to Staci Criswell at _Redacted _Privacy_; by the close of business on Friday, June 10, 2011, to reserve your seat at the
table. We are eager to discuss our plan with you and to take the next step in creating an effective action-oriented coalition to
insure the ability of our members to provide and receive optimal care for pain.

For the oxycodone testing, making sure oxymorphone was included in the analysis is a good point. The lab should

I have often seen cases of patients taking high doses of both hydrocodone and oxycodone having primarily

but it still may be worth checking into.

We have a 60 yo male
who is on high doses of oxycodone for pain control. The family
medicine doc gave him an immediate release dose of oxycodone 150mg (10 x 15mg tabs), and then
had a level drawn 1.5 hours after the dose. The level came back as 20ng/ml.
The lab is a drug analysis laboratory, that has a long history of excellent work, good
quality control.
So let us rule out the laboratory error stuff.
Micromedex states levels are 9 to 38ng/ml 1 hour after a 5mg immediate release dose.
No drug interactions/inducers/inhibitors present. No short bowel syndrome, no TPN.
Have any
of you had this experience? If so, would an extensive metabolizer do something to this
extent?
I've only worked on a couple of 2D6 extensive metabolizers...but I haven't observed
anything like this.

Hi Everyone,
I had a moment to take a look at a new leave behind for our OER targets, the Journal of the American Academy
of Pain Medicine, Volume 10 (Oxymorphone). While this is strictly a leave behind, to be left in the plastic
covering, it is very insightful for our own education and understanding. There are several articles that
comprise the journal with the focus being on Oxymorphone. The introduction is a nice overview of Opana ER
and oxymorphone pointing to the basic but key factors that differentiate OER such as delivery system and linear
pharmacokinetics.
The first article that is of interest is titled "Enteral Controlled-Release Opioid Delivery Systems" which is located
on page S30. It reviews the delivery systems of our competitors such as MSContin, Kadian, Avinza and
Oxycontin as well as OER and highlights the importance of the delivery systems while clearly describing the
pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of these agents.
The other article that I found enlightening is located on page S39, titled "Oxymorphone and Opioid Rotation."
The article states what we already know, "Owing to the vast variation in clinical responsiveness to opioids,
clinicians have observed that changing opioids can sometimes improve analgesia while simultaneously
reducing side effects." But, the article does continue to specifically address OER in opioid rotation and
strategies to allow for successful rotation. This can be very useful for a prescriber who has had some
challenges rotating and converting patients and highlights the lack of interaction with CYP450.
While this is a good review/reference for us, it is a great reference for our physicians and another tool that
brings additional value to our day to day interactions with providers. I hope this helps.
Rosalie

Dear Vicente,
'Tis the holiday season with so much to do and we bet at the top of your list is
planning which conferences to present at next year. Ho! Ho! Ho!
'Tho the holiday cheer is in the air, we must push forward with the serious
topic of opioid prescription. We invite you to submit your important
proposals for Papers, Posters, Presentations, Symposia and Corporate
Satellite Symposia for presentation at the 2016 International Conference On
Opioids (ICOO 12016), June 5-7, 2016 in Boston.

 Click here to submit your presentation.
Building on the success of our past conferences, this unique forum will be
comprised of renowned specialists in all aspects of opioids. This includes the
latest advances in basic science, neurology, clinical application,
pharmacology, pharmacogenetics, public health, opioid addiction, ethics,
legal and compliance. The program is designed to enlighten healthcare
providers with new data, essential information, and best practices every
medical professional needs to know when prescribing opioid analgesics.
The ICOO12016 Program Committee requests proposals representing all
areas of opioid research, treatment, ethics, opioid abuse and addiction.
Proposals from individuals and panels are accepted. Multidisciplinary panels
are encouraged to include perspectives from physicians, nurses,
psychologists, basic scientists, pharmacists, etc. Moderators should seek
participation from a varied group of faculty with a maximum of four
participants per proposal. Proposals that include both basic and clinical
science are encouraged.
The ICOO12016 Program Committee suggests the following partial list of
topics for submission:
* Translational Opioid & Pain Research
* Basic Science Research in Opioids and Opioid Pharmacology
* Current Topics on Opioid REMS
* Interventional Pain Management Opioid Techniques
* Inequalities in Pain Experience and Pain Management
* Clinical Practice Guidelines for Opioids
* Ethical Issues in the Use of Opioids
* Legal & Regulatory Issues of Prescribing Opioids
* Abuse and Addiction Issues and Opioids
* Pain Management for Cancer Survivors
* Opioids in Acute Pain
* Perioperative Pain Management
* Pharmacogenetics and Targeted Prescribing
* Pain Management in Opioid Addicted Patients
Proposals for previously presented or published work may not be submitted
to ICOO12016 without modification. Original work must be changed or
expanded, resulting in a new proposal.

information before January 2, 2016.
A complete proposal submission should include the following:

Subject: NY unanimously passes prescription drug monitoring/abuse legilsation with study language to examine use and
substitution of Tamper Resistant Opioid Formulations
Importance: High

Last night, the New York legislature unanimously passed the Attorney General's initiative, Internet System for
Tracking Over-Prescribing Act, or I-STOP.
The tamper resistant formulation study language is below. We believe this will enable us an opportunity to educate
the Commissioner of Health and Commissioner-appointed working group of health professionals on the important
role of tamper resistant opioids in appropriate treatment of pain.

(ii) No later than January first, two thousand thirteen, provide

outreach and assistance to health care professional organizations to
encourage and facilitate continuing medical education training programs
for their members regarding appropriate prescribing practices for the
best patient care and the risks associated with [prescription] overprescribing and underprescribing pain medication; [and]
(iii) Provide information to the commissioner for use in the development and continued update of the public awareness campaign, including
information, resources, and active web links that should be included on
the website[.]; and
(iv) Consider other issues deemed relevant by the commissioner,
including how to protect and promote the access of patients with a
HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL

EPI001919743

 legitimate need for controlled substances, particularly medications
needed for pain management by oncology patients, and whether and how to
encourage or require the use or substitution of opioid drugs that employ
tamper-resistance technology as a mechanism for reducing abuse and
diversion of opioid drugs.

The legislation does the following:
I-STOP will make New York the first state in the nation to mandate that physicians (or their
designee) consult a database of a patient's prescription history before prescribing a schedule II,
III, or IV controlled substance.
I-STOP will make New York the largest, and only second state in the nation, to require real-time
reporting by pharmacists when schedule II, III, IV or V prescriptions are filled.
I-STOP will make New York one of the first states to schedule the universal mandate of
e-prescribing for controlled substances in December of 2014. The regulations will be promulgated by
December 2012. This will nearly eliminate the problem of forged or stolen prescriptions—used both
by addicts, and criminal organizations obtaining pills to resell on the street.
I-STOP will reschedule hydrocodone to Schedule II, ending automatic refills for this abused drug.
I-STOP will schedule tramadol to Schedule IV (it is currently unscheduled).
I-STOP will require an unspecified amount of CME for prescribers of controlled substances.
I-STOP will establish a safe disposal program providing a place for New Yorkers to get rid of expired
and unneeded drugs to ensure that they are not left in medicine cabinets for children or addicts to
access.
I-STOP will also create a working group of medical professionals- pain treatment, addiction
treatment, etc who will advise the Health Commissioner to create CME, a public awareness campaign,
and medical awareness campaign.
The tamper resistant opioid study language is a huge step forward in New York toward raising awareness among
policy makers and medical professionals of their critical role in pain treatment and reducing abuse.
Thank you all for your support and guidance throughout the last year and a half. This was a team effort and

Casey Seiler, Capitol bureau chief HI Eric Schneiderman. Health Care

EPI001919744

 Not in Albany: Eric Schne derman. (Lori Van Buren/Times Union)
The prescription drug oversight legislation known as the Internet System for Tracking Over-Prescribing Act, or I-STOP, passed both houses
with ease this afternoon: 58-0 in the Senate; 116-0 in the Assembly.
The bill will result in a real-time database that gives physicians information on a patient's prescription history before prescribing the most
powerful and addictive drugs; will require pharmacists to provide information for that purpose; reclassify hydrocodone and tramadol to reflect
the risk of abuse that comes with their use; and kicks off the process to establish "e-prescribing" of controlled substances by the end of 2014
to prevent runaway prescription fraud.
The bill also establishes a safe drug disposal program for expired or unused medication.
The legislation has spent a long time near the top of Attorney General Eric Schneiderman's agenda. Nevertheless, the former Democratic
state senator chose not to be in Albany for the bill's passage. Spokeswoman Jennifer Givner had no explanation for the AG's latest display of

January 28, 2011

News for the biotech, medical device, drug and food regulatory profession

Drugs & Biologics i

■ Lobbyists, GOP push to ditch Medicare advisory board
The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, the American Medical Association
and the American Hospital Association, among others, are lobbying Congress to weaken or cancel
the Medicare Independent Payment Advisory Board created under the PPACA to rein in costs. The
House will attempt this year to repeal the relevant provision, an aide said, with some Democrats
expected to support the repeal. Kaiser Health News/The Politico (Washingtoa, D.C.) (1/26)
x

■ Expert proposes regulatory measures for biosimilars
James Sykes, The AIDS Institute's director of global policy, lists in this blog post
recommendations for the FDA in implementing a pathway for the approval and marketing of
biosimilars. "Biosimilars must not be treated like traditional generic drugs," he writes. The
Hill/Congress Bloq (1/26)

■ Senators reintroduce pay-for-delay bill
Sens. Herb Kohl, D-Wis., and Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, reintroduced a bill to restrict deals
between brand-name and generic drugmakers that critics say keep lower-cost generics off the
market. "It is past time to put an end to these backroom deals and pass this bipartisan
legislation," Kohl said. Pharmalot.com (1/26)

■ FDA accepts King's resubmission of painkiller Remoxy
The FDA accepted King Pharmaceuticals' second marketing application for pain medicine
Remoxy, or oxycodone. The controlled-release drug, co-developed by Pain Therapeutics, is made
using a drug-delivery technology from Durect. Drug Store News (1/27) x

Baxter is warned about violations at 2 Puerto Rico plants
Baxter International received a warning letter from the FDA regarding violations at two
manufacturing plants in Puerto Rico. The issues have not caused serious adverse effects, a
spokeswoman said. "Baxter continues to manufacture the products referenced, which continue to
be safe and effective if used in accordance with the labeled instructions," she said.
Bloomberg/The Associated Press (1/27)

■ Arena will cut 66 jobs to pursue regulatory approval of lorcaserin
Arena Pharmaceuticals plans to reduce its workforce by about 25%, or 66 positions, to conserve
cash and focus on resubmitting weight-loss drug lorcaserin for FDA approval. Arena expects to

for Provider Education. Dr. Grichnik is in charge of this effort. As we discussed the general aspects and features of the LAO

want to get in touch with you a bit further down the road to discuss whether longer-term outcomes studies have been
considered as yet within the REMS program development task force and/or by FDA personnel focusing on the LAO REMS. Any

Bruce
Thank you for the opportunity to review the VHA 2009 Pain Directive and to offer my thoughts
regarding clinical support for Endo's approach.
Highlights from the Guidelines:
• The VHA Pain Management Directive 2009 outlines various Performance Expectations at
all levels of the health system, from the top levels on out to the regional VISN affiliates
• Primary care providers must have access to pain consultative and treatment sources
• At the VISN level, Point of Contact responsibilities, and Multidisciplinary Pain committees
are to be established
• Each VISN by 2014 to have an accredited tertiary care interdisciplinary pain care program
• Each VHA medical facility to are to utilize published clinical practice guidelines and pain
management protocols (available on the VHA Pain Management website)
• "Effective pain management often requires consideration of the use of one or more of
several different classes of medications and other treatment modalities prescribed
simultaneously. "
• Patients with TBI are specifically mentioned as meriting consideration
• Special attention to Risks including adverse side effects of these medications, development
of addiction, and risks to the public through diversion of prescribed medications
• Written opioid pain care agreement is strongly encouraged between provider and patient
• Quality of pain assessment and effectiveness of pain management interventions must be
monitored (including medication safety)
Opportunities for possible discussion, collaboration with the VHA:

Have you seen this? Is this separate from the RPC??
Assessments of a novel Continuing Medical Education (CME) initiative showed meaningful changes in opioid prescribing behavior and improvements in
pain-patient outcomes. These assessments of REMEDIES (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies — An Employer-Driven CME Initiative for Efficacy and
Safety) — were presented this past week at PAIN-Week, the nation's largest conference for clinicians with an interest in pain management.
Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals (NYSE: MNK) provided the regulatory framework for and served as the sole funder of this continuing medical education
(CME) initiative_ which trains prescribers on evidence-based approaches to optimize the evaluation, treatment and management of chronic pain. Opioid
analgesics are a class of prescription medications intended to treat chronic pain_ but they have a significant potential for abuse.
The REMEDIES program was developed to meet the goals of the class-wide Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) for extended-release and
long-acting opioid analgesics, as required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration
"REMEDIES is a novel educational platform for prescribers and is intended to improve the quality of care for opioid-tolerant pain patients:" said Van Vette_
President of Applied Clinical Education, a medical education company with 20 years of programming experience in the area of pain management. "The key
factor that differentiates REMEDIES from other CME programs is an intensive assessment that measures changes in prescribing behavior and improvements
in patient outcomes."
The REMEDIES initiative was jointly provided by Global Education Group. an Accreditation Council for Continuing Medical Education
(ACCME)-accredited provider_ with commendation_ and Applied Clinical Education.
"As a leader in prescription pain medicine. Mallinckrodt is committed to supporting programs that educate and encourage behavioral changes for health
providers and patients to ensure that analgesic opioid use is beneficial_ not harmful_ to people in need of pain relief" said Mario Saltarelli. MD_ Chief Science
Officer. Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals. "This report confirms that practical and engaging content_ conveyed through a blend of learning methods_ has a
measurable impact as gauged by positive participant feedback and observed behavioral changes in opioid analgesic prescribing practices and use."
The REMEDIES curriculum incorporates a variety of tools that include live symposia_ interactive web-based activities_ a three-stage performance
improvement program_ and a series of three patient screening and education activities that help healthcare providers navigate the clinical challenge of opioid
prescribing.

 Key Learnings From Pilot
We identified early on as a district that our biggest challenge was gaining subsequent scripts after
the initial prescription. We have felt that this challenge is due to 2 main areas:
Lack of Sufficient Education of Prescribers
o Initiation of Opana ER therapy
o Proper titration
o Setting realistic patient expectations
Patient Profiling/Identification thru Managed Care opportunities
We have employed the following tactics to overcome these challenges:
Speaker Programs & KOL Involvement
o We have went "back to the basics" with prescribers getting them to attend educational
speaker programs that specifically cover these areas
o We conducted 6 Opana ER Speaker programs during the pilot period (8/20, 9/14, 9/16, 10/21,
10/22, 10/24)
Assisting HCP's to identify patients thru Managed Care opportunities has been best addressed
at the individual physician level
o For the most part, HCP's don't want to single out patients by plans - they just want overall
ease of writing within their opioid patient population
o We are identifying patients by either Med D opportunities (elderly patients in need of
long-acting opioid therapy) or younger patient populations (commercial plans, Tricare,
Workman's Comp patients in need of long-acting opioid therapy)
o We initiated 1 Specialty-Pharma KOL Managed Care dinner with Joe Sirna

Sent:

Subject:

North Central Region Task Force RE: Medicaid and Health Reform Scorebook Updates

From:

Knuth, Jennifer <JKnuth©phrma.org>

Redline- State-Specific Medicaid Scorebook 03-23-12.PDF; Redline- State-Specific Health Reform
Attachments: Scorebook 03-23-12.PDF; State-Specific Medicaid Scorebook 3_23_12.DOC; State-Specific Health
Reform Scorebook 3_23_12.DOC
To: North Central Regional Task Force Members
From: Linda Carroll-Shern
Fyi.
Attached please find the State Medicaid Scorebook and the State Health Reform Scorebook, as well as redlines illustrating
information that we have received or identified since these documents were last circulated on March 9, 2012.
In addition, below are several updates regarding health reform, including in particular the health reform litigation, which will
be heard by the Supreme Court at the beginning of next week. Other health reform updates include updates related to health
insurance exchanges, other consumer protection aspects of the health reform law, and efforts to reform Medicare and
Medicaid. There are also several updates related to Medicaid, including the health reform law's expansion of Medicaid
eligibility and the dual-eligible insurance market.

Health Reform Litigation
• In anticipation of the oral arguments to be held before the Supreme Court next week regarding the
constitutionality of the Affordable Care Act, there has been significant press coverage about the issues presented, the
positions articulated by both sides, the industry and consumer groups that support each side, the lawyers appearing
on behalf of each side, and the legal and political consequences of the Supreme Court's decision. A brief summary of
the schedule of the argument by issue is included below:
o Monday March 26:
■ Whether the Anti-Injunction Act bars a challenge to the law's individual mandate (90 minutes)
o Tuesday March 27:
■ Whether the law's individual mandate that requires the purchase of health insurance is
constitutional (2 hours)
o Wednesday March 28:
■ Whether the law's Medicaid expansion is constitutional (1 hour)
■ If the individual mandate is ruled to be unconstitutional, whether it is severable from the rest of the
law (90 minutes)
o The Supreme Court has promised that it will make audio recordings of the oral arguments available to the
public by 2 pm each day.
Health Insurance Exchanges
• The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued its final rule —more than 600 pages long—regarding
the implementation of state health insurance exchanges. The Obama Administration stated that the rule is designed
to give state officials broad discretion to decide the operational details of the exchanges, such as the freedom to
choose to run an exchange through an existing state agency or through a nonprofit entity established by the state, to
allow larger employers to participate, and to decide what role agents and brokers should have in selling insurance
through an exchange. However, HHS officials also noted that the federal government would set up and operate an
exchange in any state that refused to do so. A fact sheet about the rule is available here:
http://www.healthcare.gov/news/factsheets/2011/07/exchanges07112011a.html
Health Reform Consumer Protection
• The Commonwealth Fund issued a new report finding that 49 states have taken at least some action to implement
some of the consumer protection elements of the Affordable Care Act, such as prohibiting lifetime limits on coverage,
requiring plans to cover young adults on their parents' coverage and requiring preventive care without cost-sharing,
among others. A copy of the report is available at:
http://www.common. alt''f.J1d.orgt-/media/Files/Publications/Issue%20Brief/2012/Mar/1586 Keith state action early market reforms v2.pdf
•
A Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) report cautioned that in a "worstcase scenario" as many as 20 million Americans could lose employer-based healthcare coverage as a result of
President Obama's healthcare reform law, as employers might drop their coverage and send their employee to the
individual insurance exchanges. Employer-sponsored health insurance has already declined since 2007 as a result of

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07359676

 the weak economy. The report also found that fewer people than previously projected are expected to receive health
insurance coverage through insurance exchanges, and more are expected to receive coverage from Medicaid and the
Children's Health Insurance Program.
• The Department of Health and Human Services' (HHS) Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight
Director Steve Larsen found that two insurers—the John Alden Life Insurance Company and Time Insurance
Company—proposed "unreasonable" health insurance premium rate increases and called on the companies to
rescind those rates.
Medicare & Medicaid
•
On March 22, 2012, the House passed a bill repealing the Medicare Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB)
established under the health reform law to help control Medicare costs. The bill is not expected to pass the Senate.
• Republican Representative Paul Ryan introduced a budget proposal to reduce federal government spending by $5
trillion over 10 years, which calls for the repeal of the health reform law and includes proposals to dramatically
overhaul both Medicare and Medicaid. Although the proposal differs in some respects from the controversial
Medicare reform proposal Rep. Ryan introduced last year, the budget proposal still plans to achieve savings through
partial privatization of Medicare, in which government subsidizes purchases of health insurance on the private
market. The budget also proposes to transform Medicaid into a federal block grant program.
•
Meanwhile, insidehealthpolicy.com reports that a House GOP budget proposal would keep in place the health
reform law's $500 billion in Medicare savings, gleaned through major cuts to health care providers and insurers, but
repeal the law's health insurance subsidies to individuals in the exchanges and the Medicaid expansion provisions.
•
HHS issued its final rule implementing the Medicaid eligibility expansion (to individuals not already eligible for
Medicaid with incomes at 133% of the federal poverty level) required under the Affordable Care Act starting in
January 2014. The rule also contains numerous provisions designed to ease the application and eligibility renewal
process for the program, including a modernization of eligibility verification rules to rely primarily on electronic data
sources and streamlining the systems for processing Medicaid and CHIP applications.
• Forbes magazine reported that a new paper in the Health Services Research journal concludes that expanding
Medicaid may actually reduce access to care because Medicaid reimbursement is too low and many physicians opt
not to take Medicaid patients.
Dual-Eligibles
• Dow Jones Newswires reported that major health insurers, including potentially companies such as UnitedHealth
Group Inc., Molina Healthcare Inc., WellPoint Inc., and Amerigroup Corp, are preparing to target the MedicareMedicaid dual eligible patient market, touting their abilities to better manage the care for the very sick, very poor
population. Consumer advocate groups expressed concern about pushing dual-eligibles into managed care and
expressed doubts about whether these companies could in fact offer more proactive, higher quality care.
Prescription Drugs
• The Senate Finance Committee Subcommittee on Health held a hearing on March 22, 2012 about how Medicare
and Medicaid programs are working to combat the problems of prescription drug abuse, particularly of opioids.

Robert,
Not to worry, I haven't made any commitments or even "quasi-commitments," I was just letting you know what
my thinking was at the present time so you would know I did have a plan (albeit one we still need to discuss).
I have a suggestion, since I agree with you that this requires face-to-face discussion in early Jan. (And since I
don't want to consume your entire vacation with email correspondence!!)
1) I will ask Jackie/Tina to get time scheduled on the calendar for early Jan
2) In the interim, I will send Demir the "what we will be doing" part of the Clin Aff top 3 objectives, but will
not insert any "numbers." I will let him know the numbers will be inserted following the discussion you/I have
scheduled in early January.
This way we can address this in a systematic way... That sound OK to you?

Linda

on migraine while CL positions in the field go unfilled. We need to discuss this.
I am happy to hear that we have CL candidate. Unless they have a PharmD and some relevant CL experience,
would like to review the CV and discuss the candidates before hiring. There is a clear and defining business
need to have PharmDs in most, if not all, of these open slots. Please keep this in mind as you review potential
candidates.
Looks like you and I need some time in early January.
Best
Robert

* Elizabeth - who would cover the mid-Atlantic area plus the nat'l prof societies & also handle the
development/coordinate the implementation of the strategic/tactical plans for migraine.
* 3 regionally-based liaisons (aligned geographically to the key therapeutic experts/headache centers of
excellence, provided we don't already have an existing CL in that same geopgraphy). This will still involve a
lot of travel, but it will be manageable and consistent with the business needs.
Again, we can work out the details once we get final approval of the headcount, but this is what I will base this
round of "objectives" on, and we can adjust if needed.
With regards to a hiring plan... already in the works...
* 2 promising candidates from internal CL referrals (interviews in Jan); 1-2 other internal referrals possible
(awaiting CV's)
* 3 referrals from Field Sales Mgmt; phone interviews already conducted; live interviews in Jan
* 1 promising in-house CME candidate (awaiting call back regarding interview date)

promising candidate out of the 2)

Linda

The organization of our resources are our issue. We must be aligned with corporate goals. That being said, there
is a real interest in having regionally deployed CLs. Therefore, I would keep any "specialty" small at this point
and we can reconsider it size and scope as we hire the new CLs. The most important activity is to have a hiring
plan with HR to bring these new folks on in the 1-2Q07. Absent a plan, we may have openings all year and
never achieve the regional coverage envisioned.

Compensation Advisory Board

Ellen,
I wanted to thank you for selecting me to serve on the Compensation Advisory Board and give you a brief update.
Prior to our initial conference call with the Towers Perrin group, I sent a voicemail out to about 65 of my friends across Endo.
The end result was conversations with about 40 of them and emails from another 8-10. All identities were promised to be
kept anonymous.
As you know, this is a topic full of passion and opinions. My intent was to harvest from that group their primary concerns and
ideas.
The discussions centered along the following points:
1. Base salary is an issue for established, tenured representatives on the Specialty side. Some new Pharma hires are
being paid more than long term Specialty reps that have been productive for years. This is a serious issue.
2. Bonus structure: The perception is that the current system rewards growth and does not include contribution as part
of the bonus structure. There is perceived and evidence of inequity in the payouts. The dissension seems to be not so
much with the goal setting, but the lack of credit for the effort required to maintain the higher volumes. Total
contribution needs to be part of the equation. If it is currently, it is not being explained or understood.
3. Recognition: The recognition programs are too narrow. They need to be broadened and include recognition for
contribution, RX or $. This is not about straight cash but more along the lines of simply being recognized and feeling
appreciated.
4. Cell phones and internet. We are addressing the internet. Almost every rep is getting killed on their cell phone
charges. The under current is one nearing oppression. The sentiment is that we have ample cash and need to cover
the cost of doing business. Other companies range from direct billing of cell phones to fixed amounts of $100 to $175
per month.
5. Differentiation between Pharma and Specialty. There is a narrowing and blurring of the lines between Specialty
and Pharma with bonus and salary. Pharma reps can make more bonus with a volume that is much smaller than the
Specialty reps. Many Specialty reps see that their contributions can be multiples of their Pharma partners but the
bonus is on par.
6. Bring back the Fun! Many mentioned how much they enjoyed contests. By contests they do not mean the ones
which are narrow in the number of winners but ones like the Tsunami Launch for Percocet 325. This contest enabled
many of us to win points each month depending on announced criteria and rankings. Hundreds won points that could
be exchanged for internet catalogue items including gift cards, TV's and other prizes. The contest was structured so
that there were two big prizes, a BMW for a year, but more importantly, a very broad opportunity for many to win and
accumulate points. It made a positive difference and drove a lot of business.
7. District Level Monthly Contests: Another suggestion was for monthly contests at a District level. Empower the local
DM's to set the criteria and award the prizes or points toward prizes or even time off with pay.
8. The Presidents Club: This is perceived as a lucky combination of timing and goals. Again, it is way too narrow in
scope and not seen as obtainable by most reps. The trip is great if it works for you, but few really see that they have
a viable chance to win. Also, a simpler trip or get away weekend might be nice for the Top 20. It is not a positive
incentive.
There was an abundance of other ideas and issues. In the interest of brevity, I will limit this note to those above.
Please understand that I have a great deal of passion about making ENDO a better place to be. I bring to the table the
unusual combination of having been in field operations in home office and a current field prospective. I came to ENDO to
build a culture and great work environment.
When asked about his tremendous success as CEO of Coca Cola, Roberto C. Goizueta, said the success was the
result of the following attitude: "At the end of every day of every year two things remain unshakable; Our constancy of

 purpose and our continuous discontent with the immediate present."
A little healthy discontent is a good thing.
I am concerned that the Advisory Board is a single meeting event as the consultants did not seem to know if we would
meet again.
Please keep me involved with this issue. I want to help make ENDO a better place to be.
Together, we are working to build a better ENDO.

Date:
Subject:
From:

Friday, September 29 2017 01:09 PM
FDA Takes Important Steps to Stem the Tide of Opioid Misuse and Abuse
Middleton, Rosanne
To:
Chapman, Tara <Chapman.Tara@Endo.com >; Rotman, Harris <Rotman.Harris@endo.com >;
Attachments: image001.gif; image002.png
https://blogs.fda.gov/fdavoice/index.php/2017/09/fda- takes-important-steps- to-stem-the-tide-of-opioidmisuse-and-abuse/
FDA Voice Blob from Scott Gottlieb
America is awash in immediate-release (IR) opioids. About 90 percent of all opioid pain medications prescribed —or
160 million prescriptions a year —are for IR formulations like hydrocodone and acetaminophen or oxycodone and
acetaminophen combinations. Many people who are currently addicted to opioids became medically addicted. Their
first exposure to opioids was from a legal prescription, and for many, that prescription was written for an IR formulation
of these drugs. Many addicted patients may then move on to higher dose formulations or more accessible illegal street
drugs.
At FDA, we believe it's necessary to continue to take steps to address both ends of this continuum, the potential
gateway to addiction that is often the IR formulations, and the higher dose, extended-release formulations, both of
which carry a significant risk of overdose and mortality. We are taking several actions to address these challenges.
This week, we issued letters notifying 74 manufacturers of IR opioid analgesics intended for use in the outpatient
setting that their drugs will now be subject to a more stringent set of requirements under a Risk Evaluation and
Mitigation Strategy (REMS). The REMS requires that training be made available to health care providers who
prescribe IR opioids, including training on safe prescribing practices and consideration of non-opioid alternatives.
FDA also will soon issue a final guidance document that will assist potential applicants who plan to develop, and
submit to FDA, an application to seek approval of a generic version of abuse-deterrent formulations (ADFs) of opioid
drugs. Most of the currently approved opioids with labeling describing abuse-deterrent properties are extended
release/long-acting (ER/LA) formulations of opioids. These drugs are generally formulated to be more resistant to the
sort of manipulation that would otherwise make them amenable to snorting and/or injecting. Addicted patients who
start by using the IR drugs will sometimes migrate onto the ER/LA formulations, and then try to manipulate those
higher-dose formulations in ways that can provide a more immediate "high" through injection or snorting. But there are
currently only brand name ADF formulations. These steps that FDA is taking are aimed at addressing each end of the
spectrum of abuse and addiction.
With respect to the new REMS measures to address the safer use of the IR opioid pain medications, these short-acting
drugs will now be subject to the same regulatory requirements as the ER/LA opioid analgesic formulations. Since
2012, manufacturers of ER/LA opioid analgesics have been subject to a REMS, which requires, as its primary
component, that training be made available to prescribers of those products. To meet this requirement, the sponsors of
the ER/LA opioid analgesics have been providing unrestricted grants to accredited continuing education providers for
the development of education courses for health care professionals based on content outlined by FDA, which the
agency calls the "Blueprint." FDA is now extending these REMS requirements to the IR manufacturers.
While some of the ER/LA manufacturers also make IR opioids, today's action will greatly expand the number of
products covered by the REMS. The existing REMS currently includes 64 ER/LA opioid analgesic products. Once the
action is finalized, an additional 277 IR opioid analgesics will be subject to these REMS requirements.
In addition to expanding the REMS to include IR products, FDA is modifying the content of the educational "Blueprint"

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_ANK_CHI_0192922

 required under the REMS. The agency is adding content on pain management, including non-opioid alternatives. This
includes principles related to the acute and chronic pain management; non-pharmacologic treatments for pain; and
pharmacologic treatments for pain (both non-opioid analgesic and opioid analgesic). The revised Blueprint will also
cover information about the safe use of opioids, and basic information about addiction medicine and opioid use
disorders.
For the first time, this training will also be made available to other health care professionals who are involved in the
management of patients with pain, including nurses and pharmacists, which is in addition to prescribers of opioid
analgesics. FDA believes that all health care professionals involved in the management of patients with pain should
be educated about the safe use of opioids so that when they write or dispense a prescription for an opioid analgesic, or
monitor patients receiving an opioid analgesic, they can help ensure that the product is properly indicated for the
patient and used under appropriate clinical care.
FDA's new Opioid Policy Steering Committee is also considering whether there are circumstances when FDA should
require some form of mandatory education for health care professionals, and how the agency would pursue such a
goal. The agency's purpose is to reduce overall exposure to opioids by making certain that prescribing doctors are
properly informed about appropriate prescribing recommendations, that providers understand how to identify the risk
of abuse in individual patients, and know how to get addicted patients into treatment. In fact, today, the agency issued
a public notice to solicit input on a detailed series of questions related to these goals. FDA has also been scheduling
meetings with provider organizations and sponsors engaged in dispensing drugs — including health systems and
pharmacy chains, in an effort to solicit additional input on new strategies.
Sending out the manufacturer notification letters is the first step in extending the REMS to the IR drugs. This process
could take about a year to finalize. The modified REMS will continue to include a requirement for patient Medication
Guides, patient-counseling documents, and plans for assessing the effectiveness of the revised REMS. The crisis of
opioid addiction is a public health tragedy of enormous proportions. By putting in place safety measures for IR opioid
analgesics, and creating a more robust path to converting the high dose opioids to formulations that are more resistant
to manipulation, we are addressing both ends of this crisis. Our hope is that we can help prevent new patients from
becoming addicted, and keep some individuals from experiencing the serious adverse effects associated with these
medications.

RE: Conference call follow-up notes

Hey Tom,
Finally out of bed today (Sunday). Thanks for the notes of the conference call and I'll be back on the road on Monday. It
has been a tuff few days with a bad stomach virus. I am feeling much better now and I apologize I missed the conference
call.
Matt

From: Lennox, Thomas
Sent: Friday, October 06, 2006 3:55 PM
To: Cantrell, Douglas; Desai,Sudir; FigureIli,Robert; Giordano,Matthew; Lupisella,Phyllis; Muldowney,Thomas; Naser,Carl
Cc: Darling, Valerie
Subject: Conference call follow-up notes
Team,
Thanks for your participation on the conference call today. We didn't have as many successes to share today, as compared
to most weeks. I challenge each of you to find a success each and every day. Remember to celebrate the small wins, as
the big ones don't come along every day.
• Synera is really beginning to gain some substantial traction nationally. Weekly sales doubled last week. The trend is
very encouraging. In addition, the following significant national accounts approved Synera for formulary. You should
use these accounts to leverage your accounts. After all, if it's good for these accounts, it must be good for yours.
We've got to push, pull, grab and drag through the sales in your accounts.
o San Diego Children's Hospital
o Stanford
o St. Jude's
o Arkansas Children's Hospital
o Boston Children's Hospital
• Spend time with your key influencers who can make decisions. Hold their hands the whole way through the process &
hold them to their commitments. We have a lot of formulary reviews coming up. We need to execute on them now,
so that we can pull it through during November & December! Lets maintain or improve our national standing with
DepoDur sales.
• Tom Muldowney shared his success this week with getting to the QA/QI folks at Children's of Buffalo & Golisano
Children's. According to him, there was strong interest in their pain initiative & selling these folks will really help to
overcome pharmacy
• Phyllis shared her experiences:
o She & Doug displayed at the CLS convention & got many good leads out of it for their territories. I encourage
you to find your local chapters & display at their events.
o Phyllis shared a success story of a patient who was going to have to discontinue chemo, because they couldn't
get her veins. They gave Synera a shot & it really helped get the vein. Now she's working to get Synera
approved for all patients in the infusion center. Nice job Phyllis!
• There are still available slots for the Meet the Experts dinner @ the ASA. Please continue to drive attendance to this
vital meeting. The speakers can discuss all aspects of DepoDur and can really help reinforce your selling efforts. To
date, we have 2 territories participating. Please drive attendees from your territory. I'd like to see all territories
represented.
• There will be another visiting professorship program upcoming for DepoDur. This one will be at Thomas Jefferson in
Philly, on November 6-7. More details will follow, however this program is a perfect place to send someone from an
account that is ready to break open. These accounts should include the following as targets: Metro West (Arkoff or
Lewis), Roger Williams, Kent, Mid State (CT), Danbury, Winthrop, S. Nassau, LIJ, St. Lukes/Roosevelt(Me), Sisters
HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - ATTORNEYS EYES ONLY INFORMATION

ENDO-NY-00071470

 (Buffalo), MF Suburban, St. Barnabas (NJ). If we can get a few attendees, it can make all the difference in the
world, in terms of vial usage.
• Speaker program budget — we were allotted another $35k, giving us about $80k left. We have some spoken for, but
we have to drive programs into all accounts where DepoDur is about to begin. This should include all of the accounts
mentioned in the previous bullet, and any others where we need a bump in the business. It is expected that all of you
will have programs on the books by the end of next week
o Good speakers include Koncelik, Gerancher, Martin, Abrams, Grant, Hutchinson, Rosenfeld (hot & cold, iffy) —
get `em booked!
o Wrap programs across 2 or more days, to include round tables, VPs, non-CME Grand rounds, etc. Call Matt
& see what he did w/ Dr. Hutchinson. His turnout for his programs was phenomenal! Way to go Matt!
• Opana ER — we need to continue to leverage accounts where we have users. This means that you need to continue
to coordinate w/ your Specialty & Pharma counterparts to identify early adoptors. Your most likely accounts will
revolve around them. Get them to submit the requests & leverage the pain management teams, appropriate
surgeons, HEM/ONCs & appropriate anesthesiologists to support the review. As we anticipate increased selling time
in 2007 for Opana & Opana ER, it's vital that you set the stage early & effectively to drive for results now. In the end,
if you accomplish this, you'll maximize your MBO earning potential.
Thanks again for your participation! I know it's tough out there, but everyone is making a difference. Keep the faith. It's
beginning to happen.
Have a great weekend.
Best,
Tom Lennox
District Manager-Northeast
Hospital Division
