July 2004 Oxymorphone Update
• Convened two managed care advisory meetings - one East coast group (July 12) and a second
comprised of MCO's from the West coast (July 25). The group from the East coast was
very receptive to the Opana product concept and was optimistic that it would be put on
formulary. There was a great deal of dissatisfaction with Purdue among members of this
group. The West coast group was less receptive and claimed that they would need to see
some advantage over OxyContin to warrant placement on formulary. Price was the only way
to differentiate according to this group.
• Held speaker training session (July 18) with key Opana advocates - Chris Miaskowski,
Dermott Fitzgibbons, Charles Argoff, Perry Fine and Bob Dworkin - to enable them to
better present Opana data at advisory meetings, managed care presentations, CME
meetings, etc. Rollin Gallagher and Jim Cleary will be trained in one-on-one sessions due to
schedule conflicts on the 18th.
• FDA has still not rendered a decision on the trademark. Have been able to confirm with
Regulatory Affairs that we can manufacture injectible product and ship to another facility
to label and package at a later date, avoiding the issue of labeling 2004 supplies of
injectible as Numorphan.
• Held Hospital Pharmacy advisory meeting (July 11) to better understand the needs of this
group as we plan for relaunch of Opana injectible and introduction of IR and ER
formulations in the hospital setting. Science was not of primary interest, packaging was.
• Held two advisory meetings in Las Vegas July 24/26. Pain Management and Oncology
Nurses meeting takeaway was that these groups of nurses play not only a very critical role
in influencing the choice of drug treatment, but actually do a lot of the prescribing
themselves. They are also the critical link with the patient and have a lot of influence with
compliance and management of side effects. The PCP advisory meeting was most valuable
for contacts with two very influential editorial board members to the AAFP who may be
able to steer us through the landmines of getting posters accepted and manuscripts
published.

Mary Jo,
I hope this finds you well and enjoying the summer, despite the heat & humidity!!
As you may have read, after years of planning, the FDA approved the Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) for
Extended-release (ER) and Long-acting (LA) Opioid Analgesics on Monday of this week.
For the educational element of the REMS, the opioid analgesic manufacturers (REMS Program Companies [RPC]) will be
making available unrestricted educational grant funds to support accredited continuing education, which will be developed
by CE Providers based on the FDA Blueprint that was published as part of the REMS.
http://w,vw.fda.gov/downloads/Drugs/DrugSafety/InformationbyDrugClasqUCM27791.6.pdf )
The CE Sub-team of the RPC has drafted a Request for Grant Application (RFA) document, to help provide specifics for
educational providers wishing to submit grant application(s), as well as a Letter of Agreement (LOA), which incorporates both
the Standards of Commercial Support and the REMS specifications FDA is requiring of the RPC.
To assure that the educational grant process proceeds smoothly and without unanticipated delays/issues, we thought it
would be appropriate to seek a review of these drafts by the CE Accrediting Bodies prior to the RPC finalizing the documents.
We would very much appreciate if you, or a colleague from ANCC, could provide a courtesy review of these documents, and let
me know whether there are any concerns that we should be aware of/address.
If at all possible to receive any comments by noon on Monday, July 16 so that we can proceed with the final internal RPC
approvals, and then post the RFA, we would very much appreciate it. (Wherever possible, we tried to utilize the standard
language in the ACCME SCS sample LOA to minimize potential issues, however, we did have to insert some of the REMSspecific details that FDA is requiring of RPC).
Thank you in advance for your input/assistance — it is very much appreciated!

Cc: Jackson,Ronald
Subject: 2H08 Planning
Good afternoon — As we head into this Holiday weekend and start the second half semester, I wanted to give some
direction for business planning over the next couple of weeks. It goes well with the Mid Year Review and reflecting on
what do I keep and what do I change:
1. Print your new call plan and compare to first half call plan. Who is different besides the Rheums? What is their
potential based on call priority/decile? Who do I not see that expected to? How can I quickly qualify the new
adds?
2. In recent ride alongs we looked at calls made since Jan 1 to see where your time has been allocated. Was the
frequency in the right places? What were the results of high frequency? Did I have docs with too little frequency?
3. Look at your 2 week routing. Who are the new targets that will replace the Rheums? Do I have targets that no
longer need to be in my routing? Who needs adding to the Franchise targets as absolute see every week or 2
weeks? How is my 2 week routing going for days of the week to see docs, access, etc?
4. Where do I need to plan strategic breakfasts, lunches, and dinners? What targets do I need to get exposed to a
KOL?
5. Using May PTD and June Weekly, where did I finish in goal attainment for the first half for each product? Does my
focus need tweaking and do I have enough targets in my routing to accomplish my second half goals?
6. Looking at the 3 vs 3 Analytics File saved on my desktop — What key targets are up for last 3 months and what
targets are down? What the rolling 12 months for growth and loss?
7. What is the status of my key Opana ER targets in relation to 8 key messages, new MVA, Davis Reprint, MCO,
routing?
8. Do I have my MCO lists up to date and using them effectively for Aetna, Humana, United, Coventry,
CVS/Caremark, Tricare?
9. What selling skills do I need to use as strengths and which ones continue to develop?
10. What daily/weekly/monthly process can I do consistently to assure preparation, knowledge, and results from
every call?
This is meant to give thought to where changes or continuity might be needed. It will also help update our business plan
for the second half.
As we do your mid year review, we can discuss these questions and the thoughts you have toward success this semester.
Thank you for your daily focus.
Remember it is the sum of the parts - MDs to Territories, Territories to Districts, Districts to Regions, Regions to Divisions,
Divisions to Company.
Billy Roberts

Good Morning,

 In 2002, the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) issued its "Code on Interactions
with Healthcare Professionals" ("PhRMA Code"). At that time, Endo adopted this voluntary code and made it part
of our Company policies. The principles set forth in the PhRMA Code reaffirm that our interactions with
healthcare professionals should always be focused on providing information about the benefits and risks of our
products, providing scientific and educational information, and supporting medical research.
PhRMA and its member companies, including Endo, have revised and strengthened the PhRMA Code. The
PhRMA Board of Directors unanimously approved the revised PhRMA Code in June 2008. The revised PhRMA
Code is attached and becomes effective in January 2009.
Endo is committed to continued compliance with the PhRMA Code. By expressing our intent to follow the
revised PhRMA Code, we are signaling to our stakeholders our commitment to uphold the highest ethical and
professional standards relevant to interactions with healthcare professionals. We recognize that in order to help
advance patient care in America, it is essential that educational information about the benefits and risks of
medicines is responsibly conveyed to physicians.

Among its changes, the new Code:
• Prohibits distribution of non-educational items (such as pens, mugs and other "reminder" objects adorned with
a company or product logo) to healthcare providers and their staff, even if accompanied by patient or physician
educational materials. The Code acknowledges that such items, even if they are of minimal value, "may foster
misperceptions that company interactions with healthcare professionals are not based on informing them about
medical and scientific issues."
• Specifies that it is appropriate for companies to offer items intended primarily for the education of patients or
healthcare professionals if they are not of substantial value — $100 or less — and do not have value to a
healthcare provider beyond his or her professional responsibilities.
• Prohibits company sales representatives from providing restaurant meals to healthcare professionals, but
permits occasional, modest meals in a physician's office or hospital in conjunction with representatives'
informational presentations. The Code also reaffirms that companies cannot present any entertainment or
recreational benefits to healthcare professionals.
• Requires companies to ensure their representatives who visit healthcare professionals are sufficiently trained
about applicable laws, regulations and industry codes of practice — including this Code — that govern
interactions with healthcare professionals. Companies are also asked to assess their representatives periodically
and to take appropriate action if they fail to comply with relevant laws and standards of conduct.
• Provides that each company will state its intentions to abide by the Code and that company CEOs and
Compliance Officers will certify each year that they have processes in place to comply. In addition, the Code
encourages companies to get external verification of these processes periodically. PhRMA will post on its
website a list of all companies that announce their pledge to follow the Code, contact information for company
compliance officers, and information about the status of companies' annual certifications and/or external
verifications.
• Provides more detailed standards regarding pharmaceutical company support of continuing medical education
(CME). The revised Code specifies that company funding of CME should support education on a range of
treatment options rather than promoting a specific medicine; urges companies to separate CME grant-making
activities from its sales functions; and states that companies should not provide advice or guidance to CME
providers regarding the content or speakers at CME courses.
2

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-08207377

 • Provides principles on the responsible use of non-patient identified prescriber data, highlighting some of the
essential uses of such data, including communicating safety and risk information to prescribers of a particular
medicine.
Offers additional guidance for speaking and consulting arrangements with healthcare professionals, including
disclosure requirements for healthcare providers who are members of committees that set formularies or
develop clinical practice guidelines and who also serve as speakers or consultants for a pharmaceutical company.
I will be reaching out to many of you as we implement these changes. In the meantime, please contact me if you

Final minutes on the FDA and IWG teleconference that occurred on 7/14/11 from
3:30 to 4:30pm

These minutes are considered finalized. No additional comments were received.

FDA participants:
Jane Axelrod (Associate of drug policy and research),
Terry Toigo
Bob Rappaport,
Mary Willy,
Denise Hinton,
Patrick Frey,
Carla Cartwright:
FDA Office of Chief Counsel.
**John Jenkins was not be able to attend as he has a conflict.
The FDA started off the meeting reviewing their comments on questions that the IWG had submitted
to them.
July 6th questions

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06542928

 1. no further question
2. early next week they hope to get it to us — ie. Earlier than July 22
3. no further questions
4. no further questions
5. to be clear, we see that what you sent is an expanded outline and that the key messages still
need to be added. Permissible for IWG to develop some key messages — FDA conversation
with ACCME made it apparent that IWG developing key messages is ok. Suggested set up
call to pull FDA, ACCME and IWG together. Dr. Haddox asked for some examples from FDA
of key messages to make it clear what FDA is asking us to do. FDA agreed to provide some
examples.
6. no further questions
The IWG then proceeded to review the following questions that were submitted to the FDA earlier in
the morning on 7/14/11. A summary of the questions sent and their response is summarized below:
1. The IWG has actively engaged with the continuing education community to ensure that our
submission, if approved, will facilitate the development of relevant educational training content
that will encourage participation by the prescribing community. In feedback from accrediting
bodies, CE providers, and key opinion leaders who are engaged in continuing education for
health care professionals, the IWG has learned that those who are regularly involved in CE
believe that certified continuing educational activities that completely cover the Blueprint would
entail more than 10 hours, with some estimates being significantly longer. As you may be
aware, there have also been a number of surveys performed by various entities unrelated to
the IWG, comprising a sample of over 1000 prescribers. These surveys suggest that, as
educational time burden increases, the number of prescribers participating will
decrease. Further, they suggest that a significant number of prescribers may simply cease
prescribing the drug products subject to this REMS. The time burden that is acceptable to a
majority of survey respondents is in the range envisioned by FDA that was mentioned at our
May 16th meeting — "at least a couple of hours."
Clearly, in order for REMS-related education to have any favorable impact on the public health
issues in which we are all interested, there has to be uptake by the prescribers. Thus, IWG
intends to submit a modified Blueprint that is somewhat scaled back in scope from the first
draft, that would constitute what we propose as the "essential safety core" material from the
expanded Blueprint. We see this as the first step in prescriber training — a step that would be
both palatable to prescribers in terms of scope and time commitment and would provide
essential information that is likely to promote safer use of these medicines. This would be
followed by sequential educational activities that would be tailored to the individual needs and
circumstances of the prescriber as determined by the accredited CE providers.
Because this represents a change in our initial approach, the IWG would like to engage FDA in
a discussion of this approach, so that our submission can represent a common understanding
among all parties and facilitate FDA's review and approval of the REMS and its Supporting
Document.
FDA collaborate with liNG on this issue'? DH/SN
FDA comments:
Yes we will collaborate you with it on this. We have to define what "it" is before we can move
forward. We want to understand the depth of discussion /training and time it will take so we can
determine what is reasonable. So yes we will need to have a discussion on the level of training,
timing and content.
2

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06542929

 2. We are proposing to send out the Dear Prescriber letter after CE training is made available by
accredited providers. There will be a lead time prior to the first CE training therefore IWG
would like to provide the PMIS, PPA, and med guide in a manner that would allow easy access
to prescribers. In addition to the IWG website and other methods to make these documents
available, would FDA be amenable to providing the PMIS on their website immediately? SN
FDA comments:
When the REMS and appended material is approved it will be posted on the FDA website and we will
issue some sort of communication to the public informing them that they are available. We can
create links when the document is approved (safe use initiative web site) and will send it out to med
watch.
3. There are a number of terms that have very specific meaning to accredited CE providers and
CE accrediting bodies. To assure transparency and to remove the potential for
misinterpretation of what the REMS education will entail, IWG would propose that FDA & IWG
agree to use terminology in the REMS & REMS Supporting Document that will minimize the
potential for confusion & misinterpretation with the CE community & their learners. For
example, the term "training" has a different meaning than "education" in the adult education &
CE communities, and as such, the CE accrediting bodies have suggested, and IWG concurs,
that we utilize the term "education" to avoid the potential for confusion and misinterpretation.
The second example is the term Sponsor vs. NDA/ANDA holder. Is this acceptable to the
Agency? LK/SN
FDA comments:
We are not able to give you a definitive answer but will work with you regarding the definitions. The
reason we use training is because that is what is in the statutes.
We will have to talk among ourselves if we can shift and use the term "education". Quote from Jane
"I am sure we can come up with some clarifying definition".

4. The IWG wants to make FDA aware of our concerns about the request in Appendix B in the
FDA letter regarding patient information for links to web sites with additional information about
the safe use of opioid products. The concerns stem from our lack of industry authority or
influence over the information provided from any of these sites and the uncertainty on which
sites would be the best sites to link to. Our thinking is that it would be more appropriate for
FDA to provide these links and we are interested in the Agency's thoughts or
recommendation. KJ /SN
FDA comments: We need to take this question up among ourselves and are not able to comment on it at this
time.
5. FDA had indicated in one teleconference that they are working on a Patient-Prescriber
agreement (PPA) that will be made available to the public. Will the PPA include information
that the patient can retain which would than satisfy the requirement referenced in point 8 of
Appendix B. IWG is seeking some clarification on item 8 in Appendix B of Post-Approval
REMS Notification letter. FDA has seen that IWG included the concept, use, and importance

75% of drug industry stakeholders see the FDA's intent to reform individualized REMS programs as a good thing.

standardized REMS. Here's how ...

Standardizing REMS: What's the Status?
An FDAnews Webinar

Register now
What can you do now to assure you're ready to comply — and benefit from — the standardization of REMS?
Plenty.
That's because various industry groups and associations are hard at work hammering out real-world REMS
reference guides that map out what you can do today to improve your programs and anticipate what the FDA
guidance is likely to include.
These include:
• Industry Work Group (IWG): The IWG is a consortium of pharma
companies — primarily opioid sponsors — working with FDA to
provide feedback and input on a classwide REMS.
• Physicians Insurers Association of America (PIAA): This trade group
represents medical liability carriers and is increasingly involved in
shaping REMS CME programs.

medical societies, liability carriers, sponsors, trade groups and the FDA,
provides REMS- and AER-related tools to safeguard patient safety
and protect provider interests and liability as healthcare moves to

U.S Pain Position Statement:
Substitution of Opioids incorporating Tamper- Resistant Technologies
While the benefits of opioids in treating and managing pain are widely recognized, the potential for
misuse and abuse of these products has long been a concern of manufacturers, state and federal law
enforcement, healthcare providers, legislators and regulators. Given the critically important public
health and law enforcement goals of preventing the abuse and misuse of opioids, state lawmakers should
work to approve policies that encourage manufacturers to:
• Work with patient advocacy groups in order to develop educational programs on the use and
misuse of opioid products.
• Develop opioid products with tamper-resistance technologies without increasing cost to
patients.
• Protect prescribing physician decision with respect to such products.
Because healthcare providers are a critical line of defense in identifying and preventing opioid abuse,
U.S. Pain Foundation fully supports prescribing physicians' ability to write prescriptions for opioid
products incorporating tamper-resistance technologies when it is their medical judgment that such
prescriptions are in the best interests of the patient. It is imperative that medical judgments are not
undermined by inappropriate substitution at the pharmacy level without first determining that the
substitute incorporates substantially similar tamper-resistance properties or without obtaining explicit
physician authorization.

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07117518

 As a nation, U.S. Pain sees the need for all individuals to become better informed regarding effective
pain management treatments as well as the risks of abusing prescription drugs. From 1991 to 2009,
prescriptions for opioid analgesics nearly increased threefold (to over 200 million). According to the
Drug Abuse Warning Network System, which monitors drug-related emergency department visits and
drug-related deaths, emergency room visits related to the non-medical use of pharmaceutical opioids had
also doubled between 2005 and 2009.
It is no question that opioid medications are vital for pain management treatment. Yet the wide
availability may result in leftover pills in family medicine cabinets, which therefore increase
opportunities for abuse as well as a host of serious medical consequences, including addiction.
Considering about one in every three individuals will experience chronic pain in his or her lifetime,
abuse-deterrent and tamper-resistant technologies can help mitigate risk for those with legitimate need
for pain control.
U.S. Pain Foundation is an independent, nonprofit 501(c) 3 organization dedicated to serving those who live with pain conditions
and their care providers. Created by people with pain for people with pain, our mission is to inform, empower and advocate for the
pain community.

From: GerritsenvanderHoop,Roland

Subject: RE: Opana "Unleashing Our Power" Cluster Meetings
Dave,
Thanks for your approval. It is already quite clear that the CD&E organization has understood the "wake-up call" and is trying to
respond. That does not mean, of course, that they like it and will really change, but it is a start. When we start to uncouple the
CME money from the CL efforts, reduce it in size and change the direction to be more regional, we will see how that is received.
This one time rally is one thing, but having to do it every day is a very different thing and I still wonder whether that can be
achieved without organizational changes.
I think what is really needed from your side is clear direction where you want the focus of the effort to be (like you are providing
in the e-mail) and how you (and I) are going to assess the performance (so we need clear measurements, something you like
anyway).
The phasing in of new FTE's needs to match regional needs and the most urgent priority(ies). By the way: do you have an
opinion on whether CLs should be handling all products, or should be specialized? This is something we have been struggling
with. On the one hand you could argue our portfolio is not so diverse someone could not cover all products and this would help
regional coverage. On the other hand specialization adds focus and credibility, but decreases coverage.
If we present a closed front we will get change going, and at there is momentum here.

Kind regards,

 Roland
From: Kerr, David
Sent: Thursday, November 02, 2006 9:09 PM
To: GerritsenvanderHoop,Roland
Cc: Baglin, Mark; Santilli,Nancy
Subject: RE: Opana "Unleashing Our Power" Cluster Meetings
Roland,
Wow. Thank you, this is really leadership in action and will go a long way to showing those that are concerned about our change
in direction the "way ahead" for CD&E.
You are helping deliver on the expectation that we will have a detailed plan on path forward between us for CD&E. You have my
full support. I want to do my part of course.
Do you need me to put something formal together that describes the rationale for change in direction of CD&E? Here's my
top-of-mind rationale and direction if you want to integrate it into the R&D plan for 2007.
I tried to lay out at our Friday-last meeting with Linda K. and Miss Craven what the change in direction and priority was:
A1, Selling the "science" to impact Regnl KOL, Thought-leader cascade, MCO P&T, IIS etc in support of Opana Sharp Stick
with/in support of Field Sales (less national CME and KOL, more support for the clinical utility of C-II with novel activity);
A2. Using the data and clinical evidence for Menstrual Migraine Dx and Tx to establish awareness, build support for clinical
intervention, and build network of clinical support/cascade for the entry of new therapies for MM in 2007 (less emphasis on
National CME and more emphasis on regional KOL, P&T support, IIS, clinical experience, etc);
C. P&T support for pediatric pain, JACHO standards/survey for pediatric pain, venipuncture procedures and clinical practice
for pain; Identify and support data within the 16-20 clinical studies on local anesthetics for venipuncture in pediatrics that
would be persuasive in building support for action at major pediatric centers for new therapies available in the recent past.
D. Support of the positioning of local analgesia (as opposed to anesthesia) for difficult-to-treat neuropathic pain conditions
like PHN; work with our marketing and sales training staff to better understand how to truly "sell" the science of
Lidoderm's MOA so that we can grow the use of this therapy in PHN patients, which is going to help underscore it's
clinical utility for these difficult to treat neuropathic pain patients. The MOA story has been under-valued in our support of
localized pain treatment and this may pay benefits with other localized pain products in our pipeline.
Overall While being fully compliant with the highest standards of professional conduct and regulatory guidance... ..less national
CME, less national long term KOL focus, more regional KOL, more P&T clinical/science support, more "selling" of the data that
underlies our portfolio & pipeline more IIS linked to clinical experience on the science and clinical practices underpinned by our
learnings from the labeled clinical trial packages and other supportive studies, more transparency on what work is being done by
whom, for whom, when, and with what impact; more alignment top-to-bottom with our CD&E, Commercial, and Executive teams.
In the absence of knowing what the CD&E team is really doing, we are probably assuming the worst, and that's not good for any
involved.
It's a more pragmatic approach that in the past, but I don't apologize for it — that's truly what I believe we need to do for the
advancement of our mission as a mid-sized specialty pharma. Leveraging clinical experience and data for focused change in
awareness, clinical utility, and pharmaco-economic rationale for analgesic and CNS therapies. I realize we aren't developing
NCE's, but that doesn't mean we can't advance clinical experience and utility with the data and science we create.

I am ready to support your proposal for additional 5-10 CD&E staffers to support the mission per your proposed expansion last
Spring, but the part I want to see from Linda is how this expansion would be phased in support of the company's launch
effectiveness priorities.
If we need to get more senior commercial input to the CD&E organization revitalization, I can arrange time with my staff as you
need us.
Regards,

Nick,

I just wanted to give you some of the information and extremely useful feedback that I
acquired at this past VFAB meeting. We touched upon everything from information about how
physicians view OA and Voltaren Gel to some of the great tools we will be receiving soon.
We were also able to come up with some ideas for patient profiles that will be great tools
to have in the field, and all the ideas that everyone sent me from the region were a great
resource to use in developing those profiles.
So here are some bullet point notes from the meeting:
- When a study was conducted questioning PCPs about OA and Voltaren Gel some information
that stood out
1. PCP main focus when prescribing was managed care
2. They saw Voltaren Gel more as a 2nd line or switch agent
3. Celebrex was seen more as their 1st line agent
- So what is important to take away here is that even though managed care stands out
in a physicians mind when prescribing a NSAID, it is still very important to sell efficacy
first because Celebrex is still seen as a 1st line agent over Voltaren Gel

- Two thirds of patients stop taking their medication(Patient Compliance)
- For reasons of not enough relief,feel they are taking too many pills,GI problems
- Importance of this is making sure we are informing the physicians to set patient
expectations
- PCPs are not usually just treating pain, more than often they are treating a lot of
things at once(CV issues,allergies,GI,etc etc). With that most of OA pain sufferers were
diagnosed years before and their pain problems may no longer be a primary focus when
visiting their primary care physician for a check up, if anything maybe just a refill of a
previous medication. So what may help us in selling to our doctors is to focus on the
comorbidities that may be masking their OA pain(Examples Diabetes, CV, Obesity,
Depression). These are things that many OA pain patients suffer from and that primary care
doctors see everyday, with this we can funnel the physicians focus down to perhaps
re-diagnosing these patients and giving them a NEW treatment like Voltaren Gel that will
give them the efficacy they need to relive their OA pain.
-A great targeting tool is to look at physicians who may be large Evista/Boniva/Fosamax
writers, these physicians are seeing female patients over the age of 65 that are suffering
from osteoporosis who also happen to be at risk for OA
-March 16th is 3&5 pack launch day, most of the larger pharmacies are being drop shipped
with the new packs and information
- The NDC # for the single pack is being discontinued, so that there is no loss of
scripts pharmacy calls are going to be very important considering the new 3&5 packs are
going to have new NDC #s when the pharmacy tries to order more VG or fill a script

On Tuesday October 12, 2010, 8:43 am NEW YORK (AP) -- Pfizer Inc., the world's
largest pharmaceutical company by revenue, said Tuesday it will buy pain drug maker King
Pharmaceuticals Inc. for $3.6 billion in cash. Pfizer is paying $14.25 per share for King. That's a premium
of 40 percent to the stock's Monday closing price of $10.15. In the deal Pfizer gains products including the
pain drug Avinza and EpiPen, a pre-filled injection designed to quickly treat serious allergic reactions. The
deal is Pfizer's largest since it bought rival Wyeth for $68 billion in 2009. That deal closed last October. King
has struggled in recent years as patents on several of its key drugs have expired or been thrown out. But
the Bristol, Tenn., company is heavily involved in developing pain drugs that are intended to be abuseresistant. Abuse of pain drugs like oxycodone has become a major concern for health officials and
regulators in recent years. The drugs are often crushed or dissolved to defeat their time-release
mechanisms, allowing users to get high. King's Embeda is one pain treatment that is designed to resist
abuse attempts. King plans to file new applications for two similar drugs in the next few months, filing for
approval of Remoxy in the fourth quarter of 2010 and Acurox in the first quarter of 2011. Remoxy and
Embeda are extended-release drugs, while Acurox releases its painkilling ingredient immediately. King's
other products include the bleeding control drug Thrombin-]MI and the Flector pain patch. The boards of
both companies approved the deal. Pfizer said the purchase will add about 2 cents per share to its profit in
2011 and 2012, and 3 to 4 cents per share in each of the next three years. In premarket trading, King
shares soared to $14.13, up 39 percent from Monday's close. Pfizer shares dipped 3 cents to $17.35.

 Dear Chairman Upton:
On behalf of the patient and health professional groups listed below we would like to express our support for H.R.
4641, to provide for the establishment of an inter-agency task force to review, modify, and update best practices for
pain management and prescribing pain medication, and for other purposes. We appreciate your leadership in fighting
to establish a new model opioid prescribing guidelines development process that is open and includes the input of a
broad range of government and external stakeholders.
The need for opioid prescribing guidelines is clear. However, we do not want confusion among medical practitioners,
which is why we have developed the following amendment that allows for a single clear unanimous set of guidelines
issued by the federal government.
"(g) Effect on Other Guidelines.--- The guidelines issued by the Inter-Agency Task Force pursuant to
subsection 101(d) of this Act shall, upon issuance, be the onLy valid opioid prescribing guidelines issued by the
federal government."
As Congress continues to address the prescription drug abuse epidemic in the United States, we applaud your taking
the lead to ensure that there is a single model set of prescribing guidelines. We look forward to supporting this
initiative.

Subject POPAN activities in the past months
A Lot of activity has been occurring in the past months in WA state.
1.

Pain Care Forum a group in Washington DC has been listening and strategizing with WAKPI President and POPAN state Professional leader (Dionetta) about the situation in WA state. We have had 2 meetings so far.

2.

Position statements from 8 major state and national pain organizations have been received stating their concerns about the current Pain Guidelines in WA state and these have been forwarded to Dr Gary Franklin and his Agency Medical
Directors group members. Copies were also given to legislators, the governor and key pain groups in WA state. The organizations that wrote position statements are:
a. American Pain Foundation (APF)
b. American Pain Society (APS)
c. American Cancer Society jointly with the Alliance of State Pain initiatives (ACS &ASPI)
d. American Academy of Pain Management (AAPManagement)
e. Washington Chapter of the Academy of Pain Management (WAPM)
f.
Western Pain Society (WPS)
g. Washington Alaska Pain Initiative (WAKPI)

3.

We have had 3 major news articles in the papers on east and west side of state which have increased public awareness. Letters to the editor have been written, I have not seen any published yet though. All POPAN state leaders have
responded to the Alerts given by POPAN —APF re: news articles
a. Brenda's article in the Puyallup paper in November
b. Dionetta's article in the Yakima paper, (January) which was picked up by 2 west side papers.
c. Recent article from WAPM Doctors (February) in response to the NY times Fibromyalgia article.
d. Thank you letters have been written or being written and sent to reporters who did the stories as well as the paper's editor.

4.

Brenda and Fred have started a support group in Puyallup area, with good attendance and positive response

5.

We have identified at least 2 new community leaders in WA state. One in Seattle area (Sheri) and one in the Spokane area (Robert). And Alaska has 2 more that are being invited to join us (can't recall the names at the present moment).
Sue and Jeff are getting their feet on the ground and ready to go.

6.

We have scheduled our first joint POPAN-WA-AK telephone Conference for Feb 12th at 8 pm. We will be using the ACS phone conferencing service.

7.

WAPM members (physicians)met with Gary Franklin last week...VERY positive outcome...More to come on that once the document is reviewed by both parties. I am not at liberty to divulge the particulars at this time but just know that we
are gaining some ground here thanks to the work of many concerned and dedicated individuals in the state.

8.

Dionetta met with the WA end of life coalition Last Friday via phone conference and they are looking at the guideline and its possible effect on end of life pain. Some interesting dialogue occurred...will talk more about this at our
POPAN-WA-AK meeting on the 12th.

9.

Dionetta had scheduled Meetings with legislators on Nurse legislative day on Feb 4th. They are all still very interested in hearing continued updates on what is occurring in WA around the pain issue. We need to stay on their radar. Our
influence with the legislators at the Pain Rally is paying off. We are a face to them now. We all need to send emails, letters, and meet with them as we can. Right now they are in session but will be back to their local community offices in
Mid March. Call and set up an appt for coffee and a chat. They need to see your face and hear your story to stay connected to the issues.

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-04061191

 10. Newest strategy for POPAN-WA to work on at the moment --- Suggested by WAPM doctors who feel that it is necessary to be able to factually document as many of these occurrences. (Carol, Brenda, Robert and Sheri You all know
some of these individuals or have been in contact with these individuals via email)
We need to find any person who is in pain in WA state and
1. has had their pain meds — decreased or discontinued in the past 2 years
2. or has been dismissed from their physician's practice due to their chronic pain diagnosis, And if they received a letter to that effect it would be helpful to have a copy of that letter.
3. or has not been able to get in to see any physician about their pain due to their diagnosis and/or their insurance coverage.
4. Or is on a waiting list to see a pain specialist or has an appt that is/was more than a month away.
5. We need to help them to write a one page and no more than 2 page factual story about what happened, (it is as easy as answering the following questions)
a. Physician's name, clinic location
b. What is their pain diagnosis or problem?
c. what they were on and how much and how long were they on it?
d. What was their quality of life before and after?
e. What reason was given for the decrease or discontinuation of meds?
f. Dates - when was it decreased or discontinued?
g. How were they notified that this would occur ?
h. how was it done i.e. abruptly or gradually
i.
If they were discharged from Physician's practice, can't get in to see anyone about their pain or are on a waiting list to see a pain specialists.
i. We need date, name of physician, Clinic location, reason given, and how long they have been on waiting list or have been trying to find a physician to see them for their pain problems.
6. These stones will then be collected and WAKPI Leadership will send copies of them to Dr Franklin, MOAC, the Governor and legislators.
Let's keep the momentum going.
Looking forward to our first POPAN-WA-AK meeting on the 12th.
Got to listen into the POPAN meeting today, excited about some of the new tools for leaders that will be available soon.
Dionetta

Alabama, Pennsylvania and Connecticut Updates

Updates for Keri meeting...
Alabama R&D Tax Credit
Nearing the end of the 2015 Regular Session, our legislation has not yet been scheduled for debate on the House Floor. HB 304 is
not alone. None of the Governor's Economic Development Bills are moving nor are they likely to for the remainder of the Session.
Approximately three weeks ago, House Leadership put the brakes on any of these Bills moving forward until the General Fund and
Education budgets are finalized citing the potential cost to the state.
The Education budget has passed the Senate but neither the Education budget nor the General Fund budget have been heard in
the House Committee. As we've discussed previously, filibusters in both the House and the Senate are further slowing down any
legislative action. The tactic has been used by Democrats, representing the minority party, which various members filibustered
legislation including simple election law legislation, representation on Birmingham Water Board and even honorary proclamations.
Further complicating movement of HB 304 during the few remaining days of the legislative session is our Sponsor, Phil Williams (RHuntsville) and his waning relationship with Speaker Mike Hubbard. Williams was previously given the Speakers approval to lead
the R&D legislative effort in the House. The House Leadership last week proposed a series of new taxes in an attempt to fix the
holes in the budgets. In Committee on Wednesday, Williams joined three other Republicans voting against the adoption of a tax
raising the tax on lubricating oil from $3.30/barrel to $200.00/barrel prompting the Speaker to burst into the Committee Room and
as one press outlet described his tirade as "becoming unhinged". The Committee then quickly scheduled a rare second meeting for
Thursday to reconsider the tax legislation. In that second meeting the previous wayward votes all changed their vote to yes with
the exception of Williams further enraging the Speaker. As ethics violation charges surround Speaker Hubbard, there is a strong
possibility he will not return as speaker for 2016.
On May 11th we gathered the coalition members, all who agreed this package would not pass if split apart and it is purely mired in
politics. Our new tact is to pass the budget and then attempt a special session on Economic Development.
Pennsylvania
In February, Rep. Maria Donatucci circulated a memo detailing her interest in creating a joint "Heroin and Opioids Addiction
Eradication and Treatment Committee". Understanding she is seeking input from the drug addiction prevention and treatment
community as well as having also cited opioid addiction as part of this committee, there was a strong possibility the composition of
the committee would not adequately include patients appropriately using therapies and might result in patient adverse
recommendations. Additionally, we felt the legislation redundant as a panel was already assembled in 2014 to provide
recommendations on this subject.
Having worked with Representatively Doyle Heffley in 2014 to expand his advisory committee to include patient societies (via an
amendment Endo drafted and which was adopted via a unanimous vote) we asked Rep. Heffley to reach out to his colleague. Rep.
Heffley did speak with Re. Donatucci and, to date, the legislation has not been introduced. Endo has also spoken to other
interested parties, including Pennsylvania Bio and the Pennsylvania Medical Society, to make them aware of the February
Donatucci memo.
Connecticut
Connecticut SB 1130, if enacted, would implement a 6.35% tax on manufacturers of controlled substances.
Given the composition of the legislature in Connecticut, legislation such of this has a better chance of passing than it would in other
states.
As we know, the national press has an appetite to report on controlled substances. While many of the stories are not entirely
accurate, they are fueling the debate in state legislatures across the country. For that reason, in addition to the financial impact to
our branded and generic business in Connecticut, of great concern is the likelihood that should SB 1130 pass it is very likely that
this legislation would appear next session in numerous other states. The financial impact in a more populous state or numerous
small states would be significant.
Since introduction, the bill has undergone two significant edits. 1) only impacting schedule II and I controlled substances (despite

Additionally, the 5-7-15 substitute bill language describing the fund use reads specifically "grants-in-aid to regional opioid abuse
prevention and treatment programs that follow state and federal treatment protocols in accordance with section 5 of this act"

 REMS UPDATE:

The MedBiquitous standards (the national standards used by all Accrediting Bodies to report on
CE/CME) have been revised to include REMS-specific data fields. I've been participating as a member of
the MedBiq Working Group, and am really thrilled to see this project successfully completed, since it is
absolutely essential to being able to aggregate data from all CE Providers, and all CE Accrediting Bodies so
that RPC can report it to FDA.

I'm particularly pleased that the Working Group consented to include all of the data fields that RPC
requested, including one that caused a lot of discussion among the CE stakeholders: "Have you
prescribed at least 1 ER/LA opioid in the past 12 months?" It was a major step (since you all know info on
prescribing practices and CME are generally like oil & water), however the Working Group agreed this was
the only "simple, yet de-identified"way of being able to report to FDA on whether the REMS CME was
actually "reaching"the HCPs who write scripts for ER/LA opioids.

The grant approvals for the first round of RPC-supported REM-compliant CE have been completed,
letters of agreement have been signed with Providers, and the Providers are in the process of finalizing

Hamburg: FDA Budget Cuts Would Have `Devastating' Effect
(3/14, David Belian, Drug Industry Daily) reports "...In response to a question from Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), the former chair of the
subcommittee, Hamburg said that if the agency does not receive the funding it requested, the progress it has made in addressing the backlog of
generic-drug applications could be reversed. This cut would set us back, it would mean that our backlog would increase [and] we would hay e fewer
drugs being reviewed and approved,' Hamburg said. `A small cut to that program is going to have repercussions in terms of costs to the healthcare
system.'" Paid Subscription Required
Hamburg Says Generic Drug Reviews ould Slow In Wake Of GOP-Backed Budget Cuts
(3/11 The Pink Sheet Daily) reports "FDA's progress in addressing the backlog of generic drug applications would be a casualty of House
Republican efforts to cut the agency's non-user fee funding levels for the remainder of fiscal 2011, Commissioner Margaret Hamburg warned the
House Appropriations Subcommittee on Agriculture/FDA March 11." Paid Subscription Required
The Difficult Fight Against Counterfeit Drugs Dr. Sanjay Gupta Investigates Fake Medications on His First Assignment for "60 Minutes"
(3/10 CBS News: 60 Minutes) reports "...What is even more alarming is these counterfeit medications are not just being sold on the Internet. They
are also making their way into mainstream pharmacies and hospitals. FDA Commissioner Margaret Hamburg says that while the vast majority of our
drug supply is safe, there's reason for concern. You know, we don't really know the full dimensions of the problem. But, we do know that in certain
countries somewhere between 30 and 50 percent of really important drugs for health arc, in fact, counterfeit,' Commissioner Hamburg said." Full
Video
Administration Pushes Track And Trace System To Stem Drug Counterfeiting
(3/11 Insidehealthpolicy.com) reports "The Obama administration, in an interagency task force report released Friday (March II), is recommending
legislation to authorize a track and trace system for pharmaceuticals, longer sentences for counterfeit pharmaceutical convictions, and requirements
that importers and manufacturers notify agencies when they discover counterfeit products. The initiatives are supported by the drug industry to
prevent the proliferation and trade of counterfeit drugs." Paid Subscription Required

(3/13, Peter M. Jaensch, John R. Fleder, FDA Law Blog) reports "...Although some agencies already post online much of this type of information,
FDA's website has not provided a comprehensive picture of the agency's activities in court. We believe that making all public information available
online will promote consistency in FDA actions, and permit industry and the general public to make informed decisions about FDA-regulated
products. Whether FDA will agree — or respond — remains to be seen." Full
Durbin Takes Aim at Obama's Detente with Drug Industry
(3/12, Alexander Bolton, The Hill) reports "...Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-I11.) and Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-I11.) have introduced
legislation that would require the secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate lower prices for beneficiaries of the Medicare prescription
drug program." Full
CBO Keeps Idea Of Mandatory Rx Rebates For Medicare Part D Low-Income Members In Play
(3/11 The Pink Sheet Daily) reports "An idea for bringing the government more revenues from the pharmaceutical industry is being kept alive in a
budget option listed by the Congressional Budget Office in a new report: mandating Medicaid-level rebates on drugs used by Medicare Part D
beneficiaries who are also eligible for Medicaid." Paid Subscription Required
Physician Payments Sunshine Rule From CMS Expected By Year's End

reporting payments made to physicians if the agency meets its current timeline for issuing the rules." Paid Subscription Required

Manufacturers of America." Paid Subscription Required

UPDATE 1-J&J pain drug Nucynta ER gets FDA nod

* Approved with a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (Follows alerts)
Aug 26 (Reuters) - Johnson and Johnson unit Janssen Pharmaceuticals got U.S. regulatory approval to market its
oral pain
drug Nucynta ER for moderate to severe chronic pain when an opioid analgesic is needed for extended use.
Nucynta ER is an extended-release version of the company's already approved pain drug Nucynta.
The drug has been approved along with a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy, also known as REMS, to
educate
prescribers about the potential for abuse, misuse, overdose and addiction from exposure to the drug.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the American Pain Foundation suggests that more than 42
million
Americans age 20 and over suffer from chronic pain, the company said in a statement.
Johnson and Johnson shares closed at $64.55 Thursday on the New York Stock Exchange. (Reporting by Esha

Subject: RE: Bloomberg News: FDA Will Act on Pain Pill Abuse After Senate Blocks Nominee
Dear All,
Here is a little more detail on the FDA plan.
FDA Opioids Action Plan
The FDA is deeply concerned about the growing epidemic of opioid abuse, dependence and overdose in the United
States. In response to this crisis, the agency has developed a comprehensive action plan to take concrete steps
toward reducing the impact of opioid abuse on American families and communities. As part of this plan, the agency is
committing to work more closely with its advisory committees before making critical product and labeling decisions;
enhancing safety labeling; requiring new data; and seeking to improve treatment of both addiction and pain. At the
same time, the FDA will fundamentally re-examine the risk-benefit paradigm for opioids and ensure that the agency
considers the wider public health effects. The FDA is committed to taking all of these steps transparently and in close
cooperation with its sister agencies and stakeholders.
The FDA's actions include:
• Expand use of advisory committees. Starting today, the FDA will convene an expert advisory committee
before approving any new drug application for an opioid that does not have abuse-deterrent properties. And
the Pediatric Advisory Committee will make recommendations regarding a framework for pediatric opioid
labeling before any new labeling is approved. The FDA will consult an advisory committee on abuse-deterrent
formulation (ADF) opioids when they raise novel issues. Outcome: Review and advice from external experts
with opportunity for public input before approval of any new opioid that does not have abuse-deterrent
properties and expert advice on pediatric opioid labeling.
• Develop warnings and safety information for immediate-release (IR) opioid labeling. The FDA is developing
changes to IR opioid labeling, including additional warnings and safety information that incorporate elements
similar to the extended-release/long-acting (ER/LA) opioid analgesics labeling update that occurred in 2013.
Outcome: Better information for doctors about the risks and how to prescribe safely.
• Strengthen postmarket requirements. Because the evidence base to guide the use of opioid medications,
particularly in the setting of long-term use, is substantially lacking, the FDA is strengthening the requirements for
drug companies to generate postmarket data on the long-term impact of using ER/LA opioids. Outcome:
Better evidence on the serious risks of misuse and abuse associated with long-term use of opioids, predictors
of opioid addiction and other important issues.
• Update Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) Program.ER/LA opioids are currently subject to a
REMS program that requires sponsors to fund continuing medical education (CME) providers to offer, at low

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-02799815

 or no cost, CM E courses on the appropriate use of these products. The FDA will update the REMS program
requirements for opioids after considering advisory committee recommendations and review of existing
requirements. Outcome: Increase the number of prescribers who receive training on pain management and
safe prescribing of opioid drugs in order to decrease inappropriate opioid prescribing.
• Expand access to abuse-deterrent formulations (ADFs) to discourage abuse. The pharmaceutical industry has
shown significant interest in developing ADFs and the technology is progressing rapidly. ADFs hold promise as
their abuse-deterrent qualities continue to improve and as they become more widely available. The FDA will
issue draft guidance with its recommendations for the approval standards for generic abuse-deterrent
formulations. Release of this guidance is a high priority, since the availability of less costly generic products
should accelerate prescribers' uptake of ADFs. Outcome: Spur innovation and generic ADF product
development.
• Support better treatment. The FDA is reviewing options, including over-the-counter availability, to make
naloxone more accessible to treat opioid overdose, building on the agency's recent approval of intranasal
naloxone. The agency actively supports the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidelines for
prescribing opioids for the treatment of pain and will facilitate the development of evidence and improved
treatments. Outcome: Broader access to overdose treatment, safer prescribing and use of opioids, and
ultimately, new classes of pain medicines without the same risks as opioids.
• Reassess the risk-benefit approval framework for opioid use. The FDA will seek advice from the agency's
Science Board in March 2016 and is already engaging the National Academy of Medicine on how to take into
account our evolving understanding of the risks of opioids, not only to the patient but also the risks of misuse
by other persons who obtain them. These reports will be publicly available. Outcome: Formal incorporation of
the broader public health impact of opioid abuse in approval decisions.

face of a drug abuse epidemic in the U.S., a move that may also help get the administration's nominee to lead the
agency through the Senate.
Opiod addiction has become a major issue in the presidential race, at the White House and in Congress, where Robert

To: Thomson, Heather
Subject: Re: New text book
Hi Heather,
I don't know if you noticed, but in our chapter outline we mention that we will include text from "Four MS-PREP graduates,
where they will describe the value that pursuing postgraduate education about pain has had for their careers, the ongoing
application of this education in their busy everyday practices, and the role this specific guide can play for other busy
clinicians".
Would you be interested in writing a short piece (about 3 paragraphs) for this section? It would be great to get your input.
Best wishes and thanks,
Ewan
— Original Message -From: Thomson, Heather
To: Ewan McNicol
Sent: Tuesday, August 19, 2008 8:57 AM
Subject: RE: New text book

Em, an —
I applaud your project! The content and format should really be of assistance to primary care
practitioners and others faced with treating pain. Now, you will get way more useful feedback from the
clinicians you have contacted, and I seriously hesitated to respond because of my background and narrow
professional focus; that said, I have decided to offer a few minor observations which I trust you will temper
with more valid advice than mine.
Based on my involvement with the design of educational programs from a funding standpoint, I

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-08384702

 endorse your case scenario approach. This format is consistently rated as a preferred learning tool, and
should especially fit into your "busy clinician's" needs. (The book title is great, by the way.) I will offer one
point for consideration, though. The standard Continuing Medical Education objectives frequently use the
"you will learn" language that appears in your proposed chapter headings, and I wonder if that will make the
book seem like one of those CME offerings that clinicians get that are frequently supported by industry. An
alternative as similar as, "The objectives of this chapter include," or "Topics to be addressed," or something
like that might be just different enough to avoid that impression. But see if anyone else had that response.
Secondly, your intention to use tables will be most helpful, as they are a speedy way to find quicklyneeded information. Here's a caveat: my recent exposure to the area of osteoarthritis (because of diclofenac
topical gel) has had me puzzled over how some drug tables can be a jumble of headings, including route of
administration, class of drug, and mechanism of action, all in the same guide. So, for example, diclofenac
gel gets listed with capsaicin in a table titled "Topicals" but isn't mentioned in the next table, which is
headed "NSAIDs." Cross-referencing so that a therapy appears in more than one place if you use more than
one kind of heading is one solution, or just stick to one method of categorization for all the therapies in your
tables, so your reader doesn't flip to the table where he thinks the information should be, but you've put it
somewhere else.
Finally, from my tiny view of the universe, where everything is an opioid, I'll make a plea for you to
consider whether there is a place in your book for a paragraph on urine drugs tests as part of an opioids
monitoring program, even if it's just to advise your readers not to order them unless they know what they're
doing. Some of the questions I field from primary care physicians imply that they think these tests can
provide information that they can't, and also suggest that a fair number of practitioners are not adequately
equipped to evaluate the results, from which they make egregious clinical decisions.
Oh, I lied about the "finally" — I have one more thing for you to run by people with better insight than
me. Wherever you are advising the practitioner to take some action that requires communication that may
be new or difficult, go ahead and offer the specific verbiage they might consider using. Telling someone to
do something gently, with tact or with some other consideration is no good if the person has no idea what
that sounds like. Go ahead and put some good examples in quotations.
All right, really finally, I am a pretty good copy editor. If you want someone to go through your final
draft looking for spelling mistakes and the like, I won't guarantee I'll get every one, but I would be happy to
scan the text with a pair of fresh eyes. For some reason I see that stuff in flashing neon on the page, so it
doesn't take me long to do, and I would offer that as my best potential contribution to the project when the
time comes.
Warmest regards on a great undertaking,
Heather

Heather Thomson, MS
Clinical Affairs Manager
Endo Pharmaceuticals
15 Pine Ledge Way
Norfolk. CT 06058
Redacted - Privacy ! (phone and fax)
From: Ewan McNicol
Redacted - Privacy .
Sent: Thursday, August 14, 2008 11:23 AM
To: Undisclosed-Recipient:;
Cc: Carr, Daniel; Carol Curtiss
Subject: New text book
Dear Present and Former MSPREP Students,

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-08384703

 Dr. Dan Carr, Carol Curtiss and I are about to begin authoring a new text book "The Busy Clinician's Guide to
Pain". As the title suggests, we hope to create a comprehensive, yet concise text that clinicians from
multiple disciplines can quickly use to help them in their daily practice. The book is not aimed at pain
experts (sorry!), but hopes to cover basic concepts and offer practical, useful advice for the non-specialist.
One of the unique aspects of the book is that we will incorporate feedback and comments from students of
MSPREP —the only program of its type in America. We figured that what you all find relevant and important
will translate to what is relevant and important to clinicians in general.
I have attached an outline of the chapters of the book, and a single chapter format draft. If you have the
time, we would really appreciate your input as to the usefulness of this text. Would you add anything? In
addition, we would value your thoughts on using case scenarios to illustrate key points from each chapter
(please refer to the example in the chapter draft). Do you find these useful as a learning tool? Do they draw
you into the text? If yes to both, what about them makes them useful? And is there a specific way that you'd
like them to be incorporated?
Please contact me directly with your comments, or if you have any questions about the project.
Thank you all very much,
Ewan (and Carol and Dan)

On May 2, 2011, at 9:01 AM, <elizabeth.ernst@boehringer- ingelheim.com> wrote:
Dear Michie and Team,
Below are several questions that the IWG would like to obtain clarification on so that we can continue to
move forward and finalize our REMS proposal. I have tried to break them down into categories for your
convenience:
Administrative

I. Does the FDA plan to continue their review and approve new products both ANDAs and NDAs that
fall into the category of LAO? How will these new companies be integrated into the IWG process and

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07049661

 what is FDAs expectation regarding when their interaction begin with the IWG?

2. Can the agency please clarify by what is meant by "stepwise approach" ? This is in reference to Janet
Woodcock's comment at the teleconference where she stated that the agency sees the opioid class REMS
as being a "stepwise approach".

3. Can the FDA please send the IWG a list of companies who have products that fall into the category of
extended release products so that we can ensure that they are part of the process for finalizing the class
wide REMS program currently being developed.? What are FDAs expectation when it comes to those
companies who do not have an approval but have received a pre-approval letter as part of the review of
their NDAs/ANDAs.

4. The ANDA REMS requirement letters (we should confirm that this is true for all ANDA holders)
did not indicate that assessments were a requirement - could you confirm that assessments would not be
mandated to the ANDA holders?

5. What is the filing expectations for the FDA regarding the draft REMS proposal that is due in 120
days. Is it the FDA's expectation that each company must file an proposed REMS to them for review or
would we be able to file one draft program until we are in agreement to what the final plan shall look
like?

Medication Guides
1. What does the FDA mean by drug specific: Are we talking about each product individually? Are we
considering brand products vs generic products? Do we need to separate different dosage forms? Or do
we define it more broadly by its active molecule? For example, would all oxycodone products regardless
of the formulation fall into one category and be assessed as one? Therefore medication guides, metrics
and assessments will be done via molecule not via the individual products. Please confirm your
understanding.

2. Can the FDA clarify what their expectations are in regards to the medication guides for the class wide
REMS. The verbiage currently written is open to interpretation and therefore is it FDAs expectation that
each company will be responsible for developing their own medication guide which should include
common content applicable to all extended-release and long-acting opioids. OR should the IWG
continue to focus on developing medication guides based on opioid categories for example (Methadone,
Fentanyl, extended release OS products)?

3. IWG had previously presented the concept of class Medication Guides (IWG draft REMS document
including 3 medication guides: Oral long-acting opioid analgesics, Long-acting opioid transdermal

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07049662

 patches, and Methadone formulations) however, the REMS requirement letters seem to indicate that
FDA is moving towards individual product Medication Guides. Can you discuss the path that IWG
should evaluate when developing Medication guides? Should all the medication guides under this
program adopt a common template? Is there a preferred format that the FDA can recommend (number of
pages in particular)?

4. Appendix B in the REMS letter to manufacturers has a very different lay out then a medication guide
or the Patient Medication Information Sheet (PMIS) as previously proposed by IWG. Is it the FDAs
expectation that the patient education document be presented in the format outlined in Appendix B. Does
the FDA want the IWG to create patient education document which are product specific or by molecule?
Training

1. What did FDA intend regarding the content development for training (ACCME indicated that an
approved provider should develop everything beyond the outline FDA has already provided)?

2. IWG understands from Dr. Woodcock that it is the IWG responsibility to develop the education
material/content for prescribers' and that it would be reviewed and approved by FDA and then provided
to CME providers who will be responsible for the implementation. Is that correct?

3. Item #6 of the REMS assessment plan states "Include methodology for monitoring patterns of
prescribing to identify changes in access to these products" in regards to an evaluation of drug utilization
patterns. It will take at least 6 to 7 months to develop detailed methodology with a research organization
(that has yet to be selected and a contractual agreement put in place) that is approved by at least 19
companies. IWG proposes a high-level overview of the proposed methodology for this assessment in the
proposed REMS, with more detailed methodology to be developed after the REMS is approved. Does
FDA concur?

4. The FDA had indicated in one of the teleconference that they are working on a patient/prescriber
agreement. Can the FDA please send the IWG a copy of this agreement so we can review and included it
in our final proposal? We want to make sure we are consistent with the direction that the FDA is going.

Subject: Advocacy Alert - People with pain need your help with FDA
From:

U.S. Pain Foundation & INvisible Project <paul@uspainfoundation.ccsend.com >

To:

Byrne, Timothy <Byrne.Timothy@endo.com >;

Having trouble viewing this email? Click here

U.S. Pain Foundation would like to hear from you. As an organization created by
people with pain, we believe it is the voices of those with pain that generate the
most change. Our goal is to advocate on behalf of the 100 million Americans
living with pain as well as provide support and inspiration. We feel it is
important to our individual recoveries that we, as patients, become empowered
and proactive.
As we send this latest advocacy alert email, we want you to know why we do
continue to do so. Mainly, we send these alerts to make sure everyone within the
pain community is informed about issues pertaining to our current and future
healthcare. Additionally, we believe it is the pain community speaking out and
becoming involved in advocacy that evokes positive action.
In July, the group, Physicians for Responsible Opioid Prescribing (PROP), sent a
letter to the FDA requesting they place set regulations and caps on opioid
analgesics for chronic non-cancer pain. Click here for full letter.
While U.S. Pain understands the reasoning behind new prescribing protocols to
ensure safety, we feel the recommendations of a maximum daily dose,
equivalent to 100 milligrams for non-cancer pain, and a maximum duration of
90-days for continuous daily use are extreme measures. It concerns us that the
patient, the person living with unrelenting pain, will suffer severe consequences
from such drastic actions.
Today an article ran by NPR, read article. US Pain would like to applaud those
physicians who want to give the best care possible to people with pain and as you
can see they voiced there opinion and concerns. WE NEED YOU TO VOICE
YOUR OPINION!
Below you will find our response to the PROP letter. If you would like to become
involved by sharing your stories or opinions on this matter, please contact the
FDA. Tell them what your thoughts are as a person with pain and a U.S. Pain
Foundation member. Together, we stand strong ... and together, we will generate
change. The FDA is meeting this week and they need to hear from people with
pain.

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07022819

 To contact the FDA, copy and paste this link:
http.//www.regulations.gov/#!documentDetail D FDA2012-P-0818-0001
Thank you again. You are warriors. I hope today is a low-pain and high-spirits
day for each of you.
With gratitude,
Paul Gileno
Founder & President, U.S. Pain Foundation

U.S. Pain Foundation response letter
September 28, 2012

The July 25 petition from the Physicians for Responsible Opioid Prescribing (PROP)
requesting the FDA place set regulations and caps on opioid analgesics for chronic noncancer pain concerns U.S. Pain Foundation. Although we acknowledge the medical
literature suggesting, "that long-term use of opioids may be neither safe nor effective for
many patients, especially when prescribed in high doses," we feel the recommendations of
a maximum daily dose, equivalent to 100 milligrams of morphine for non-cancer pain, and
a maximum duration of 90-days for continuous daily use are extreme measures. It is our
opinion that the patient, the person living with unrelenting pain, will suffer severe
consequences from such drastic actions.
U.S. Pain Foundation aims to empower, educate and support the 100 million Americans
living with pain. As an organization created by people with pain for people with pain, we
advocate for patient rights and access to proper treatment. It is our goal to make patients
more proactive and accountable in their recovery while also demanding the best care from
physicians.
Doctors need to be better educated regarding pain management modalities so they can
treat patients with the appropriate care. A doctor-patient relationship is very important
when looking at overall outcomes of patient care. We want to make sure that relationship
is not only protected, but also nurtured. Patients need to feel a doctor is working with
them, looking at their entire history, before deciding on the most appropriate care.
U.S. Pain does not feel a "one-size-fits-all" mentality will help the medical or pain
community. We agree there is a problem, and are committed to finding ways to remedy it.
However, we do not think strict mandates are the answer. We look forward to
collaborating with all sides in order to find a solution to this undeniable problem, while
also making sure the right to needed access are protected for our members.
Kindly,
Paul Gileno

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07022820

 Founder and President, U.S. Pain Foundation

Subject: State Law Updates Relevant to Marketing

Brand Teams —

In the past few weeks, there has been a lot of activity around state laws affecting the pharmaceutical industry. The following is
a high level summary of some changes in Vermont and Massachusetts. In addition, I have included a reminder with respect to
Brand Team Sponsored Giveaway Programs in Minnesota. I will be meeting with the Brand Teams in the near future to further
address these issues and answer any questions that you may have.

Vermont
Effective July 1, 2009, the state of Vermont enacted amendments to its existing law that affects what types of items
pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturers can provide to Vermont health care providers. (Note: The term "health
care provider" in Vermont has expanded and now includes prescribers, nursing and front office staff, hospitals, pharmacists,
health plan benefits administrators, nursing homes, and individuals authorized to recommend prescribed products such as
social workers or psychologists.)
Meals — The only time we are permitted to provide a meal to a Vermont health care provider is when the meal is provided in
conjunction with a bona fide service being performed (e.g., meal at an advisory board). Therefore, any Endo employee may
not provide a meal to a Vermont health care provider unless it is in conjunction with a consulting service.

Massachusetts
Disclosure Requirement — Effective July 1, 2009, the Commonwealth of Massachusetts now requires pharmaceutical and
medical device manufacturers to disclose the value, nature and purpose of certain items (e.g., food, educational items,
honorarium) that have been provided to a Massachusetts "covered recipient," if the value of the item is over $50. (A
Massachusetts "covered recipient" includes prescribers, nursing and front office staff, hospitals, pharmacists, nursing homes,
and health benefit plan administrators.

Meals — The only time a meal may be provided to a MA health care practitioner outside of the office or hospital setting, is when
the meal is being provided in conjunction with a bona fide service being performed (e.g., meal at an advisory board).
Therefore, any Endo employee may not provide a meal to a Massachusetts health care practitioner, outside of the office or
hospital setting, unless it is in conjunction with a consulting service.
(A Massachusetts "health care practitioner" is a prescriber, the nursing and front office staff, and any individual who is licensed
to provide health care in the commonwealth.)

 Minnesota
The state of Minnesota mandates that the total retail value of gifts/educational items and meals provided to a Minnesota
licensed prescriber must not exceed $50 per year. This $50 limitation includes meals/snacks provided by the sales
representatives to Minnesota prescribers. In order to ensure we are complying with this law and not exceeding the $50 limit,
giveaway programs sponsored by the Brand Teams must exclude Minnesota prescribers. If you are working with a vendor on
these types of initiatives, please make sure they are aware of the restriction in Minnesota.

If you have any questions regarding these state laws, please do not hesitate to contact me directly.

 2) for Providers who wanted to capture detailed specialty info, arrange the questions on the form so that practice type and
specialty questions were "adjacent" to each other; that way participants would understand that the information in both was
requested/complimentary to each other. (Perhaps a brief explanatory comment, as Julie suggests below in point 1 would
