From: White, Julie L [mailtollwhite@bu.edu]
Sent: Wednesday, January 16, 2013 4:16 PM
To: Valerie Smothers; Kitlinski, Linda
Subject: RE: professions and specialties
Hi Valerie and Linda — we discussed this this morning internally with Dr. Alford, our course director/content expert (he is board
certified — internal medicine and addiction medicine) and are still struggling. I agree with Murray that this is a different
question from specialty but I think it could be very confusing to participants. We are concerned that if a PCP selects primary
care at this juncture then they will not bother to select a specialty and we do want to know that. Could you order the questions
so that specialty comes first? I guess if it is paper, that wouldn't really be effective; just a thought. Let me propose a new way of
getting to where we want to be (still to be verified with Dr. Alford but I want to see what you think). There are three steps as
follows:
1) The participant is first asked:
To be sure that we are targeting our education in the best way possible, please define your current prescribing practices (all
information is confidential ):
1. Are you currently licensed to prescribe schedule II and schedule III opioid analgesics (drop down list) ? Y/N/Not
sure
2. Do you currently prescribe opioids for any patients for equal to/greater than 3 months ? Y/N This is beyond what
we have talked about collecting, but you are certainly welcome to collect it.
3. Have you prescribed extended release long-acting opioids within the last 12 months ? Y/N
2) Then we ask the participant to select a specialty using a slightly paired down version of the MedBiquitous list
(eliminating medical genetics for example). [Process question — does this need to be endorsed by the group,
understanding that this is optional data for the FDA but wanting to ensure that all grantees use the same specialty
types ?— in which case I can forward our list to you ...)
I think it would be helpful for you to share your list and for the group to discuss. I think it's also helpful for you to share
your concerns about primary care vs. specialty (ie why you would like to collect specialty data in addition to primary
care/pain specialist).
3) Then we ask:
Do you consider yourself a pain specialist ? Y/N (with the definition - A specialist whose practice predominantly involves the
evaluation and treatment of patient pain.)
Regarding Profession — we would like to take out veterinarian as we decided since we are not addressing their needs, it would

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_FLAG-01177075

 be misleading to have this here. We would like to replace this with Other which would then include a drop down for us to
include other allied health subsets that we are interested in capturing. [Process question — does this need to be endorsed by
the group, understanding that this is optional data for the FDA but wanting to ensure that all grantees use the same specialty
types ?— in which case I can forward our list to you ...)
I don't think that needs to be endorsed by the group, but you can certainly share how you plan to execute this so that others
can learn from you. If you plan to use the healthcare lom professions in both the initial list and the other drop down, you are
conforming to the recommendations in the spec and that should be fine. I think it sounds like a very good approach.
What do you think ?
Thank you for thinking through this, Julie!
Julie

Subject: IWG - Dispenser bullet points
Hi Nancy and Lisa,
Per our discussion please see below as bullet points re: the Medication Guide —
• It is IWGs understanding that the REMS requires individual Medication Guides (MG) for each specific product.
The MG's will consist of common content applicable to all ER and LA opioids as well as product specific information
that is necessary for safe and effective use of the drug.
o The MG's will be based on format and information contained in the most recently approved products (with
MG's) in this class (i.e., we believe we can identify the "common content" from several recently approved
MG's)
o Contingency: If FDA responds that MGs by active drug substance — identify differences within generic
products that will need to be somehow conveyed (i.e., fentanyl reservoir vs. matrix formulations, morphine
doses reserved for opioid tolerant patients only) and different risks based on formulation (i.e., morphine
formulations having a pharmacokinetic interaction with alcohol [affects on delivery system potentially
resulting in increased/rapid release])
•
IWG considers the information in Appendix 8 (Patient Education) to be a list of information required for inclusion
in patient information, not format [i.e., headings or order] requirements. The list of required information will be
applied to both the information presented to the patient at time of prescribing (i.e., PMI by the physician) and at the
time of dispensing (i.e., MG by the pharmacist).
o IWG intends to move forward with the PMIS as presented in our draft REMS program for use by the
physician at the time of prescribing for patient education
• Individual sponsors with products that have an existing approved MG will assess whether their MG includes the
common content applicable to all ER and LA opioids and determine if the currently approved MG is acceptable or
whether updates are required
o If FDA clarifies that those that are currently approved must be included as they are, then this point is
irrelevant.
Please edit!
Thanks,
Tara

PressReleases
21 DEC 2011 / Product

Actavis to Launch Novel Pain Medication in the US

Strategic partnership with QRxPharma to commercialise MoxDuo® IT for the $2.5 billion US acute pain
market
Morristown, NJ (Dec. 21, 2011) - Actavis Group, the international generic pharmaceuticals company,
today announced that its US subsidiary, Actavis Inc, has entered into a binding letter of intent (LOI) with
QRxPharma Limited (ASX: QRX and OTCQX: QRXPY) to commercialize MoxDuo® IR in the United States.
Under the terms of the LOI, Actavis gets exclusive rights to launch and market MoxDuo® IR, a
patented 3:2 ratio fixed dose combination of morphine and oxycodone for the $2.5 billion US acute pain
market. The product launch in the US is expected in Q3 2012. Pre-launch preparations will begin
immediately.
Claudrio Albrecht, CEO Actavis:
"This partnership represents a major step in our strategy to further strengthen our position as one of
the major players in the segment of pain management in the US. Furthermore, as this latest development
highlights, Actavis is serious in its quest to be ahead of the changing generic pharmaceutical industry. In
the future, there will not be such a clear difference between innovator and generic companies. The lines
between the two models are blurring. The generics business as we know it today will be gone within the
next 10 years."
Actavis intends for MoxDuo® IR to be a flagship product in the Company's growing pain management
franchise. This transaction builds on Actavis success with the currently marketed Kadian® Extended
Release Morphine Sulfate capsules, and a broad array of generic scheduled narcotics offerings. Kadian®
has been manufactured by the Company for 15 years and marketed by Actavis since 2008. The
Company's analgesic sales force for its branded products will expand significantly and have MoxDuo® IR
as a primary focus in the US pain market.
Actavis' CEO for the US, Doug Boothe:
"Actavis Inc. is a company with deep experience and solid results in pain management. Building on the
success of Kadian®, we believe the QRxPharma partnership offers significant opportunity to leverage the
talent of our team to establish MoxDuo® IR as a preferred option in the US acute pain marketplace. We
believe MoxDuo® IR has tremendous sales potential."
As one of the world's largest manufacturers of branded and generic opioids, Actavis may serve as a
contract supplier for MoxDuo® IR in the US market. Under the terms of the LOI, QRxPharma retains full
flexibility to market MoxDuo IR outside the US.
Dr. John Holaday, Managing Director and CEO, QRxPharma:
"After analysis of several other licensing proposals, it was clear Actavis was the strategic choice for the
Company. Their experience in the manufacturing, distribution, marketing and sales of both patented and
generic opioid products enabled a partnership structure with QRxPharma that will accelerate revenues and
maximise shareholder value."
3

Demir From the Managed Markets perspective, the following approach addresses Mark's points regarding Managed Care (iii in the
first set and iv in the second set) below.
1) Dedication of a new Segment Marketing Manager, Al Weeks, who will work closely with TJ Fuller and will have
responsibility for ensuring that Field Sales is equipped with the knowledge and the appropriate messages to take best
advantage of the access for OPANA ER nationally. This includes both pull through efforts to support contracted accounts and
push through efforts to generate prescriptions in the absence of a contract or advantaged formulary position.
2) Develop and communicate processes and clear, detailed instructions to ensure that representatives and their DMs are
able to target customers that have tier 2 or 3 formulary status without PA, using the tools, such as Reimbursement Viewer
and MC Pull Through Report on Endonet, along with the TREX system and other custom pull-through tools, for incorporating
this information into appropriate call planning.
• DMs would then review on a regular basis the targeting/routing activity for key customers for OPANA ER and provide
a summary report for Sales Management to ensure that appropriate targets are being called upon.
3) Development of workshops to be presented at the POA meetings, beginning in January, that demonstrate for
representatives how to incorporate pull-through messaging in sales calls with key physicians, including PCPs, and reinforce
the need for ongoing DM counseling and follow-up to ensure appropriate execution.
4) To the extent that the use of Managed Markets personnel can be of assistance with key physicians when strong Managed
Care messaging can help move a physician toward either initial prescribing or greater prescribing, develop a process for
making Account Executives or Segment Marketing personnel available for interactions with these key physicians. These
interactions can be either on calls or within other interactions (e.g., dinner programs), with appropriate oversight to
ensure efficient and effective use of these relatively limited Managed Markets resources. We have not done this in a
systematic way and it may help solidify for key physicians the message regarding access for OPANA ER.
The process will remain consistent with the ongoing educational road map or baseline for MC knowledge with primary
care field personnel, will incorporate closer coordination among Segment Marketing, Corporate Accounts, and Field
Sales, and will provide greater confidence for representatives regarding MC pull-through discussions.
These are some of the things we discussed last week. Please let me know if additional information is needed. Thanks.
Art Vrecenak
Sr. Director, Segment Marketing

Guys,
We need an explicit plan of action for driving Opana ER penetration into PCP. While there are a number of issues contributing to slow
penetration into primary care, my conclusions, based on all of the inputs I've seen over the last few months, are that there are three main
factors behind our lack of penetration:
i) Messages are not tailored to address PCPs needs and to succinctly overcome objections
ii) Reps feel unable to close for business (consistent feedback from our own and others' field visits)
iii) We continue to hear that MC access is an issue. However, it's unclear at present whether we are capitalizing on the access we do
have.

C,
I know them all well and worked with them for years at DuPont (Jeff Fetterman, Gary Slatko, Nancy Mayer-Mihalski, and Bill
Lynch (watch out for Bill — he's a bit of a "snake oil salesman" in an RPh disguise....).
Be aware, however, that they are working on the promotional side of the business, and as such, we should not consider them
for any CME stuff...
Also, thanks to pressure from Brian/Tom, they tried VERY HARD to convince me that the CL's could play an important role for
Depo in working with individual hospitals to generate "practice guidelines" or "pathways." I told them IN NO UNCERTAIN
TERMS that while we would be happy to work with a national prof soc such as ASRA or ASA to facilitate development of thirdparty independent guidelines, that we could not (and would not) work with individual institutions.
I explained to them that first of all, that's a hospital rep's job, not a CL's job, and that secondly, we don't even have enough CLs
to handle the national/key regional initiatives that have to be taken care of, let alone getting down to a local level. I think they
"got it" but just be sure they (or Brian/Tom) don't try to box you/Frank into anything like that.
One other item of interest that just came out of a mtg with Scott yesterday (I'll fill all the CLs in soon as I get the final "written"
version from Brad/Scott, but this is good enough for the purposes of your conf call.....) I told Brad/Scott that we absolutely
needed some guidance/priorities as far as what approx % of CD&E time should be devoted to chronic pain vs migraine vs
periop pain vs opioids for 2006.
Here's what came out of the discussion: For base case (until we get oxymorphone approval), it would be something like 60%
on chronic pain (neuropathic, LBP, OA, etc), 30% menstrual migraine, and 10% periop. After oxymorphone approval, it would
shift to something like 35% chronic pain, 35% opioids, 20% menstrual migraine, 10% periop. (this latter scenario is the one
that hasn't yet been finalized)
These would be "national averages," and would vary from CL to CL based upon the project team the CL belongs to, the
opportunities and therapeutic experts located in a given geography, etc. So, for example, you & Frank would spend more than
10% of your time on periop, but less than Vin or Bobbie Sue on chronic pain....etc. Overall, across the team, we'd shoot for the
60%, 30%, 10%.
Bottom line (Scott & I had good conversation on this yesterday, and he is in total agreement) — when it comes to Depo, we can't
afford a lot of time intensive CD&E initiatives. We have to focus our time on developing the top therapeutic experts, and
working with the nat'l prof societies to try to develop initiatives that are going to have "legs" and educate a wide audience. I
told Scott that rather than a lot of personal time, we'd have to rely on obtaining adequate resources to develop impactful
national initatives (e.g. publications, guidelines, key symposia/enduring materials, etc.)
Therefore, the value that I think Paragon Rx can bring to the table is for them to be "surrogate MSLs (not CLs, but the "glorified
hospital rep type of MSL" that Mktg is looking for) and work with the Sales/Mktg side of the business on addressing institutional
issues (e.g. creating a turnkey package that would facilitate institutions getting Depo on board... I'd recommend they talk to
the Chief of Anesth at St. Luke's in Bethlehem who was very clear about what he had to go through: developing his own
training materials for both anesth/nursing, developing materials for P&T, developing orders for how to get the drug
ordered/stored from pharmacy, etc.) If Paragon Rx could develop this "package" which could then be rolled out by the reps, we
could really expedite the process/time needed to get Depo into use once an institution has approved it for formulary.
Sorry for being long-winded, but I knew we wouldn't get to talk before your conf call, so I wanted to just share this background

Attachments: prb042507[1].pdf; prb042507a[1].pdf
Dear All,
Attached please find a press release and accompanying report from the
Senate Finance Committee (SFC) entitled "Use of Educational Grants by
Pharmaceutical Manufacturers." As you know, the SFC's investigation of
educational grant activities has been underway for approximately two
years, and included two rounds of letters requesting voluminous amounts
of information from 23 pharmaceutical manufacturers.
The Committee Staff Report concludes that while companies have adopted
policies to ensure educational grants are provided for lawful and
appropriate purposes, "risks remain for fraud and abuse in several
areas." The Report singles out the following four areas: "(1)
kickbacks, (2) veiled advertising, bias in clinical protocols; and (4)
off-label promotion." (p.16).
The Report includes interesting data about current industry practices
with respect to educational grant activities, including with respect to
accreditation, grant review and approval processes, and funding for
clinical practice guidelines. For example, the Report states:
-"Only one pharmaceutical manufacturer reported allowing field
representatives to collect grant requests from customers." (p.10)
-"With one exception, the major pharmaceutical companies are not
overtly giving educational grants to individual
physicians or physician group practices." (p.17)
The Report also includes data about the volume of grant activities in
2003-05. For example:
-- Educational grant budgets reported by individual companies for 2004
ranged from less than $2 million to $117 million. In 2004, total
expenditures by commercial sponsors to support CME exceeded $1 billion
(p.9).
--18 of the 23 companies providing information to the committee broke
down grant funding by therapeutic area. In 2005, the top therapeutic
areas were oncology ($218 million), cardiovascular disease ($112
million), and neurology/psychology ($104 million).
The Committee press release states that Chairman Max Baucus (D-MT) and
Ranking Member Charles Grassley (R-IA)"will follow up on its findings
with participating drug companies and with organizations that have
issued guidelines for educational grants, including the FDA, the
Inspector General at the Department of Health and Human Services, the
participating drug companies, and ACCME."

from the Strategic Planning Summit for the Advancement of Pain and Palliative Care Pharmacy (attached).
Sponsored by a grant from the Mayday Fund and in-kind support from Southern Illinois
University Edwardsville (SIUE), the Strategic Planning Summit for the Advancement of Pain and Palliative
Care Pharmacy (Summit) was held in October 2009. The Summit was developed by a multidisciplinary
advisory board including pharmacists, physicians and nurses, and was constructed to examine the
education and development of pharmacists on pain and palliative care (PPC) across the entire professional
continuum. Individual working groups were created with specific assigned objectives as they related
to PPC education or assessment of pharmacists or pharmacy students. Each working group developed
recommendations and presented them to the advisory board for adoption and dissemination. Summit
participants included individual invitees as well as professional organization representatives. Eighty
persons attended the Summit with 25 professional stakeholder organizations represented.
The objectives of the summit were:
• Develop curricular recommendations for schools of pharmacy on the delivery of PPC education
• Identify collaborative opportunities with accrediting bodies and licensing boards to assure the
assessment of PPC knowledge
• Recommend general competencies for pharmacists pursuing formal post-graduate education
• Develop a model certificate program for provision of high quality continuing education to pharmacists
in practice, regardless of practice setting (i.e. community, hospital, etc.)
• Reach consensus on best methods for demonstrating expertise in PPC for pharmacists

THERE IS A NEW REPORT FOR OPANA ER. Opana sales will appear in the report as soon as the first Rxs are received. All
products in this report are shown as normalized TRxs.
- All reports are now aligned to the new territories.
A FEW KEY POINTS:
- There are 4 tabs per file: Lidoderm report, Frova report, Opana report and a tab with three line graphs.
- Each report contains TRxs for your call plan doctors individually and a last line for all other profiled prescribers in your
territory combined.
- Manager reports contain summarized data for each of their territories or districts.
- The arrow indicates whether the Lidoderm or Frova TRxs are up or down for the most recent 4 weeks compared to the
previous 4 weeks.
- This information should be close to, but not the same as, your monthly IC TRxs. Weekly TRxs are provided to help you
monitor your prescribers, but IC is based on final monthly data.
- Weekly data is naturally more volatile than monthly data. Please do not overreact to week-to-week changes.
- When opening your report in Excel, click the "Enable Macros" button. This is necessary to turn on some of the features of
the report.
TO SORT THE REPORTS:
- Above the Endo logo, there will be a toolbar with 4 pull-down lists and three buttons.
- The lists work in pairs to allow you to sort by one or two fields.
- The buttons will apply or remove the sort you choose.
- You can sort by Prescriber Name, Prescriber ID, Specialty, Zip Code, Current Week TRx, Current Four Week or Prior 13
week total TRx in either Ascending or Descending order. The default order is Ascending.
- In the first drop-down list on the left, select the primary sort field.
- In the second drop-down list, select the order for the primary sort field.
- (Optional) In the third drop-down list, select the secondary sort field.
- (Optional) In the fourth drop-down list, select the order for the secondary sort field.
- When you have specified your sort options, click the "Sort" button to apply the sort.
- If you want to return to the original sort order, click the "Reset" button.
- The "Exit" button will close the report.
TO PRINT:
- The report and graph tabs are already formatted for reporting.
- To print any tab, click the "File" menu and choose "Print...".
- When the print window opens, select the options you want and click the "Print" button.
Please DO NOT reply to this email or call WK. If you have any questions about this file, please contact Chris Speaker by email
(speaker.chris@endo.com) or phone (x4052).

RESTRICTED DATA:
- New data restrictions were implemented with the data reports for week ending August 11. There are two different
restrictions affecting the pharmaceutical industry: one in New Hampshire, and the other nationwide based upon an AMA
Opt-Out (PDRP) program.
- In New Hampshire, we cannot show Rxs for any physician who prescribes in that state. We also cannot show any Rxs that
are filled in NH but are written by prescribers in other states. We WILL have this data at the zip code level for IC purposes.
- In the rest of the country, we cannot show Rx data for any physician who has asked the AMA to restrict the use of their
information. These prescribers will be listed at the bottom of the report. We WILL have this information for use in calculating
IC, but will not be able to share it with anyone in the field.
- We will continue to show the historical data for prescribers in both categories.
A FEW KEY POINTS:
- There are 4 tabs per file: Lidoderm report, Frova report, Opana report and a tab with three line graphs.
- Each report contains TRxs for your call plan doctors individually and a last line for all other profiled prescribers in your
territory combined.
- Manager reports contain summarized data for each of their territories or districts.
- The arrow indicates whether the Lidoderm or Frova TRxs are up or down for the most recent 4 weeks compared to the
previous 4 weeks.
- This information should be close to, but not the same as, your monthly IC TRxs. Weekly TRxs are provided to help you
monitor your prescribers, but IC is based on final monthly data.
- Weekly data is naturally more volatile than monthly data. Please do not overreact to week-to-week changes.
- When opening your report in Excel, click the "Enable Macros" button. This is necessary to turn on some of the features of
the report.
TO SORT THE REPORTS:
- Above the Endo logo, there will be a toolbar with 4 pull-down lists and three buttons.
- The lists work in pairs to allow you to sort by one or two fields.
- The buttons will apply or remove the sort you choose.
- You can sort by Prescriber Name, Prescriber ID, Specialty, Zip Code, Current Week TRx, Current Four Week or Prior 13
week total TRx in either Ascending or Descending order. The default order is Ascending.
- In the first drop-down list on the left, select the primary sort field.
- In the second drop-down list, select the order for the primary sort field.
- (Optional) In the third drop-down list, select the secondary sort field.
- (Optional) In the fourth drop-down list, select the order for the secondary sort field.
- When you have specified your sort options, click the "Sort" button to apply the sort.
- If you want to return to the original sort order, click the "Reset" button.
- The "Exit" button will close the report.
TO PRINT:
- The report and graph tabs are already formatted for reporting.
- To print any tab, click the "File" menu and choose "Print...".
- When the print window opens, select the options you want and click the "Print" button.
Please DO NOT reply to this email or call WK. If you have any questions about this file, please contact Chris Speaker by

Endo Pain Solutions Sales Team,

Endo announced Second Quarter 2011 Financial Results: Second Quarter revenue increased 53% to $607.6M from
$396.5M same quarter 2010. Second quarter adjusted net income rose 36% to $128.7M from $94.7M same quarter
2010.
Over the past quarter, we've successfully completed the acquisition of AMS, a leading provider of world-class devices
and therapies for male and female pelvic health. AMS brings Endo scale in its device and services business segment,
and the combination of AMS and Endo's existing platform will provide additional cost effective solutions across the
entire urology platform. In the branded segment, brand pain sales rose 8% year-over-year with Opana ER growing
64% and Voltaren Gel growing 39%. In the generics segment, Qualitest announced approval of three generic
products: dexamethasone elixir, USP, 0.5mg/5mL, Orsythia tablets, and telmisartan/HCTZ tablets. In R&D, the FDA
accepted Endo's Complete Response for the New Formulation of Opana ER with a PDUFA date of December 13,
2011.
Very strong performance by the Pain Solutions Team,
Thank you,
Larry Romaine

Weekly Retail Report - 310501 - for the Week Ending February 2, 2007
END01_112948_310501_20070202.xls

RESTRICTED DATA:
- Data restrictions were implemented with the data reports for week ending August 11, 2006. There are two different
restrictions affecting the pharmaceutical industry: one in New Hampshire, and the other nationwide based upon an AMA
Opt-Out (PDRP) program.
- In New Hampshire, we cannot show Rxs for any physician who prescribes in that state. We also cannot show any Rxs that
are filled in NH but are written by prescribers in other states. We WILL have this data at the zip code level for IC purposes.
- In the rest of the country, we cannot show Rx data for any physician who has asked the AMA to restrict the use of their
information. These prescribers will be listed at the bottom of the report. We WILL have this information for use in calculating
IC, but will not be able to share it with anyone in the field.
- We will continue to show the historical data for prescribers in both categories.
A FEW KEY POINTS:
- There are 4 tabs per file: Lidoderm report, Frova report, Opana report and a tab with three line graphs.
- Each report contains TRxs for your call plan doctors individually and a last line for all other profiled prescribers in your
territory combined.
- Manager reports contain summarized data for each of their territories or districts.
- The arrow indicates whether the Lidoderm or Frova TRxs are up or down for the most recent 4 weeks compared to the
previous 4 weeks.
- This information should be close to, but not the same as, your monthly IC TRxs. Weekly TRxs are provided to help you
monitor your prescribers, but IC is based on final monthly data.
- Weekly data is naturally more volatile than monthly data. Please do not overreact to week-to-week changes.
- When opening your report in Excel, click the "Enable Macros" button. This is necessary to turn on some of the features of
the report.
TO SORT THE REPORTS:
- Above the Endo logo, there will be a toolbar with 4 pull-down lists and three buttons.
- The lists work in pairs to allow you to sort by one or two fields.
- The buttons will apply or remove the sort you choose.
- You can sort by Prescriber Name, Prescriber ID, Specialty, Zip Code, Current Week TRx, Current Four Week or Prior 13
week total TRx in either Ascending or Descending order. The default order is Ascending.
- In the first drop-down list on the left, select the primary sort field.
- In the second drop-down list, select the order for the primary sort field.
- (Optional) In the third drop-down list, select the secondary sort field.
- (Optional) In the fourth drop-down list, select the order for the secondary sort field.
- When you have specified your sort options, click the "Sort" button to apply the sort.
- If you want to return to the original sort order, click the "Reset" button.
- The "Exit" button will close the report.
TO PRINT:
- The report and graph tabs are already formatted for reporting.
- To print any tab, click the "File" menu and choose "Print...".
- When the print window opens, select the options you want and click the "Print" button.
Please DO NOT reply to this email or call WK. If you have any questions about this file, please contact Chris Speaker by
email
(speakerchris@endo.com) or phone (x4052).

7/20/2009 2:13:57 AM
UCD - SF Pain Conf...first day news!

Hi y'all —
Sunday was the first day of the UCD-SF Pain Conf and we're off to a good start.
There were about 140 pre-registered attendees and more people doing same-day registration at the desk. The
anticipated total is 200 attendees.
First day, we are the only pharmaceutical company displaying, so we had steady traffic by the table. The
physicians, nurses, physical therapists, and psychologists who came our display either asked really good
questions about our products, seemed genuinely interested in learning more about the medications, or provided
good feedback on the efficacy of our medications as they use them with their patients. (It's always nice to get
good feedback about our medicines and the benefits they bring patients.)
Highlights:
Bobbie-Sue Brown is participating in the conference as attendee... and getting to know some key
participants... like....
Jeffrey Reinking, MD (Yippee!) and his associates Robert Kelly Otani, MD and Linda Glazier, NP.
Had time with Drs Scott Fishman and Gagan Mahajan from UCDavis Dept Anesthesia & Pain Medicine.
Discussed Dr Charles Argoff coming out here Oct 1 and they are looking forward to seeing him.
Munish Lal, MD from Chico Pain Clinic is an attendee, spent time speaking with us at the booth extolling
Lidoderm's benefits and is signed up for the breakout session taught by Daniel Rockers, PhD on use of hypnosis
in the management of chronic pain.
Physicians from Kaiser (Oakland & Vallejo) stopped by the table to ask questions about Opana-ER. They told us
that Kaiser pharmacy has done an excellent job of instructing Kaiser physicians about how to dose, convert, and
titrate Opana-ER because the physicians have been instructed to convert OxyContin patients to Opana-ER.
Opana-ER is on Kaiser formulary and is in preferred position ahead of OxyContin. (Yeah!) Their questions
revolved about understanding the food effect, for the most part. Also of interest, the Kaiser doctors said they saw
great benefit for their patients from Lidoderm and were willing to do the necessary paperwork to get Lidoderm for
them as Lidoderm is a non-formulary medication.
Family Practice doctor, Alhers/Albers (sp?) from Minden, NV is very interested in learning more about Opana-ER.
She had not heard of this medication, asked questions, took literature, and said she would come back to the booth
with more questions through the duration of the conference. She said she doesn't get to see many reps as she is
in a small clinic in the very rural area around Minden, NV.
Other interesting feedback comments include being familiar with Voltaren Gel because it has been available
overseas for many years... learned about it there... now glad it is here... and Frova is rooted in many physician
minds as the triptan that starts slowly, lasts a long time and is great for their long-duration migraine sufferers.
That's all folks (at least from me!),
-Cherry

Subject: Weekly Report Week Ending February 6th 2004
Good Morning,
Attached are the weekly reports of prescription and tablet activity for the week
ending 2/6/2004. Please use caution when interpreting weekly numbers.
For the WE 2/6/2004 Lidoderm TRx's were up +9.2% to an all time high 32,524
prescriptions from 29,789 prescriptions the previous week. New Rx's were up +9.4%
for the week, while Refill Rx's were up +8.8%. Lidoderm dispensed patches were up
+9.7 for the week.

For the WE 2/6/2004, the total 7.5/325 and 10/325 market, brand and generic, was
up +8.8% to 50,445 prescriptions from 46,366 prescriptions the previous week.
Percocet 7.5/325 and 10/325 scripts were up +6.7% to 13,743 prescriptions from
12,875 prescriptions the previous week. Generic 7.5/325 and 10/325 variants
captured 72.8% share of the total 7.5/325 and 10/325 market for the week. Within
the generic 7.5/325 and 10/325 market Endocet has 57.3% share while Watson's
Oxycodone APAP has 42.7% share of the generic market.
Percocet 2.5 mg prescriptions were up +9.0% to 1,040 scripts from 954 scripts the
previous week, 2.5mg tablets were up +13.6% for the week.

In comparison, the total Oxycodone market and the Oxycodone Acetaminophen markets
were up +8.5% and +6.3% respectively for the week, Total Percocet scripts were up
+7.3% for the week, and total Oxycontin scripts were up +14.8% for the week
For the week ending 2/6/2004 the Long Acting Morphine market was up 13.3%. Endo
captured 77.4% share of the total market, while share for all other generics was
13.4%.

For the WE 2/6/2004 the Hydrocodone market was up +4.8%

Please let me know if you have any questions.

Date:

Tuesday, January 20 2004 11:23 PM

Subject: Bob Barkin Review
From:

Aron, Carey

To:

Kitlinski, Linda <Kitlinski.Linda@Endo.com>;

CC:

Tormo, Vin <Tormo.Vin@Endo.com >;

Linda,
Vin and I were able to speak live about this today, but I wanted you to also have the info...
Bob spoke for almost 2 hours on The Pharmacological Treatment of Pain: Opioid and Non-opioid at the Pain Management
Seminar jointly sponsored by AAPMed, the CA Assn of Neurological Surgeons, and the Assn of CA Neurologists this weekend
in S. Cal.
Bob is an extremely knowledgeable pharmacologist and that certainly came through in this very educational presentation. As
one attendee told me "Bob was able to wrap the entire world of pain pharmacology into one neat 90 minute package".
Couple of flaws noted in Bob's presentation 'style' (nobody's perfect!) - he does come off as being a bit pompous, but it is
tolerable in comparison with certain other pompous presenters who make it almost painful to sit through a presentation. Also,
probably because this was a presentation that Bob has given innumerable times before, he comes across as a bit 'overrehearsed'. His presentation style is rapid-fire anyway, and when he rattles off various lists, they are done with such rapidity
that anyone who might be trying to take notes might as well just throw away their pencil.
Those comments aside, Bob was tremendous when it came to elucidating the positive attributes of both Lidoderm AND
oxymorphone. As I wrote in a previous message to Deb T, she should seriously consider Bob for upcoming 3202 ad boards he would be a valuable addition. Based upon his Lidoderm comments, I would certainly not turn him down when an
opportunity to support a talk on NP or other topic where Lido will be covered is involved. (VIN - he does, however, need to
correct his title slide from "transdermal" to "topical" - I hope you have quicker success with that than I've had with Scott F on the
same issue!!!!).
Did you know that he "coined" the term opioiphobia in the late 50s/early 60s? At least, HE thinks he didiiiiiiiiii
Another tip for Vin - Bob's boss at Rush is Anthony Ivankovitch (anesth) who very well may want to become involved with
DepoMorphine in the future.
Thanks for listening!!
C

Subject: What's going on? Another PFE buyout?

2. Report: Endo, in a world of hurt, may be looking for a savior
By Eric Palmer Comment I Forward I Twitter I Facebook I LinkedIn
Endo Health Solutions' ($ENDP) is feeling the generics pain this year as its key products face copycats and that may
be enough to have sent it looking for a buyer.
Reuters, citing unnamed sources, says the pain drug specialist in recent weeks has had conversations with potential
suitors, including Warner Chilcott ($WCRX) and serial buyer Valeant Pharmaceuticals International ($VRX). The
news service said the talks are preliminary and no official "auction" process has yet been started. There are no
comments from any of those players.
In December, the company downgraded its earnings prospects and announced that CEO David P. Holveck would
retire by May. After the report surfaced of a possible buyout, 113S analysts told clients that they wouldn't be
surprised, since "The company is searching for a new CEO and a potential sale of the company quite often
accompanies this process."
Endo's best-selling product, a Lidoderm pain-relieving patch, will face generic competition later this year as its Opana
ER already does. Endo tried to forestall generic competition by kicking dirt all over its original formulation of Opana
ER and trying to force the FDA to declare it unsafe. It wanted the agency to require generics makers to provide
tamper-proof versions like Endo is now doing. But a judge found its argument wanting and copycats have already
been launched in Canada.
The FDA is in the midst of deciding if it will require opioid makers to produce only tamper-resistant drugs that can
help deter drug addicts from abusing the popular prescription painkillers. It will hold hearings this month to collect
information about how that might best be done. That decision is some months, or more, away and by then it might be
to the benefit of whoever then owns Endo.

CHRONIC PAIN

Covidien Receives FDA Approval for Morphine Sulfate Oral
Solution
• In hospital oral morphine sulfate therapy - Competitor to Endo's
generic morphine sulfate extended release tablets
ST. LOUIS--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug 1, 2011 - Covidien (NYSE: COV), a leading global provider of
healthcare products, today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recently
granted approval to the company's Mallinckrodt business for morphine sulfate oral solution, used to
relieve moderate to severe acute and chronic pain in opioid-tolerant patients. The solution will be
available as a generic in 100 milligrams per 5 mL (20 milligrams per 1 mL).
"FDA approval of this drug represents a key component in palliative care treatment," said Matthew
Harbaugh, Chief Financial Officer and Interim President, Pharmaceuticals, Covidien. "It is important
that we are able to respond to the concerns of the hospice and palliative care community."
Morphine sulfate oral solution has been used to manage pain for many years, and Mallinckrodt
began marketing the 20 milligram per 1 mL strength in 2005. Prior to 2010, however, this form and
concentration of morphine had never been approved by the FDA.
In April, 2009, the FDA announced that manufacturers could keep morphine sulfate oral solution on
the market, but only until the product was approved, or an equivalent, approved therapy was
available. Accordingly, upon approval of a new drug application (NDA) by another manufacturer in
January 2010, Mallinckrodt removed its product from the market. Mallinckrodt undertook the current
approval process to ensure adequate supply of this medication to patients.

• New U.S. contract sales agreement with unknown pharmaceutical
company for knee pain therapy - Competition with Voltaren Gel
PARSIPPANY, N.J., Aug. 1, 2011 /PRNewswire/ PDI, Inc. (Nasdaq: PDII) today announced that,
through a newly formed business unit, Interpace BioPharma, LLC, it has entered into a two-anda-half-year, fee-for-service agreement with a pharmaceutical company to market in the United States
and its territories a treatment for pain of the knee.
The agreement is expected to generate approximately $10 million of revenues to PDI in 2011 and
$55 million over the life of the contract. The agreement, which runs through December 31, 2013,
includes an option for a contract extension. Under the agreement, Interpace will provide a dedicated
full-time sales team and a fully integrated strategic and operational management team that, together
with the pharmaceutical company, are responsible for the U.S. commercialization of the product.
"This major new agreement reflects the expanding capabilities of PDI and our commitment to
growour company through new service offerings like those delivered through Interpace BioPharma,"
said Nancy Lurker, PDI's Chief Executive Officer. "In promoting this pain therapy, we intend to
demonstrate again the value and strategic flexibility that PDI can deliver to clients while gaining an
additional and steady source of revenue for PDI. PDI now has the ability to offer clients the
opportunity to outsource the full range of PDI's product commercialization services, thus providing a
compelling option beyond traditional co-promotion deals or out-licensing agreements. We look
forward to realizing the full potential of this opportunity."
PDI established Interpace BioPharma, LLC as part of its ongoing strategy for managing new
commercial platforms, such as today's agreement. Interpace is structured to provide the flexibility for
additional fee-for-service agreements and other product commercialization opportunities.

CO-PAY CARD VENDORS

Do the co-pay card vendors that we identified in the Implementation

of co-pay cards?

In our September 12, 2014, letter to you, we identified the following two vendors that
Endo considered Covered Persons: (1) Market Share Movers LLC and (2) TrialCard.
These two vendors assist Endo with its co-pay card programs. Endo contracts with
Market Share Movers LLC in relation to its Frovat, Opanat, and Voltaren Gel® copay card programs and TrialCard in relation to its Sumavel® co-pay card program.

Endo policy is to only distribute co-pay cards and related program materials to health
care professionals ("HCPs") on the current call plan (i.e., the universe of physicians
eligible to be called on as determined by the HCP's specialty). Endo considers copay cards and the related program materials (e.g., Business Reply Cards) to be
promotional materials. As such, co-pay card program materials are subject to the
restrictions around distribution applicable to other promotional materials.

materials during calls to HCPs on his or her call plan. When these materials are
distributed by Endo through direct mail, Endo's Promotional Planning team verifies

Bret:
I participated in the quarterly Compliance Teleconference today. Here are the items we discussed that could be
relevant to the region:
Representatives should take all appropriate steps to guard against calling on excluded clinicians for Lidoderm
and Opana. The Compliance and Sales Operations teams have discussed greying-out' excluded clinicians so
that reps will not be able to make calls on them. Sales Operations is reviewing this for technical feasibility.
PAs with a Ghost-busters (0) sign attached to their names but supervised by a non-excluded clinician are
excluded from being called on by representatives.
Non-excluded PAs supervised by excluded clinicians are not to be called on as well for the specified product.
In case of inadvertent sampling, promptly report the situation (clinician, product, number of samples left for
clinician and the date) to the compliance team and the samples compliance team (John Doyle and Tracy
McAleenan). Please let Bret know as well.
Some offices in some parts of the country are asking reps to sign documents to gain access to clinicians.
Please refer such cases to the compliance team. No one should sign any documents since legal has a review
process in place for such requests.
Compliance and marketing has discussed bringing back Voltaren gel stampers. The marketing team is
reviewing the request.
Reps may have lunch with a speaker clinician who is conducting a "specialist-for-a-day" program.
Representatives cannot have meals with clinicians outside their normal practicing office. Late, after-hours
meals in an office, served with alcohol, may create an atmosphere of a `happy hour.' Please discourage your
reps from any such activity.

All,
As you know, NY Medicaid has shifted approximately 3Million lives into Managed Medicaid plans. In
response to this event, I would like to propose that we take advantage of the communication opportunity
of this event by considering the following:
1. Select targets to communicate the favorable formulary status changes for OPANA, Lidoderm and
VGel. We have selected a 4000 doc target list that is based upon the following parameters:
a. Limited to doctors with at least 20% of their TRx in NY Medicaid
b. Selected doctors that had at least 2 NY Medicaid Market TRx per month in PHN and LAO.
For VGEL we went to 50TRX per month
c. Understand and implement a plan to deal with targets that show utilization for two or more
of products in our portfolio ( example, Dr. Smith writes for Opana , Lidoderm and or VGel
d. We have identified multi targets among all brands - LAO=322 out of 461 ; PHN = 1259 out
of 1618 and OA=1001 out of 2,842
2. Execute a rapid response program that will perform the following task:
a. Communicate the change in NY Medicaid
b. Communicate the change in a way that will allow for multi product interactions. In the
following manor:
i. Identify the change in NY Medicaid
ii. Offer to send information mail/fax
iii. Follow-up with target after information has been received
iv. Offer to have a rep visit
The approximate cost of implementing a rapid response program will be $150k for 4000 targets. There
will also need to be a concept review with MARC to facilitate an understanding regarding our strategy for
our multi target approach. The strategy overall will be to communicate the change in NY Medicaid and
forward product information via mail and or fax during the first contact, then follow-up with messaging
during the second call. The critical factors to this initiative will be the following:
1. Approval of funding
2. MARC approval with the initiative communication strategy

Please contact me with any questions and recommendations for moving forward.

This provides an overview regarding my 'field visit' with David Branch, Dallas Texas. David
made several calls to 'high' decile pharmacies providing them with introductory information for
Belbuca. The response was favorable from the pharmacists, some who stated they were looking
forward to stocking the product due to many patients being prescribed buprenorphine.
Pharmacists asked which strengths they needed to stock and David responded by stating he
would provide that information once he begins promoting the product.

1

upper and lower extremities.

Guide, dosing/titration and the rough draft MVA. We focused more so on the Belbuca PI, the
clinical studies, 12 week studies for Opioid-Naive, Opioid-Experienced Patients with lower back

Subject: Leadership Advisory Board Meeting Notes
NE Leaders,
Below are my notes from today's Leadership Advisory Board conference call with Larry. Thanks for all the feedback
you provided leading up to the call!
Consensus is less field reps, more offices closed to reps, more flow of reps to higher deciled targets
What's worked well in past might not work at all in future — need to change the way we do business
3 key objectives: 1.42 billion, grow market share, create culture of accountability — continue to reinforce with
reps
Discussed value of the PHN target listing — consensus is PHN targets don't offer a lot of new opportunity —
hope is that there will be 4 or 5 solid targets — have to give them time, don't give up too soon but have a sense
of urgency in growing them.
What's worked following the POA?
o Better utilization of the OER patient profiles
o Better utilization of the TBR
o Appreciation of more steady flow of reports: RTLs, rebate redemptions, etc...
Challenges we need more help with:
o Competitive selling tools (similar to the OER Messaging Tool)
Comfort isn't an option in our business: we all should always be hungry to overcome obstacles
Mandated changes to APAP will probably take years - shouldn't have a concern about Percocet or it affecting
the health of Endo
Q&A:
o Any thought on giving credit back to Opana IR? Yes but we won't do it. Our future is with ER. Larry will
communicate to the sales force shortly.
o Sales force realignment — all under one RD? Lot of things being done to optimize our business right
now. Last time we changed was 2006. Right now there aren't specific plans in place for a change. We
are looking at what smaller changes (without reductions) could be made to better serve the customer.
o IC Comp — need to overhaul our entire IC program — more of a level setting between field forces
(possibly as early as 2010)

of interest for MTM at Humana, but so was PHN and other neuropathic type of pain (with a focus on diabetes I'm sure there is
also a focus on diabetic neuropathic pain). Plans are looking for patients that are receiving Pregabalin, Neurontin, Lidoderm,
etc. and focusing on providing MTM for pain. There would be an interest in a program specific to PHN—it would be a smaller
potential group of patients, but there is nothing available right now that focuses on this disease state.
The program should be patient-focused, primarily phone followed-up by mail. I will be talking with Si in the next few days to
develop our ideas in greater detail and also determine which components from the existing INFORM program could/should be

Weekly Retail Report - 310502 - for the Week Ending April 20, 2007
END01_112948_310502_20070420.xls

RESTRICTED DATA:
- Data restrictions were implemented with the data reports for week ending August 11, 2006. There are two different
restrictions affecting the pharmaceutical industry: one in New Hampshire, and the other nationwide based upon an AMA
Opt-Out (PDRP) program.
- In New Hampshire, we cannot show Rxs for any physician who prescribes in that state. We also cannot show any Rxs that
are filled in NH but are written by prescribers in other states. We WILL have this data at the zip code level for IC purposes.
- In the rest of the country, we cannot show Rx data for any physician who has asked the AMA to restrict the use of their
information. These prescribers will be listed at the bottom of the report. We WILL have this information for use in calculating
IC, but will not be able to share it with anyone in the field.
- We will continue to show the historical data for prescribers in both categories.
A FEW KEY POINTS:
- There are 4 tabs per file: Lidoderm report, Frova report, Opana report and a tab with three line graphs.
- Each report contains TRxs for your call plan doctors individually and a last line for all other profiled prescribers in your
territory combined.
- Manager reports contain summarized data for each of their territories or districts.
- The arrow indicates whether the Lidoderm or Frova TRxs are up or down for the most recent 4 weeks compared to the
previous 4 weeks.
- This information should be close to, but not the same as, your monthly IC TRxs. Weekly TRxs are provided to help you
monitor your prescribers, but IC is based on final monthly data.
- Weekly data is naturally more volatile than monthly data. Please do not overreact to week-to-week changes.
- When opening your report in Excel, click the "Enable Macros" button. This is necessary to turn on some of the features of
the report.
TO SORT THE REPORTS:
- Above the Endo logo, there will be a toolbar with 4 pull-down lists and three buttons.
- The lists work in pairs to allow you to sort by one or two fields.
- The buttons will apply or remove the sort you choose.
- You can sort by Prescriber Name, Prescriber ID, Specialty, Zip Code, Current Week TRx, Current Four Week or Prior 13
week total TRx in either Ascending or Descending order. The default order is Ascending.
- In the first drop-down list on the left, select the primary sort field.
- In the second drop-down list, select the order for the primary sort field.
- (Optional) In the third drop-down list, select the secondary sort field.
- (Optional) In the fourth drop-down list, select the order for the secondary sort field.
- When you have specified your sort options, click the "Sort" button to apply the sort.
- If you want to return to the original sort order, click the "Reset" button.
- The "Exit" button will close the report.
TO PRINT:
- The report and graph tabs are already formatted for reporting.
- To print any tab, click the "File" menu and choose "Print...".
- When the print window opens, select the options you want and click the "Print" button.

From:

Team Epic- FYI, so you're aware of changes made to the Tricare co-pays. The bottom-line is a $3 change for our products — all
tier coverage for our products will stay the same. Let me know if you hear of any concerns from your customers.
Marcia

As of October 1, 2011, Tricare Management has made several changes that will impact copayment for both mail and retail RX
fills. Asa point of reference, Tricare's copayment program is administered and managed by Tricare. The changes below should
not have any impact on the marketing and selling of Endo's product portfolio. The most significant change is that the copay will
go from $9 to $12 for branded drugs in retail pharmacies.

Tricare Changes:
Tricare Retail Rx
•

Generic formulary drugs purchased at retail pharmacies will go from $3 to $5.

•

Brand name formulary drugs from retail pharmacies will go from $9 to $12.

•

Copayment is for 30-day supply when purchased at a retail pharmacy.

TMOP/Mail/Home Delivery Rx
•

Brand name formulary drugs purchased through Home Delivery will have the same $9 copayment.

•

Generic formulary drugs filled via home delivery are now zero copay versus $3 previously

•

Copayments for prescriptions filled through Home Delivery cover a 90-day supply

•

Non-formulary medications will go from $22 to $25 in both retail and Home Delivery

Summary of Impact on Endo Products

• This change will be applied to Opana ER, Lidoderm, Voltaren Gel and Fortesta (T2/Uniform
Formulary) making the copay $12 instead of $9
• Frova (T3 non formulary) will change to $25 from $22
• Specialty products, Valstar, Vantas and Supprelin LA are still available via the DoD nonformulary request process at the local DoD facility

MEMPHIS, TN - Drug Enforcement Administration

agents arrested a doctor and charged him with writing illegal prescriptions after a raid at a

D.E.A. agents and Shelby County Sheriff's Deputies raided Wickman Family Medical Care in the 8400 block of Highway 64, Friday, October 30,
2009.
According to a news release issued by the Department of Justice, 57-year-old Daniel Fearnow was indicted on 12 counts of illegally issuing
prescriptions. Fearnow is accused of conspiring to distribute controlled substances by writing prescriptions "for drugs outside the normal course
of practice and for no legitimate medical purpose," the news release stated.
Authorities say Fearnow, on several occasions between February and October 2009, prescribed Oxycodone, Lortab and Alprazolam (Xanax).
This is not the first time Wickman Family Medical Care has been scrutinized by law enforcement. In June of 2009 Dr. John Wickman's medical
license was suspended for six months after he was accused of "unwanted and inappropriate sexual conduct" with two of his patients. According
to the Tennessee State Medical Board, the alleged attacks happened in 2007 and April of 2008. The suspension came after a previous
complaint, of an unknown nature, was filed.
Authorities say Wickman admitted himself into a treatment program for sex addiction earlier this year. Wickman will be able to file a petition to
practice medicine again after his six month suspension is completed.
Department of Justice :
Memphis Doctor Arrested and Charged with Illegally Writing Prescriptions
Memphis, TN- Daniel Fearnow, 57 of Cordova, has been charged in a 12 count indictment charging him with illegally issuing prescriptions
announced Lawrence J. Laurenzi, United States Attorney for the Western District of Tennessee, Keith Brown, Resident Agent in Charge of the
Drug Enforcement Administration , and Mark Luttrell, Sheriff of Shelby County. The indictment was unsealed today after Fearnow was arrested.
According to the indictment, Fearnow was licensed as a medical doctor and operated a medical practice in Shelby County. Fearnow was
currently practicing at Wickman Family Medical Care located on Hwy 64 in Memphis. The indictment alleges that Fearnow, from February 2009
to October 2009, conspired to distribute Schedule II, III, and IV controlled substances by issuing written prescriptions for drugs outside the
normal course of practice and for no legitimate medical purpose. Allegedly, Fearnow illegally wrote prescriptions on several occasions for
Oxycodone, Lortab, and Alprazolam (Xanax). Federal Regulations prohibit prescribing and dispensing of controlled substances when not in the
normal course of treatment according to Title 21, Code of Federal Regulations, Section 1306.4.
Fearnow is charged with six counts of illegally writing prescriptions for a Schedule II drug. Each of those counts carries a penalty of up to 20
years in prison. Fearnow is charged with two counts of illegally writing prescriptions for a Schedule III drug. Each of those counts carries a
penalty of up to five years in prison. Additionally, Fearnow is charged with three counts of illegally writing prescriptions of Schedule IV drugs.
Each of those counts carries a penalty of up to three years in prison. The Conspiracy charge carries a penalty of up to 20 years in prison.

Endo Pharmaceuticals Launches FORTESTA(TM) (Testosterone)
Gel for Topical Use Class Ill for Adult Men in the U.S. With Low
Testosterone
CHADDS FORD, Pa., March 3, 2011 /PRNewswire/ -- Endo Pharmaceuticals (Nasdaq: ENDP)
announced that FORTESTA Gel recently approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the
treatment of low testosterone, or 'Low T in adult males is now available by prescription in
pharmacies across the country. The clear, colorless and odorless gel comes in a small (60 g)
canister with a pump that delivers 10 mg of testosterone with each actuation (pump). FORTESTA
Gel is applied once-a-day with one finger directly to the front and inner thighs not to the upper
body.
The introduction of FORTESTA Gel in the U.S. comes at a time when only about 1.3 million (9
percent) of the estimated 14 million men with Low T are actually receiving treatment.
"We are excited to bring FORTESTA Gel to market in the United States and are confident that once
men try it, FORTESTA Gel will quickly become a significant treatment option for many men with Low
T," said Julie McHugh, Chief Operating Officer, Endo Pharmaceuticals. "Endo is committed to
providing additional treatment options for the millions of men with Low T who are currently not being
adequately treated for the condition."
In a 90-day, multicenter, open-label, non-comparative, pivotal Phase III trial involving men with
hypogonadism, 78 percent of patients using FORTESTA Gel had an average testosterone blood level
within the normal range at day 90. The most common side effect in this trial was application site
reactions.
Back to Top

Opioid Pain News Releases

ZX002 (Hydrocodone) Clinical Update
(From March 3, 2011 press release) Zogenix has completed enrollment in the Phase 3 safety (Study
802) and efficacy (Study 801) trials of ZX002, a novel, oral capsule, single-entity, controlled release
formulation of hydrocodone for the treatment of moderate to severe chronic pain in patients requiring
around-the-clock opioid therapy for an extended period of time. Results from the Phase 3 efficacy
trial are anticipated in the third quarter of 2011.
Pending positive Phase 3 clinical results, Zogenix expects to submit a new drug application (NDA) for
ZX002 with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) by early 2012. If approved, ZX002 has the
potential to be the first oral controlled-release version of hydrocodone and also the first hydrocodone
product that is not combined with another analgesic.
Stephen J. Farr, Ph.D., president and chief operating officer of Zogenix, said, "ZX002 does not
contain acetaminophen, which can cause liver toxicity at high doses over time, and may address the
FDA and the public's safety concerns surrounding acetaminophen-containing prescription pain
products. Clinical studies of ZX002 to date have demonstrated a pharmacokinetic profile that
supports twice-daily dosing. We believe ZX002 represents a beneficial treatment option for patients
using immediate-release hydrocodone combination products on a chronic basis, and an alternative for

NUCYNTA® ER (tapentadol extended-release tablets) Receives FDA
Approval for the Management of Moderate to Severe Chronic Pain
Clinical Trial Data Demonstrate Efficacy, Safety and Favorable Tolerability
Raritan, N.J., August 26, 2011 /PRNewswire/ — Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Inc. today announced the U.S. Food and
Drug Administration (FDA) has approved NUCYNTA ® ER, an oral analgesic taken twice daily, for the management of
moderate to severe chronic pain in adults when a continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extended
period of time.
Although the exact prevalence is unknown, information from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the
American Pain Foundation suggests that more than 42 million Americans age 20 and over suffer from chronic pain. Chronic
pain is the most common cause of long-term disability, and almost one-third of all Americans will experience severe chronic
pain at some point in their lives. Yet despite the treatments available, additional treatment options still are needed to help
patients manage their pain appropriately and effectively, according to research published by the American Pain Society.
"In clinical trials, NUCYNTA ® ER demonstrated proven efficacy for treating moderate to severe chronic pain," said Paul
Chang, M.D., Vice President, Medical Affairs, Internal Medicine, Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Inc. "We are pleased with the
FDA's decision to approve NUCYNTA ® ER as it represents an important new option to help people with chronic pain."
Johnson & Johnson Pharmaceutical Research & Development, L.L.C. and GrOnenthal GmbH, a privately-owned
pharmaceutical company based in Aachen, Germany, conducted the double-blind, randomized, active- and/or placebocontrolled phase 3 studies that evaluated the efficacy and safety of NUCYNTA ® ER for the treatment of moderate to severe
chronic low back pain and painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Additionally, safety also was evaluated in more than
1,100 patients with moderate to severe chronic pain over a one-year period. The findings demonstrate efficacy and safety,
a favorable tolerability profile and favorable discontinuation rates.
"Chronic pain is difficult to manage, and even with the treatments available today, it can be a challenge to balance pain
relief with a patient's ability to tolerate the medicine," said Sunil J. Panchal, M.D., President, National Institute of Pain.*
"People with chronic pain will continue to need additional options, so an approval like this is welcome news for this
community and the people who suffer from this often debilitating condition."
To support the appropriate and effective management of chronic pain, Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Inc. believes it is also
essential to support educational programs about the safe and responsible use of pain medicines and the prevention of
inappropriate use.
Since 2008, the company has supported educational programs that reach a range of audiences, including patients,
physicians, caregivers, parents, teens and educators. These include: Prescribe Responsibly
www.PrescribeResponsiblv.com ) for physicians seeking information on the appropriate prescribing of opioid pain
medications; the Let's Talk Pain Coalition (www.LetsTalkPain.orq ) to help enhance communication between patients with

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_MA_00201605

 pain, caregivers and physicians; and Smart Moves, Smart Choices (www.SmartMovesSmartChoices.orq ) to increase
awareness among educators, parents and teens about the serious problem of teen prescription drug abuse in the U.S.
To help ensure the risks of NUCYNTA ® ER are communicated accurately, Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Inc. has developed a
Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) for the medication, in collaboration with the FDA. This REMS, which is
similar to those developed for other medicines in this category, educates prescribers about the potential for abuse, misuse,
overdose and addiction from exposure to NUCYNTA ® ER. To supplement the REMS, the company also utilizes
surveillance methodologies to monitor for inappropriate use of its products.
About Tapentadol, NUCYNTA® ER and NUCYNTA®
Tapentadol is a centrally-acting synthetic analgesic. The tapentadol molecule is classified as Schedule II of the Controlled
Substances Act.
NUCYNTA ® ER (tapentadol extended-release tablets) represents the ongoing commitment of Janssen Pharmaceuticals,
Inc. and Johnson & Johnson Pharmaceutical Research & Development, L.L.C. to bring new and innovative products to
patients and physicians for the treatment and management of pain.
NUCYNTA ® ER is an oral analgesic indicated for the management of moderate to severe chronic pain in adults when a
continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extended period of time. It is taken twice daily and available
in 50 mg, 100 mg, 150 mg, 200 mg and 250 mg strengths.
NUCYNTA ® (tapentadol immediate-release tablets) was approved by the FDA on November 20, 2008, for the relief of
moderate to severe acute pain in patients 18 years of age or older. It is available in 50 mg, 75 mg, and 100 mg strengths.
Both NUCYNTA ® and NUCYNTA ® ER are available by prescription only.
Outside the United States, tapentadol is marketed by Janssen Inc. in Canada; Grunenthal GmbH discovered tapentadol
and markets immediate- and extended-release formulations of tapentadol (PALEXIA®) in various countries in Europe.
Johnson & Johnson Pharmaceutical Research & Development, L.L.C. and Janssen Pharmaceutical KK, Japan, are
developing tapentadol in Japan. In addition, Janssen Pharmaceutical companies have rights to develop and market
immediate- and extended-release formulations of tapentadol in select European countries and certain countries in Latin
America, the Asia-Pacific region, Africa and the Middle East.

SBC,
Trying to get finished up here in my hotel on time sensitive email before I come over to the BW3.
I think Bret's slides look great and didn't want to nitpick, but a few typos and things that would not have been clear to me
(if I were someone seeing these for the first time)
Slide 1 — "Elevating" should be capitalized
Slide 2 — Seems like this is missing the 'so what' .... Perhaps move the "outcomes" slide (#10) up to follow slide 1,
paraphrase it somehow so the objective becomes more meaningful to the reps & DMs
Slide 3 — need to be sure they don't pick times that overlap with APS, AAPMR, and other key Congresses if they want
major CAM participation. Suggest to Brett that he contact Voletta Santiago who maintains the Conventions calendar. I
haven't rec'd it yet.
Slide 7 — should be "deeper dive into pharmacology." Also, perhaps reword the slide so they know there are multi
10
min lecture followed by 5 min audience response. Bret probably thought this was intuitive since the first sentence says
"delivered during 1.5 hr general session" but someone might read that to mean that there will be a 1.5 hr general session,
of which 15 min will be devoted to the expert speaker....
Slide 8 - is it members of Endo's "Clinical" and "Medical" teams, or is it "Clinical Affairs" and "Medical Affairs" teams? (My
question is whether folks like Harry Ahdieh, Robert, Ernest, etc will be presenting... If not, then Brett should add "Affairs"
after "Clinical" and "Medical" )
Also, the last point on slide 8 seems to imply the questions would be the type that have a "right" and "wrong" answer...I
presume then that addresses the question you/I kicked around yesterday about what type of questions they'd be....
Last slide: I think the last bullet is again missing the "so what." Perhaps "Firm foundation of pharmacology on which to
better position Endo's products with customers" or something like that.
Again, I didn't want to be nit-picky with Bret and the rest of the group, but since these slides will presumably be shown to
an audience who knows very little about what is being proposed, I think we want to be as clear/explicit as possible.
MANY THANKS AGAIN for your leadership of this for us, Steve!
Lk

Date:

Subject:

Re: [pain] Urine Toxicology

From:

UCSF Redaction

To:

Pain and Palliative Care PRN <pain@prn.accp.com>;

Attachments:

JAT part Il.pdf; UDT monograph - dispelling myths and designing strategies.pdf; Utility of UDT for
Opioids.pdf

I have attached a few references. There is a definite chance of a false negative for opiates, given that

the following from a local pharmacist), beginning March 1st the long acting opioid class would require a generic prior to a
branded medication. I know that this is common and many health plans have a similar step therapy in place. My
question is that the pharmacist said that oxymorphone ER was listed as one of the generics that might be required prior
to a branded medication. As you know, Endo markets Opana ER (oxymorphone hydrochloride) with INTAC technology
which is designed to be crush resistant. Opana ER w/INTAC is the only oxymorphone product on the market with this
technology. My question is, will a patient have to try oxymorphone ER prior to receiving a prescription for Opana ER
w/INTAC?
If you or someone on your clinical team is willing, I would like to set up a meeting and bring in a member from our
clinical team to further discuss Opana ER with INTAC.
I look forward to hearing from you.

TRF_TX_Pfizer Amends.pdf

Hi Tara,
I just wanted to double back with you on this email. I believe you had previously indicated that we need
the language pointing to a `laboratory study' therefore, we would be opposed to Pfizer's recommendation
regarding Point #1 below. Am I recalling this correctly?
Thanks,
Tim
From: Byrne, Timothy
Sent: Wednesday, March 23, 2011 1:42 PM
To: Thomas,Greg (Thomas.Greg@endo.com); Bingol, Demir; Chapman, Tara; Barto, Bob; Clark, Michael; Benedek, Irma;
Fiske, William
Cc: Phipps, Candice; Munroe, Brian (Munroe.Brian@Endo.com)
Subject: Opana Crush Resistance Legislation

All
As we introduce our legislation in state legislatures to prevent the substitution of TRF products with
non-TRF generics, we are being asked to modify the language by various interested parties. Attached
are suggested amendments by Pfizer. In short, they are asking that we amend our language to:
1. delete the language that allows a company to submit as evidence "a laboratory study comparing
the tamper- or abuse resistance properties of the drug to one or more opioid analgesic drugs that
(a) have been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration; and (b) serve as a positive
control."
2. Add "abuse deterrent" to the type of qualities that the product must demonstrate.
3. To prevent therapeutic substitution, add language to provide that, in addition to having
substantially similar tamper resistant properties, the drug must be "deemed equivalent in the most
recent version of the Food and Drug Administration's publication Approved Drug Products with
Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations."
I attached a copy of the bill and Pfizer's suggested edits. We would be interested in the groups input as
to whether these amendments would jeopardize or compromise the protections for Opana ER.
Thanks in advance for your input.
Tim

Confidential

END00307383

Hi Greg —
I spoke with Alicia and the Palio medical team will be reaching out to Bill directly to review our recommended references.
Attached are four solid references that are a combination of refs from Bill's list and new refs Meleik has identified.
Our literature search to support the finding of social isolation in patients with chronic pain focused on the parameters below,
and we want to make sure this thinking is aligned with Bill.
• Reference published after 2001
• Article's main focus was not quality of life parameters
• No discussion of depression related to chronic pain
• Patients with chronic pain from lower back pain or osteoarthritis (articles discussing neuropathic pain or
fibromyalgia were not considered)
• Patients across broad age range
• Patient reported isolation/feelings of loneliness
• Article did not discuss medication abuse associate with patients in chronic pain
Consequently, we have attached highlighted articles named in recommended order of review; for example, Recommendation
1 should be reviewed and considered first and so on.
I will cc the brand team on our correspondence to Bill. Let me know if you have any questions.

Jess

Hi Dan,
I looked into the Fraud Risk Assessment for 2009 and compared the worked performed to the 2012 Assessment and here are
my observations. There was a different layout in the information but our procedures were the same:
• Identification of fraud risks factors
• Identify relevant fraud schemes and scenarios based on industry guidance
• Identified existing internal controls that would mitigate the risk of fraud and map these controls to the fraud
schemes
• Residual Risk Assessment
We accomplished these testing procedures in both reviews. In 2009, there was a bit more documentation and a different
format, while the information in the 2012 review was consolidated and scaled down a bit.
Some differences:
• 2009 we held Fraud Brainstorming sessions with select Finance personnel in addition to the well as interviews
• 2012 we only held interviews
Minor changes except for the layout but the same testing objectives were met. I am attaching the report from 2009 and the

10-year sentence for owner of Ohio 'pill mill'
By ANDREW WELSH-HUGGINS
The Associated Press
COLUMBUS, Ohio —
A judge has handed down a 10-year prison sentence for the owner of a medical clinic in southern Ohio that authorities
allege was a notorious drug house.
George Adkins had pleaded guilty last month to five felony counts involving drug trafficking, corrupt activity and forgery
related to the clinic he ran until December 2011.
Authorities say Adkins' Greater Medical Advance was the last so-called pill mill in Scioto County before it was shut down.
They say the Wheelersburg clinic was a well-known destination for addicts that existed to generate money for its
operators.
Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine says Adkins allowed an overwhelming amount of prescription drugs to leave the
clinic knowing they would be abused.
Scioto County judge William Marshall sentenced the 69-year-old Adkins Friday afternoon.

The purpose of this email is to summarize the RD Prescriber Removal Process. This process is intended to be
consistent, fair, resource feasible, and compliant — the guiding principles of our effort to improve governance around
prescriber crediting adjustments.
Criteria/Guidelines
This process provides you with a mechanism to proactively address prescriber issues that have a significant impact at
the territory level while maintaining accountability within your Region.
Examples:
Inappropriate for reps to call on* — safety issues, valid license but suspicious practices, apparent "pill-mill" that
cannot be located, etc.
o *Suspicion of diversion should continue to be submitted to Compliance for investigation and removed
through that process
No Access** — no reps are allowed in the building (Kaiser, UPenn, etc.) so rep time is better spent elsewhere
o **In evaluating requests you should look at not only at goal impact but also whether prescribers can be
reached via other means (HOPE, non-personal programs, etc.)
