- In New Hampshire, we cannot show Rxs for any physician who prescribes in that state. We also cannot show any Rxs that
are filled in NH but are written by prescribers in other states. We WILL have this data at the zip code level for IC purposes.
- In the rest of the country, we cannot show Rx data for any physician who has asked the AMA to restrict the use of their
information. These prescribers will be listed at the bottom of the report. We WILL have this information for use in calculating
IC, but will not be able to share it with anyone in the field.
- We will continue to show the historical data for prescribers in both categories.
A FEW KEY POINTS:
- There are 4 tabs per file: Lidoderm report, Frova report, Opana report and a tab with three line graphs.
- Each report contains TRxs for your call plan doctors individually and a last line for all other profiled prescribers in your
territory combined.
- Manager reports contain summarized data for each of their territories or districts.

Redacted - Non-Opioid Product
- This information should be close to, but not the same as, your monthly IC TRxs. Weekly TRxs are provided to help you
monitor your prescribers, but IC is based on final monthly data.
- Weekly data is naturally more volatile than monthly data. Please do not overreact to week-to-week changes.
- When opening your report in Excel, click the "Enable Macros" button. This is necessary to turn on some of the features of
the report.
TO SORT THE REPORTS:
- Above the Endo logo, there will be a toolbar with 4 pull-down lists and three buttons.
- The lists work in pairs to allow you to sort by one or two fields.
- The buttons will apply or remove the sort you choose.
- You can sort by Prescriber Name, Prescriber ID, Specialty, Zip Code, Current Week TRx, Current Four Week or Prior 13
week total TRx in either Ascending or Descending order. The default order is Ascending.
- In the first drop-down list on the left, select the primary sort field.
- In the second drop-down list, select the order for the primary sort field.
- (Optional) In the third drop-down list, select the secondary sort field.
- (Optional) In the fourth drop-down list, select the order for the secondary sort field.
- When you have specified your sort options, click the "Sort" button to apply the sort.
- If you want to return to the original sort order, click the "Reset" button.
- The "Exit" button will close the report.
TO PRINT:

Safety Alert: Voluntary Recall
July 5, 2011
Pain Medications Voluntarily Recalled for Mislabeling

Endo Pharmaceuticals, Inc., and Qualitest, a generic drug manufacturing subsidiary, issued voluntary recalls of certain lots of oxycodone
with acetaminophen (Endocet), hydrocodone with acetaminophen (generic Vicodin) and butalbital, acetaminophen and caffeine (generic
Fioricet) because some bottles may contain different strength tablets, resulting in individuals taking more than or less than the intended
doses of active ingredients.
According to the Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) safety alert:
Qualitest Pharmaceuticals issued a voluntary nationwide recall at the retail level for
• generic butalbital, acetaminophen and caffeine tablets USP, 50mg/325mg/40mg, and generic hydrocodone bitartrate and
acetaminophen tablets, USP 7.5mg/500mg. One bottle of butalbital, acetaminophen and caffeine tablets was found incorrectly
labeled with a hydrocodone bitartrate and acetaminophen tablets, USP 7.5mg/500mg, 1000 count label, printed with lot number
C0590909B.
An accidental dosage of generic butalbital/acetaminophen/caffeine (Fioricet) could cause sedation, lightheadedness, dizziness, nausea,
hypersensitivity, tremors, irritability and difficulty sleeping. Those who normally take generic hydrocodone bitartrate/acetaminophen
(Vicodin) could experience withdrawal symptoms and worsening of pain due to missed doses of that opioid.
Endo Pharmaceuticals issued a voluntary nationwide consumer level recall for

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07757814

 • Endocet (oxycodone/acetaminophen) USP tablets, 10 mg/325 mg 100 count bottles, NDC 60951-712-70, lot numbers 402415NV
and 402426NV. One bottle from each lot was found to contain a higher acetaminophen dose. This can be recognized by their larger
size, and different shape and markings.
Unintentional administration of tablets with increased acetaminophen content may result in liver toxicity, especially in people taking other
acetaminophen-containing medications, people with liver dysfunction, or people who consume more than three alcoholic beverages a day.
If you are taking a generic version of Fioricet (butalbital products) or Vicodin (hydrocodone products) or the brand Endocet, please
check your lot numbers immediately.
Lot numbers can be found on the side of the bottle. The medications look different from each other. The two Qualitest products are:
• The white, round-shaped tablet with "2355" debossed on one side is the butalbital/acetaminophen/caffeine tablets (generic form
of Fioricet).
• The white with green specks, capsule-shaped tablet and debossed with "3594" on one side is the hydrocodone
bitartrate/acetaminophen tablets (generic form of Vicodin).
The Endo brand formulations of oxycodone/acetaminophen (Endocet) are:
•
•

Capsule-shaped 10 mg/325 mg tablets with an "E712" marking on one side and a "10/325" marking on the other.
Oval-shaped 10 mg/650mg tablet with an "E797" marking on one side and "10" on the other.

I Individuals who have these lots in their possession should:
•

Stop using the product and contact the manufacturer for disposal and reimbursement information.
o Qualitest at
o Endo's agent Stericycle ati.511! 5v.:(m,5O

• Notify the pharmacy where this medication was filled and report that you are in possession of an affected lot.
• Notify the health care provider who writes your pain medicine prescriptions and ask for guidance.
• Notify you insurance provider should a new prescription be written, so that it will be covered.
• Contact the FDA and report if you have had any adverse reactions described above or trouble receiving replacement medication
by:
o Online using FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program at www.fda.gov/medwatch/report.htm;
o Regular mail by using the postage-paid, pre-addressed Form FDA 3500 available at:
www.fda.gov/MedWatch/getforms.htm. Mail to address on the pre-addressed form;
o Fax: (800) FDA-0178.
Consumers with questions may contact the manufacturers for more information.

First of all, THANK YOU for all your work on this. I know that all of us are just trying to do the right thing for the business.
With regards to your question, there would be absolutely no reason any organization could not approach/receive grants from
Endo. (Whether because someone was on the speakers bureau or for any other reason — grant requests are evaluated strictly
on the merits of them being a sound educational program and Endo having the budget to support them.)
I have to say that after my email below, I am really struggling with why folks are still asking questions about the CME
implications of someone being on a promotional speaker bureau. I had hoped that by sending a plainly worded message in
writing, there would be no further potential "misinterpretation" issues.
But, just for the record.... Someone on the promotional speaker bureau would still be able to do CME but Endo would not be
able to suggest his/her name when CME providers or professional societies request potential speaker names or author names
for a CME program or CME publication in the therapeutic area for which the person is a promotional speaker.
Just to make sure I had my facts straight and that nothing had changed in recent weeks, I spoke to Colleen this morning and
did confirm that my understanding of the CME/promotional speakers bureau issue is correct. Hopefully, if everyone reads the
email I sent below, we'll all be on the same page. (I also bounced a possible idea off Colleen that may help us out if we get in a
bind, but any discussion of that is premature until Dr. Argoff decides what his path forward is.)
To avoid anyone thinking I am trying to intentionally or inadvertently influence any outcomes here, I'm going to take myself out
of the middle of this, and if I receive any further calls from the faculty, I will ask them to please give you guyz a buzz.
I'm out of the office on a sick day today (either the shrimp I had for dinner last night was bad, or I have some GI bug) but if you
need to reach me, I'm at my celICIiii4ii:iiiiiiii:3

Subject: KY TRF Bill Passed Unanimously by House Health & Welfare Committee

Yesterday, members of the Kentucky House Health & Welfare Committee voted unanimously (13-0) in favor
of TRF legislation (HB 377). In addition to the bill sponsor, Rep. Wuchner, compelling testimony was heard
before the Committee by KY State Police Commissioner, Rodney Brewer, Circuit Court Judge William
Roberts, Michael Barnes, Exec Dir. CLAAD, and a mother who lost two of her young adult children last year to
opioid abuse.
Prior to the hearing, representatives of the Hospital Association and the Association of State Health Plans met
with the sponsor and expressed several concerns which we were able to quickly address with further
explanation of the bill and minor language adjustments (inpatient exemption). Representatives of pharmacy
and retail merchants were in attendance at the hearing, however, there was no opponent testimony given.
Because HB 377 was approved unanimously, it was put on the House Consent Calendar.
As a matter of expediency, the House allows bills to accumulate on the Consent Orders and will periodically
pass the entire Consent Calendar with one vote without dealing with each bill individually on the House floor.
We are now meeting with Senate Leadership in efforts to get the bill passed by the Senate.

NE Leaders,
Here is a summary of today's Lidoderm call from Nancy, my Lidoderm District Champ. If you've received some
you'd like to share send them on.
Leslie
From: Bowie, Nancy
Sent: Tuesday, May 11, 2010 8:18 PM
To: Tucker, Nicholas; Saucier, Jeffrey; Heindl, Leslie; Giovanni, Jodie; McKnight, Michael; Carmody, Christina; Smith, Eric;
Felz, Andrew; Donaldson, Mark
Subject: Qutenza Call
Hi Team,
Just wanted to send a summary of the Lidoderm call this morning. The call centered around our newest competitor —
Qutenza. As we have talked before, the sales force is small and is mainly focusing on high PHN pain specialists and they may
expand to high PHN prescribers in the PCP world, but that probably won't happen until next year.
As of now, only 2 Rxs for Qutenza have shown up. Physicians have to order the product directly and the data will show up
under non-retail data in IMS. If the prescriber orders through a specialty pharmacy (such as CVS.com), the Rx will show up in
your weekly data. The fact that the physician has to order the product may cause problems with reimbursement — any
specifics as to reimbursement for either the product or the application process are still unknown.
We will be receiving updated MVAs and slim jims the week of May 19th. The new ones will have a change on pg. 3 to reflect
the capsaicin patch. Keep in mind that Lidoderm is still the only topical PHN treatment that can be applied by the PATIENT at
HOME.
Market research on physician feedback showed that they would try Qutenza AFTER Lidoderm and they had a positive reaction
to the data; however, there were concerns about application site reactions and frequency of those reactions as well as
administration and reimbursement concerns.
What are we hearing back from physicians? 390 docs (pain specialist and PCPs) were surveyed. Only 5% reported that they
had been detailed about Qutenza; details for Qutenza lasted 7.6 minutes, Lidoderm lasted 6.3 minutes, and Lyrica lasted 6.8
minutes. Doctors were asked about the relevance of the data and they rated it a 5.2 on a 7 point scale. 40% of the Qutenza
details finished with a close or call to action by the rep.
When asked about their awareness of any new PHN treatments (and the answer had to be filled in) — zero providers said
Qutenza
When given a list of agents, 38% stated they had heard of Qutenza.
Remember we have the PI Training Tool we received after the NSM with PI info on Qutenza, as well as Lyrica and Lidoderm.
We also have via the Force Resource, the Qutenza training tool that reviews the 5 key messages for Qutenza and the approved
Lidoderm messages. Remember when responding to an objection to use the CRCT model.
Other highlights:
The application process and the pain potential are the major drawbacks of this product —the entire process includes 9 steps
and 9 items that are needed. Also, the process could take up to 3 hours with the prep work and the actual application and this

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_MA_00166303

 needs to happen in a dedicated room or area to reduce the chance for the capsaicin to be inhaled. Also due to the pain that
can occur with this product, the patient may require opioids for up to 5 days after application — as pointed out in the call, no
physician would allow a patient to drive home after taking an opioid and the patient may need to bring someone along to take
them home.
The brand team seems to think one of the points the Qutenza reps will point out is the compliance. Obviously if the pt has to
come into the office for the patch to be put on, compliance is taken out of the hands of the patients to some degree (they still
have to show up). Also, the patch provides pain relief for up to 3 months.
Again, this is not something we should be seeing a lot of in our offices, but it is always good to be knowledgeable about the
products in this marketplace. Hope this review helps. If anyone hears anything out in the field about Qutenza, please pass it
on.
Thanks!
diranc# d3owie

ENDO_MA_00166304

Hi Nancy and Oksana,
We received the following BRC question: Does Opana ER increase the pressure on the sphincter of Oddi?
I am checking with Esther to see if she knows whether this was an AE.
We performed a search of the Opana ER PI, SRLs/FAQs, available study materials, previous ad hocs, and ran a Medline lit search (attached; no results).
Unless you are aware of any other information, may we provide the following information from the PI:
5.11 Use in Pancreatic/Biliary Tract Disease
OPANA ER, like other opioids, may cause spasm of the sphincter of Oddi and should be used with caution in patients with biliary tract disease, including acute pancreatitis.

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-02527439

 12.2 Pharmacodynamics, Effects on the Gastrointestinal Tract and on Other Smooth Muscle
Oxymorphone can cause a marked increase in biliary tract pressure as a result of spasm of the sphincter of Oddi, and transient elevations in serum amylase.
Thank you,
Nora

From: Esther Coleman
Sent: Monday, December 05, 2011 3:39 PM
To: 'Terleckyj, Oksana'; Nora Tu
Cc: David Hornshuh; Esther Coleman; Kelly Seidel; Lakeisha Leftwich; Margaret Carlson; Quyen Tran; Seneca York; Shelly Bagley; Tangela Battle; Valeria Thorpe
Subject: Opana ER and Sphincter of Oddi MITA 110810
Hi Oksana and Nora

A BRC was received with the following question!?

Does Opana ER increase the pressure on the sphincter of Oddi'?

Information below is innthe PI:

Effects on the Gastrointestinal Tract and on Other Smooth Muscle
Gastric, biliary and pancreatic secretions are decreased by oxymorphone. Oxymorphone causes a reduction in motility and is associated with an increase in tone in the antrum of the stomach
and duodenum Digestion of food in the small intestine is delayed and propulsive contractions are decreased. Propulsive peristaltic waves in the colon are decreased, while tone is increased
to the point of spasm. The end result may be constipation. Oxvmorphone can cause a marked increase in biliary tract pressure as a result of spasm of the sphincter of Oddi_ and transient
elevations in serum amylase. Oxymorphone may also cause spasm of the sphincter of the urinary bladder.
Is there anything else to add'?

Subject: Opana ER Hospital Rollout - Credentialing Communication
Sent by Kathleen Cronshaw on behalf of Bill Leinhos & Rhianna Trice
Hello Everyone,
Please immediately cascade this message to your reps that our part of hospital rollout.
I've received several questions regarding Vendormate registration fees. We are finalizing the additions to our Corporate Open
Access Plan now and should have everyone registered within the next couple of days. We've had a slight delay due to the
holidays and I apologize for any confusion or inconvenience this may have caused. Please DO NOT pay the $250 Vendormate
registration fee at this time. For those who may have already registered, I'm working to get those charges reversed through
Vendormate. I will send further communication shortly on how to proceed with Vendormate registration. Again, I sincerely
apologize for the inconvenience and VII update you as soon as possible.
In the meantime, please use the link below for the required AORN Certifications.
http://www.addlearner.com/
Select the "Vendor Credentialing" assessments on the Scott Physician Training form. Once submitted, your login information
will be sent in a separate email.
Complete the following modules:
• Bloodborne Pathogens
• Environmental & Electrical Safety
• Fire Safety
• HI PAA
• OR Protocol I — Aseptic Technique
• OR Protocol II — Sterile Technique
You must receive a 90% on each module to pass (out of 10 questions, you can only get 1 wrong— but you can retake
immediately if necessary).
To complete ALL modules should take approximately 90 minutes. Once all modules are complete you can receive your
certificate.
Please inform your manager when you have completed all training & receive your certificate. Tracey Bentz will draft a letter of
"product training/service competency" for you ( the letter includes proof of employment, drug/criminal background screen
and all certifications as well as product training).

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

 Immunizations:
Ask the hospital which immunizations they require (before spending time getting ones that you may not need).
Here is a list of the most common:
*TB (annually)
*Hepatitis B (3 shot series)
*MMR (Measles, Mumps and Rubella)
*Vericella (Chickenpox)
*Influenza
*Some hospitals also require a Tetanus shot
If you're not sure about the status of your immunizations, ask your physician for a Titer — a blood check for antibodies. Allow
time for this — results take up to one week.

**Finally, Endo's Tax ID # is 522035829 and I've attached the Proof of Liability Insurance. You will need both
when registering with any vendor service provider.
Sorry for the lengthy email! Please let me know if you have any further questions.
Warm Regards,
Rhianna

Subject: [EXTERNAL] FDA issues guidance for generic abuse-deterrent opioids
From:

POLITICO Pro Health Care Whiteboard <politicoemail@politicopro.com >

To:

Byrne, Timothy <Byrne.Timothy@endo.com>;

ATTENTION: This email came from an external source. Do not open attachments or click on links from unknown senders or
unexpected emails. Click the "Report Phishing" button in Outlook if it is suspicious.

By Luis Sanchez
11/21/2017 09:44 AM EDT
The FDA today issued final guidance to help develop generic versions of abuse-deterrent opioids as part of its
effort to transition the painkiller market toward formulations with properties such as being difficult to crush or
dissolve.
"This is an effort designed to encourage the shift
only when opioids are clinically necessary
from
existing, easily abused products to those that are harder to manipulate," FDA Commissioner Scott Gottlieb said
in a statement.
New abuse-deterrent formulations are only available as brand-name products, Gottlieb noted. Generic versions
could bring expanded access.
The FDA's final guidance includes recommendations about studies companies should conduct to demonstrate a
generic medicine is as effective an abuse-deterrent as a branded drug. The FDA is taking additional steps to
ensure generic ADF developers can quickly and efficiently navigate the regulatory process to market, including
"taking a flexible, adaptive approach" when evaluating and labeling the opioids, Gottlieb said.
The agency is trying to make new, safer formulations of opioids more commonplace without encouraging more
painkiller use, Gottlieb said. Even with ADFs, people should only take opioids when appropriate, because they

FDA) Lie ctearty indicated they were s'iti evacuating the options a:1d that additional comments submitted to the
docket would be considered in their fins' decision. The September 30 extension provides an excellent

recommendations to withdraw propoxyphene. (I know, I know...hard to believe given the drug's "efficacy," but
a notable precedent nonetheless!)
Kit

Acetaminophen Information
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) convened a public advisory committee meeting on June 29 and June 30,
2009 regarding acetaminophen use in both over-the-counter (OTC) and prescription (Rx) products, the potential for
liver injury, and potential interventions to reduce the incidence of liver injury.
The FDA will keep the docket for this meeting open until September 30th 2009 to receive comments. Electronic
comments should be submitted to www.regulations.gov. Enter "FDA-2009-N-0138 Liver Injury Related to the Use of
Acetaminophen" and look for the Joint Meeting of the Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee,
Nonprescription Drugs Advisory Committee and the Anesthetic and Life Support Drugs Advisory Committee: Notice
of Meeting. Click on "Send a Comment or Submission." Written comments should be submitted to the Division of
Dockets Management (HFA-305), Food and Drug Administration, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rim 1061, Rockville, MID

Subject: Request Pain Care Forum Organizations to co-sign letter to CMS

As discussed at yesterday's Pain Care Forum meeting, we are circulating the attached
letter and urging that your organization co-sign this letter to the Centers for Medicare &
Medicaid Services. Please let us know by March 16th if you will be able to join us in this
effort to help to encourage the development of Abuse Deterrent Formulation of abused
medicines.
Abuse deterrent medications help to achieve the goal of the White House Drug Plan that
is described as a "balance between our desire to minimize abuse of prescription drugs
and the need to ensure access for their legitimate use." It makes little sense for the White
House, the FDA, DEA, CDC, SAMHSA and other federal agencies focused on
prescription drug abuse to propose policies that would lead to the expanded availability of
Abuse Deterrent Formulations of medicines, only for CMS to undercut these important
policies by penalizing Abuse Deterrent drug manufacturers by proposing a distorted
definition of line extension.
Please review the attached letter and consider joining us in this effort to incentivize the
continued development of Abuse Deterrent technologies.

 Colorado has second-worst rate of pain pill abuse
By Michael Booth The Denver Post The Denver Post
Posted: DenverPost.com

Colorado has the second-highest rate of prescription-painkiller abuse in the nation, according to a new federal report,
boosting the urgency of various state efforts to curb rampant overuse of the pills.
Six percent of Coloradans said they used prescription painkillers - such as Percocet or Oxycontin — for nonmedical
purposes in 2010 and 2011, according to the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. That was second only to
Oregon, where the rate was 6.37 percent.
Iowa had the lowest abuse rate, about 3.62 percent among people over the age of 12. Among people age 18-25,
Colorado's misuse rate for the painkillers was a much-higher 14 percent of the population.
Seven of the 10 worst states were in the West, noted Art Schut, chief executive of the Arapahoe House treatment
centers. The number of Arapahoe House clients who named prescription drugs as a problem substance has quintupled
in the past six years, Schut said.
The painkillers are everywhere, and many clients assume they are relatively safe because they are pure, come from a
medical source and have legitimate uses, he said.
"It's hard to get around the idea that all medicine is good for you," he said.
Once people get addicted, they increase their dosage, then look for cheaper sources of high, Schut said. "It's a very
dangerous, slippery slope."
State policy and health leaders are working on various fronts to stem the flow of painkillers, with prescriptions
quadrupling in a decade as doctors moved to treat chronic pain directly rather than dismiss it as a symptom.
The opiate-based pills are highly addictive, and the mass increase in their prescription opens them to misuse or theft
by family members, addicts and dealers. Law enforcement and treatment experts also have seen an increase in young
addicts switching from painkillers to cheaper heroin. Overdose deaths are rising in parallel with prescriptions.
"There's not one solution," said Laurie Lovedale of the state Division of Behavioral Health, who is advising Gov. John
Hickenlooper about prescription drug policy.
Hickenlooper co-chairs a task force on pain-pill abuse at the National Governors Association, and the group expects a
report on policy changes by the end of February, Lovedale said.
Answers must include a combination of doctor education on how the pills are being abused, greater use of a state
prescription database to identify at-risk patients, and better disposal methods for leftover pills, Lovedale said.
Massachusetts, for example, requires doctors to take pain management and opiate courses to renew their licensure,
she said.
State officials also support efforts by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency to change rules to allow pharmacies to
accept leftover medicine for destruction. Currently they can't, and law enforcement instead conducts periodic
"takeback" days to accept prescription drugs.
If there is good news in the report by the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, it is that
rates of pill misuse have leveled off in Colorado and most states. Colorado's abuse rate dropped slightly from 6.23
percent in 2009 and 2010, although it rose among 12- to 17-year-olds and 18- to 25-year-olds.

From: Stempek, Cynthia

To: Chung, Kelvin
Subject: ClinTopics Review with Dr. De Leon-Casasola, MD
Hi Kelvin,
Just wanted to provide you with a quick recap of "pearls" from the newest Opana ER resource,
"ClinTopics: Clinical Considerations When Prescribing Reformulated Long-Acting Opioid Analgesics, by
Dr. Oscar A. De Leon-Casasola, MD".
AS A REMINDER, THIS recap IS NOT TO BE USED OUT IN THE FIELD
As I mentioned on our call, I had the opportunity to share this with three prescribers in my footprint,
and thus far, they have found it to be a valuable resource. As I mentioned on the call, being that it is a
"limited" resource, I will be providing Aaron a list of names of where I have shared the information so
that we will not be duplicating our efforts, and so as to stretch this valuable tool in our footprint.
The article is set up nicely in that it starts off by establishing Dr. De Leon-Casasola's credentials and
background. (p.3) and moves into the first, and very important question of, "What are inherent
challenges to consider when prescribing reformulated long-acting opioids?" This first question
establishes the importance of discussing the topic, and the relevance to the prescribers patients. The
response, "An inherent challenge when using a reformatted long-acting analgesic is the need to establish
pharmacokinetic equivalence with the previous formulation, to ensure that the reformulation provides
similar analgesic efficacy as the original formulation." It also states, " Additional considerations include
enabling (HCPs) to continue prescribing the product as they have traditionally, and ensuring that the
accessibility and reimbursement coverage for patients remains unchanged."
The second question on page 3 is: "How does the reformulation of Opana ER (oxymorphone HCI) with
INTAC technology differ from the original formulation of Opana ER? What studies have been conducted
to examine the pharmacokinetics of Opana ER with INTAC technology in comparison with the original
formulation of Opana ER?"
"The original formulation of Opana ER was formulated using TIMERx technology, which
reduced fluctuations in drug concentrations and provided consistent 12-hour dosing. The
Opana ER reformulation uses INTAC technology with oxymorphone embedded in a hard
polymer matrix."
"Opana ER (oxymorphone HCI) with INTAC technology is designed to deliver the same
therapeutic dose and efficacy as the original formulation."
"The pharmacokinetic (PK) behavior of Opana ER with INTAC technology was evaluated in 3
open-label, randomized studies conducted at a single site in the United States."
"The primary endpoints for all 3 studies included systemic oxymorphone exposure in terms
AUC(0-inf), AUC(0-t), and C(max)."
The third question on page 4: "What did these studies show regarding the rate and extent of absorption
of Opana ER with INTAC technology in comparison with the original formulation of Opana ER over 12
hours?"
2

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO_SF-00038610

 -

-

"In all 3 studies, there were no significant differences between Opana ER with INTAC
technology and the original formulation of Opana ER with respect to the rate and extent of
oxymorphone absorption.
"Results showed that, under fasted and fed conditions, the oxymorphone plasma
concentration vs time profile was not significant different for the 2 formulations."
"The bioequivalence between Opana ER with INTAC technology and the original formulation
is clearly illustrated in Figure 1 (p. 4)"
The 0% confidence interval of the geometric mean ration between the original formulation
of Opana ER and Opana ER with INTAC technology for all PK endpoint parameters was
between 0.80 and 1.25, satisfying the predefined criteria for bioequivalence."
*Dr. De Leon-Casasola gives his opinion (starts below Figure 1) and continues up at the top
of the page, and it is important to note, "the correlation of pharmacokinetics to clinical
effects has not been established"

The fourth question on page 4: "Both the original formulation of Opana ER and Opana ER with INTAC
technology offer 12-hour dosing. What studies were conducted to determine whether the original
formulation of Opana ER offered true 12-hour dosing?"
"Clinical data show that the original formulation of Opana ER delivered consistent plasma
levels, with low peak and trough fluctuations, for 12 hours after administration (Figure 2). /
have found in my experience that this has translated into a consistent and reliable 12-hour
dosing interval."
"These studies not only established dose proportionality for the 5-mg, 10-mg, 20-mg and 40mg tablet strengths with respect to peak plasma levels (Cmax) and the rate of absorption
(AUC) but also showed a half-life of 9.4 to 11.3 hours."
"Based on these data, along with the study results showing bioequivalence between the 2
formulations, I believe that Opana ER with INTAC technology should provide a reliable full
12-hour dosing interval." (bottom of page 4, column 2)
** "Again, the correlation of pharmacokinetics to clinical effects has not been established."
The fifth question on page 5: "What clinical data exist showing effective oxymorphone pain relief with
Opana ER?"
See Figure 3 from the Hale reprint
The sixth question on page 5: "What was the AE profile seen with Opana ER in this clinical study?"
See Table 1 from Opana ER prescribing information and Hale trial
"In my experience, the incidence of opioid-related AEs declines once patients are on a stable
dose, and the results in this study confirmed this "
"I will discuss this point with my patients when initiating therapy with long-acting opioids, to
help set realistic expectations...."
The seventh question on page 6: "What are the differences in shape and color of the reformulated
Opana ER (oxymorphone HCI) with INTAC technology tablets in comparison with the original formulation
of Opana ER tablets?"
"I was very pleased to see that the tablet colors used for each dose of the reformulated
Opana ER with INTAC technology are the same as those used with the original formulation
of Opana ER."
"In my opinion, many patients, particularly those taking multiple medications, tend to
identify their medications by tablet color rather than by name, and keeping the same
dose/color assignment may help avoid confusion."

3

ENDO_SF-00038611

 The eighth question on page 6: "Opana ER with INTAC technology contains the proven pain reliever
oxymorphone. What is the recommended dosing of Opana ER with INTAC technology for both opioidnaïve patients and opioid-experienced patients?"
See Table 3, taken from Opana ER prescribing information
"In my experience, some patients may interpret inadequate pain relief upon opioid initiation
as a failure of the medication being used, rather than as the result of inadequate
dosing. This provides clinicians with an opportunity to set realistic expectations for their
patients and counsel them on the importance of the titration process."
LAST QUESTION, end of page 6: "What measures will help ensure that patients who have been using the
original formulation of Opana ER will gain access to Opana ER with INTAC technology?"
"....patients who have been using the original formulation of Opana ER will be able to
transition easily

RESTRICTED DATA:
- Data restrictions were implemented with the data reports for week ending August 11, 2006. There are two different
restrictions affecting the pharmaceutical industry: one in New Hampshire, and the other nationwide based upon an AMA OptOut (PDRP) program.
- In New Hampshire, we cannot show Rxs for any physician who prescribes in that state. We also cannot show any Rxs that
are filled in NH but are written by prescribers in other states. We WILL have this data at the zip code level for IC purposes.
- In the rest of the country, we cannot show Rx data for any physician who has asked the AMA to restrict the use of their
information. These prescribers will be listed at the bottom of the report. We WILL have this information for use in calculating
IC, but will not be able to share it with anyone in the field.
- We will continue to show the historical data for prescribers in both categories.
A FEW KEY POINTS:
- There are 4 tabs per file: Lidoderm report, Frova report, Opana report and a tab with three line graphs.
- Each report contains TRxs for your call plan doctors individually and a last line for all other profiled prescribers in your
territory combined.
- Manager reports contain summarized data for each of their territories or districts.

Redacted - Non-Opioid Product
- This information should be close to, but not the same as, your monthly IC TRxs. Weekly TRxs are provided to help you
monitor your prescribers, but IC is based on final monthly data.
- Weekly data is naturally more volatile than monthly data. Please do not overreact to week-to-week changes.
- When opening your report in Excel, click the "Enable Macros" button. This is necessary to turn on some of the features of
the report.
TO SORT THE REPORTS:
- Above the Endo logo, there will be a toolbar with 4 pull-down lists and three buttons.
- The lists work in pairs to allow you to sort by one or two fields.
- The buttons will apply or remove the sort you choose.
- You can sort by Prescriber Name, Prescriber ID, Specialty, Zip Code, Current Week TRx, Current Four Week or Prior 13
week total TRx in either Ascending or Descending order. The default order is Ascending.
- In the first drop-down list on the left, select the primary sort field.
- In the second drop-down list, select the order for the primary sort field.
- (Optional) In the third drop-down list, select the secondary sort field.
- (Optional) In the fourth drop-down list, select the order for the secondary sort field.
- When you have specified your sort options, click the "Sort" button to apply the sort.
- If you want to return to the original sort order, click the "Reset" button.
- The "Exit" button will close the report.
TO PRINT:
- The report and graph tabs are already formatted for reporting.
- To print any tab, click the "File" menu and choose "Print...".
- When the print window opens, select the options you want and click the "Print" button.

Request to Retain: Dr. Michael Brennan--Opana ER Speaker's Bureau

Hi Janett,
I'm forwarding on April Dove's response concerning retaining Dr. Brennan as our Opana ER speaker for 2013. I'd
like to also include my strong support in keeping Dr. Brennan as one of our primary speakers for Opana ER. He is
a major thought leader in Connecticut and has been instrumental in the training and mentoring of many of the pain
specialists who currently practice in Connecticut and in some parts of New York, Massachusetts, and Rhode
Island. In addition, he has been a key advocate and vocal supporter of maintaining the integrity of using long
acting opioids despite the harsh criticisms and attempts of the Connecticut state government to impose harsh
constraints on physicians who incorporate LAO's within their practice. He works tirelessly to educate his medical
community on the necessity and appropriate use of opioids and is sought out by the primary care physicians for
advice or to provide referrals for tough to treat patients.
Unfortunately, due to events beyond our control in 2012, he was limited to speaking on behalf of our company for
one event. April provides the details below. I would greatly appreciate that a positive outcome is reached and that
Dr. Brennan is retained on our Speaker's Bureau for 2013. I will be following up with my peers across the country
to promote Dr. Brennan's disease state knowledge, medical background and real-world expertise on leveraging
LAO's. This will ensure that the value he has historically brought to our district will be shared with more consistency
to other medical communities abroad. I appreciate your support. -Marvin
From: Dove, April
Sent: Wednesday, February 20, 2013 7:59 PM
To: Sepulveda, Marvin
Cc: McReddie, Warren
Subject: Re: Potential Removal of Dr. Michael Brennan from the Speaker Bureau
Dear Marvin,
Here are just a few reasons why Dr. Brennan should not be removed from our speaker bureau.
1.

I was only allocated two programs during 2012 and Dr. Brennan was the speaker for one program on
October 17th. Marvin, as you know, Dr. Brennan has been used extensively in the Connecticut area. As a
result, I thought it would be a good idea to have a speaker from a different region and I utilized one from
New York for the second program.

2.

Dr. Brennan has been a tremendous asset and advocate for Endo. He has been a speaker for many of
our products since 2001. It would be a huge loss to lose someone with his passion, leadership and
expertise of educating on long-acting opioids. He is a thought leader and has had a very positive impact
on the medical community. He brings a cutting edge perspective because he is both a Rehab and Pain
Management Specialist. As we discussed, I am looking to promote Dr. Brennan to my peers in our area
as well as other areas around the country. Three programs have already been confirmed for him in 2013.

3.

Dr. Brennan spent a lot of time during 2012 taking care of two very ill family members, his wife and
mother-in-law. Offers to speak may have been rejected because of his inability to travel outside of the CT
area.

I strongly suggest that we retain him as a speaker for Endo.
Sincerely,

10/20/2008 06:42:27 PM EDT -- Chicago Tribune
FDA rejects Abbott's extended-release Vicodin
Published Date: October 20, 2008 04:00:00 AM EDT
Author: Bruce Japsen, Chicago Tribune
Oct. 20--The U.S. Food and Drug Administration did not approve Abbott Laboratories' extended-release
formulation of the painkiller Vicodin, the North Chicago-based drug giant confirmed Monday afternoon.
The FDA's decision to issue a "complete response letter," essentially a rejection of Abbott's product, comes
amid a period of intense scrutiny by the federal agency, lawmakers and consumer groups on drug approvals,
particularly pain killers. In 2004, for example, Merck & Co. pulled the pain killer Vioxx from the market after
studies showed users had an increased risk of heart attacks and strokes. In the wake of that decision, the FDA
has faced much criticism for approving Vioxx.
"Abbott is evaluating the FDA Complete Response Letter, will discuss the letter with the FDA and will provide
an update when appropriate," Abbott said in a statement issued after the close of trading on the New York Stock
Exchange.
Abbott was seeking the approval of controlled-release hydrocodone with acetaminophen as the "first extended
release medication in the class to provide extended relief over 12 hours," the company said. Currently available

HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-07588045

 "short acting" versions must be taken every four to six hours. Some doctors and consumer groups have also
voiced concerns over the potential for abuse of pain killers such as Vicodin.
The FDA could not be reached this afternoon for comment.
Abbott had been projecting the controlled-release formulation of Vicodin would eventually reach $500 million
in annual sales. Abbott has total annual sales of more than $26 billion.

 a.) A pre-doctoral student at an AOA-accredited college of osteopathic medicine at the time that the

2.

The poster should clearly state the following:

a.)

Hypothesis:

State the primary objectives and scope of the study or the reasons why the document was
written. Also, state the rationale for your research. Why did you do the research? Is the topic that you
are researching ignored or a newly discovered one?

b.)

Materials and Methods:

Design: Clearly state the study design, identifying it as observational or experimental. For
observational studies, specify the temporal profile of the study as prospective, retrospective, or crosssectional. Other description terms such as cohort, case control, or survey should be used as
appropriate. Blinding should be described where relevant.

c.)

Setting: For clinical investigations, describe the study site and/or,

Participants/subjects: Indicate the study population, study dates, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and
method of sampling. If matching was employed, specify the criteria by which subjects were matched. If
controls were utilized, identify them as concurrent or historical and/or,

d.) Interventions/observations: For experimental studies, clearly describe interventions. The data
analysis section should include the type(s) of descriptive or inferential statistical methods used. The
observations should be a list of major data elements or outcome measures relevant to the study
objective. Negative studies should be accompanied by a statement of power, beta error, or confidence
intervals and/or,

For most clinical research abstracts, the following areas are specifically mentioned: research design;
research setting; number of patients enrolled in the study and how they were selected; a description of the
intervention (if appropriate); and a listing of the outcome variables and how they were measured. Finally,
the statistical methods used to analyze the data are described and/or,

For basic sciences abstracts, include enough detail for comprehension about study or program design
and methods, sample size, type, selection method, instruments, protocols, procedures, interventions,
treatments, highlight new techniques, validity, reliability issues, data sources, analysis, manipulation,
techniques and/or approached used in your study.

e.)

Results:

November 1, 2011

News for the biotech, medical device, drug and food regulatory profession

Drugs & Biologics

■ High court won't consider Barr appeal regarding Temodar patent
The Supreme Court declined to review Barr Laboratories and Barr Pharmaceuticals' appeal of a
decision affirming the enforceability of Schering-Plough's patent for brain cancer medicine
Temodar. Last year, the Merck & Co. subsidiary reached an agreement that allows the Teva
Pharmaceutical Industries units to launch generic Temodar in August 2013 if the patent is upheld.
Bloomberg (10/31)

■ Pacira's local anesthetic Exparel receives FDA approval
Pacira Pharmaceuticals obtained FDA approval for Exparel, an extended-release local anesthetic
found to provide pain relief after surgery for as long as 72 hours. The injectable drug is a
combination of Pacira's drug-delivery technology DepoFoam and AstraZeneca's anesthetic
bupivacaine. San Diego Union-Tribune (10/31)

FDA approves Sun's generic of Valeant's Cardizem CD
The FDA approved Sun Pharmaceutical Industries' application to market a generic version of

EN3202-402 Euphoria study -- Positive (topline) Pharmacodynamic data and successful submission of
2 abstract to the 2010 APS

Attachments:

Endo archive notification. Click here to View the original item
Dear Euphoria Study Team

Just a quick note to share the good news that the topline PD data for the Euphoria study were extremely
positive and completely supports the anecdotal reports received from Patients and Prescribers regarding the
cognitive improvements when patients are switched from equianalgesic doses of Oxycontin to Opana ER. As
a result, 2 abstracts, one on euphoria & positive subjective effects (such as drug liking, good effects etc)
and one on Cognition (alertness/drowsiness and divided attention (driving) test) were submitted yesterday
for publication and presentation at the 2010 APS conference in Baltimore.

So far, we have only received the topline PD data inc AEs (4 days ahead of schedule in order to allow us to
submit to APS if positive) and we now expect final data on 16NOV09. Once we have received and digested
all of the data, we will present all study results to the Clinical subteam and then senior management,
probably near the end of NOV. In the meantime, pls find attached PDFs of the Euphoria & Cognition
abstracts -- these for your information only and must not be communicated externally.

I would like to end by thanking everyone involved with the study - it is super that the study is positive but
even if it wasn't, the team needs to be recognized for doing a great job to deliver the study on time and on
budget.
Big thanks go to Nancy, Demir & commercial for pushing this through; Errol &Tim Victor for initial
discussion and topline designs; Kathy Zerbe in Clin Ops who is the heart and soul of the study and all of
the clinical subteam inc Anita, Cindy & Munira for getting the drug into Canada, Stats for their continued
input; DM for their oversight, PVRM for finding solutions to unexpected problems; DMPK for handling the PK
& Phase 1 for their expert advice ..... and anyone else I've forgotten! Thanks also go to Matt, Chad & Todd
for helping to review the data and bash out the abstracts yesterday!

Finally, it is important to acknowledge the great job by Kendle Early Stage CRO (formerly Decisionline in
Toronto) who recruited all of the subjects on time, conducted the study without too much fuss and worked
above and beyond to provide topline PD data 4 days earlier than agreed in order to allow us the possibility
of submitting to the APS if the results were good .... which they were!

Hi Bryan,
Here are all of the FAQ's that I have created:
1. Adding an HCO/Pharmacy: This guide will provide assistance with adding HCO/Pharmacies to your Engage application.
2. Downloading CLM: This guide will provide assistance with downloading and utilizing Digital Master Visual Aids.
3. Engage Adding an HCP Account: This guide will provide assistance with gaining visibility to an HCP that is currently not in
your Engage system by walking you through the steps of self-aligning the HCP to your territory, or adding the HCP to the
Engage universe.
4. Engage Affiliating an Address: This guide will provide assistance with adding new addresses to an HCP's current list of
addresses . (Please note that this task requires a manual sync whether executed in the Engage iPad app or Engage Online)
5. Endo Data Request: This guide will provide you with an explanation of each of the data requests in Engage and how they
work.
6. Engage Global Exclusion Data Request: This guide will provide you with instructions for submitting a Global Exclusion Data
Request
7. Password Reset Instructions: This guide will provide you with instructions for resetting your Engage Password if you get
locked out.
8. (Sample Teams Only) Correction Call in Engage: This guide will provide assistance with performing a correction call to
correct a call that you mistakenly added the wrong sample product, sample lot #, and/or sample quantity
9. Engage Change IC Address: This guide will provide assistance in submitting an Change IC Address Data Request. Please note
that requests submitted today will be processed for P12016 (not P42015)
10. Engage Coaching Report: This guide will provide assistance in approving Field Coaching Reports
11 Engage Specialty Challenge: This guide will provide assistance in submitting an Specialty Challenge Data Request. Please
note that requests submitted today will be processed for P12016 (not P42015)
12. Trigger Letters: This guide will provide assistance with sending trigger letters to HCP's
13. Search Bar: This guide will provide assistance in opening the search bar in Engage Online
14. Engage Synchronization: This guide will provide assistance in synchronizing your Engage system
Please let me know if you have any questions.

Amy,
Thanks for asking for clarification, I should have been more specific with my answer, sorry for the confusion.
Express Scripts merely adjudicates and handles the "back office" reconciliation to all parties concerned on Tricare's behalf in
the RETAIL environment. So if a patient brings an Opana script to let's say Walgreens or CVS, NO MATTER WHERE THEY
ARE IN THE COUNTRY, if they present their Tricare card, they will pay a $9 co-pay. However currently, if they take that
same script on to a military base and try to have it filled at the outpatient pharmacy, they will be either be diverted to a base
formulary product, or told to go out to a retail pharmacy for filling at the $9 co-pay. (Since we are currently not on ANY base
formulary with Opana) (Or use mail order, again at a $9 co-pay for up to 90 days of any product) All prescriptions filled at
any base outpatient pharmacy (regardless of company or disease state or product cost) are filled at $0 co-pay; but to be
dispensed, they MUST be on the base formulary, which is a SUBSET of the National Tricare formulary. Each base is
allowed to tailor their formulary to "fit the clinical need in that local geography". Additionally, any script filled on base is
currently blinded to you, and you would not get credit for it. However, VERY soon we will be introducing a pilot program that
will allow you to take advantage of this on-base opportunity, and get credit for business that flows through these pharmacies
that you generate, so stay tuned...

The investigators, from the Government Accountability Office, said Medicare officials had been slow to recognize and act on the evidence
of abuse, which is to be presented at a Senate hearing on Tuesday.
"Our analysis found that about 170,000 Medicare beneficiaries received prescriptions from five or more medical practitioners" for 14 types
of drugs that are frequently abused, said Gregory D. Kutz, director offorensic audits and special investigations at the accounting office.
The medications were obtained through Part D of Medicare, which provides coverage for prescription drugs. The drugs most commonly
abused by Medicare beneficiaries included powerful prescription painkillers like oxycodones and hydrocodone products. Oxycodones
include Oxygontinmad Percocet.
In one case described in the report, a Medicare beneficiary in Georgia received a 15o-day supply of oxycodone in just 27days by obtaining
seven prescriptions from four doctors. Over the course of a year, the woman received prescriptions for a total of 3,655oxycodone pills(a
1,679-day supply) from 58different prescribers, and she filled them at more than 4o pharmacies.
In another case, a California man received prescriptions fora total of1,397 fentanyl patches and pills(a1,758-day supply) from 21 different
prescribers in a year. In a third case, a Texas beneficiary received prescriptions fora total of4,574hydrocodone pills(a 994-day supply)
from 25 different doctors.
Senator Thomas R. Carper, Democrat of Delaware, said: "Federal dollars intended to address the health needs ofthe elderly and the poor

Mr. Carper called the hearing as chairman of a Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs subcommittee.
The accounting office said prescription drug abuse threatened the health ofbeneficiaries and increased costs to taxpayers. "Medicare

others, the report said.

Damn it. I meant to send that to my Government Affairs team. It's been a long day on top of a
long week. I guess it's good for y'all to know as well. Any way, they make Suboxone. It's
actually used to treat opioid addiction and off label for pain. Here's the low down:
Category profile
SUBOXONE is the first opioid medication approved under DATA 2000 for the treatment of opioid
dependence in an office-based setting. SUBOXONE also can be dispensed for take-home use, just
as any other medicine for other medical conditions.
The primary active ingredient in SUBOXONE is buprenorphine. Because buprenorphine is a partial
opioid agonist, its opioid effects are limited compared with those produced by full opioid
agonists, such as oxycodone or heroin. SUBOXONE also contains naloxone, an opioid antagonist.

CONFIDENTIAL - SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-03137748

 The naloxone in SUBOXONE is there to discourage people from dissolving the tablet and
injecting it. When SUBOXONE is placed under the tongue, as directed, very little naloxone
reaches the bloodstream, so what the patient feels are the effects of the buprenorphine.
However, if naloxone is injected, it can cause a person dependent on a full opioid agonist to
quickly go into withdrawal.
SUBOXONE at the appropriate dose may be used to:
* Reduce illicit opioid use
* Help patients stay in treatment

by
* Suppressing symptoms of opioid withdrawal
* Decreasing cravings for opioids

Kitlinski, Linda
Subject: OPANA Brand 3 Year Anniversary Message!
Endo Sales Team:
As you know, today marks the third anniversary of the approval of OPANA and OPANA ER. Congratulations on helping to make
the OPANA brand a genuine success story in the CII opioid market over the past three years!
Today also marks the end of the brand's three year marketing exclusivity period granted by FDA. While OPANA ER has been
issued a patent, which Endo continues to defend, there is no patent for OPANA. This means that a generic for OPANA could
potentially launch as early as today. However, over the past several weeks, Endo National Account Executives have been
canvassing their customers to understand if a generic oxymorphone launch is imminent. These customers report that they have
not been approached by generic companies seeking to launch oxymorphone.
So the good news is that it appears an OPANA generic is not coming in the next several weeks. Since there is no patent against
which a generic manufacturer must certify, we really do not know if an OPANA generic is coming next month or next year. The
NAEs will continue to monitor their customers and will report any updates with regards to competitive activity as it occurs.
Furthermore, our Generics Division will not introduce the authorized generic of OPANA until Endo is confident that a competing
generic product is set to launch. In the mean time, we all need to keep focused on helping as many patients as possible with
OPANA ER. We need to continue our mission - we need to continue the trend.
Thank you all for your hard work and happy anniversary!
Demir Bingol

EndoI have summarized the pertinent articles below and attached the drug liking and LBP HOPE-related articles.

1. Opioids in the Publihed Articles
Drug Liking of Interest:
Link: Measuring attractiveness for abuse of prescription opioids.
Authors and affiliations: Butler SF, Fernandez KC, Chang A, Benoit C, Morey LC, Black R, Katz N. Infle)aion, Inc.,
Newton, Massachusetts, USA.
GOALS: A major focus of the present method was to attempt to separate the effect of formulation from other possible
variables that might impact drug preferences. This point deserves special emphasis as it is apparent that the particular
formulation of a drug is only one piece of a larger mosaic of factors that may interact in various and changing ways to
result in individuals' preferences.
CONCLUSIONS: OxyContin was the most preferred drug, followed closely by Dilaudid, Duragesic, MS Contin and
Avinza. The relevance of the model is discussed along with possible modifications that might allow prediction of
"attractiveness" of "abuse deterrent" formulations that have not yet been marketed.
NOTE: they did not have OPANA or OPANA ER as one of the selected drugs evaluated in study 2. The drugs
evaluated included OxyContin®, Percocet®, Vicodin®, Dilaudid®, MS Contin®, KadianO, Avinza®, Dolophine®,
Duragesic®, Stadol®, and Talwin0 NX.
HOPE-related of interest:
Link: The course of opioid prescribing for a new episode of disabling low back pain: Opioid features and dose
escalation.
Affiliations: Liberty Mutual Research Institute for Safety, University of Massachusetts Lowell, USA
CONCLUSIONS: These results reinforce recommendations to limit opioid duration, and suggest that consideration of
opioid features, purity as an important one, can be part of a strategy to prevent escalating dosages.
Link: Evaluation of study discontinuations with tapentadol inmmediate release and oxycodone immediate release in
patients with low back or osteoarthritis pain.
Affiliations: Clinical Development, Ortho-McNeil Janssen Scientific Affairs, LLC
CONCLUSIONS: A lower percentage of patients discontinued because of nausea and/or vomiting or constipation with
tapentadol IR versus oxycodone IR while receiving comparable pain relief suggesting tapentadol may improve the
management of low back and OA pain
Drug Interactions
Link: Oxycodone concentrations are greatly increased by the concomitant use of ritonavir or lopinavir/ritonavir.
CONCLUSIONS: Ritonavir and lopinavir/ritonavir greatly increase the plasma concentrations of oral oxycodone in healthy
volunteers and enhance its effect. When oxycodone is used clinically in patients during ritonavir and lopinavir/ritonavir
treatment, reductions in oxycodone dose may be needed to avoid opioid-related adverse effects.
Clinical Trials
Just added: Official Title: A Multi-center, Primary Care-Based, Open-Label Study to Assess the Success of Converting
Opioid-Experienced Patients, With Chronic, Moderate to Severe Pain, to EMBEDATM Using a Standardized Conversion
Guide, and to Identify Behaviors Related to Prescription Opioid Abuse, Misuse, and Diversion

Endo ASAM Abstract Comments/Response
ASAM2013_Abstract_Final_10 12 12. pdf

Hi Matt,
Thank you for your comments and helpful revisions to the ASAM abstract. Attached is a copy of the revised and final
abstract submitted to ASAM. We included the changes suggested by Endo in the final abstract however, we did omit
the addition of text "before and" in the third sentence ("Initial observations regarding abuse of oxymorphone ER...") as
the data provided include observations from NAVIPPRO only after the reformulation of oxymorphone ER. In
response to your general comments, we also made the revisions described below.
(1) it is not clear what the stated percentages represent (changes vs old formula? Proportion of current
population? Are these ASI-MV data?)
The percentages presented in the draft abstract represent the proportion of individuals assessed by
the ASI-MV during the second quarter of 2012 who reported abuse of reformulated oxymorphone ER,
hydromorphone and morphine ER. The abstract was revised to include the total number of ASI-MV
assessments during Q2 2012 (total ASI-MV sample) and past 30-day abuse is presented as rates (i.e.
cases per 100 assessments) rather than percentages.
(2) Are there no data on rates of snorting or injecting reformulated OPANA ER?
Data on the percent of individuals who reported abuse of reformulated OPANA ER via injection or
snorting was included in the abstract.
(3) Observation period was unclear so we have restated it as release in 2012 to December 2012.
(4) Meetings don't favor submissions promising to present data that hasn't yet been acquired (ie, data to
December 2012)
•

Reference to "data through December 2012" was removed.

I hope this helps. Have a great weekend.
Janine

Confidential

END00645432

 As mentioned, we have Bedford Breakaway, our Clinical Education Series Conference taking place this weekend, March 7-9,
2008. At this conference, we have two session on Chronic Pain (a therapeutic area familiar to Endo).
• Self-Assessment Module on Chronic Pain (Friday March 7: 8am-3pm)
• Identifying and Managing Chronic Pain (Saturday, March 8: 2:14-3:15pm)
While I realize it is too late to secure grant funding for these sessions, I would be happy to pass materials on Endo's pain
medications to the sessions' faculty in the event they want to pass them out.
We do have a few exhibitor spaces remaining (cost $850), but again realize it may be too difficult for Endo to have a
representative this late in the process.

Lodge and Conference Center. We will have numerous cancer-related sessions (in collaboration with Fox Chase Cancer
Center) that not only deal with cancer issues but certainly the pain associated with cancer.
We will also have sessions on pain related to orthopaedic issues such as:
• Knee & Hip Pain in children
• Orthopaedic Injuries in Fingers, Hand, and Wrist
• Weekend Warrior: Overuse Injuries
In November, PAFP/F will hold a conference in Philadelphia; sessions have not been planned as yet for this conference.
I would like to submit a proposal for funding from Endo Pharmaceuticals in the near future.
In addition, PAFP/F hopes to reinstate a new version of its former Pain Management Program--offering further education to
family physicians on pain management. (This was a former program which Endo supported in the past.) We will be taking it to

RE: Kroger Pharmacy Trade Show

Melanie and Sue,
Thank you for all your help and I'm glad the trade show was a success. Please take time on your next conference call
with the district or region to share your insight into Kroger's and all that you learned from the pharmacist. It is such
valuable information and I would think many of your peers would benefit from the knowledge you gained. All the best
and let the trade team know how we can help you.
John
From: Etheridge, Melanie
Sent: Wednesday, May 08, 2013 6:03 PM
To: Bullock, John
Cc: Price, Kenneth; Wolfe, Robert; HefnerBraun, Sue
Subject: Kroger Pharmacy Trade Show
John:
Again this year, the Kroger pharmacy trade show was a valuable opportunity to speak to so many Kroger pharmacists
in one setting! This year it was even larger because pharmacy techs were included too.
Rob, Sue and I had about 25 rotations of 5-8 pharmacists each from 1:30-3:30.
OpanaER:
We were able to educate them about INTAC technology. While most knew something was new about OpanaER,
some were not sure exactly what the INTAC technology meant. Very few were aware of the generic availability, but
most expressed no interest in stocking or filling any generics that do not have crush resistant technology. They also
expressed that it would be rare to call a doctor to request a switch to a non AB rated CII. Someone explained that
Kroger chose to block seeing the generic available because not AB rated. They all understood what AB rated means.
Many were unaware of OpanaER rebates and inquired about getting them.
We took advantage of the empty booth next to us and got twice the bang for our buck. We divided and conquered to
cover more products.
Voltaren gel:
Still hearing that doctors do not write the number of joints being treating. Pharmacists said when it's not specified on
the script, they are required to dispense the lowest dose. When asked what that is, they said 1 tube. Too many did not
know that 3 tubes is a minimum therapeutic dose for a single OA upper joint. Most said they call doctors on a regular
basis to inquire about number of joints or amounts to apply. (Docs write tubes, not grams). Dosing still not correct in
all electronic scripts. Several asked how the patients knew how much to apply and were very interested to learn about
the dosing card inside the boxes.
Frova:
They were interested to know that it was still available. Most do not stock it, but can get in quickly.
Fortesta gel:
While some had never heard of it, others said they are starting to see increased prescriptions for it. They did not know
dosing was un upper inner thigh, but said it sounded smart.
Thanks for having us participate,
Melanie

Simone,
I want to pass on a success story with Dr. Gumina, one of my Primary Care physicians. Dr. Gumina was a new physician
for me. I utilized TReX analytics to identify my Embeda writers and it turned out that Dr. Gumina was on top of this list.
The Embeda situation gave me a great opportunity to have Dr. Gumina try OpanaER. I presented the overall benefits of
OpanaER and we went over how to convert those patients over to OpanaER. He asked about Managed Care and we
went over that in detail because coverage was very important to him. It took time, but patience and persistence paid
off. He wrote 7 Rx's of OpanaER in September and two calls ago he told me "I wrote 3 Opana Rx's for you" and those
Rx's showed up in my first week of October numbers. He told me he really likes the overall tolerability, the CYP450, the
coverage seems to be good, and finally he likes the dosing because he does like to start his patients on a smaller dose.
The same day he told me he wrote 3 OpanaER Rx's, he also told me he wrote 2 Fortesta Gel's for me. I was really
excited after that call and was going to write a success story at that point. I decided to wait to see if the Fortesta Gel Rx's
were actually going to show up, because I have been having major problems with these getting denied. I need to give
you a little history at this point. Dr. Gumina initially told me he really liked Fortesta Gel because of its' 2% concentration,
convenient application and that it was less volume. He said he was using Androgel and that when he had to titrate it up,
he would resort to compounding because of the larger volume of gel the patient had to apply. So he started to utilize
our rebate cards and then he later told me he was having major problems getting it authorized. He then wrote a few
Axiron's but then stopped. He wrote another Fortesta Gel for me after that until he told me that he was fed up with
getting gels approved and that he was just going to go back to compounding because it was cost effective and there

FDA and GAO Examine Drug Shortages in Reports to Congress;
Subject of House Energy and Commerce Hearing
Two reports released by the FDA and GAO were part of the discussion of the House Energy and
Commerce Health Subcommittee's February 10 hearing entitled, "Examining Drug Shortages and
Recent Efforts to Address Them." Testimony was provided by Douglas Throckmorton, Deputy
Director of Regulatory Programs for the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and Marcia Cross,
Director, Healthcare at the Government Accountability Office (GAO).
According to the FDA's report, "First Annual Report to Congress on Drug Shortages for CY 2013"
(February 5) 140 product shortages were successfully prevented between January 1 and
September 30, 2013, due to the work of the agency's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research
(CDER) and pharmaceutical manufacturers. Additionally, there were 38 new drug shortages
tracked within that time period, compared to 117 in 2012.
Required by the Food and Drug Administration Safety and Innovation Act of 2012 (FDASIA), the
report summarizes the major actions FDA took during the first three quarters of 2013 to prevent or
mitigate drug shortages and provides information about the shortages that occurred. It further
summarizes, that "... increased notifications resulting from actions by the President, Congress and
FDA are helping the agency respond more effectively to shortages and potential shortages."
Meanwhile, the GAO report, "Drug Shortages: Public Health Threat Continues Despite Efforts to
Help Ensure Product Availability" (released February 10) indicates that while FDA has prevented
further shortages by increasing its responsiveness, the "... total number of drug shortages active
during a given year— including both new shortages reported and ongoing shortages that began in
a prior year— has increased since 2007."
The GAO recommends that FDA strengthen its internal controls over its drug shortage data and

Hi Brian,
I hope you're well. I previously reached out to you when I was a counsel on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on
Investigations to set up a briefing on Endo's opioid products. I've since followed Sen. McCaskill over to the Homeland Security
and Governmental Affairs Committee, and I'm hoping you can assist with another briefing on a similar issue—Endo's efforts to
combat opioid diversion. The recent Washington Post article on the DEA investigation into Mallinckrodt has raised concerns
about the level of cooperation between manufacturers, distributors, and pharmacies in monitoring and reporting suspicious

CONFIDENTIAL-SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER

ENDO-OPIOID_MDL-06982505

 opioid orders, and it would be helpful to hear about Endo's efforts in this area. Specifically, it would be great if Endo's
representatives could cover these topics during a call:
■ Efforts by Endo to monitor, investigate, or report suspicious opioid orders, including transactions between
distributors and pharmacies (through a review of chargebacks, for example);
■ Any requirements Endo imposes on its distributor partners in terms of their anti-diversion efforts, and methods
Endo uses to monitor and review these efforts;
■ Efforts Endo undertakes to audit or investigate specific pharmacies that receive its products and the
standards/analysis Endo uses to determine when an audit or investigation is necessary;
■ Endo communications with DEA, and whether DEA officials have provided clear standards concerning suspicious
order monitoring and the company's anti-diversion obligations generally.

Would it be possible to schedule a briefing for some time in the next few weeks? As with our inquiry last fall, a phone briefing
would be fine. Happy to discuss further at your convenience.
Thanks,
Brandon
